name: Nevada Current
title: Ford says he’ll pause data center tax abatements if elected
description: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Attorney General Aaron Ford says as governor he will pause the state’s tax breaks for new data centers to make sure Nevadans are getting their money’s worth.  “Data centers are swarming into Nevada communities, draining our water, and jacking up our energy bills – and Joe Lombardo is handing them Nevadans’ tax […]
text:
“Data centers are swarming into Nevada communities, draining our water, and jacking up our energy bills – and Joe Lombardo is handing them Nevadans’ tax money to do it,” says a plan on data centers released Wednesday by Democratic nominee for governor Aaron Ford. (Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)Democratic gubernatorial candidate Attorney General Aaron Ford says as governor he will pause the state’s tax breaks for new data centers to make sure Nevadans are getting their money’s worth. 
“Data centers are swarming into Nevada communities, draining our water, and jacking up our energy bills – and Joe Lombardo is handing them Nevadans’ tax money to do it,” reads a position paper released by Ford’s campaign Wednesday.
Ford was among the state lawmakers who co-sponsored legislation in 2015 to grant tax abatements to data centers that set up shop in Nevada. Now, with affordability issues top of mind for voters and a water shortage threatening the state’s future, Ford appears to be having second thoughts. 
The state extended $97 million in tax breaks to data centers in the 2021-22 biennium, according to the Department of Taxation’s Tax Expenditure Report. That number more than doubled for fiscal years 2023-24 to almost $240 million. 
“When I’m Governor, Joe Lombardo’s gravy train for data centers is coming to an end. I’m going to implement some of the strictest rules in America: data centers will need to bring their own water or coolant, pay for their own electricity so ratepayers’ bills don’t go up, and actually deliver the sustainable high-paying jobs and tax revenue they’ve promised,” Ford said, adding he intends to make data centers “pay up.” 
Ford’s plan calls for making data centers pay not only for the energy they use, but for the infrastructure required to deliver it. NV Energy says it intends to build close to $3.5 billion in capital projects in the next three years to accommodate the increased demands of data centers on the electrical grid.
Ford also intends to ban water-intensive evaporative cooling methods used in data centers. 
Ford’s Democratic primary opponent Washoe County Commissioner Alexis Hill, who called for ending data center subsidies during the campaign, supports her former opponent’s plan. 
“Gov. Lombardo is handing over our state’s precious water and energy resources to his biggest donors,” Hill said in a news release from Ford’s campaign. “Nevadans must come together to vote for Ford and other Democrats who will guarantee transparency and center local community needs.”
Ford says he intends to see that all data centers, including those that don’t receive subsidies, are held accountable when it comes to water use, community benefits, and transparency in the local permitting process. 
Data centers are an election issue in Nevada and elsewhere. 
“People really effing hate data centers,” Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said while campaigning in July.  
Lombardo has repeatedly professed his support for data centers, including in an opinion piece in the Reno Gazette-Journal. 
Lombardo’s Better Nevada PAC has also hauled in large data center-related donations, including $500,000 each from data center pioneer Ben Horowitz and his wife, Felicia in May, and $1,000,000 the same month from Jessica Roy, wife of Switch founder Rob Roy.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Debate between the 2 US Senate candidates highlights their differing backgrounds
description: In their only debate before voters choose between them, U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman pointed to his years of experience on Capitol Hill, while U.S. Sen. Darline Graham used it against him. Early voting starts Wednesday in the special primary runoff that will decide who replaces the late Lindsey Graham as the GOP nominee for the […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman responds to U.S. Sen. Darline Graham during their debate Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026, at the Newberry Opera House. (Screenshot from the SCETV livestream)In their only debate before voters choose between them, U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman pointed to his years of experience on Capitol Hill, while U.S. Sen. Darline Graham used it against him.
Early voting starts Wednesday in the special primary runoff that will decide who replaces the late Lindsey Graham as the GOP nominee for the next six-year term in the U.S. Senate.
The Aug. 25 runoff comes two weeks after his younger sister, Darline Graham, led the 10-candidate primary with 33% of the vote, followed by Norman at 25%, according to state Election Commission data. Both want to get their supporters back out to the polls while winning over the more than 40% of voters who didn’t choose either one of them.


When to vote
Early voting is 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Wednesday through Friday.
Click here for early voting locations in each county.
On Tuesday, polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.
Click here to find where you vote Tuesday. Many locations have changed for the runoff.


The contest pits a 62-year-old first-time candidate, who was sworn in a month ago as the appointee to complete her brother’s fourth term, against a 73-year-old congressman who’s held elected office since 2004. That’s when Norman first won a seat in the state House.
With very little separation in their political stances, both argued their different backgrounds as advantages. He touted 40 years as a developer, saying “unlike my opponent, I’ve owned a business.” She emphasized her 30 years in state government, the last seven leading the state Commission for the Blind, as serving South Carolinians.
Graham’s answers also highlighted how she’s different from her brother.
Voting records
“I’ve got a proven record,” Norman said in his introductory statement. “You know how I’m going to vote.” As for Graham, he continued, “we have an unknown candidate I am running against.”
Graham, who started by thanking President Donald Trump for his endorsement, accused Norman of working against the president as a holdout on last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill. Norman, who sits on the House budget committee, said he worked to make it better before ultimately voting for it.
“We had another bite at the apple. When you’re in the business arena, you drive the hardest bargain as long as you can,” he said, adding he told the president the subsidies for electric cars and solar and wind projects are “stupid.” “I was cutting it out. … I would do it over again. I don’t apologize for it,” he said to cheers from his supporters in the audience.
Graham argued she’s “done more in 20 days than you’ve done in 20 years,” referring to Norman’s combined time in the Legislature and U.S. House.
As Trump did last week in a pre-primary call-in rally, she pointed Tuesday to her votes enabling Todd Blanche to be sworn as U.S. attorney general as well as passage of sanctions against Russia as negotiated and championed by her brother.
Two days after being sworn in, she introduced a new sanctions bill renamed in Lindsey Graham’s honor, which the Senate approved overwhelmingly as an amendment to separate legislation on education. It is not yet law, however, as the changes await action in the House.
As for Norman’s bills, Graham said, the only one he’s sponsored that became law in his nine years as the 5th District congressman “named a post office. Good job.”
That referred to the 2018 law designating the building in Fort Mill as the J. Elliott Williams Post Office. Congressional records show Norman did sponsor one other bill that became “private law” earlier this year. It authorized Trump to award the Medal of Honor to retired Marine Maj. James Capers Jr. for his heroism during the Vietnam War.
Taiwan flub
During the debate’s section on foreign policy, Graham blanked on a question about Taiwan.
Asked whether Taiwan is a national security issue for the United States, Graham initially asked the question to be repeated before acknowledging she’s not informed on the issue.
“I’m just going to be honest up here,” she said. “I’m not a polished politician. National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise.”
However, she stressed her support of the military, noting her father was in the Army, and her brother was in the Air Force for 33 years: “So, I will do everything I can to support the military,” she said.
In his response, Norman called Taiwan a “definite ally” and trading partner.
“What the president is doing right is enabling Taiwan to defend themselves against China,” he said, adding that he believes the “peace through strength” Trump is showing with Iran is what’s really dissuading the Chinese from attacking.
Graham has said she’ll concentrate more on domestic issues than her brother, a frequent world traveler who focused on foreign policy. Her answer demonstrated that difference, probably not in a way she wanted.
Immigration
On a later question about immigration, she highlighted another difference. Lindsey Graham was part of the bipartisan “Gang of Eight” who worked to get a bill overhauling America’s immigration laws through the Senate in 2013. The effort ultimately failed, and Republicans who didn’t like the bill labeled him with the nickname Grahamnesty.
Norman and Darline Graham were in agreement over opposing birthright citizenship and letting people live in the country illegally.
“This is where I differ from my brother,” she said. “It’s real clear to me if you’re here illegally, you need to be deported immediately. I’ll support deporting any illegal immigrant.”
Norman said he believes in “legal immigration, not illegal immigration. You have to get illegals out of the country now.”
But Graham accused Norman of not practicing what he preached in his own business.
During his 2006 run for the U.S. House, Norman made illegal immigration a central part of his campaign against then-U.S. Rep. John Spratt. When The Charlotte Observer reported several workers on a job site of his development company acknowledged being in the country illegally from Mexico, Norman said they worked for subcontractors, whose employees his company doesn’t get involved in vetting. Norman’s campaign also said their presence showed a failure in federal policy, as businesses shouldn’t be burdened with enforcing immigration law. But the discovery helped sink Norman’s bid that time.
When Graham brought it back up Tuesday, Norman said, “I don’t hire illegal immigrants. It’s just false.”

Both praised Trump’s policies. But Graham mentioned him in nearly every answer, making clear she supports his decisions.
The president will travel to Myrtle Beach on Friday in a get-out-the-vote rally for Graham.
The rally at the Myrtle Beach Convention Center starts at 7 p.m. Doors open at 3 p.m.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Lawmakers appear poised to take some big swings against competitive electric suppliers. How big is the question.
description: The pushback comes as Democrats on Beacon Hill are on the cusp of a long-sought breakthrough to rein in what critics contend are shady energy companies that rip off unwitting customers.
text:
NEARLY TWO MONTHS after the Senate followed the House in passing sprawling energy affordability legislation that lays the foundation for a crackdown on competitive electric suppliers, the industry’s opposition to the measure is starting to come into clearer view. 
The Retail Energy Supply Association and Retail Energy Advancement League, which share member companies like Constellation, NRG, and Shell that generate or purchase electricity to sell directly to customers, have spent a combined $80,000 in lobbying through the first half of this year — about as much as the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce and Associated Industries of Massachusetts have each spent. 
That would put the groups on pace for $160,000 this year, the most since REAL launched in 2022 and since RESA started lobbying in Massachusetts in 2018, state records show. The two groups have combined to spend roughly $1 million lobbying state government since 2018. 
Plus, the energy companies and their trade groups are drawing lawmakers’ attention to a new poll that ostensibly shows the industry’s popularity among Bay Staters, said Frank Caliva, RESA’s national spokesperson. That poll of 500 Massachusetts ratepayers, commissioned by RESA, was released just days before the Senate voted on its energy bill and found that about 9 in 10 respondents support “maintaining the ability to choose their electric supplier.”  
The pushback comes as Democrats on Beacon Hill are on the cusp of a long-sought breakthrough to rein in what critics contend are shady energy companies that rip off unwitting customers by signing them up for electricity at a reduced cost only to then raise prices later. 
The industry is supporting a slew of reforms — including stricter oversight for direct sales to customers and removing certain customer fees — put forward by Gov. Maura Healey and advanced by both the House and Senate. But a new effort this year to grant individual municipalities the ability to ban the companies from directly selling to customers is a bridge too far, Caliva said. 
Even as the industry has beaten back past attempts to ban it from selling to consumers, this new proposal gaining traction means this moment is different, he added. 
“We are certainly very concerned about this bill, and I think the risk here is pretty significant,” Caliva said in an interview. “We are trying to sound the alarm that even this version of the approach, which is different than an outright state ban, will have significant negative repercussions for the market. There’s really no equivocating about it: It’s a concerningly fraught moment.” 
Both chambers advanced language that would allow municipalities to vote to ban competitive electric suppliers from selling directly to individual customers in the face of scathing reports that they lure consumers into enrolling in too-good-to-be-true electricity contracts. Lawmakers believe the move would save ratepayers hundreds of millions of dollars over 10 years, representing a concrete way to stem soaring energy costs. 
The alignment on stronger-than-expected guardrails through this novel approach is even more notable given the deep divisions that have emerged regarding the shape of the rest of the sweeping energy legislation now under negotiation between the two chambers.  
It’s a stark reversal from last session, when an effort to crack down on the industry failed in a contentious uproar that included allegations of conflict of interest against a key lawmaker amid a protracted legislative battle. 
Larry Chretien, executive director of Green Energy Consumers Alliance who has long advocated for tougher measures against the companies, also known as third-party suppliers, said that the industry has been “effective” in stopping the Legislature from banning it in the past, but that now it should “adjust to reality” as the legislative compromise enjoys broad support. 
“I just don’t know how you get that conference committee to do anything other than say, ‘Oh, let’s look at our language on this. Let’s look at your language. Oh, it’s pretty much the same,’” Chretien said. “Why would they do something different?” 
In Massachusetts, residents can get electricity one of three ways: through their investor-owned utility, like Eversource and National Grid; a municipal aggregation program, if the customer lives in one of nearly 250 communities where such an option exists; or through a third-party supplier, which the state has allowed to directly sell to individual residents since the 1990s and compete with the utilities and aggregation programs.  
Nearly 500,000 electric customers are currently served by third-party suppliers as of March, the most recent data from the state Department of Energy Resources. 
Yet the attorney general’s office has found that the industry has engaged in widespread deceit, targeting vulnerable and lower-income populations with misleading marketing, costly contracts, and automatic renewals. 
The industry has cost these customers $739 million in total net losses over the past 10 years, according to Attorney General Andrea Campbell’s latest report. At least 30 percent of low-income residents in the Boston neighborhoods of Mission Hill, Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan are enrolled with third-party suppliers.  
Campbell said in a statement that those figures only “exacerbate” electricity costs that are already staggering in Massachusetts — the price of electricity in the Bay State is roughly double the national average — and that she’s “eager to continue working with the Legislature to protect Massachusetts ratepayers from this predatory industry.” 
In the last five years, the Department of Public Utilities has settled with eight different competitive suppliers, resulting in refunds for customers, bans on specific types of marketing, or, in one case, forcing the company to exit the market altogether for two years. 
Caliva blamed “bad apples” for past harms committed by the industry but said these examples don’t justify “shutting down the market.” 
The $80,000 in lobbying spent by the competitive suppliers’ two trade groups so far this year doesn’t count lobbying from those groups’ individual member companies, leaving the full scope of the industry’s influence efforts unknown until the next lobbying report is released, likely after lawmakers presumably reach agreement on a broader package and Healey signs it into law.  
CleanChoice, a competitive supplier confronting an active state investigation into its marketing and advertising practices, has spent $27,500 on lobbying so far this year, roughly in line with what it’s spent in years past. 
Constellation, NRG, and Shell have all spent around $50,000 so far on lobbying in Massachusetts this year, though those are large energy companies likely lobbying on multiple issues. That’s in line with what they’ve reported spending in previous years.  
Individual third-party suppliers like NRG, Shell, and CleanChoice declined or didn’t respond to requests for comment.  
Emily Kennedy, a spokesperson for Constellation, a member of both REAL and RESA, said that the company “supports competitive energy markets and policies that preserve customer choice” and opposes restrictions on Massachusetts residents’ ability to choose their electricity supplier.  
The two Democrats leading the joint energy committee in the Legislature, Rep. Mark Cusack and Sen. Michael Barrett, did not comment on the lobbying push. 
Past efforts to ban the industry from selling to customers statewide, initially led by then-AG Healey in 2019, have failed to advance. 
Even if communities do vote to prohibit the suppliers through the legislative provision under consideration, the industry would still be able to operate in Massachusetts — just on a more limited basis.  
Third-party suppliers would be able to contract with businesses and bid on contracts through municipal aggregation programs, a process by which a town or city purchases power in bulk from a competitive supplier to serve its residents.  
Chretien said municipal programs are vetted and approved by regulators, are carefully crafted by local officials who in theory are looking out for their constituents, and are generally more stable long-term agreements that can be an attractive low-cost option. There more than double the number of residential electric customers in Massachusetts served by the municipal aggregation programs compared with those served by competitive suppliers. 
“We’re not putting them out of business overall,” he said. “We’re just saying: Leave these poor residential consumers alone.”  
For its part, RESA is supportive of provisions included in both the originaly energy legislation filed by Healey and the versions that have advanced in the Legislature that would prohibit automatically renewing customers without receiving their consent, bar cancellation or early termination fees, and raise fees for the companies to operate in the state, Caliva said. 
That shows the industry is making a good-faith attempt to encourage commonsense reforms that can fix its reputation and root out problematic actions without impacting customer choice, Caliva said. 
“People jokingly say, ‘Use a scalpel instead of a hammer,’” he said. “In this case, we’re saying, ‘Use a saw instead of a wrecking ball.’” 
But, to Chretien, the industry’s charades have gone on too long. This time, he hopes the door is shut to its influence on Beacon Hill. 
“I don’t know how the industry is going to persuade legislators to reverse direction now,” he said. “There’s an energy affordability crisis, and this is the most glaring opportunity to do something about it.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Given chance to take a stand on NV Energy’s demand charge, state lawmakers take a pass
description: When given the opportunity to take a public stance on the controversial NV Energy rate scheme set to go into effect next year, seven state lawmakers on Tuesday opted to say nothing at all. Approved by the Public Utilities of Commission of Nevada last year and set to go into effect Jan. 1, NV Energy’s […]
text:
Attendees hold up signs at a press conference hosted by utility customers and advocates outside the utility companies summit over rising electricity bills, AI-driven power demand and utility CEO pay on June 03, 2026 in Las Vegas. (Photo by Bryan Steffy/Getty Images for People's Action)When given the opportunity to take a public stance on the controversial NV Energy rate scheme set to go into effect next year, seven state lawmakers on Tuesday opted to say nothing at all.
Approved by the Public Utilities of Commission of Nevada last year and set to go into effect Jan. 1, NV Energy’s “demand charge” will be based on a customer’s highest 15-minute period of energy consumption each day. It is unprecedented among investor-owned utilities in the U.S. and has garnered much public outcry. It’s also become a gubernatorial campaign issue, with Democratic nominee and Attorney General Aaron Ford criticizing the PUCN, whose members were appointed by Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo.
State lawmakers have had relatively little opportunity to get involved with the rate restructuring, which was proposed by NV Energy after the 2025 Legislative Session ended and is scheduled to go into effect Jan. 1, before the next regular legislative session convenes.
But on Tuesday, Assemblymember Howard Watts (D-Las Vegas) asked the interim legislative committee on growth and infrastructure, which he chairs, to advance a bill draft request “prohibiting mandatory daily demand charges for residential electric utility customers.”
It was one of 10 BDRs up for consideration and the only one not advanced because of a lack of support.
Watts asked for a motion to approve the BDR and was met with resounding silence from the committee’s other seven members. The committee is made up of four Democrats and four Republicans.
The committee’s inaction was met with frustrated utterances and groans from audience members, many of whom had spoken during the meeting’s public comment period and urged the committee to back the bill.
Watts, in an interview with the Nevada Current after the meeting, said he was disappointed in the outcome. The BDR would have been “the Legislature’s opportunity to step in” and discuss whether the structure is good public policy, he added.
“It could have been a statement,” he added. “Ultimately, the committee decided not to move forward.”
Watts said NV Energy has a history of breaking promises and hasn’t been transparent about the impact the daily demand charge will have. 
“The public is deeply concerned,” said Watts. “I didn’t want to leave my time in office without trying to address this.”
Watts this year ran for a fifth Assembly term but was defeated in a Democratic primary. His term ends after the November general election.
No comment
State Sen. Rochelle T. Nguyen, a Las Vegas Democrat and vice chair of the committee, declined to comment on the daily demand charge when approached by the Current after the meeting adjourned. She offered to speak on the issue “later” but did not respond to attempts to follow up.
Assemblymember Venise Karris (D-Las Vegas) said she didn’t support the BDR because she believes “there are better ways” to address energy pricing issues.
Assemblymember Cinthia Zermeño Moore (D-Las Vegas) said only that she is working on two BDRs of her own related to NV Energy. She did not elaborate on whether those proposals address the daily demand charge. Moore has sponsored extreme-heat protection bills in previous sessions and used to work for the Nevada Environmental Justice Coalition, a group actively opposing the daily demand charge.
Moore was a substitute for Assemblymember Max Carter (D-Las Vegas), who did not attend the meeting. Carter said via text message he was unable to attend due to family matters.
State Sen. Carrie Buck, a Henderson Republican now running against U.S. Rep. Dina Titus in Nevada’s 1st Congressional District, initially responded “no” when approached by the Current and asked if she’d like to comment on the failed BDR.
“I don’t know how it got on” the agenda, she added. “It’s being litigated.”
The Nevada Attorney General’s Office, along with its consumer protection bureau and solar offices, are legally challenging the demand charge. In late May, a judge ruled in favor of NV Energy, but AG Ford vowed to appeal to the Nevada Supreme Court.
Assemblymember Greg Hafen (R-Pahrump) also declined to comment on the daily demand charge — “I don’t know enough about it.” He noted he is not a sitting member of the growth and infrastructure committee. Hafen was filling in for Assemblymember Heidi Kasama (R-Las Vegas), whose absence at the meeting was expected after the recent death of her husband.
Democratic state Sen. Fabian Doñate and Republican Assemblymember Jason Patchett, the final two committee members, could not be reached for comment Tuesday.
Outside the Las Vegas Legislative Building, opponents of the demand charge expressed their disappointment with the lack of action from lawmakers.
“All they would be doing is writing a BDR,” said Janet Carter, a member of the Sierra Club Toiyabe Chapter. “That BDR can obviously change and still has to go through the legislative process. … They weren’t even willing to let it get to the point where it would get to be discussed. That is not answering to the people that they represent.”
While Janet Carter and others were disappointed, they were not surprised.
“The public overwhelmingly is asking (lawmakers) to do the smallest first step to avoid walking down a very dangerous road,” said Nick Christenson. “They were so cowed by NV Energy that they refused to do even that.”

The Ohio burgee. (Getty images file photo.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Catching Our Eye

• Wow. The Cleveland Scene’s Mark Oprea reports, “He Helped Erase $1.2 Million in Medical Debt for Cuyahoga County Residents. It Took Him Just Two Months.”
Khorana, a 20-year-old college student from Shaker Heights, encountered another one this summer when he was schooled in the realm of unpaid medical bills. With the right planning, he found, millions of dollars of his neighbors’ medical debt could be relieved for the price of a used sedan. All by making a few calls.
So, Khorana did just that. In partnership with Undue Medical Debt, a nonprofit based in New York City, he raised a little over $10,000 from a short list of donors and, starting Thursday, helped buy up and cancel out $1.3 million in medical debt for 1,148 Cuyahoga County residents.
• Electric bills. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Karen Kasler reports, “More Ohio households lost power because of nonpayment in the last year than previous years.”
In the last year, more Ohio households lost their power because of lack of payment than in previous years, according to an annual report from the state’s six regulated electric utilities filed with the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio. The leader of the state agency that advocates for ratepayers says that’s a real concern.
From June 2025 to May 2026, 344,589 Ohio households had their electric shut off for not paying. That’s an average of 7.7% of customers with AEP Ohio Power, AES Ohio, Duke Energy and the three companies associated with FirstEnergy, which are CEI, Ohio Edison and Toledo Edison.
• Not concerned. Axios reports, “Trump shrugs off concerns about dismal conditions on USS Abraham Lincoln.”
President Trump said Friday that he isn’t concerned about the state of the USS Abraham Lincoln, despite calls from lawmakers to investigate reports of mental health issues for those onboard.
Why it matters: The San Diego-based aircraft carrier has been deployed for nine months, and numerous reports have indicated that crew members’ families are concerned about a lack of food and other basic supplies.
At least one sailor has gone overboard, prompting the Navy to launch an investigation and The Military Times reported that other crew members have also tried to go overboard.
• Plane crash. USA Today reports, “Military GPS jamming linked to New Mexico plane crash that killed 4.”
A medical transport plane crash that killed four people in New Mexico this spring has been linked to a U.S. military GPS jamming exercise, a preliminary report released by the National Transportation Safety Board shows.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Poor recordkeeping muddies latest target of MassHealth fraud probe
description: ATTORNEY GENERAL Andrea Campbell’s office has recovered almost $12 million from a string of settlements with Massachusetts medical transportation companies it accuses of defrauding MassHealth, the state Medicaid program – […]
text:
ATTORNEY GENERAL Andrea Campbell’s office has recovered almost $12 million from a string of settlements with Massachusetts medical transportation companies it accuses of defrauding MassHealth, the state Medicaid program – and it’s got more in sight.  
For those on Medicaid, coverage will pay for non-emergency medical transportation, either through certain state-approved providers or reimbursement. Companies that bill for services they never provide can find themselves in prosecutors’ crosshairs. 
The latest defendant is fighting the fraud charges. But he’s also blaming any errors on years of shoddy recordkeeping on the part of brokers and vendors that handle scheduling, patient records, and billing for the state’s Medicaid-covered rides. 
Worcester resident Ardit Islamaj and his company, Instant Transportation, LLC, were indicted last year on 17 counts. They are accused of billing MassHealth more than $3 million for rides that never happened — to patients who were dead, hospitalized, or had canceled rides — between August 2018 and August 2023. Prosecutors also allege patient abuse and neglect, identity fraud, and witness intimidation.  
“The attorney general’s office conducted a one-dimensional investigation and simply got this one wrong,” said Islamaj’s lawyer, Amy Crafts. “We will continue pushing to dismiss these charges and clear his name.” 
Islamaj’s lawyers argue the company can’t properly defend itself because Coordinated Transportation Solutions — the vendor that scheduled and billed Instant Transportation’s rides — won’t hand over records they say would let them prove that some of the bills they submitted were either legitimate or honest mistakes. Separately, Islamaj has accused CTS of feeding prosecutors curated information to help build the case against him. 
CTS is a Connecticut-based nonprofit that administers non-emergency rides for some MassHealth members. It told the court that it has already provided the attorney general’s office with all documents relevant to scheduling, patient information, and billing information for the defendants’ services to MassHealth clients. 
Worcester Superior Court Judge James Gavin Reardon, Jr. wasn’t persuaded that even potential gaps in CTS’s files help Islamaj’s case.  
“The defendants have provided no facts indicating that CTS is in possession of, or has withheld, potentially exculpatory evidence,” Reardon wrote in his May 21 order. 
He noted prosecutors have said they’ll rely only on specific bills, trips, and patients — not on anything CTS might be missing. 
The case is due back in Worcester Superior Court for a motion hearing September 16. 
Islamaj’s case is one of seven the attorney general has pursued against Massachusetts transportation companies in the last few years. Roughly $11.6 million has been recovered through settlements.  
“MassHealth serves millions of residents, and every dollar improperly billed is a dollar that cannot go toward legitimate health care,” a spokesperson for Campbell said in a statement. “The AG’s office will continue to vigorously pursue these cases to protect the integrity of our public programs, both with respect to patient safety and to ensure taxpayer dollars are appropriately spent.” 
Islamaj is one of two current indictments, according to the AG’s office. Waltham operator Bakali Mukasa was indicted in February for billing $770,000 for almost 17,000 rides to methadone clinics that the indictment alleges were never provided, with the proceeds allegedly funneled to Uganda, where he now lives.  
Last August, Weymouth’s Brewster Ambulance and EasCare — the state’s largest medical transportation provider — paid $6 million over inflated claims.  
In July, Traveler’s Transit paid $1.045 million to settle charges on routes it never drove. Two North Dartmouth ambulance companies paid $1.6 million in February 2024 for billing more expensive services than the ones provided. Leominster’s MedStar Ambulance paid $2.6 million in August 2023 for similar false billing. In October 2024, Swampscott’s RM Transportation paid $380,000 for billing rides for MassHealth recipients with take-home methadone doses who had no reason to travel that day — roughly the same behavior for which a grand jury indicted Mukasa. 
Most of the cases have targeted the companies that provided the rides, not the brokers or vendors responsible for verifying the bills. But in 2020, under then-Attorney General Maura Healey, the AG’s office and the US Department of Justice settled with the Montachusett Regional Transit Authority (MART) for $300,000, resolving allegations that the organization billed for and received reimbursement from MassHealth for thousands of rides between 2011 and 2015 that its transportation subcontractors did not provide. 
A May 2025 audit by the state auditor’s office examined the $283 million in MassHealth business paid to MART and the Greater Attleboro Taunton Regional Transit Authority. The office found the state had paid for rides with no matching medical appointment on record, and for rides without adequate documentation.  
“Without sufficient evidence of trips, MassHealth may be paying for transportation services that did not take place,” auditors wrote.  
The Executive Office of Health and Human Services responded that brokers are now rolling out software to centralize trip logs and driver records. Some cases without documentation, the health office said, may reflect circumstances where the member did receive the medical service but it was not properly logged or documented. 
That audit did not cover the transportation broker CTS, the Connecticut nonprofit at the center of Islamaj’s argument. No state audit or attorney general settlement has yet examined whether the recordkeeping there passes muster. 
But Crafts, Islamaj’s attorney, says years of poor documentation by transportation brokers should cut in his favor. 
“Both the [attorney general’s] prior settlement with a transportation broker and the auditor’s recent report made clear that brokers like CTS are not properly documenting contracted rides, and they are now out to scapegoat my client,” Crafts said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: A national divide over holding back students: Some states do it young, others wait until high school
authors: Eric Sagara, Megan Tagami, Ariel Gilreath, Devna Bose, Carli Brosseau and Denisa R. Superville
description: Western Line School District Assistant Superintendent James Johnson, ceneter, and Superintendent Lawrence Hudson, right, greet students while visiting Riverside Elementary School, Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026, in Avon.
text:
High school came with more responsibility and less accountability for Josiah Ulukita. Courses were much harder, teachers were less strict about attendance, and it was easier to skip school with friends or go on his phone during class, said 16-year-old Ulukita, who attends Kaimuki High School in Honolulu. 
He went from easily passing middle school to failing freshman English and social studies. After missing roughly half of his freshman year due to poor attendance, he found out he needed to repeat ninth grade. Ashamed, he began to skip more school, he said — until his counselor warned him that he may not graduate on time. 
“I was acing all my classes, and then I hit freshman year,” Ulukita said. “I thought it was going to be easy.”
Throughout the country, states and school districts approach retention — often considered a last resort to catch students up academically — in very different ways. In some states, like Hawaii, schools often wait until ninth grade or later to retain, or hold back, students. Other states, like Mississippi and Florida, tend to retain students at much younger ages, between kindergarten through third grade, according to numbers from 2021-22, the most recent year for which national data was available. 
As concern about student performance nationally intensifies, a growing number of states are mandating this approach: More than two dozen states now have laws requiring or allowing schools to retain third grade students who are not reading at grade level, according to an analysis from the Education Commission of the States, a nonprofit that tracks state legislation in the U.S. 
Despite these laws, the rate of students who were retained in school fell across the U.S. from the 2011-12 to 2021-22 school years, according to data from the federal Office for Civil Rights compiled by the journalism organization Big Local News in partnership with The Hechinger Report. Overall, very few students are held back each year: Less than 2 percent of students in the U.S. repeated a grade level in 2021-22, down from about 3 percent of students a decade prior. (The Office for Civil Rights, the only source for consistent data across all states, is now eight months behind in releasing new data.) 
The research on retention is mixed — there’s little consensus on whether retention can catch students up to grade level. Historically, most studies indicated that students who had to repeat a grade often benefited very little and had long-term negative consequences. Research from the past decade complicates that picture: Younger students may see some positive effects from retention if schools are also combining it with high-intensity tutoring and support, some studies have shown.
“If the retention happens in earlier grades and is combined with help — not just a threat, but some kind of positive intervention — the results, at least in the short-run, tend to be good,” said Dan Goldhaber, director of the Center for Education Data and Research at the University of Washington.
There is less proof that students in middle and high school, like Ulukita, ultimately benefit from repeating a grade.
Students at the all-boys public school A&T Four Middle College find their home rooms on the first day of school in Greensboro, N.C., on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. A&T Four Middle College recently started a program to help ninth graders adjust to high school.  Credit: Matt Ramey for The Assembly
“The evidence suggests that it leads to higher rates of student disengagement from schooling, it leads to higher rates of high school dropouts, less likelihood of high school graduations, and it leads to lower likelihood of enrolling in college. Basically, worse outcomes,” said Umut Ozek, a researcher and senior economist at the policy think tank Rand Corp., who has studied retention.
In every year measured, schools in the South held students back more than any other region, according to the data. Boys were held back more than girls, and Black boys were retained at nearly three times the rate of white boys — a gap that did not narrow over the decade even as retention fell. 
In Hawaii, roughly 1 in 10 freshmen in public high schools had to repeat ninth grade in the 2021-22 school year. That was more than double the national rate for this group of students.   
In the state, freshmen must earn five credits — the equivalent of five year-long classes — to move on to 10th grade. Students and teachers attribute the spike in ninth grade retention to those strict credit requirements, along with more difficult coursework and increased peer pressure to skip class and dodge assignments.
Schools work to avoid holding students back by offering summer school, counseling, personalized learning plans and other resources, Hawaii Department of Education Deputy Superintendent Heidi Armstrong said in a statement. Students may be held back when they’re struggling to make academic progress and earn enough credits to advance to the next grade, she said. 
“The Department’s goal is to ensure students are prepared for continued academic success and remain on track toward earning a high school diploma,” Armstrong said, adding that schools decide to hold students back on a case-by-case basis. 
Mississippi has taken a markedly different approach. In 2013, as part of an overhaul of literacy instruction, the state introduced a policy to retain third graders if they couldn’t pass the reading portion of the state’s English Language Arts assessment.
Rachel Canter, an education policy expert who helped craft the 2013 Literacy-Based Promotion Act, said Mississippi lawmakers looked to Florida in particular, where former Gov. Jeb Bush made ending “social promotion” — the practice of passing students because of their age — one of his signature policies.
“The Legislature was desperate,” Canter said. “The argument that won was, ‘We have to do something, and we know how harmful it is when kids pass with no skills.’”
The state’s third grade retention policy has had a trickle-down effect: Retentions in Mississippi are concentrated in kindergarten through second grade, too. 
Researchers such as Canter say that’s because the literacy legislation established more monitoring and higher standards in those grades as well.
A&T Four Middle College students find their home rooms on the first day of school in Greensboro, NC on Thursday August 6, 2026. Credit: Matt Ramey for The Assembly
That holds true at Western Line School District, a small district with schools on the banks of the Mississippi River. Western Line held back 68 students in kindergarten through third grade during the 2021-22 school year, compared to 56 students in all other grades combined, according to the Big Local News/Hechinger analysis. 
Not all of those retentions are tied to reading, Superintendent Lawrence Hudson said, but the policy raised the bar for students in early grades.
“We want to make sure kids are successful for the rest of their life,” he said. “We know if children have deficits at younger grades, they’ll get to third grade with those deficits.” He added: “The longer you wait, the harder it is to clear those deficiencies.”
But Canter said students don’t automatically improve when they’re retained. To help students, schools have to get them the academic support they need in that year they repeat. The decision to retain a student is difficult, she said, but combined with intervention, it can pay dividends. 
“Any time a child is retained, it is a signal that we have not done what we needed to do as adults,” Canter said. But the retention policy paired with additional support has “done great things for kids,” she said. 
Yet some educators worry that, even in relatively well-funded school districts, resources to provide that support are falling away. Shana Richards has been a school counselor for 19 years in North Carolina, which holds back more students in ninth grade than in any other grade. 
“You used to have teachers that would stay after school, provide tutoring,” said Richards, who now works at A&T Four Middle College, an all-boys public high school on the campus of North Carolina A&T State University in Greensboro. “But now those people are having to leave to go to another job when the school day ends.”
The stipends for educators to provide after-school programming dried up years ago, she said, and the buses that used to carry students home from their after-school activities no longer run, either.
Richards helped design a program for her school’s incoming ninth graders that she hoped would help reduce the need for supports that are now harder to come by. She applied for a grant from the NEA Foundation to help fund the program, an expanded version of the summer orientation the school was already doing. 
The program, which just completed its second year, is called “Welcome to the Brotherhood” and primarily serves the population with the highest retention rates: Black boys. Students learn study skills and hear about academic expectations from their English and math teachers. They also have time to make friends and tour the college campus that surrounds their school.
Richards meets with every student before the program begins to get a sense of their anxieties and where they might need extra support, and she meets with them again in the first month of the school year to get a sense of any emerging problems.
“We know if we can get them to and through ninth grade,” Richards said, “then they have a higher chance of actually staying until graduation.” 
In Washington state, more students were held back just before graduation, in 12th grade, than at any other grade, according to the data from 2011-12 to 2021-22. That’s not because of any state policy though; decisions are made at a district level. 
A&T Four Middle College guidance counselor Shana Richards greets incoming ninth graders on the first day of school in Greensboro, N.C. Richards says that in recent years in the state, the sorts of services that help keep students on track to graduation have been disappearing because of funding and other challenges. Credit: Matt Ramey for The Assembly
Still, Liz Trautman, the executive director of the Washington affiliate of Stand for Children, an advocacy organization that works to boost high school graduation rates, said she was not surprised by the trend.
“I would argue and suggest that when we see those high rates of retention in senior year, we’re actually seeing a cumulative effect of missed opportunities to intervene and to support students that started much, much earlier,” Trautman said.  
Washington officials say retained students include those who were behind in credits for a variety of reasons, including from absences related to medical issues or involvement in the juvenile justice system. Many are also enrolled in transition programs for students who receive special education services and are counted as 12th graders until they’re 22 years old or exit the program, officials said.
Daniel Lee, who has spent 14 years as a counselor at Garfield High School in Seattle, said a high student-to-counselor ratio means counselors aren’t able to work with students and parents as closely as they would like to ensure students have everything they need to meet requirements before 12th grade.
The American School Counselor Association recommends a 250:1 ratio. Washington’s was 364:1 in the 2024-25 school year. 
“In order for us to be effective in all facets of our job, not just interventions, but every aspect of our job — whether it’s college and career-readiness or social-emotional health — all of that hinges on the 250:1 ratio,” he said.
But, he said, counselors check in every quarter with students who are struggling to find out what’s hindering them. That could include finding ways to help them attend regularly or setting up mental health support if that’s the barrier, he said.
Tutoring and summer classes are available for those who aren’t grasping the material or need to recover credits, he said, though access to them is uneven.
“They do have an incentive to finish,” Lee said. “It’s pretty rare to say, ‘I am not doing it.’”
Ulukita, the high schooler in Hawaii who repeated ninth grade, is on track to graduate with the rest of his peers in 2028. Now a junior, he was able to earn the credits he needed to complete both his freshman and sophomore years through additional courses, after-school work and a better attendance record. 
Said Ulukita: “You’ve got to lock in more, do all your classes, make sure you get all your credits — and graduate on time.”
Contact editor Caroline Preston at 212-870-8965, via Signal at CarolineP.83 or on email at preston@hechingerreport.org.
This story about being held back was produced by Big Local News and The Hechinger Report, a nonprofit, independent news organization focused on inequality and innovation in education, in collaboration with The Assembly in North Carolina, Honolulu Civil Beat, Mississippi Today and The Seattle Times. 
The data analysis was conducted by Eric Sagara, senior data journalist with Big Local News. Reporting was contributed by Megan Tagami, Ariel Gilreath, Devna Bose, Carli Brosseau and Denisa R. name: Nevada Current
title: Group tasked with exploring how to pay for regional rail tosses task back to legislators
description: State lawmakers on Tuesday approved a slate of legislative recommendations proposed by a regional rail working group that are supposed to aid the state to potentially develop mass transit, such as light rail, in metro areas.  None of the proposals, which are expected to be discussed in the 2027 Legislative Session, include concrete suggestions about […]
text:
On average states pay for nearly ten times as much of the cost of public mass transit as the state of Nevada pays to support public transit in the Las Vegas metropolitan area. (Graphic: Guy Hobbs, financial advisor to RTC) State lawmakers on Tuesday approved a slate of legislative recommendations proposed by a regional rail working group that are supposed to aid the state to potentially develop mass transit, such as light rail, in metro areas. 
None of the proposals, which are expected to be discussed in the 2027 Legislative Session, include concrete suggestions about what stable revenue streams or taxes should be considered to pay for a potential rail system, let alone to address overarching concerns around how public transit at large could be funded in the state.
The interim Committee on Growth and Infrastructure instead approved drafting legislation to “support the planning, construction, operation, and maintenance of high-capacity transit in metropolitan areas.”
The bill draft requests approved also includes formulating a separate study on funding sources and creating a statewide group to coordinate the development of rail transit. 
State lawmakers didn’t publicly discuss the proposals, nor any of the rail working group’s findings, prior to approving the measures Tuesday. 
The proposals look as though the state Legislature created “a committee that recommended forming another committee to recommend ways of actually implementing rail,” Willie Chalmers, president of Las Vegas for Better Transit, told lawmakers Tuesday.
“With all due respect, I do not believe we need another study,” he said. “I asked that the committee draft legislation that allocates funding from the state’s general fund to support the planning and construction of high capacity and, ideally, rail-based rapid transit in the region.”
Assembly Bill 256 passed in the 2025 session authorized the creation of a Regional Rail Transit Working Committee and charged it with identifying sources of state, federal, private and nonprofit funding that could potentially be used to develop and support regional rail.
After six meetings, the group concluded in June with general consensus that the state would benefit from a mass transit system in metro areas like most states. 
Speakers from nonprofits, business industry, environmental groups that address the working group this year laid out a plethora of benefits Nevada could see from building out rail infrastructure, specifically in the Las Vegas and Reno metropolitan areas. 
Chalmers reiterated on Tuesday that funding transit is about helping the “everyday people who power this economic region” move across cities. 
The working group came up against deeper structural issues about the state’s lack of revenue streams, Democratic Assemblymember Max Carter, who chaired the working group, said in an interview
“I will say that in my two terms now, it’s become abundantly clear that Nevada has a revenue problem,” Carter said. “Every single issue out there that needs to be done in our state hits the same block wall of revenue streams.”
Assemblyman Max Carter. (Photo: Richard Bednarski/Nevada Current)
Between a reluctance to embrace specific revenue sources and a 7-month timeframe for the group to complete its recommendations, there wasn’t enough time to “find a magic funding stream,” Carter said. 
“I don’t believe there was a shortage of time, but rather a shortage of ambition for creating robust transit in Southern Nevada,” Chalmers said in an interview, adding that “It’s not like what we’re trying to do in Nevada is completely unprecedented,” pointing to light rail systems in the neighboring states of Utah and Arizona. 
The state’s existing public transportation infrastructure, which is operated at the local level, already is experiencing funding issues, the committee was told. 
The Regional Transportation Commission relies on local funding one and a half times higher than the national average, Guy Hobbs, financial advisor to the RTC of Southern Nevada, said during an April meeting.
Across the country state general fund dollars make up on average a quarter of public transit funding. In Nevada, state contribution to public transit is less than 3%.
The members of the working group weren’t named until December, first met in January, and then had until July 1 to submit their findings to the Legislative Counsel Bureau. 
Cater said it wasn’t enough time to dive deeper into revenue streams and tax structures, kicking it to the 2027 session to carry on the work of finding a funding stream. 
“We think the (committee) should use one of their committee bills to do what we said: find a way to fund this, and not only fund high capacity but also sustainable funding for existing mass transit,” Carter said during the working group’s final meeting in June. “Get the thinking caps on and make some hard decisions.” 
Don’t say taxes
When it comes to paying for public transportation, most states rely on a combination of federal, state, and local funding sources, Hobbs told the working group in April. 
Other states have “general fund appropriations, different identified and earmarked revenues, income tax, which are words we never say here, property tax, fuel tax, tolls, and sales tax,” Hobbs said.
In Nevada, local transit’s primary funding source is sales tax revenue, which is unpredictable.
“That is a revenue that is not a linear growth revenue,” Hobbs said. “It experiences ups and downs, and right now we’re going through somewhat of a flat period.”
Hobbs added that if he could give sales tax as a revenue source “little stars for stability and predictability, it might get a half a star.”  
Though sales tax revenue can fluctuate and be unpredictable, “no funding source is without limitations,” M.J. Maynard-Carey, the CEO of the Regional Transportation Commission of Southern Nevada, said in an email, adding that  “the goal is to identify a long-term funding strategy that can preserve essential service, keep pace with growth and provide a reliable foundation for future transit investments.”
“The conversation isn’t about any one funding source,” Maynard-Carey said. “As our policymakers consider future transportation needs, there may be opportunities to examine how other states fund transit and determine what approaches best fit Nevada’s needs and priorities. It’s also important to recognize that Nevada’s Constitution prohibits the use of motor fuel tax revenues for public transit, which shapes how transportation funding is structured in our state.”
A list compiled by Hobbs presented at the April meeting of the working group listed taxes other states rely on to fund public transportation and rail transit including wealth taxes, payroll taxes, real property transfer taxes, casino revenue taxes, corporate income taxes, congestion pricing, lodging rental fees, and a live entertainment tax.
Hobbs again noted the list included “things that are not to be spoken of” in Nevada, where personal income taxes are unconstitutional, and taxes on wealth and corporate income have never garnered significant support from elected officials, be they Republican or Democratic. 
When asked about the various taxes identified on that list, Carter said changing some of those structures, including property taxes or payroll taxes, could hurt Nevadans already struggling to get by. 
As for the gaming tax, Carter said “I don’t think we need to mess with that.” 
The majority of Nevada elected officials in both parties have historically avoided efforts to raise Nevada’s lowest-in-the-nation gaming tax unless the state’s most powerful industry has signaled acceptance, as was the case when Republican Gov. Brian Sandoval, a close ally of the industry, and a bipartisan group of legislators enacted a gross receipts tax in 2015. 
“People compare our tax structure on gaming to other states, but we’re not like other states,” Carter said. “I believe they’re doing their fair share. If we raise taxes on them, then we impede the ability to pivot, to constantly grow.”
Carter said if any new taxes are created or current tax rates increased, he’d prefer to see voters do it instead of legislators like himself. “I would like to see it put on the ballot.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Thune calls energy development permitting reform a rare opportunity for bipartisan action
description: SIOUX FALLS — U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota, said this week that permitting reform could offer a rare opportunity for bipartisan action in Congress.  Thune discussed the issue on Tuesday during a summit hosted by Northwestern Energy, which has about 65,000 customers in the state and plans to merge with Black Hills […]
text:
U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota, speaks with Northwestern Energy President and CEO Brian Bird in Sioux Falls on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)SIOUX FALLS — U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota, said this week that permitting reform could offer a rare opportunity for bipartisan action in Congress. 
Thune discussed the issue on Tuesday during a summit hosted by Northwestern Energy, which has about 65,000 customers in the state and plans to merge with Black Hills Energy to become Bright Horizon Energy Corporation. 
Thune told attendees lawmakers are considering shorter federal reviews for energy projects and time limits on legal challenges from project opponents. 
“As soon as they’re ready to go, we’ll put it on the floor” of the Senate for a vote, Thune said. 
The politics around the issue, Thune said, have shifted because developers of coal, natural gas, wind, solar and nuclear projects have run into similar obstacles, and have brought those concerns to their elected officials. Democrats have watched renewable energy projects encounter those hurdles, which he said has created momentum for reform.
Support from Democrats matters in the Senate, he said, where major legislation requires 60 votes to overcome a filibuster. Republican senators need some Democratic support. 
The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and Energy and Natural Resources Committee are hashing out potential permitting reform, he said. 
South Dakota inches toward studying nuclear power as data center energy demands loom

Ranking Democratic members of the two committees said in March they want a bipartisan bill to speed up development, lower energy costs, and create jobs. The Democrats warned, however, that progress depended in part on the Trump administration backing off its opposition to  renewable energy projects. 
Among other policy shifts, the administration has argued that offshore wind is a national security threat, tightened eligibility requirements for wind and solar tax credits and moved to pull back Biden-era “Solar for All” grants. Last October, the Bureau of Land Management cancelled what would have been the nation’s largest solar energy project.
Thune said the negotiations come at a time when Congress is more partisan and polarized than he has ever seen. That makes bipartisan policymaking difficult, but energy permitting reform may be an exception. 
“I’m a realist,” Thune said. “But I feel good about where things stand.” 
Permitting reform
Northwestern and other utilities anticipate rapidly growing demand, including that associated with data centers. Thune said faster and more predictable permitting could unlock more private investment at a time when the nation needs additional electricity generation and transmission.
Congress should put permitting reform into federal law rather than rely on regulations that can change from one presidential administration to another, Thune said. He said different administrations will continue to treat fossil fuels and renewables differently. Thune, for his part, said he favors an “all of the above” energy strategy. 
A permitting “shot clock” to establish deadlines for the review process is one possibility, he said. He also wants Congress to address litigation after permits are issued, including how quickly courts deal with litigation and who can file legal challenges.
Nuclear power
Nuclear power could also draw bipartisan support, he said, particularly small modular reactors. The reactors are designed to be smaller than traditional nuclear plants, looking more like a warehouse than a large power plant. They produce up to 550 megawatts of electricity, according to information shared by Northwestern Energy. 
“Nuclear is, you know, it’s kind of back in vogue, especially the smaller modular reactors,” Thune told Searchlight. “We want to, as much as we can, create conditions that are favorable for investment there.” 
Northwestern Energy has spent more than $800,000 studying small modular nuclear reactors in South Dakota. The company is evaluating potential sites and is helping establish a nonprofit to educate the public about nuclear power, dubbed the “South Dakota Nuclear Collective” in documents filed by the company with  the state Public Utilities Commission.

title: All incumbents appear likely to advance in Alaska House and Senate primaries
description: Primary voters have not removed any of the Alaska Legislature’s incumbent lawmakers, according to preliminary, incomplete vote tallies published late Tuesday by the Alaska Division of Elections. Of the 40 state House and 10 state Senate races on ballots across the state, only five had more than four candidates.  That matters because the top four […]
text:
Poll workers pose for a photo at the polling site at the Mat Su Fire Station 5-1 in Palmer on primary Election Day on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Primary voters have not removed any of the Alaska Legislature’s incumbent lawmakers, according to preliminary, incomplete vote tallies published late Tuesday by the Alaska Division of Elections.
Of the 40 state House and 10 state Senate races on ballots across the state, only five had more than four candidates. 
That matters because the top four vote-getters advance to the general election, and if a race has four or fewer candidates, the primary eliminates no one. 
Vote-counting is expected to continue through Aug. 28, the deadline for absentee ballots to arrive by mail and be counted. 
Candidates who qualify for November may still withdraw before the general election. The deadline to quit is Aug. 31.     
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

Success in the August primary doesn’t always equal success in November: Two years ago, Sen. Scott Kawasaki, D-Fairbanks, received fewer votes in the August primary than his Republican challenger, Leslie Hajdukovich, in a head-to-head race. 
Just three months later, Kawasaki reversed that result and remains a member of the Senate today.
House District 37 – Bristol Bay
In southwest Alaska, three candidates were on course late Tuesday to be eliminated from contention for House District 37, where Speaker of the House Bryce Edgmon, I-Dillingham, is not seeking re-election.
With 20 of 35 precincts reporting at 12 a.m. Wednesday, Republican candidate Brenda Wilson led with 29.5% of the vote. The district leans Democratic, but there were two Democratic candidates and four independents, which likely split Tuesday’s vote. 
Democratic candidate Dennis Robinson was second, with 23.8% of the vote, followed by nonpartisan Mark Smith (15.4%) and Democrat Evelynn Trefon (14.5%). 
On track for elimination were Kim Johnson (6.7%), Peter Angasan (6.2%), and Cade Woods (4%). 
Senate District S – Southwest Alaska
After Sen. Lyman Hoffman, D-Bethel, announced his retirement, five candidates signed up to replace the longest-serving member of the Alaska Legislature. Among them is Edgmon, who had 33.1% of the vote with 27 of 59 precincts reporting results at 12 a.m. Wednesday. 
Republican candidate Darren Deacon (24.7%) was in second, with nonpartisan candidate Richard “Rick” Robb (17.1%) in third and Democratic candidate Wassilie Guy (16.8%) in fourth. 
In fifth place and on track to be eliminated was undeclared candidate Wayne Morgan, with 8.3% of the vote.
House District 23 – Eagle River
In Eagle River, Republican Rep. Jamie Allard faced four challengers in Tuesday’s primary vote. On Wednesday morning, with all precincts reporting results from election day, Democratic candidate Lee Hammermeister had just 5.8% of the vote and was on track to be eliminated. 
That would leave Allard, who had 41% of the vote, to face two other Republicans — Nick Capozzi (9.1%) and Ruby Jones (13.3%) — as well as one Democrat, Jim Arlington, with 30.9% of the vote. 
House District 29 – Eastern Mat-Su
Gov. Mike Dunleavy appointed Republican Garret Nelson of Sutton to represent this district after its former Representative was selected to fill a vacancy in the state Senate.
Now, Nelson is running for a term of his own and facing five challengers.
On Wednesday morning, with all precincts reporting results, Nelson had just 23.7% of the vote, behind Republican challenger Steve Menard, with 40.5%. Also in the top four were Democratic challenger Kimberly Slone, with 21.6% and nonpartisan challenger Jessica Kusner-Kalarchik, with 7.7%.
On pace to be eliminated were Libertarian Candice Frisby (4.5%) and undeclared candidate Amber Hansen (2.1%). 
House District 30 – Big Lake
Republican Rep. Kevin McCabe is an outspoken member of the Alaska House’s minority caucus and faced four challengers — three of whom are Republicans — in Tuesday’s primary.
With 12 of 12 precincts reporting results, McCabe led the field with 33.2% of the vote. Democratic challenger Sandra Loomis was second with 27.2%, followed by Republican Doug Massie (20.9%) and Republican Doyle Holmes (13.9%).
Republican Mike Alexander, with 4.8% of the vote, was on course to be eliminated. 
Other races to watch
While no other candidates will be eliminated in the primary election, the statewide trend in the primary was favorable for Democrats. No incumbent Democrat trailed a Republican on election day, but several incumbent Republicans trailed Democrats. 
In Anchorage, with all election day precincts reporting, Democratic candidate Denny Wells led Republican Rep. Mia Costello by 57 votes out of 3,651 cast in the race for House District 15, Sand Lake. 
Wells narrowly lost to Costello two years ago and had an even closer loss to former Republican Rep. Tom McKay in the same district in 2022. 
In Fairbanks, nonpartisan candidate Joy Cottle led Republican candidate Harmony Tomaszewski by four percentage points in a district where President Donald Trump won over 58% of the vote two years ago.
Tomaszewski is the spouse of the incumbent, Republican Rep. Frank Tomaszewski, who is running for Senate this year. 
In Homer, nonpartisan candidate Brent Johnson had 55% of the vote, compared to 45% for incumbent Republican Rep. Sarah Vance. 
The lone incumbent Democrat trailing on election day, Rep. Nellie Unangiq Jimmie, was trailing another Democrat, CJ McCormick, who held the seat until Jimmie won it two years ago.
With just 7 of 24 precincts reporting in House District 38, Jimmie had 24.2% of the vote, while McCormick had 41.7%. Republican candidate Willy Keppel had 23.3% and nonpartisan candidate Joseph Amik had 10.8%. 
In all of these races, the results could be different in November, when the same candidates are scheduled to run against each other again.
