name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas chemical plant where acid spill occurred operated without a permit, state regulators say
description: A Fort Smith chemical plant that spilled thousands of gallons of highly acidic chemicals last spring lacked a permit to operate and had not disclosed to Arkansas authorities it was handling hazardous chemicals, according to state agencies and public records obtained by the Advocate.  The spill killed thousands of fish in nearby waterways, crossed state […]
text:
The interior of the C&S Chemicals facility in Fort Smith, Arkansas, on May 3, 2026, including the ruptured acidified aluminum sulfate tank that caused the spill. (Photo courtesy of the Arkansas Department of Energy and Environment) 


Key points:

A tank at a poultry litter manufacturing plant in Arkansas ruptured, spilling corrosive acid on May 2. 
C&S Chemicals had not obtained the stormwater permit required to operate a chemical plant, according to state agencies.
The spill killed thousands of fish in a nearby creek and is being investigated by Arkansas authorities.

This summary was produced by an Arkansas Advocate reporter. Read our AI policy here. 



A Fort Smith chemical plant that spilled thousands of gallons of highly acidic chemicals last spring lacked a permit to operate and had not disclosed to Arkansas authorities it was handling hazardous chemicals, according to state agencies and public records obtained by the Advocate. 
The spill killed thousands of fish in nearby waterways, crossed state lines and severely damaged a city fire truck responding to the incident. Georgia-based C&S Chemicals had been making its sulfuric-acid based product Poultry Guard at the plant since opening in November 2024, according to a former employee and a Linkedin post announcing its opening. 
But Arkansas Department of Energy and Environment officials say the agency was “not aware” of the C&S Chemicals plant before the May 2 spill — and the facility never received a permit required to operate. It had never been inspected by state regulators either, the agency said. 
Local and state emergency management officials have confirmed C&S Chemicals also hadn’t filed a report needed to help local officials prepare for such disasters — until two hours after the spill. 
Spilled acid damaged the bay doors at the C&S Chemicals facility in Fort Smith, Arkansas, on May 2, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Sebastian County Emergency Management)
Now, as authorities from Arkansas, Oklahoma and the federal government deal with the aftermath of the acid spill, elected officials are demanding answers on how the chemical manufacturing plant could have operated with such little oversight. 
“You had this stuff for two years or more, and you didn’t fill out the permits before you started filling tanks?” said Rep. Zack Gramlich, a Fort Smith Republican. The company had purchased the property in February 2024, according to county tax records. 
Asked how C&S Chemicals was able to operate completely unpermitted before the spill, the Arkansas environmental regulator reiterated its lack of knowledge about the operations. 
“E&E was not aware of the facility prior to the spill,” an agency spokesperson said.
C&S Chemicals declined to answer questions from the Arkansas Advocate, including whether it would pay for infrastructure damages, why it did not report the chemicals to the state, and why it hadn’t obtained permits before starting operations. 
The company directed the Advocate’s inquiries to the FAQ page on the public website it created about the spill. The FAQ page gives a brief overview of the spill, including what happened, the chemicals that spilled, the affected area, remediation efforts, and instructions and contact information for residents. 
Upon investigating the facility after the spill, the Arkansas Department of Energy and Environment determined that C&S Chemicals operated without a legally required stormwater permit. 
The permit is mandated by the federal National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System, a provision of the Clean Water Act that protects waterways from industrial pollution. Without the permit and its requirements to track industrial runoff, the state agency and EPA were unable to monitor whether harmful pollutants were being discharged from the facility. 
“E&E has notified the facility that they must obtain a NPDES permit,” the agency told the Arkansas Advocate in an email on July 30. It is unclear how this stormwater permit will apply, as C&S Chemicals has not confirmed plans to continue operations after the disaster. 
Poultry Guard trucks parked near the loading dock of the C&S Chemicals facility in Fort Smith, Arkansas, on July 11, 2026. (Photo by Evey Weisblat/Arkansas Advocate)
According to the EPA, failure to obtain an NPDES permit when required is a violation of the Clean Water Act and comes with serious penalties. Operating without a water permit when required is also a violation of state law. 
The EPA did not dispute that C&S Chemicals lacked environmental permits but declined to comment on whether the facility was legally required to have numerous environmental permits, including the stormwater permit. The EPA forwarded all permitting questions to the Arkansas Department of Environmental Quality, noting the agency is the “delegated primary authority for NPDES permitting and enforcement in Arkansas.” The EPA could not comment on potential or ongoing investigations into C&S Chemicals for permit violations and negligence, a spokesperson said on July 13. The agency reiterated this in an Aug. 8 email to the Arkansas Advocate, noting it “does not comment on enforcement matters.”
C&S did not answer questions about why it did not obtain the stormwater permit, whether it plans to obtain one now or if it will resume operations at the Fort Smith plant. 
‘An oversight’ 
Despite storing up to 368,350 pounds of sulfuric acid on site — more than 730 times the reporting threshold for sulfuric acid set by the Arkansas Department of Emergency Management — C&S Chemicals had also never reported the chemicals to the state, according to public records obtained from the agency through Freedom of Information Act requests. 
Businesses handling hazardous chemicals are required to report chemical inventory annually under the federal Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act, designed to prepare communities for chemical emergencies such as the May 2 spill. 
The reports are sent by the state to local fire departments to prepare for chemical disasters. But C&S Chemicals didn’t file its report until two hours after the spill, when C&S Chemicals’ corporate safety and compliance manager sent an urgent email to the state emergency management agency attempting to file the report, which had been due two months earlier. 
“Again, this is an oversight and I am eager to correct this,” the email obtained via a FOIA request to the Arkansas Department of Emergency Management stated.
The company official said in the email they “did complete” their reporting but weren’t aware it “needed to be completed” through the Arkansas Department of Emergency Management website. The Fort Smith Fire Department and Sebastian County’s emergency management department said the company had not filed a report with them, and a spokesperson for ADEM said the state agency is the only repository of such reports, and the agency later fined C&S Chemicals for not filing its report on time.
Undated photo of dead fish in the stream near the C&S Chemicals facility where the acid accumulated. (Photo courtesy of the Arkansas Game and Fish Commission)
But the damage had already been done. Early emergency reports from local authorities confirm first responders initially believed they were responding to a building that had flooded. They discovered at the scene that a highly potent and corrosive sulfuric acid was “leaking from a container” there. 
Without the knowledge of what chemicals were stored, a Fort Smith Fire Department ladder truck responding to the incident drove directly into the spilled acid. The city is evaluating if the truck can be fixed or will need to be replaced, the city’s spokesperson said. New fire ladder trucks cost about $2 million and take several years to replace, according to the International Association of Firefighters. 
The city confirmed first responders were not injured, and the facility was closed when the spill occurred. 
State and federal investigators later determined that a tank of acidified aluminum sulfate — a product containing up to 10% sulfuric acid — had ruptured, which “broke the piping network,” causing other tanks to discharge their contents and breach the building’s walls, a May 4 internal email from a state environmental supervisor said. 
Local stream ecosystem destroyed, thousands of fish killed
The destruction didn’t stop with public infrastructure. The acid spill quickly swept into a stream along the property line, crossing state lines and flowing nearly 3 miles downstream to the mouth of the Poteau River in Oklahoma. Communications between responding agencies, including pH test results obtained by the Arkansas Advocate through FOIA requests, show the acidity of the stream quickly plummeted despite intensive efforts to neutralize it.
The acid “killed virtually every fish” between the C&S Chemicals facility and the mouth of the Poteau River, said Brandon Brown, a fisheries biologist with the Oklahoma Department of Wildlife Conservation, who spent nearly two weeks counting dead fish on the Arkansas and Oklahoma sides of the stream.
“To this creek, it was catastrophic,” Brown told the Advocate. 
The EPA described the initial release as resulting in a “complete collapse of the aquatic life in the area” of the spill.   
Brown said he counted about 2,750 dead fish. Though he was able to survey the entire stream, he estimates the number only accounts for “a fraction of the fish that actually died.”
Odie and Gina Dillard witnessed firsthand the devastation. The stream spans the length of their property off of State Line Road in Pocola, Oklahoma. The day after the spill, Odie Dillard said he walked down to the water on his property to find tanker trucks and hoses submerged in a creek. 
“And the creek was dark, dark brown, like dark coffee,” he said. He immediately spotted dead fish floating to the surface.
Although the Arkansas wildlife agency has been unable to provide an official or estimated count of the animals that died, a data collection and analysis by the Arkansas Advocate of the agency’s field observations and collected carcasses following the spill found 3,019 dead fish logged across both states, and 111 other animals. 



Quotation







I’ve seen fish kills before, but not like this.


– Brandon Brown, fisheries biologist with Oklahoma Department of Wildlife Conservation


The Arkansas Game and Fish Commission initially indicated in a May 8 statement to the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette only about 300 small fish had been impacted. But an internal agency report three days earlier confirmed that, in addition to the fish mortalities, 19 crayfish, two turtles, and one frog had also died. 
The agency blamed the “fluid” nature of the multi-agency response for the discrepancy, noting that personnel could not gather complete data until the EPA deemed the water safe to enter.  
But the delayed guidance didn’t stop Brown in Oklahoma, who began counting fish as soon as he was alerted to the spill on May 4. He soon discovered “it was a really special little creek.” 
The stream and wetland area it led to were home to a number of rare fish species in Oklahoma, such as bowfin and golden topminnow that live mostly in the area around Fort Smith, where the Ozarks, the Ouachitas and the Arkansas River Valley meet up. The stream also hosted a thriving population of redfin darters, a fish belonging to the group with the second-highest conservation status in Oklahoma, Brown said. 
The complete eradication of diverse fish species all in one place is not something Brown has witnessed in his 30 years working for the Oklahoma Department of Wildlife Conservation. 
“I’ve seen fish kills before, but not like this,” he said. 
After the spill, remediation teams work to increase the pH of the stream on May 13, 2026. (Photo courtesy of the Arkansas Department of Energy and Environment)
‘It can all be lost’
The Oklahoma and Arkansas wildlife agencies have proposed C&S Chemicals pay for restoration efforts at the affected creek rather than pay a flat restitution fee for the fish killed. The approach includes paying for restocking the sensitive fish species killed. 
The Oklahoma agency has also asked C&S Chemicals to make a donation to its planned in-house breeding program for Species of Greatest Conservation Need, Brown said. 
The Arkansas Game and Fish Commission said “C&S was very open to the remediation plan and would be talking with company leaders regarding implementation of recommendations.”
The immediate aftermath of the spill was complicated by conflicting reports of the spill’s volume, with initial reports to the National Response Center — the federal point of contact for chemical spills — of a 140,000-gallon spill downgraded repeatedly by agencies overseeing the spill to the final number C&S Chemicals provided to regulators, 77,877 gallons of acidified aluminum sulfate and 2,900 gallons of sulfuric acid. 
The EPA told the Arkansas Advocate the initial number was based on the assumption that “all the tanks released their materials,” but the sulfuric acid was contained within the facility. The agency said the rupture “appeared to be related to the manufacture of that specific tank,” and “all other similar tanks” had been drained.  
It remains unclear what penalties or enforcement action C&S Chemicals could face from environmental regulators. The EPA has declined to comment about enforcement actions. The Arkansas Department of Energy and Environment said the agency had not determined penalties yet.
“As E&E’s investigation of the incident and facility is still ongoing, E&E is still evaluating appropriate enforcement actions,” the agency told the Advocate on July 30. 
Dave Owen, an environmental law professor at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco and an expert on the Clean Water Act, said states are granted a “huge amount of discretion” to implement penalties recommended by the EPA, “much the same way as a police officer who pulls you over for speeding doesn’t have to give you a ticket.” 
“If Arkansas DEQ tried to impose a penalty that is more harsh than the guidance recommends, that might lead to litigation,” Owen said. “But if Arkansas DEQ opts for a less harsh penalty, or no penalty at all, there’s not really anything anyone else can do about it.”
The only confirmed penalty C&S Chemicals has faced has come from the Arkansas Department of Emergency Management, which fined it $790 for failing to file its chemical report by the March 1 deadline, a spokesperson said.  
The affected stream on May 7, 2026. (Photo courtesy of the Arkansas Department of Energy and Environment)
The city of Fort Smith said “responsibility for the costs has not yet been determined or finalized,” which includes damage to the fire truck and a sewer pipe.   
Gramlich said C&S Chemicals should face enforcement action for operating unpermitted. The lawmaker said the spill should serve as a wake-up call for other facilities, too. 
“If there’s other organizations out there, companies out there, who are operating like this, I want to figure out a way to help compel them or encourage them, rather, to come out of the woodworks and make sure we know they exist, so other municipalities don’t lose fire trucks — or worse,” Gramlich said. 
More than two months since the spill, the Dillards said they have still not seen any fish in the creek, and the large egrets that hunted the fish have also disappeared. A few turtles and frogs have come back, but other animals like deer and geese have largely stayed away.  
Odie Dillard expressed frustration over the lack of information he has received but said he is hoping for answers. 
“How did it happen? Did somebody screw up? Was it neglect, or what?” he said. 
For Brown, who spent days traversing the river, only to encounter dead fish at every turn, it’s a matter of respecting the “intrinsic” value of the fish and wildlife that surround us. 
“This is an example of just how fragile it is,” Brown said. “It can all be lost.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Report: Children in the Black Belt see worse health, education outcomes
description: Children raised in the Black Belt continue to see worse health and education outcomes than the state as a whole, University of Alabama researchers said at a press briefing on Monday. In the 24 counties that stretch across the southern part of Alabama, children are likely to have higher rates of mortality, live in single-parent […]
text:
Children playing with colorful wooden building blocks. Children who live in the Black Belt have worse health and educational outcomes than those who do not live in the region, according to research from the Education Policy Center at the University of Alabama. (Getty Images)Children raised in the Black Belt continue to see worse health and education outcomes than the state as a whole, University of Alabama researchers said at a press briefing on Monday.
In the 24 counties that stretch across the southern part of Alabama, children are likely to have higher rates of mortality, live in single-parent households and have fewer quality education resources compared to their counterparts, according to researchers.
“The Black Belt of Alabama is a historically underserved region and is no stranger to policy failures as it regards to the wellbeing of children and to the wellbeing of other citizens in these counties.” said Tessa Pickens, a graduate student at the University of Alabama Education Policy Center who led the media briefing.
The briefing highlighted a report from the Education Policy Center, part of an ongoing series to highlight various issues in the Black Belt region.
Alabama has long struggled with infant mortality. In 2024, Alabama’s infant mortality rate was  7.1 deaths per 1,000 live births, according to the Alabama Department of Public Health, versus 5.5 deaths per 1,000 live births for the United States.  There are major racial disparities in the rate. White Alabamians saw an infant mortality rate of 5.4 per 1,000 live births, while the rate among Black Alabamians was 11.8 per 1,000 live births.
That figure is worse for counties in the Black Belt, whose infant mortality rate is more than 9 deaths per 1,000 live births versus 6.5 deaths per 1,000 live births in non-Black Belt counties.
Butler County has an infant mortality rate of almost 30 deaths per 1,000 live births. Conecuh County’s infant mortality rate was 30.3 deaths per 1,000 live births. Wilcox County’s infant mortality rate was 31 deaths per 1,000 live births.
Researchers also said on Monday that a lack of access to health care for pregnant women plays a significant role in the disparities. According to the media briefing, only three counties in the Black Belt, Montgomery, Dallas and Escambia, have hospitals with obstetrics services targeted toward addressing the infant mortality rate, whereas 23 of the 43 counties in the non-Black Belt region have such services.
Dallas and Escambia counties have infant mortality rates that are 5.9 and 6.7 deaths per 1,000 live births, which places them in the upper third of the ranking among all counties in the state.
“Expectant mothers in most of these Black Belt counties are expected to travel outside of their county of residence to receive pregnancy-related healthcare,” Pickens said. “Barriers to transportation, as well as financial barriers, do prevent the utilization of services.”
Alabama’s refusal to expand Medicaid has also made it harder to sustain hospitals in rural areas like the Black Belt, according to Pickens.
The researchers also said that about 35% of households in the Black Belt are led by a single parent versus 23% in non-Black Belt counties. The statewide number is about 24%, which is higher than the national rate of 21%.
“Single-parent households are dependent on one income stream versus two,” Pickens said. “Single parents are more likely to have jobs with lower income potential and job security, and are more likely to face mental health issues, such as higher rates of depression and limited social support for helping to raise children.”
Researchers also said that fewer parents in the Black Belt enroll their children in childcare compared to parents who do not live in the region. Some of the barriers to enrollment could be affordability due to lower household incomes, or problems accessing transportation.
The report states that Lowndes County does not have any licensed childcare service providers, which forces parents to drive outside the area. The average occupancy rate for a childcare center in the Black Belt is about 73% but it is 79% for a childcare center that is not based in the Black Belt.
“This could indicate that families in the Black Belt are less likely to enroll their children in licensed childcare services, either turning to non-licensed options or choosing to not work to care for their children,” the report states.
This is problematic because childcare centers offer programming that could help put children on a successful path in school.
The Education Policy Center recommended expanding the Well Woman Program, provided by the Alabama Department of Public Health for women ages 15-55, which promotes healthy living and includes services such as preconception and/or inter-conception health planning.
Researchers also suggested expanding pre-kindergarten programs for children who are four years old.
“I believe the policy recommendations discussed at the briefing are great steps to address some of the needs of Alabama’s children,” said Katie Jeter, executive director of Children First, in a statement. “I would also like to add that it is imperative that children remain at the forefront of our minds as decisions are made for our state. Children are our future, and it is our responsibility to provide them with the opportunity to be successful in whatever endeavor they choose.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Data centers are not inevitable. It’s time for state laws to catch up.
description: As the midterms approach, data centers are dominating the discourse. It’s a rare issue that most people actually agree on: A May Gallup poll found that over 70% of Americans don’t want an AI data center built near them. The problems with data centers run deep. It’s not just that they broadcast constant noise and […]
text:
A server room in a data center.  A recent poll found more than 70% of Americans don't want a data center built near them. (Getty Images)As the midterms approach, data centers are dominating the discourse. It’s a rare issue that most people actually agree on: A May Gallup poll found that over 70% of Americans don’t want an AI data center built near them.
The problems with data centers run deep.
It’s not just that they broadcast constant noise and keep the lights on all night, making the neighbors crazy. Or that they’re ravenous for electricity and water. Or that they’re inescapable eyesores to the people who have to live near them.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
It gets right down to what these facilities are built to do.
They’re not like the mills and factories of an earlier America, which might have been ugly as sin and spewed smoke into the sky but at least provided jobs, woke up sleepy local economies, and made real products. 
Instead, inside their gray walls, rows of processors nibble away at the world as we know it. They hum along, day and night, powering the AI models replacing human workers, filling the internet with slop, and facilitating mass surveillance. 
Instead of producing cars or blue jeans — things we can understand and touch — these factories run the algorithms that have plunged humanity into the uncanny valley, fracturing our understanding of what’s real and human.
Not even the creators of this technology fully understand what it’s capable of or how to keep it in check. Unlike old-fashioned computers with their binary limitations, AI models sometimes go rogue. Last month, an OpenAI test model broke out of its sandbox testing environment, accessed the open internet, and conducted a cyberattack on another company. 
“Move fast and break things,” indeed. Of course, no one wants a data center in their neighborhood.
But the billionaire technocrats have already barged through the gates, extracting our land and water to feed their machines and make themselves even richer. Local communities have little power to stop them.
The ball sits squarely in the Alabama Legislature’s court.
As John Sharp wrote recently for AL.com, our state operates under a model of limited home rule, which means local governments cannot assume powers not explicitly given by the state. It’s why, every year, the Legislature must spend time passing a long parade of local bills that don’t apply to most Alabamians. And it’s why county commissioners throw up their hands in despair when angry citizens confront them about data centers. 
In lieu of local control, we have to look for answers at the state level. 
First and foremost, data centers are eligible to receive subsidies that don’t make any sense in the current climate. In Alabama, data centers can receive both a general sales tax incentive and a property tax abatement (excluding education) for up to 30 years, per the National Conference of State Legislatures. This might be an acceptable trade-off for an industry that creates jobs, but most data centers function with minimal permanent staff. The only thing a community stands to gain from a data center is tax revenue. If we give up that money, we have nothing.
We also need a more robust regulatory framework for water usage, noise, and siting. In Texas, the second-biggest data center market behind Virginia, Gov. Greg Abbott this month announced that new data centers must pass a comprehensive audit before connecting to the state energy grid.  
By contrast, while Alabama’s Public Service Commission has been tasked with making sure data centers don’t push up everyone else’s energy costs, it has no authority over a center’s water usage or other community impacts. That’s woefully inadequate.
Finally, local communities need the power to decide whether they want to host a data center or not. 
Some counties might find the promised windfall outweighs the risks, especially in rural areas that desperately need money for education, public safety, and infrastructure. In 2018 Google opened a data center on the site of a former coal plant in Jackson County, in the farthest northeastern corner of the state. In return for the county’s hospitality, Google has contributed a running total of more than $1 million to local schools, and they’ve promised an additional $2.5 million to the community for student STEM kits and energy efficiency upgrades to homes and schools. 
The relationship has been symbiotic enough that when Google announced plans earlier this summer to expand the Jackson County campus to the tune of $1.5 billion, they didn’t get much local pushback. It’s a case where the stars have aligned: The right site, plus enough local incentives to sweeten the deal, equal an agreement that seems to be palatable in this one particular corner of the state. 
And that’s the point: Counties should be empowered to look at construction proposals on a case-by-case basis and decide whether they fit into the fabric of their communities.
The AI industry is creating tectonic shifts in an already fast-moving world. It’s overwhelming and maddeningly ephemeral, impossible to fully understand. 
But we have a measure of control over the physical spaces that keep AI’s engines running. As it turns out, the cloud is not a cloud at all. It’s just a series of buildings, each with four walls and a roof and a plug that can be pulled. These buildings are not inevitable. They are the product of choices. 
Choices that should belong with the people who would have to live with them.

title: SCC commissioner, former NextEra attorney declines to recuse herself from merger case
description: On Tuesday, Virginia lawmakers heard from utility regulation experts on the potential impact of the proposed merger between Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy. If approved, the merger would create the largest electric utility in the country. In the days preceding this week’s Commission on Electric Utility Regulation meeting, legislators asked State Corporati[...]
text:
A protester displays a sign opposing the Dominion-NextEra merger outside the Virginia General Assembly on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)On Tuesday, Virginia lawmakers heard from utility regulation experts on the potential impact of the proposed merger between Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy. If approved, the merger would create the largest electric utility in the country.
In the days preceding this week’s Commission on Electric Utility Regulation meeting, legislators asked State Corporation Commission Chair Kelsey Bagot, a former attorney for NextEra Energy, to clarify if she planned to recuse herself from presiding over the $67 billion merger between Dominion and her former employer.
On Monday, Bagot replied that she saw no reason to do so.
 Commission won’t step back from merger case

Bagot resigned from her position as a senior attorney for NextEra following her appointment to the SCC, where she took office in April 2024. She had worked for the Florida utility for two years prior. 
In an Aug. 12 letter, Sen. Scott Surovell, D-Fairfax, stated “several members of the General Assembly and other third parties that have raised questions about your continued participation as a commissioner in this matter due to your prior employment by NextEra Energy especially in light of your prior recusal in a prior NextEra Energy case.”
In a response letter dated Aug. 17, Bagot wrote that her previous NextEra-related recusal during her SCC tenure concerned a high-voltage transmission line that would stretch from Leesburg to Winchester as the state’s segment of the Mid-Atlantic Resiliency Link. 
Bagot had provided legal counsel for the project in 2023, she wrote, which prompted her to notify the commission at the outset that she would recuse herself from that specific case.
Bagot explained that she consulted independent counsel concerning the NextEra-Dominion merger and whether her previous employment would violate the Canons of Judicial Conduct. Following those conversations, she said, she did not feel a recusal would be necessary.
“As has been demonstrated by long-standing historical Commissioner practice, mere work history with a regulated entity has not served as a categorical basis requiring recusal,” Bagot wrote.
 Experts testify about potential merger’s risks while residents rally

At Tuesday’s meeting, a slate of energy regulation policy experts shed light on possible impacts of the deal, which Dominion has said is necessary for the companies to purchase energy infrastructure equipment in bulk, bringing down the price and benefitting their credit ratings. 
The combined companies would be responsible for 10 million customers and 110 gigawatts of power – with 130 GW of power demand in the pipeline waiting to be connected to the grid.
Part of the merger deal includes a $2.25 billion shareholder-funded bill credit for customers that will be distributed across Dominion’s coverage states. This would equate to about $10 a month for the average Virginia residential customer.
“If approved, our Virginia customers will benefit from $1.78 billion in NextEra Energy shareholder-funded bill credits,” a Dominion representative said in a statement Tuesday. “Over the longer-term our projects will be more efficient to finance, purchase, and build due to the stronger credit and buying power of the combined company.”
The experts told the Commission on Electric Utility Regulation members there’s no guarantee that rates will not increase once the bill credit runs out. 
Lawmakers also heard from experts about NextEra’s past attempts to acquire utilities in other states. 
In Hawaii, NextEra attempted to acquire Hawaiian Electric Companies but regulators determined the merger wouldn’t be in the public interest.  
In Texas, NextEra also considered merging with the utility Oncor but regulators said it did not have tangible benefits for ratepayers and it would put them at substantial risk of taking on NextEra’s debt, which currently totals over $110 billion. 
Surovell asked Yale Law School Professor Joshua Macey, who presented to the board about potential risks posed by the merger, if NextEra considers Dominion a strategic acquisition because of the data center expansion in the commonwealth that is driving energy demand.
Macey responded by explaining a capital bias by utilities called “gold plating,” where companies with a high return on investment percentage approved by regulators would have incentive to potentially overbuild.
“You want the utility’s return on equity to equal its cost of capital,” Macey said. “This might provide evidence that rates in Virginia are too high.”
About 50 Dominion customers and community advocates rallied outside the Virginia General Assembly building before the CEUR meeting began. 
Speakers including Melissa Thomas said they believe the merger is driven by the proliferation of data centers in Dominion’s coverage area – the company currently serves over 400 – which are driving the companies’ quest to build more energy infrastructure. 
“We do not need any more data centers in Virginia. And what is next —– more gas plants next to the data centers,” Thomas told the crowd. “Do we need more polluting gas plants here? We need clean energy, affordable energy.” 
 Legislators request special session, Spanberger to intervene in case

A bipartisan group of lawmakers has asked Spanberger to call a special legislative session to pass a measure allowing  the SCC review process of the merger to be extended. Commissions have less than six months to approve or reject the project. 
So far, the governor has not responded to that request. Lawmakers have also not convened a special session on their own, which each chambers’ leadership is legally permitted to do. 
Gov. Abigail Spanberger and Chief Energy Officer Josephus Allmond officially filed notice to intervene in the SCC case for the merger on Monday.
Becoming an official intervenor, an unusual step by a sitting governor, will allow Spanberger to cross examine witnesses in the case and have access to confidential information about the possible merger.
“As Governor, I remain skeptical of the benefits this merger would deliver to Virginia — particularly if those benefits come at the expense of affordability, existing jobs, or meeting our homegrown clean energy goals,” Spanberger said in a statement on Monday.
The public testimony portion of the merger case will begin Nov. 5 and continue on the 9th and 10th. The evidentiary portion of the hearing will be Nov. 17. A decision must be made by Jan 11.
For the merger to succeed, North Carolina and South Carolina’s utility regulatory boards will have to approve it, in addition to Virginia regulators, as well as the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission,  the U.S. Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Disease experts urge safe animal practices amid ‘unusual’ rabid beaver attacks
description: Despite headline-grabbing stories of rabid animal attacks – including three attacks by beavers, at least two of which were confirmed rabid – experts say there is not any greater risk to public safety this summer compared to previous years.
text:
Environmental disease experts say Marylanders should familiarize themselves with expected animal behaviors so they can identify atypical behavior that may indicate a rabid animal. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)Despite headline-grabbing stories of rabid animal attacks – including three attacks by beavers, at least two of which were confirmed rabid – public health officials and zoonotic disease experts say there is not any greater risk to public safety this summer compared to previous years.
But they say the increased publicity from those cases is an opportunity to brush up on rabies, how it works and how to protect yourself, your family and your pets – which includes keeping your distance despite the temptation to get a great social media video.
“This is unusual, but it’s not out of character for this disease,” said Meghan Frost Davis, an environmental microbiologist and associate professor with the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, of the recent spate of cases. “We’re accustomed to hearing about rabies in raccoons and foxes, we’re less accustomed to hearing about them in beavers.”
So while rabid beavers, bats and other infected animals made news this summer for behaving erratically, the disease itself is operating as it always has.
Rabies is a virus that transmits through the bite of rabid animals and attacks the nervous system of mammals, causing deterioration in the brain.
It’s almost always fatal within 10 days of the onset of symptoms, which includes disorientation, foaming at the mouth and aggression typically associated with rabies.  Infected animals can also appear extremely lethargic, timid and suffer from paralysis.
The Maryland Department of Health reports that there were 226 laboratory-confirmed rabies cases in Maryland in 2025, with 141 cases so far this year.


“Rabies exposures increase during the summer months primarily because both humans and wildlife are significantly more active outdoors, which sharply increases the frequency of unexpected interactions,” state health officials said in an email Tuesday.
Over the last eight years, raccoons made up at least 50-60% of all confirmed rabies cases in a year, according to state data going back to 2018. Other animals commonly confirmed to have had rabies in Maryland are foxes, cats, skunks and even groundhogs.
But a string of beaver attacks have brought new attention to rabies cases this summer.
In late-July, a 13-year-old visiting Cunningham Falls State Park in Frederick County was bitten by a beaver while swimming in a designated swimming area, according to county officials. Later that day, county animal controls confirmed that a beaver in that area was infected with rabies. Rabies testing requires the animal to be euthanized.
Two weeks later, a 19-year-old was also attacked by a beaver, bitten on the ankle while fishing near Hunting Creek Lake in Cunningham Falls State Park. That beaver also tested positive for rabies.
And just last week, a 10-year-old in Montgomery County was attacked by a beaver at Seneca Creek State Park. That beaver was not found but is presumed rabid due to the typically docile nature of beavers.
“Every couple years, it seems that we have animals that people are not as accustomed to hearing about as being rabid,” said Alicia Evangelista, an environmental health program manager for Frederick County’s health department. “This year we have these beavers.
“The thing is they’re actually attacking people who are doing nothing to cause them to be attacked, so that catches people’s attention,” she said.
That said, it’s not the first time a rabid beaver was found in Maryland or even in Frederick County. Evangelista noted that there was another case of a rabid beaver in Frederick back in 2009, and state data shows rabid beavers encounters as recently as 2021.
While frightening for those attacked by rabid animals, high-profile cases involving unexpected animals are good for public awareness and could potentially lead to more cases being found.
The Anne Arundel County Department of Health released three alerts for rabid bats in the last few weeks. Rabid bats are more commonly found due to the number of bats in a colony and the tendency of them ending up in people’s homes. Those cases may not warrant public notice, said Tom Burja, zoonotic disease specialist with the Anne Arundel County health department.
10-year-old girl attacked by beaver at Montgomery County park, leading to closure of park

He said the county issued alerts because those rabid bats were found outside, not in a home or building, leading to a greater risk of a pet or child accidently interacting with the rabid bats.
But tracking the severity of rabies in an area can be challenging due to how the virus operates and other variables that effects how the disease plays out, he said.
Animals infected with rabies may go weeks or months without showing symptoms, allowing those critters to travel before the virus reaches the brain, which triggers the symptoms associated with rabies. The size of the infected animal and the location of the bite wound can affect how long it takes from the initial infection before symptoms appear.
“That’s why it’s so hard to contain and deal with,” Burja said.
He added that rabid animals in rural areas may go unreported simply because there are fewer people out in those counties to interact with. Or, the local farmer may end up “taking care of things” and “dispose of wildlife that’s harming them or their pets.”
Anne Arundel County has an oral vaccine program that drops off bait covered in fish paste. When trick raccoons and other critters bite into the bait, they puncture a packet filled with liquid rabies vaccine.
That said, rabies is all around us all the time and Marylanders should not feel any more concerned about the recent beaver and bat cases than they would be in previous years, Burja said.
“It’s a very old virus that’s been around for a very long time,” he said. “What we’re seeing right now is not that big of a deal.”
Rabies is also one of the few diseases that has an effective vaccine after infection.
“One of the most remarkable things about rabies is that we can give a vaccine after you’re exposed,” Davis with Johns Hopkins said. “This is extremely rare that we can do this, and it’s because the virus moves so slowly through the nerves. The lag time can be months.”
She also urges Marylanders to get their pets vaccinated for rabies and to stay up-to-date with their boosters.
Other prevention methods includes avoiding animals that may be rabid.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Dr. Cheyenne Falat, associate medical director of the Adult Emergency Department at the University of Maryland Medical Center in Baltimore, says it’s helpful to know the natural behaviors of animals to identify when one is acting out of character.
“Beavers, for instance, are usually very shy animals. When a beaver starts coming at you or towards you or is aggressive, that’s definitely a sign that something’s not right,” she said. “When animals are normally nocturnal, like beavers, they’re mostly active around dusk, night and dawn, if you see them fairly active during the day, that might be another indication that something’s not right.”
She says to report sightings of animals that are not characteristic of expected behaviors to the county health departments or local animal control.
If there is an attack or encounter with a wild animal, Falat stresses the importance of wound care before heading to the emergency room by washing the wound with water and soap for 15 minutes. She then says to seek prompt medical attention to begin the five-shot vaccination series for rabies if needed.
But both wildlife officials and public health experts say that it’s best practice to avoid handling wild animals in the first place, regardless of whether the animal seems rabid. Falat says that social media has blurred the lines for how people should handle or be near wild animals.
“If people are trying to get close to an animal to get a photo or a video … that kind of behavior has slightly altered what is commonsense practices for humans,” she said.
Burja had the same concern with social media leading to reckless animal handling by people who are not knowledgeable about animal behavior.
“I preach. ‘Keep wildlife wild,’” Burja said.

title: Less cargo has SC Ports Authority cutting its way toward growth
description: MOUNT PLEASANT — With cargo volumes and revenue on the decline, the owner and operator of the Port of Charleston is looking to cut costs as a way to keep its budget on track. The S.C. State Ports Authority on Tuesday reported a 4.6% drop in the number of cargo containers of all sizes moving […]
text:
The SC State Ports Authority reported a drop in cargo volumes and market share for fiscal 2026 but hopes to right the ship with cost cuts and a focus on revenue-generating projects. (Photo courtesy of the SC State Ports Authority)MOUNT PLEASANT — With cargo volumes and revenue on the decline, the owner and operator of the Port of Charleston is looking to cut costs as a way to keep its budget on track.
The S.C. State Ports Authority on Tuesday reported a 4.6% drop in the number of cargo containers of all sizes moving through the port’s terminals in fiscal 2026, which ended June 30, compared to the previous 12-month period.
Financially, the authority saw revenues of about $401 million. That’s roughly 5% less than the authority had originally budgeted for at the beginning of the year.
“We knew that achieving the (container) volumes on account of what was going on in the market was highly unlikely,” Micah Mallace, the authority’s president and CEO, told the maritime agency’s board of directors. “So, we really focused on cost. I think we succeeded in a very substantial way and in a very short period of time.”
The cargo numbers are in line with what many other U.S. ports have experienced, as tariffs, the war in Iran and economic concerns have blunted imports and exports.
The National Retail Federation is warning that consumers could tighten their wallets if inflation continues to rise, but “spending has remained resilient despite persistent geopolitical uncertainty.”
SC Ports temporarily halts Leatherman operations in face of high costs, waning demand

The authority’s fiscal year operating costs — at $378.7 million — were down by 10% from the original budget and 5.3% from the previous year as the authority offered early retirement to some employees, revisited contract terms, delayed hiring when possible and kept a close watch on overtime, among other measures.
The agency expects to save more money now that the Leatherman Terminal was idled as of Aug. 1. That terminal, which is run by an all-union staff, costs more to operate than the port’s other container terminals, which use a combination of union labor and state employees to move cargo.
The authority has not said how long the $1 billion Leatherman Terminal in North Charleston will remain shut down, although many container lines have refused to call on the facility because of its higher costs.
Mallace said the authority is also being “much more selective” about the capital projects it takes on and has slowed construction of a near-dock rail yard designed to boost the number of cargo containers hauled by trains.
That $550 million project, called the Navy Base Intermodal Facility, was supposed to open last year but its debut has been delayed as its budget has swelled.
The authority recently reached initial terms with the railroads that will use the facility — Norfolk Southern and CSX Corp. — and expects to finalize agreements in the coming months. But it does not have a specific opening date.
Charleston’s Union Pier bids bon voyage to its final cruise ship

Demolition of the former WestRock paper mill adjacent to the North Charleston Terminal is also expected to open new revenue opportunities.
That demolition is expected to take about 18 months, but the authority is already looking to move some vehicle export services to North Charleston from Columbus Street Terminal in downtown Charleston.
The agency is working on a master plan for the rest of the 280-acre waterfront property, which the authority bought in 2024 for $105 million.
“We’re honing the projects that we will invest in, and we’re making sure that those projects are directly tied to incremental revenue generation or cost minimization,” Mallace said. “The team has really exemplified discipline around capital deployment.”
Charleston’s port has traditionally relied on manufacturing cargo, particularly automotive, for much of its business, and that has led to a reduction in market share compared to other Southeast ports that have a larger consumer goods base.
Mallace said the rates charged to container lines “have gotten a little out of whack” compared to regional competitors – a fact that has also contributed to lost market share.
He said efforts to cut internal costs will help the authority lower the rates it charges to container lines, “allowing us to get our rates back in line with our competitors,” and start to regain market share and growth.
“We still have other things to solve, of course, and that will always be the case,” he said. “But we’re in a much stronger position today.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Christian nationalist protest led by Jan. 6 rioter stokes tensions in Dearborn
description: Great Replacement conspiracy theorist and pardoned Jan. 6 rioter Jake Lang brought his racial grievances and “Christian Crusader March” to Dearborn and its city council meeting on Tuesday, where the right-wing provocateur told council members Muslim people are “looking to outbreed” white people and “steal our wealth.”  Dearborn, home to the largest Arab Amer[...]
text:
A Christian nationalist protest led by Jan. 6 rioter Jake Lang prompted approximately 2,000 protestors and counterprotesters to gather in front of the Henry Ford Centennial Library in Dearborn. Aug. 18, 2026 | Photo by Tyler Scott/Michigan AdvanceGreat Replacement conspiracy theorist and pardoned Jan. 6 rioter Jake Lang brought his racial grievances and “Christian Crusader March” to Dearborn and its city council meeting on Tuesday, where the right-wing provocateur told council members Muslim people are “looking to outbreed” white people and “steal our wealth.” 
Dearborn, home to the largest Arab American population in the country, has long been the target of anti-Muslim rhetoric from people outside the community. Lang had spread his anti-Muslim message in the community as recently as August 2, when he was reportedly assaulted by a Dearborn resident. The Arab American News reports the resident, Abbas Abdoush, was later detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 
“The Muslims are being used by the Democrats to instill socialism in America,” Lang said during the city council meeting as the crowd lingered outside. “Once the Muslims have power in this county, then they will start throwing homosexuals off the roofs.”
The protest before the city council meeting was defined by diametrically opposed groups of Christian nationalist and counterprotesters screaming to drown out the sound of each other. A line of police in riot gear kept the peace by standing between Lang’s group of provocateurs and the rest of the crowd that had gathered outside the Henry Ford Centennial Library, where the council meeting had been moved for safety reasons. Michigan Advance estimated the crowd size peaked at roughly 2,000 people.
“Here is to staying free from the Muslim Brotherhood takeover” yelled Lang ally Jayden Scott in a megaphone as he stood behind the police line separating him from the crowd. “We must fight back. This is a Christian nation. A Christian nation it shall remain.”
Jayden Scott uses a megaphone to exhort anti-Muslim protesters as he stood behind the police line separating him from the crowd. Aug. 18, 2026 | Photo by Tyler Scott/Michigan Advance
A throng of supporters answered with chants of “U.S.A, U.S.A.,” while a man with a megaphone of his own yelled “Jake Lang, repent”, saying Lang doesn’t follow the teachings of Jesus. 
Lang organized the protest with the help of Detroit Pastor Lorenzo Sewell, a supporter of President Donald Trump who was criticized for attempting to enrich himself through a cryptocurrency scheme after speaking at Trump’s second inauguration. Sewell is also a member of the Faith Coalition Leadership Team of Republican U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers, who faces Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a Muslim, in November’s election. 
“Michigan families deserve a Senator who will stand up to hate rather than enable it,” El-Sayed campaign spokesperson Cole Wozniak said in a press statement issued just prior to the rally. “Mike Rogers must immediately disavow this rally, his affiliation with Jake Lang and January 6th terrorists, and explain why his campaign’s faith advisor is rallying alongside out of state agitators against Michigan faith communities.”
A request for comment was made to the Rogers campaign, but was not returned. This story will be updated when a response is received.
Democratic elected leaders including Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, Michigan Secretary of State and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson, U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin and U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Detroit) all condemned Lang’s protest as an attempt to stir hatred that could directly harm Dearborn’s Muslim community. 
“Islamophobic racists are yet again marching in Dearborn to terrorize a whole faith community,” Tlaib said. “Dearborn is a beautifully diverse place, home to a vibrant, loving Muslim community, and our families do not deserve to be subjected to such hate and bigotry.”
At several moments, it seemed as if the clash between Lang’s Christian nationalist supporters and counterprotesters, mostly Dearborn residents, could turn violent. A small segment of the two groups — almost all men who appeared to range in age from their late teens to early 40s, some wearing masks or hoods to hide their faces — spewed much of the vitriolic rhetoric and tried to provoke each other into physical confrontations while denouncing the other side’s beliefs and defending their own.
“These (are) fake Christians!” One young Dearborn man yelled at a man in a U.S. Navy hat.

 “Go back to your country!” The man responded.
Both men ignored an interview request from the Advance.

Muhammad al-thihabawi in his own words.
The unity he describes here is a little pollyanna. There were some real tense moments and anger. But he says he found unity amongst people of different religious and ethnic groups who believe in the “amendments” and that Dearborn isnt bad pic.twitter.com/CK9yGQbum9
— Tyler Scott (@T_Scotttttt) August 19, 2026

A significant portion of the crowd was uninterested in violence. The Advance observed several women urging their male partners to “shut the f**k up,” and stay calm out of concern that “you’re going to get arrested.” Some seemed only interested in observing Lang’s promised spectacle or trying to keep the peace. Most of the animosity seemed verbal. Dearborn police said information about arrests or violent altercations was not immediately available. 
At the end of the city council meeting’s public comment period, Dearborn Mayor Abdullah Hammoud, who was recently the target of death threats by an Alaska man, addressed the crowd saying that word of Lang’s return to the city sparked fear across the city, with some businesses deciding not to open Tuesday. Hammoud said he met a young boy who asked “if the crusaders were going to kill him.”
Of the Christian nationalist protestors Hammoud said, “they are attacking the idea that everyone can belong to America at the same time.”
Donna Brandenburg, gubernatorial nominee of the U.S. Taxpayers Party, attended the protest and said the whole event seemed orchestrated to stoke political resentment. 
“It seems like a big act,” Brandenburg said. “It’s trying to divide people. People in Dearborn want peace. They don’t want the fighting. I saw more American flags in Dearborn than I did in Byron Center. People need to stop drinking the Kool-Aid.” 
Despite the palpable tension and verbal hostility that dominated the evening, Dearborn resident Muhammad Al-Thibabawi said he felt “unity” with people of different ethnic and religious groups and that most of the Christian nationalist protestors were uninformed about what Dearborn is. 
“I spoke to a lot of these guys who are like ‘dude we got here and this is just a normal city that practices their amendments to the fullest’” Al-Thibabawi said. “We take pride in what we have. We love America.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Childcare providers want to pursue quality for their programs, but hurdles are mounting
description: With over 30 years of teaching experience, Amy Upton prides herself on setting the bar for high-quality early education and childcare. As the executive director of East Side Learning Center in Concord, which operates both early childhood and school-age childcare, quality care is important to her and her business.  So when the state unveiled its […]
text:
The playground at the White Birch Center Childcare and Early Learning Building in Henniker. Childcare programs in the state's continuous quality program, Granite Steps for Quality, are facing issues on their quest for improvement. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)With over 30 years of teaching experience, Amy Upton prides herself on setting the bar for high-quality early education and childcare. As the executive director of East Side Learning Center in Concord, which operates both early childhood and school-age childcare, quality care is important to her and her business. 
So when the state unveiled its new continuous quality improvement program in 2022, she knew her program would join. 
The program, named Granite Steps for Quality or GSQ, is a state-run, nationally recognized, continuous quality improvement program available to New Hampshire’s childcare providers. It focuses on elevating a program, its teachers, and its classrooms through training, leadership and professional development, coaching, and assessments. 

THIS IS THE THIRD part in an occasional series exploring the Granite Steps for Quality program and its impact on statewide childcare.

According to the state’s Bureau of Child Development and Head Start Collaboration, continuous quality improvement “aims to improve the overall quality of early care and education and out-of-school-time programs in the state, thereby improving outcomes for children and families.” 
Upton and other directors whose childcare programs are in GSQ say they see improvements through that involvement. Their teachers learn skills for working with children with different needs, and their classrooms become more catered to what is best for child development. 
But they also say the program’s limited options and design make it difficult for them to understand and implement what’s required. They also say the incentive payments they get for being in GSQ do not cover the true cost of quality improvement, resulting in them using their limited financial resources to keep up. 
Data from the bureau shows that about a seventh of New Hampshire’s childcare programs are in GSQ, and some believe that low percentage is why issues with the program are overlooked and new funding rejected by state leaders. 
For providers in GSQ, frustration on all of those fronts is mounting.
It’s a ‘nightmare’ due to its design
Childcare providers’ issues with GSQ stem from its limited options that are hard to implement. 
Participating programs pick one of two “pathways” to pursue quality improvement and are provided with training, coaching, and other resources to try to increase their “step” in the pathway. What step a program is at is determined by the percent a program elevates its staff qualifications through credentialing and improvement of its learning environments. 
The Pyramid Model pathway is available to programs that offer early childhood care and education to children between the ages of 0 and 5. It focuses on improving teaching around social-emotional skills, challenging behaviors, and nurturing caregiving. 
The Environment Rating Scales pathway is available for both early education and out-of-school-time (before and after school for grade-school students) programs. It focuses on improving how a program’s experience and learning environment affect child development, including interactions between children, space, staff, and materials.
After a rebrand of GSQ in 2022, Upton said she chose to pursue the Pyramid Model pathway due to her experience being an assessor for programs using Environment Rating Scales. She said that after the pandemic, she noticed that her students’ behavior had become “super challenging,” and she wanted a way to address it. 
“I’ve never had complaints about kids, and I’ve been going all over the state for years, going in and making recommendations. Now my own program is in chaos,” Upton said. “I said to our admin team, we need to switch to the Pyramid Model because it builds on social-emotional.” 
Amy Upton looking through GSQ manuals at Early Learning Center in Concord. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/ New Hampshire Bulletin)
Leanna Lorden, chief operating officer of White Birch Center in Henniker, said their early care program had similar reasoning when they decided to join the Environment Rating Scales pathway. 
“We were kind of using that Pyramid Model approach in our behavior policies (already),” Lorden said. “So we went the ERS pathway to really improve environments, and there was coaching support available at that time.”
Upton said their perspective on each pathway is that the Pyramid Model pathway provides teachers with “more tools in their toolbox,” while the Environment Ratings Scale is a “checklist” type of quality inspection. 
Programs might want to improve their quality beyond those two pathways, but do not have another option through GSQ. Additionally, for school-age programs, their only quality improvement pathway option is the Environment Rating Scales, as the Pyramid Model does not extend past age 5. 
“When you have only one pathway for school age, then you’re excluded,” said Ana Byers, administrator at East Side and Upton’s daughter-in-law. “You’re not meeting all of the needs.”
Providers also say moving through their pathway’s steps is incredibly difficult. 
Caitlin Gelinas is the educational supporters coordinator at Rochester Child Care Center. A large part of her job is making sure teachers at the center are up to date on the N.H. Early Childhood and Out of School Time credentials and that the program is on top of its GSQ work. She said it was a “huge problem” due to the complexity of the program’s design. 
“None of it lines up, which is a huge problem because to get a credential high enough to meet GSQ standards is a nightmare, and it doesn’t align with licensing,” Gelinas said. “There’s so many hurdles to get through.” 
Under credentialing, childcare licensing rules, and GSQ – all of which are administered by the state Department of Health and Human Services – the work experience and title of an educator is different across the three systems. 
For example, under licensing, a “lead teacher” is someone with a high school degree, 18 industry-related college credits, and a minimum of 1,000 hours of work in a licensed program. Someone who qualifies as a lead teacher under licensing has different work qualifications and a different title under credentialing and GSQ. 
Gelinas also said the 2022 rebrand ended up lowering the status of providers in Rochester who had years of experience under their belt, and as a result made it harder for the center to increase what step of the pathway they were at. 
“I can get somebody to have their CDA (Child Development Associate), which makes them legally allowed to be left alone with children in all states and many countries, but for New Hampshire, if they don’t (take a class in) Child Growth and Development, they also can’t credential high enough,” Gelinas said. 
Step progression requirements for center-based programs in the Environment Ratings Scales pathway, from the GSQ guidebook. (Screenshot)
This makes administrative work more difficult, and few programs have nonteaching staff like Gelinas who have the time to figure it out. 
East Side Learning Center does, and is currently at step 1. However, Upton’s coach told her it is unlikely for her program to move up a step in less than a year or reach step 4 before 2028, the year current funding for the Pyramid Model pathway is up for renewal. 
“I’ve been here for 36 years, and it’s going to take me four years,” Upton said. “That’s an irony, and not just me, but my staff that are doing this with me.” 
East Side Learning Center’s GSQ credential hangs in their front entry hallway. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/ New Hampshire Bulletin)
A ‘perfect storm’ of issues
New Hampshire is not new to quality programs; the state’s former system started in the 2000s. But the 2022 implementation of a new quality recognition and improvement program coincided with a handful of other changes to childcare in the state that made it more difficult for providers to get a handle on it. 
Around the same time the rebranded GSQ started, New Hampshire’s childcare sector was experiencing a lot of changes. First, an influx of federal pandemic-era funding resulted in a large amount of administrative work for both the state and providers. The Bureau of Child Development was also experiencing a leadership change, on top of changes to state laws around the childcare scholarship and credentialing. 
Byers said a “perfect storm” of things caused GSQ to be overlooked.  
“The timing almost matched up perfectly. We have started GSQ at the same time,” Byers said. 
As a result, Byers, Gelinas, Lorden, and other providers said they believe the bureau does not understand how complex the program they created is. They all said they do not entirely blame the agency for the problem, but it impacts their business because it has become a provider’s job to navigate it. 
“Right now, it’s literally just them making you jump through hurdles for a system they designed that they don’t understand to get some money sometimes,” Gelinas said. 
State officials at the Bureau of Child Development do not directly work with programs to help them increase their GSQ step. The state contracted out the work to early education-based companies to facilitate it. Through the contracts, childcare programs are provided with coaches based on their pathway to help them reach their quality goals. 
Lorden said her coach through the Environment Rating Scales pathway was “amazing” and helped her not only meet her quality requirements but also with the administrative paperwork as well. With her coach, Lorden and her program had monthly meetings to develop leadership teams and goals to work toward. 
The majority of funding for the Environment Rating Scales pathway ended in June 2026 after the state rejected a contract that would have continued coaching for the pathway and brought everything under the same company that operated the Pyramid Model Pathway. 
Without her coach, Lorden said her place in GSQ is “stagnant.” 
“We always set goals, but the real lofty goal is getting to step 3, which there’s a handful of other things we would need to do, and it’s not realistic,” she said. 
Leanna Lorden in her office in Henniker. Her walls are lined with her early education credentials and certifications. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Providers have also complained that the cost of being in GSQ is not accurately reflected in the incentive payouts, resulting in providers paying more to be in it. 
Programs get three types of payments for being in GSQ, depending on their step: an additional percentage ranging from 5%-10% back on their childcare scholarship billing, a quarterly incentive up to $5,700, and an annual quality award. 
Lorden said for her program, it came out to about $10,000 a year, but about $8 a month per child. She said that because most professional development happens outside the hours of care, the benefit does not cover the cost of staff overtime, let alone other costs associated with completing the quality work. 
“It’s helpful funding, but it doesn’t come close to covering the true cost of when you’re looking at GSQ and the requirements, staff time, professional development, administrative work,” Lorden said. 
Cora Hoppe, executive director of Rochester Child Care Center, said that while she sees the quality improvement in her staff by being in GSQ, the downsides are starting to outweigh the benefits of being in the program. 
“In my eyes, (GSQ) really highlights the work that they’re doing and puts us out there as a quality provider. But it’s just the money at this point, and being able to access certain kinds of education and stuff like that, but that doesn’t even work now,” Hoppe said. 
With parts of GSQ unfunded, Upton said being in the quality improvement program is “costing even more money” because formerly free training now requires payment. Byers, who helps Upton manage their participation, says she’s worried because it is taking away from the direct care of children. 
“Everything is being held together by sheer luck, good thoughts, and glitter,” Byers said. “To truly answer the fundamental GSQ question, we will not improve quality if the administrative burden is 100% on the providers.” 
Guidebooks for the Environment Rating Scale pathway. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/ New Hampshire Bulletin)
A state funding fix
The Department of Health and Human Services is aware of some of the core issues childcare providers have with GSQ. Twice in the past year, the department has proposed a new contract to the Executive Council (the elected body that approves contracts between state agencies and third parties) that would fully fund the quality improvement program and give the company the state’s contracting with direct authority to make changes to the program. 
The most recent contract proposal, which was rejected by the council in May, would have brought coaching and resources for both pathways under one company, the Pyramid Model Consortium. Previously, support for the Environment Ratings Scale was split between multiple different contracts. 
The rejected contract would have also revived coaching for programs like Lorden’s, while also providing “streamlined administrative support for GSQ revision, development, and implementation” and “access to tools and leadership planning to increase childcare program  quality and sustain and advance progress within GSQ.” 
“This expansion amendment of this contract would have someone to then take provider feedback, implement it, change up, look at those things, and continue to improve it. Also, it could have then looked at maybe adding some more pathways for school age,” Byers said.
Byers has been petitioning the council to change its vote, advocating that the next time a similar contract is proposed, they vote “yes” because of what it could do for programs in GSQ. Earlier this month, two councilors said they would continue to reject the contract despite its implications for the program and the state’s compliance with federal rules. 
Lorden said that in a perfect world there would be a “shared understanding” of what quality means statewide with a shared understanding of how to implement it. 
“New Hampshire is known for individual silos, duplicating work, and then coming back to the table and talking about the work that’s been duplicated and feeling frustrated,” she said. “We don’t have a common definition of what quality is across the board. We understand what that looks like and know that it’s going to take work but it’s possible.” 
Gelinas said she hopes that credentialing qualifications change to accurately reflect the education and experience of the teachers in Rochester Child Care Center’s early childhood and school age programs. She wants GSQ’s steps to be reset to make it “more of an even playing field” to make it easier for programs to progress, and reflect the reality of what it means to be a quality childcare program in New Hampshire. 
“The part that people forget is that literally, if we don’t have childcare then you can’t have workers. Our economy literally depends on having safe, quality childcare in whatever that looks like,” she said. “Those people making those decisions forget that not everybody is lucky enough to have a rich parent that can stay at home and watch their children.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Hoosier Lottery to send estimated $350M surplus to state coffers
description: The lottery profits support teacher, firefighter and police pensions, plus cut costs for Hoosiers registering and plating their vehicles.
text:
Indiana's State Lottery Commission meets on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026. From left: Commissioners Luke Bosso and Alyssa Cochran. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Hoosier Lottery had nearly $1.7 billion in sales last fiscal year and will send almost $350 million back to state coffers, according to preliminary and unaudited data presented Tuesday by State Lottery Commission officials.
State fiscal year 2026 began last July and ended June 30.
The $350 million expected surplus is above the previous year’s $341 million total, but remains below record-breaking figures recorded during the pandemic — peaking at almost $376 million in 2021.
“Now, those (numbers) are not our highest year … But they do represent another very strong year for the Hoosier Lottery, particularly in an environment where many lotteries across the country are still experiencing slower or even negative growth,” Executive Director Sarah Taylor told the commission during a Tuesday meeting in downtown Indianapolis.
Hoosier Lottery Chief of Staff Carrie Stroud, left, and Executive Director Sarah Taylor, appear at a State Lottery Commission meeting on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
The surplus helps pay off pensions for teachers, firefighters and police, and takes about half the cost off the motor vehicle excise tax that Hoosiers pay when they register and plate their vehicles.
“Those retirement and pension funds are ones that we are very passionate about and have been part of our mission this whole time,” Taylor said. “In addition, the motor vehicle excise tax, what we love about it is (that) it also impacts Hoosiers throughout every county, whether they play or not. … We’re touching all the local communities and counties throughout the state with the three funds that the Legislature has designated for us.”
The $1.7 billion total is flat from the last several years.
Scratch ticket revenue hit $1.2 billion, about 38% less than was budgeted. And the lottery recorded mixed results for big jackpot draw games.
Powerball came in at $134 million, almost $48 million ahead of budget, and Hoosier Lotto was about $44 million, less than $1 million off expectations. The nearly $53 million in revenue for Mega Millions, however, was about $15 million behind budget.
Non-jackpot draw games garnered $214 million, about $17 million more than expected.
The lottery did meet its financial goals, however.
Operator Brightstar Indiana — previously named IGT Indiana — is expected to receive an incentive payment of $7 million. If the lottery had fallen short, the operator would’ve had to make a shortfall payment under the performance-based contract.
The lottery paid out about $1.1 billion in prizes last year.
Another try for i-Lottery
Hoosier Lottery signs hang in the organization’s downtown headquarters on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
During the meeting, commissioners remarked that strong digital playslip use should prompt another look at online lottery sales — an idea lawmakers have repeatedly introduced and then scrapped.
On the Hoosier Lottery app, players can build a playslip and generate a barcode for retailers to scan and print tickets.
“This is all great digital numbers,” Commissioner Luke Bosso said. “… It feels like, you know, it’s a compelling argument for iLottery.”
External Affairs Director Jared Bond confirmed the lottery has submitted an iLottery proposal to Gov. Mike Braun’s office for consideration.
The lottery has for years sought permission to sell tickets online to boost revenues. The state website could also host electronic gambling games on the site if authorized.
“We’re kind of having those discussions … again, talking to legislators about, you know, kind of, what the appetite is for that,” Bond said. “… Budget session, coming into that, the Legislature may be looking for some money. iLottery is an option for that, so we’ll see where we land with that.”
