name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Newsroom Profile: Indianapolis Recorder
description: Indy resident Karis Dix, 18, is more likely to get her news from social media than a newspaper. But every year since she was 16, she has looked to the Indianapolis Recorder for coverage about the Debutante Cotillion and Scholarship Ball. When she was a child, her mother, an avid Recorder reader, would take her […]
text:
Staff members of the Indianapolis Recorder accept awards from the Indiana chapter of the Society of Professional Journalists. (Courtesy photo)Indy resident Karis Dix, 18, is more likely to get her news from social media than a newspaper. But every year since she was 16, she has looked to the Indianapolis Recorder for coverage about the Debutante Cotillion and Scholarship Ball.
When she was a child, her mother, an avid Recorder reader, would take her to the cotillion to see the debutantes and experience the ball.
And in her junior year of high school, Ivy Endowment and the Alpha Mu Omega Chapter of Alpha Kappa Alpha Sorority, Inc. selected her to be one of them.
Now an incoming college freshman, she looks back on the Recorder’s faithful coverage of the Ball and knows what it’s like to be part of a bigger community story, and to see that story on a printed page. 
The Ball and Scholarship Program are hallmarks of Black life in Indy that the Indianapolis Recorder has recognized over the years. The newspaper publishes the photos of the young women the sorority selects to participate in the dance rehearsals, workshops, activities, and community service that make up the program. 
When Dix read about the event and saw her picture in the Recorder, she felt proud. 
“I felt recognized and acknowledged for the hard work that all of the debutantes put into the program,” she told me. 
These moments, the family reunions, the church anniversaries, the soirées, and homecomings, are all important events happening in Indy’s Black community that you won’t find captured in local mainstream news.
“By documenting our significant milestones and efforts in the community, the Indianapolis Recorder does more than report the news; it uplifts our mission, inspires future generations, and honors the rich history of Black excellence in Indiana,” said Ilisha Dowell, president of Alpha Mu Omega in Indianapolis. The African American sorority is dedicated to advancing scholarship, service and sisterhood throughout the Midwest.
To Dowell, the Recorder represents connection, legacy, and validation. She calls it an “essential cultural archive for our community.”
For this newsroom profile, I spoke with Recorder Media Group President and CEO Robert Shegog and Editor-in-Chief Camike Jones to understand the Indianapolis Recorder’s unique perspective. I also wanted to know how the news outlet is navigating shifts in the news business, so I asked Dr. Ben Chavis, president and CEO of the National Newspaper Publishers Association, the Black press trade association, to weigh in with a national perspective on Black newspapers. 
Black newspapers have thrived for decades, adjusting to shifts in the market
Black newspapers have been a vital source of news to many Black communities across the country, since the publication of Freedom’s Journal, in New York City, in 1827. 

“Historiucally, Black newspapers documented stories that other outlets ignored,” said Shegog. “They covered lynchings, civil rights activism, Black business growth, educational achievement, and community concerns long before those stories received widespread attention.”

Next year  will mark the industry’s 200th anniversary. The Indianapolis Recorder is the third oldest Black newspaper in the country.

The Black press has suffered the same blows as mainstream news organizations. More people get their news from Google searches, social media and now, AI, in the digital era. To keep afloat, Black newspapers are trying to invest in social media efforts so they can meet their younger audiences where they get news. They’ve also been impacted by the Trump administration’s attacks on diversity, equity and inclusion measures, as corporate advertisers and sponsors are less inclined to purchase ads in a Black newspaper or support events in the Black community. 

“The Trump administration has had a very negative impact on African American-owned media, particularly African American-owned newspapers, and other publications, with the drawback of Trump’s administration on diversity, equity and inclusion, which then led to corporate America retreating from diversity, equity and inclusion,” Chavis said. In addition to his role leading the Black press association, he’s also a civil rights activist and former NAACP president. “It’s had a devastating, I would say, 50% to 60% reduction in national advertising, because of the Trump administration.” 

In its heyday in the mid-1920s, there were as many as 500 Black newspapers in the United States. Today, Chavis counts 253 Black newspapers and media as part of his membership organization, including the Indianapolis Recorder.

To be clear, the Recorder’s challenges go beyond the threats from the Trump administration, Shegog points out. After a wave of public support and commitments from corporations and institutions following the murder of George Floyd in 2020, that support was “reduced, redirected, delayed, or did not materialize the way many organizations expected,” he said.

“What we are experiencing today is, in many ways, a continuation and acceleration of that shift,” Shegog said. “Some companies are changing the language they use, reevaluating programs, and becoming more cautious about investments that were previously associated with diversity and equity. At the same time, economic uncertainty and changes in advertising and philanthropic priorities are affecting the entire media industry.”
Black-owned and local from the start, Indianapolis Recorder remains an asset to the community
The Indianapolis Recorder was founded as a church bulletin by George P. Stewart and William Porter in 1895. It became a weekly newspaper in 1897, which it has remained ever since. Early issues of the paper chronicled visits to Indiana from Black dignitaries like Booker T. Washington and W.E.B. Dubois. 

Today, the paper remains an asset to the community, covering stories ignored by other media. For example, this Central Indiana Housing FAQ, created in partnership with WFYI. Recorder reporters have been recognized for their sports coverage, sweeping the local Society of Professional Journalists 2025 awards for that category.

Today the Recorder has nine staff members, including four reporters. Over the years, the paper has been passed down through family ownership by multiple families and has always been Black-owned.	


Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US




Stewart remained the publisher and editor until he died in 1924, and the paper stayed in his family until Eunice Trotter purchased the paper in 1988. In 1990, William G. Mays, founder of Mays Chemical Company, acquired the Recorder, and it stayed in that family until 2010, when Shannon Williams became the president and general manager. Robert Shegog, the current president and CEO of Recorder Media Group, took the helm in 2018. 

According to its website, the Recorder has a weekly readership of 128,000, and distributes 11,000 physical copies of the newspaper. It offers online subscriptions and can be found at grocery stores, drug stores and gas stations all over Indy. 

Seventy-six percent of their readers pay for subscriptions to the digital and print versions of the news. Their website gets 684,000 page views a month, on average. Thirty-seven percent of their readers are between the ages of 25-44 and 27% are between the ages of 45-54.

The news outlet is funded by those subscriptions as well as print and digital advertising, sponsorships, events, partnerships, grants, community initiatives, and other multimedia opportunities, Shegog told me. 

Recorder management is working to adapt the paper’s workflow to that of a multimedia organization, rather than a weekly paper, Shegog said. 

“The introduction of social media and news influencers has really changed the landscape of media and changed what people are expecting from news outlets and how they engage with news and media,” Editor-In-Chief Camike Jones said.

Jones said part of her job is maintaining journalistic standards, such as integrity and fact-checking, even as the newspaper finds different ways of delivering stories to compete with social media influencers. 

She believes the Recorder will stay relevant to its audience by continuing to cover important events and activities that make up the Black experience in Indianapolis year after year, but making sure people can find the information in their social feeds. “So those ladies’ teas and the church bazaar and some of those sorts of activities — youth programs, the men’s social clubs — I think that is still important to do and we still receive a lot of requests for that,” Jones said. 
 
The Recorder allows the Black community of Indianapolis to tell its own story. If you are looking for stories about the events, places, and traditions the African American community of the city holds dear, you will find those cultural touchstones in the Recorder. 

Karis Dix plans to study biochemistry at Florida Atlantic University this fall. Although she will be far from home, she will be checking up on her hometown newspaper to see what her community is up to. 

“I think in the future, the Recorder will continue to share great information with the Indianapolis community, like the cotillion, that other news sources don’t,” she said.



I want to hear from you! Please write to me with your questions and concerns about local press at indypubliceditor@poynter.org.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: In Hampton, a race to insulate vulnerable neighborhoods against sea-level rise
description: Millions of dollars in infrastructure improvements are helping one particularly hard-hit Hampton neighborhood cope with the effects of climate change. In the lead-up to the project’s completion, Gentian Road resident Tom Bassett saw bacteria-contaminated floodwater fill his yard, lap against his home, and pool in the street dozens of times each year during p[...]
text:
Meadow Pond, in Hampton, viewed from Gentian Road. The tidal estuary regularly floods during very high tides, spilling over into nearby neighborhoods. While the town of Hampton has worked on engineering solutions to that flooding, which is worsened by climate change, scientists are working on rehabilitating the marsh itself. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)Millions of dollars in infrastructure improvements are helping one particularly hard-hit Hampton neighborhood cope with the effects of climate change.
In the lead-up to the project’s completion, Gentian Road resident Tom Bassett saw bacteria-contaminated floodwater fill his yard, lap against his home, and pool in the street dozens of times each year during particularly high tides or heavy storms.
At first glance, the upgrades that Bassett and his neighbors on Gentian Road, Meadow Pond Road, and nearby streets spent more than two decades advocating for don’t look like much. A layer of new asphalt on the road hints at the network of new drainage pipes underneath, while an existing pump station in the heart of the neighborhood has been repurposed. Tucked behind Bassett’s home, at the edge of the marsh, a bobber swings at an automated water-level reading station. 
Yet these changes, funded with a mixture of local, state, and federal dollars totaling about $4.3 million, have had a big impact on the neighborhood. By Bassett’s estimation, they have reduced the incidence of flooding there by about 75%. 
That change was evident on Tuesday morning, if you knew where to look. Damp rings encircled the catch basins on the marsh side of Gentian Road, the asphalt still drying after water had poured in from the marsh during high tide the night before. The rest of the road was still dry, something that would not have been the case before the upgrades, according to officials.
“Roads could become impassable. I saw it first-hand,” said Executive Councilor Janet Stevens, delivering remarks during an event celebrating the upgrades on Tuesday. “Drainage outlets could be submerged for extended periods, and residents were left wondering when the next storm would bring another round of flooding.”
The stormwater drainage system serving the Meadow Pond neighborhood was built in the 1950s, according to Pauline Perkins, watershed management specialist with the New Hampshire Department of Environmental Services. The system featured an outfall pipe leading into Meadow Pond, an estuary connected to the Hampton salt marshes and, ultimately, the sea. 
But when periodic high tides brought water levels above the level of that outfall, the drainage system no longer worked — and the system wound up channeling water in the opposite direction, right back into the neighborhood, Perkins said. Other problems like cracked pipes were additional weaknesses that allowed the rising water table to inundate what was intended as a drainage network.
The worsening conditions caused by climate change and sea level rise are necessary considerations for the Hampton Department of Public Works, according to department Director Jennifer Hale and Deputy Director Joseph Lynch.
As greenhouse gases trap heat in Earth’s atmosphere, water from the melting polar ice caps is causing water levels to rise in the planet’s oceans. Liquids also take up more space as they warm, meaning that the rising overall temperature of Earth’s seas is another factor in their levels creeping upward. The global average sea level has risen between 8 and 9 inches since 1880, and the rate at which the ocean is rising is accelerating, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
Sea-level rise and the increasing intensity of storms and rainfall events, also worsened by climate change, have led to more frequent flooding in coastal areas like Hampton. 
Lynch said those changes must factor in to every decision about Hampton’s future that he makes. 
“What has happened over generations is true. If you believe in it or not, you can’t deny that there is sea-level rise,” he said Tuesday morning. “… Everything we do now in the coastal area is always in light of sea-level rise, whether it’s our wastewater treatment plant, our sewer collection systems, our drainage system, our roadway networks — everything is driven by recognition of what that future condition might look like.”
Hampton’s flooding problems aren’t limited to the Meadow Pond neighborhood. The town has paid for more engineering studies and is turning its attention to other neighborhoods for possible next steps, said Hampton Select Board Vice Chairman Jeff Grip. 
For Bassett, the upgrades to his neighborhood are a big relief. The floods brought dangerous bacteria to his door, compromised travel, and exposed his car to corrosive salt water, he said. They haven’t completely stopped; after all, the drainage solutions have their limits. But for Bassett, it’s a win in a fight that stretches on beyond Meadow Pond. 
“I think (the project’s completion) builds optimism that there are ways of coping with the problem,” he said. “But, you know, it’s a way of coping, it’s not solving it. The real issue is greenhouse gas emissions and global warming.”
Damp pavement is visible on the marsh side of Gentian Road, in Hampton, on Tuesday, Aug. 18. Before upgrades to the neighborhood's drainage system, such as the new catch basin pictured at lower left, the street would often be flooded for hours by a similarly high tide, town officials said. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)Hampton and state officials listen to remarks on the morning of Tuesday, Aug. 18, standing on the site of previously problematic flooding on Gentian Road. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)A floating bulb attached to a sensor system hangs just off the edge of the marsh at Meadow Pond, in Hampton, on Tuesday, Aug. 18. The bobber is part of an automated system that uses pumps, channels, and new outfall sites to drain tidal flooding from the neighborhood at the marsh's edge. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)Hampton residents walk through the marsh to inspect an automated water level tracker on the morning of Tuesday, Aug. 18. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)Tom Bassett, a resident of Gentian Road, addresses state and local officials, contractors, engineers, and others who helped bring a redesigned drainage system to his neighborhood. Speaking in front of his home on the morning of Tuesday, Aug. 18, Bassett said he was grateful that the new system had reduced the impacts of flooding on his property and road, which has worsened with climate change. Bassett has organized in support of improvements for more than two decades. At right is Pauline Perkins, watershed management specialist with the New Hampshire Department of Environmental Services, who managed grants for the project. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)Jennifer Hale, Hampton's director of public works, addresses a crowd gathered on Gentian Road on Tuesday, Aug. 18. "We're here today because something has been done. It started with all the outcry of, 'we need help,'" she said, referring to a tide of organizing from community members around the flooding. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)North Beach in Hampton on the morning of Tuesday, Aug. 18. Communities along Hampton's coastal strip are bordered on one side by the ocean and on the other by tidal estuaries, creating a flood hazard that compounds as sea levels rise with climate change. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)

name: Kansas Reflector
title: We cannot arrest our way out of a mental health crisis, in Kansas or elsewhere
description: For far too long, one of the greatest frustrations in law enforcement has been that we are often called because someone in our community is experiencing a substance use or mental health crisis and needs help that we aren’t trained or equipped to provide. Every police officer I know has been through this. Law enforcement […]
text:
Law enforcement officers face challenges when dealing with those in the throes of a mental health crisis. A different system has been creating better results. (Photo by Caspar Benson/Getty Images)
For far too long, one of the greatest frustrations in law enforcement has been that we are often called because someone in our community is experiencing a substance use or mental health crisis and needs help that we aren’t trained or equipped to provide.
Every police officer I know has been through this. Law enforcement responding to people with untreated mental illness or addiction consumes enormous public resources and does little to help with the crisis or the underlying problem.
Fortunately, in Kansas, we now have a better response that’s good for people in need and their loved ones as well as police officers and public safety.
Through Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics, trained behavioral health professionals partner with law enforcement to bring care instead of handcuffs to people in crisis. I’ve seen the power of the model in my community, thanks to Prairie View’s CCBHC.
Just a few years ago, my officers could spend entire shifts — and even longer — sitting in a hospital emergency department with someone waiting to be evaluated. That meant officers were unavailable to answer other safety calls, while the person in crisis often received at best temporary stabilization before being discharged.
Today, officers who respond to 911 calls about people in crisis transport those suffering directly to Prairie View, where they receive immediate care from trained behavioral health professionals. Sometimes Prairie View’s crisis response teams also come to the scene, take over once it is safe, develop a safety plan, connect the person to services, and free up police officers to return to protecting the community.
That is a better outcome for all of us.
The results in McPherson are clear. Since the implementation and expansion of Prairie View’s clinic, police responses to crisis-related calls have declined from 76 in 2022 to 42 in 2025. Protective custody placements, where officers must stay with a person in crisis, dropped by more than 80%. Average time spent in hospitals supervising people in crisis who were awaiting evaluation decreased by more than three and a half hours.
Those numbers matter. They mean people are getting connected to care faster, fewer people end up in involuntary emergency detention, and officers return to patrol faster, improving public safety for the entire community.
One of the biggest changes we have seen is that more people in crisis accept help. Many now choose treatment because they know they will be taken somewhere designed to help them.
This successful partnership between law enforcement and CCBHCs reflects a larger truth: We cannot arrest our way out of a mental health crisis. Behavioral health professionals can solve problems that police officers cannot. Better outcomes and lasting public safety depends on people receiving the right care at the right time.
For Kansas, the model is especially important because many of our rural communities have limited behavioral health resources. In parts of our state, families — and officers — have few places to turn when someone is in crisis. A model that brings trained professionals, crisis response, and coordinated care out into the communities makes all the difference.
Kansas has made meaningful progress, but there is still work to do. Every community deserves access to the kind of coordinated crisis response that has improved outcomes in McPherson.
As police officers, our job is to keep communities safe. One of the best ways to do that is by ensuring people experiencing mental health or substance use crises  receive effective treatment before their situations escalate into emergencies.
That is why supporting and expanding Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics across Kansas makes sense. They help people get well. They make better use of taxpayer dollars. They allow police officers to focus on policing, while behavioral health professionals provide the specialized care they are uniquely trained to deliver.
The result is healthier people, safer communities, and a stronger Kansas.
Mikel Golden is the McPherson police chief and president of the Kansas Association of Chiefs of Police. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Advocates say Tiffany’s vote for 2025 Medicaid cuts bodes ill for healthcare
description: A vote that U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany cast in June 2025 has become a centerpiece of healthcare advocates’ criticism of the Republican candidate for governor. Tiffany, along with all Republican members of Congress and no Democrats, joined in the passage of the 2025 HR 1 — the legislation that President Donald Trump and U.S. House […]
text:
Flanked by Corrine Hendrickson, center, and Nancy Higgs, right, Macy Buhler talks about the impact of increased health insurance costs on her workforce of childcare teachers at a news conference Tuesday criticizing Republican candidate for governor Tom Tiffany, organized by Main Street Action and Protect Our Care. (Photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)A vote that U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany cast in June 2025 has become a centerpiece of healthcare advocates’ criticism of the Republican candidate for governor.
Tiffany, along with all Republican members of Congress and no Democrats, joined in the passage of the 2025 HR 1 — the legislation that President Donald Trump and U.S. House Republican leaders dubbed “The One Big Beautiful Bill Act.”
The measure made cuts to Medicaid and federal nutrition benefits over the next 10 years, along with a range of other changes to federal programs. The Medicaid changes alone have been projected to cut $900 billion to $1 trillion from the health insurance plan for people with low incomes.
The legislation also extended a series of tax cuts that were passed in Trump’s first term — cuts that primarily benefit wealthy Americans, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities in Washington.
After the bill’s final passage in July 2025, Tiffany issued a statement praising the outcome for “providing tax cuts for seniors, parents, workers and small businesses” as well as for funding federal immigration agencies that have been deployed across the country.
Tiffany also said he would “remain committed to protecting Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid for our seniors and the most vulnerable, while rooting out waste and curbing the reckless spending that threatens future generations.”
But in press conferences last week and Tuesday, healthcare advocates said that bill was central to their opposition to Tiffany’s healthcare record.
U.S. Rep. Mark Pocan (D- Black Earth) talks about the impact that increased healthcare costs due to the loss of enhanced premium subsidies has had on small business owners he’s met. (Photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)
“When he voted for the one big beautiful bill, he essentially voted for a $1.1 trillion cut in healthcare,” U.S. Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Black Earth) said at a press conference Tuesday organized by the groups Main Street Action and Protect Our Care. “And that’s the biggest cut we’ve ever seen in this country.”
In addition to benefit cuts, advocates have focused on what HR 1 lacked. U.S. House Democrats tried to persuade the Republican majority to extend enhanced health insurance subsidies for people buying their health coverage on the Affordable Care Act marketplace.
The enhanced subsidies were enacted in 2021 and expired at the end of 2025. Democrats’ repeated attempts to extend them were rejected, not only during debate on HR 1 but several times later in 2025 as well as early in 2026.
Pocan said he’s spoken with small business owners across his South Central Wisconsin district who have been affected by the ACA premium increases that resulted.
“We’ve seen small business owners in Baraboo on the Affordable Care Act say that their monthly portion they pay in has doubled or even tripled,” Pocan said. One constituent he spoke with “just got out of the [insurance] system altogether,” setting aside the cash that would have gone to an insurance premium in hopes that it would be enough to cover a healthcare emergency.
“That’s not a healthcare plan,” Pocan said. “That’s not about making health insurance more affordable. That’s about taking insurance away from people.”
According to a July 28 report from KFF, a nonprofit healthcare policy analysis and news organization, coverage through the ACA fell nationwide by 2.6 million in 2026 from 2025 after seven years of steady increases. In Wisconsin, coverage fell 16%, by 45,000 people.
Gov. Tony Evers issued a statement Tuesday blasting Wisconsin’s Republican congressional delegation for letting the enhanced subsidies expire. 
“Congressional Republicans’ refusal to extend the tax credits caused healthcare coverage costs to skyrocket, pricing families in Wisconsin and across the country out of having coverage at all,” Evers said.
Macy Buhler, a De Forest childcare provider and Main Street Action member who joined the press conference with Pocan, said that without those additional subsidies, the cost of insurance for some of her employees rose to unsustainable levels.
Buhler said she can’t cover healthcare for her childcare teachers directly, but has been providing them a stipend to help teachers who need health insurance purchase it on the federal ACA marketplace, HealthCare.gov. She doubled that stipend for 2026, she said — a $40,000 increase in just that expense.
“Early childhood teachers deserve real access to healthcare and medication, not a Congress who makes it impossible for them to afford both,” Buhler told reporters. “Tom Tiffany voted for this bill. We cannot trust him with our healthcare.”
Buhler told the Wisconsin Examiner that she’s “lost some staff and closed a classroom because they can no longer afford to be an early childhood educator, a teacher.”
Nancy Higgs, a self-employed interior designer specializing in affordable approaches for her customers, has been in business since 2023. The ACA coverage made it possible to get health coverage, she told the Wisconsin Examiner.
After a good first year, the business struggled following the 2024 election. Because her net income was too low, she switched to enroll in Medicaid — called BadgerCare in Wisconsin — for her healthcare.
Higgs said she isn’t sure what will happen to that coverage under the HR 1 changes, which don’t take effect until January 2027.
During a virtual news conference on Thursday, Aug. 13, Dr. Sophie Kramer, a Madison internal medicine physician, said the loss of insurance coverage, whether from Medicaid or an ACA policy, will lead to poorer health. The news conference was sponsored by the Committee to Protect Health Care.
“So much of what we do depends on patients having consistent access to healthcare. I treat patients with chronic diseases like diabetes, cancer, heart disease, hypertension — and those don’t disappear when someone loses insurance, they just become harder to manage,” said Kramer. “I’ve seen too many patients suffer from treatable conditions simply because they didn’t have access to affordable care.”
Dr. Kristen Dall-Winther, another participant in that news conference, owns her own practice in Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District. Tiffany has been her U.S. representative since 2019.
“I see first hand what happens when patients struggle to afford care, when rural hospitals are under financial pressure, and when people put off seeing a doctor because they are worried about what it will cost,” Dall-Winther said. “Tom Tiffany has repeatedly voted for policies that make those problems worse.”
Dall-Winther cited forecasts that HR 1 could eventually cost more than 250,000 Wisconsin residents their healthcare coverage.
Kramer also cited Tiffany’s vote against a federal bill that would have codified a right to abortion in September 2021. The measure passed the House on a party-line vote but stalled in the U.S. Senate.  
Nine months later, in June 2022, the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the nearly 50-year-old decision in Roe v. Wade that had legalized abortion nationwide. An 1849 Wisconsin statute that was interpreted as an abortion ban went into effect as a result.
“Tom Tiffany could have voted to protect that federal right to abortion in law, but he voted against it, allowing state bans like ours to interfere in personal medical decisions,” Kramer said.
The Wisconsin Supreme Court subsequently ruled that the Wisconsin law didn’t apply to elective abortion.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Lawsuit argues SC Ports’ payout to former CEO violated state law
description: A lawsuit filed in Charleston County accuses the S.C. State Ports Authority of disregarding state laws on open meetings and public records in its handling of a nearly $1 million severance package for the maritime agency’s former director. Frank Heindel, a retired Mount Pleasant businessman and long-time public records activist, filed the suit this week. […]
text:
Barbara Melvin resigned from the S.C. State Ports Authority on Aug. 21, 2025, receiving a severance package of nearly $1 million. (File photo courtesy of the S.C. State Ports Authority)A lawsuit filed in Charleston County accuses the S.C. State Ports Authority of disregarding state laws on open meetings and public records in its handling of a nearly $1 million severance package for the maritime agency’s former director.
Frank Heindel, a retired Mount Pleasant businessman and long-time public records activist, filed the suit this week. He claims the authority violated both the state’s Freedom of Information Act and separate law governing the Ports Authority when its board of directors failed to take a public vote to approve the August 2025 severance for Barbara Melvin, the maritime agency’s former president and CEO.
State law requires the authority to publicly vote on compensation — including severance — for the agency’s executive director and division directors.
The board did not approve any resolution or take any public action approving Melvin’s severance when she abruptly resigned on Aug. 21, 2025, two days after the board held an unscheduled executive session in which the purpose was never disclosed. That, too, violated state law, the lawsuit argues.
Former SC Ports CEO to get nearly $1M severance package

The authority declined to comment on the lawsuit.
According to court records, authority lawyer Randy Lowell said the board was not required to take any action because the severance amount was less than what Melvin’s employment contract called for.
Heindel said in his lawsuit that the employment contract did not specify any severance owed unless the resignation was for good reason. Melvin did not say in her resignation letter that her resignation was for good reason, and Heindel said the severance package amounted to newly created executive compensation requiring a public vote.
“The authority cannot bypass that statutory public vote mandate by characterizing discretionary executive payouts as pre-existing contractual duties when the contract creates no such right,” the lawsuit states.
Heindel said he does not want to adjudicate Melvin’s severance package. Instead, he wants a judge to declare that the authority violated state law. He also wants an injunction banning the authority from taking similar action in the future and he wants the agency to pay his attorney’s fees.
In addition, Heindel wants the authority to post any finding that it violated state law on the agency’s website for six months.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
No court hearing has been scheduled.
Melvin, who held the authority’s top job for a little more than three years, resigned without prior public notice. She did not give a reason for her departure, other than to say she planned “to pursue other opportunities.”
The bulk of her severance package was $822,780 in pre-tax salary continuation payments through the end of 2025 and a $100,000 contribution to her state retirement account. The authority also agreed to pay her $350 an hour in consulting fees on an as-needed basis.
In addition to the money, Melvin was allowed to keep her iPad, laptop and cell phone after authority business had been wiped from them, and she received the balance of any accrued leave she had not taken.
Last fall, Heindel sued for information on how the University of South Carolina distributed money to student athletes, which resulted in the Legislature passing a law earlier this year keeping such payments secret. The exemption from the Freedom of Information Act became law after legislators overrode Gov. Henry McMaster’s veto.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Appeals court upholds ban on immigration enforcement at some churches
description: A federal appeals court Tuesday upheld an injunction that bars Department of Homeland Security agents from conducting immigration enforcement "at or near" more than 1,400 churches sprawling across 33 states and the District of Columbia.
text:
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer watches a crowd of protesters at Delaney Hall, a detention center, in Newark, New Jersey, on May 25, 2026. (Photo by Ben Ackman/New Jersey Monitor)A federal appeals court Tuesday upheld an injunction that bars Department of Homeland Security agents from conducting immigration enforcement “at or near” more than 1,400 houses of worship sprawling across 33 states and the District of Columbia.
The ruling by a three-judge panel of the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld a February 2025 ruling in favor of a coalition of Quaker, Sikh and Baptist congregations that sued to block the Trump administration’s reversal of a Biden-era policy discouraging immigration actions at “sensitive places.”
The religious groups argued that the administration’s policy would drive away immigrant attendees, burdening “their ability to worship communally and to minister to immigrant communities, both acts of which are fundamental to their religious exercise.”
U.S. District Judge Theodore Chuang agreed, issuing the preliminary injunction in 2025 that blocked the new policy at those congregations, requiring DHS to follow the more-restrictive rules of the 2021 Biden policy. He declined to apply the injunction nationwide.
In its 40-page ruling Tuesday, the appeals court panel upheld the injunction, agreeing with Chuang that the houses of worship were likely to succeed on their claim that the administration’s policy, if implemented, would decrease “attendance at worship services and other activities.”
States, cities try to keep ICE out of schools with mixed results

“The plaintiffs have presented evidence showing that the 2025 Policy is having a chilling effect on their congregations and already has caused declines in attendance among members of CBF [Cooperative Baptist Fellowship] and the Sikh Plaintiffs,” Senior Judge Barbara Milano Keenan wrote for the court.
“And our preceding analysis makes clear that this decline in attendance and the increased threat of immigration enforcement at all the plaintiffs’ houses of worship already has imposed a substantial burden on the ability of all the plaintiffs to express their religion through communal worship,” she wrote.
Keenan noted a January 2025 statement from a Homeland Security spokesperson that she said amplified the fact that the agency “intends to target houses of worship in future immigration enforcement actions.” The judge quoted the spokesperson’s statement last year that, “Criminals will no longer be able to hide in America’s schools and churches to avoid arrest.”
“DHS’s statement emphasizing the rationale for this policy change shows that the threat of immigration enforcement at their houses of worship is real and substantial,” wrote Keenan, who was joined by Judges Pamela Harris and G. Steven Agee.
When asked for a response to the ruling Tuesday, a Homeland Security spokesperson replied with a paraphrase of that 2025 statement.
“Criminals are no longer able to hide in places of worship to avoid arrest. The Trump Administration will not tie the hands of our brave law enforcement and instead trusts them to use common sense,” the statement said.
It went on to say that Immigration and Customs Enforcement “does not target places of worship. This is just another false narrative to try and demonize our brave ICE law enforcement who are facing” increased assaults and death threats.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
But Democracy Forward, the Washington, D.C.-based group that filed the lawsuit on behalf of the houses of worship, welcomed the ruling.
“The Trump-Vance administration’s policy threatened that longstanding tradition by forcing congregations to choose between fulfilling their religious mission and protecting members of their communities,” Democracy Forward said in a statement on behalf of the plaintiffs. “We are grateful that the court has preserved these protections while this case moves forward.”
The plaintiffs include the Sikh Temple Sacramento and six yearly meetings of the Religious Society of Friends, or Quakers: from Philadelphia, New York, New England, Richmond, Baltimore and Adelphi, Md. They also include the Cooperative Baptist Fellowship, a network of hundreds of churches located in 33 states.
Their lawsuit was in response to a policy, issued on the first day of the second Trump administration, lifting restrictions on enforcement activities around sensitive locations, like schools and churches. Agents instead were told to exercise “discretion along with a healthy dose of common sense” when deciding whether to act in or around a sensitive location.
It was a change from the 2021 policy that said enforcement near sensitive areas was to be avoided “to the fullest extent possible.” Such action could still be taken but, except in emergency situations, it needed agency approval first.
With new tactics, ICE reaches new high in monthly arrests

Matt O’Brien, deputy executive director of the Federation for American Immigration Reform, called the 4th Circuit’s opinion “absurd.” FAIR filed a friend of the court brief in support of DHS.
“There is zero reason, constitutional or otherwise, why immigration enforcement should be prohibited near houses of worship. This is a politically-motivated decision by an activist judge.”
But in a concurring opinion, Agee noted the “narrow scope” of the preliminary injunction, which applies only to the houses of worship that sued the federal government. In essence, it doesn’t restrict Homeland Security from conducting immigration enforcement at or near sensitive places such as mental health centers, libraries, schools and other places of worship. It also doesn’t stop all activity, he wrote.
“A host of DHS immigration enforcement actions are expressly permitted by the preliminary injunction. It states, for example, that … [it] ‘does not enjoin or restrict [DHS] from conducting arrests in or near places
of worship when authorized by an administrative or judicial warrant,’” Agee wrote.
“Further … the preliminary injunction incorporates the provisions of the 2021 Policy, which itself did not ban all immigration enforcement actions at or near a place of worship,” he wrote, noting that the 2021 policy allows agents to act without prior approval when in pursuit of a suspect, when there’s a threat of violence and in other emergency situations. “Plainly, nothing in this Court’s decision or the preliminary injunction could be construed as limiting DHS’s ability to act in accord with these directives.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Maine’s gubernatorial candidates agree on education challenges, but not solutions
description: Two of the three gubernatorial candidates vying to succeed Gov. Janet Mills this November agree on the major challenges Maine schools are facing: students are falling behind in reading and math, mental health needs are growing, educators are underpaid and stretched thin, and school buildings are aging without enough resources to replace them. Democratic Hann[...]
text:
Students work in a math class at Wasatch Junior High School in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, March 12, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Two of the three gubernatorial candidates vying to succeed Gov. Janet Mills this November agree on the major challenges Maine schools are facing: students are falling behind in reading and math, mental health needs are growing, educators are underpaid and stretched thin, and school buildings are aging without enough resources to replace them.
Democratic Hannah Pingree and independent Rick Bennett don’t diverge much over how the next governor should address those challenges either.
ButAnd while Republican Bobby Charles agrees on the need to support teachers and achieve stronger academic outcomes, he blames those challenges on “woke indoctrination” in classrooms, and proposes that schools end equity-based initiatives and return to traditional learning models.
The future governor will inherit a public education system that is grappling with the consequences of federal disinvestment. Staffing cuts at the U.S. Department of Education have disrupted special education assistance to schools. Programs that improved student mental health were cut due to ideological differences, and an ongoing lawsuit over the state’s transgender athlete policy further threatens federal support.
Bennett and Pingree’s responses to Maine Morning Star’s questions on education policy show they support strategies that include increasing teacher salaries and relying on evidence-based learning, as well as protecting Maine’s inclusive laws and continuing the state’s commitment to 55% of public education funding.
Alternately, Charles has advocated for a national Republican-led agenda that includes curriculum transparency, parental involvement in education and the end of diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives, calling it his “no-nonsense” plan.
“While schools across the state of Maine face infrastructure challenges and workforce concerns, including teacher recruiting retention and morale, the biggest challenge we face is reversing the downward slide in objective outcomes,” he said in a statement to Maine Morning Star. 
“We need a major reset that lets teachers focus on the fundamentals and clear away the anxieties and distractions that come with politicians trying to use classrooms as laboratories for social experiments.”
Pingree secures union endorsement
On Aug. 6, the Maine Education Association endorsed Pingree, with union member Sarah Abronze saying she “listens to educators on the front lines and truly wants to understand and fix the challenges we face.”.
“From serving nine years on her local school board to serving as a speaker of the House, she has an unblemished 100% MEA voting record, backing legislation that supports educators, students, public schools, and our universities in Maine,” Abronze added.
The MEA has had a long history of supporting Democratic candidates, including Mills’ re-election in 2022. Ahead of the gubernatorial primary, Pingree was not one of the three candidates the union endorsed, instead backing Shenna Bellows, now-U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson and former public health leader Nirav Shah. 
Jesse Hargrove, president of the Maine Education Association, and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree on Aug. 6 (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)
Bennett and Charles said they were not surprised by the endorsement.
Bennett said the union “always endorses the Democratic candidate, regardless of his or her credentials, plans, or support of public schools.”
Charles’ campaign manager, Dale Crafts Jr., said the Republican “will earn the support of thousands of individual teachers while their union bosses play the same political games in Augusta that have our state in a perpetual state of failure.”
MEA President Jesse Hargrove explained that the process for choosing a candidate to endorse 
in the general election — which will not be determined using ranked-choice voting like the gubernatorial primaries were —  was separate from the primary selection criteria.
Both Pingree and Bennett responded to an MEA questionnaire and were interviewed by members, who cast secret ballots to choose their preferred candidate, Hargrove explained. Charles’ team said he never received the questionnaire, although the MEA disputed that.
The union emailed Charles’ team twice, in October and November of last year, emails obtained by Maine Morning Star show. He did not respond to either invitation to participate in the endorsement process, Hargrove said. 
How Trump’s anti-DEI shift unraveled a successful federal investment in Maine schools

Pingree and Bennett’s voting records as lawmakers were also considered while making the choice, Hargrove said. According to the most recent scorecard the educator union published in 2025, Bennett, a senator representing Oxford County, scored about 50% because he voted against the Democrat-led budget supported by the union, opposed a plan to improve teacher mentoring programs, and voted in favor of an unsuccessful school voucher program bill.
At the endorsement event in Augusta earlier this month, Pingree committed to building on her support for public education and teachers.
“Public education determines the trajectory of our economy, our communities, and our democracy,” Pingree said. “The future of this state — it’s sitting in classrooms. Our job is simple: get our kids ready for the future, and get Maine ready for them.”
Educational outcomes
All three candidates agreed that Maine’s test scores — which hit an all-time low in national 2024 assessments and have slightly improved in more recent state results — indicated that students need more robust instruction in reading and math. The Maine Department of Education took on an initiative to help districts use more evidence-based learning methods last year, which experts say is a step in the right direction. 
Both Bennett and Pingree said they would rely on screenings and early interventions to help tackle poor academic outcomes. 
“Too many students fall behind in reading and math early and don’t get help quickly enough,” Bennett said in his written response. “I support regular screening, faster intervention, high-quality instructional materials, evidence-based teacher support, and better data so schools and families can act sooner.”
Pingree said she would also invest in “sustained professional development and instructional coaching for teachers, grounded in the science of reading and strong math instruction.”
Bobby Charles, the Republican gubernatorial nominee in Augusta on June 23. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)
Charles also expressed concern about plummeting test scores, but blamed it on Democratic ideology replacing traditional learning in Maine classrooms.
“Success in education must again be measured by motivating students to love learning (and) graduate with the skills they need to succeed, and maximizing freedom for teachers to teach, elevating both teacher morale and student performance in life after graduation,” he said.
School mental health
Maine schools are struggling with increasing student mental health challenges while federal resources that help districts hire and train staff to address these issues are being cut. 
“Many of our school districts are relying on federal funding for certain programs,” Hargrove said. “If that federal funding is in jeopardy, we’re going to have to be relying on state and local funding to make up that deficit.”
Both Pingree and Bennett said they would invest in expanding school-based mental health, including hiring staff.
Bennett said he would add mental health clinician and counselor ratios to the education funding formula so schools can hire needed staff with more state support. He also supports tiered frameworks currently used by schools that allow educators to offer personalized support based on student needs.  
Pingree also supports investments in student mental health, including expanding school-based health centers and telehealth access, especially in rural communities where care is hard to reach. 
“I will invest in after-school programs, sports, and music, ending pay-to-play barriers so every child, regardless of income, has the chance to connect, belong, and thrive,” she added.
When asked if he would support increasing mental health funding, Charles pointed out that counseling services are already “part of the state funding formula, and this is something that is very individualized to each student and school.”. But he also singled out counseling students about gender identity, which has been subjected to scrutiny and lawsuits by Maine parents in the past.
“Is there anything more stressful for a student than a school counselor convincing them to take steps to change their gender without informing their parents?” he added. “We need to focus on loving students just the way they are and not encouraging them to believe there is something wrong with them at such a young age.”
Inclusive education
Both Pingree and Bennett oppose changing Maine law that explicitly protects the rights of trans athletes to play on sports teams and use school facilities aligning with their gender identity. Despite President Donald Trump’s administration targeting Maine for its policy, both said if elected that they would uphold that law.
“That’s not up for negotiation because Donald Trump wants to bully our state into compliance by threatening to pull federal funding our schools and kids depend on,” Pingree said. 
“As a mom whose own kids play and love sports, I know these issues are personal for families across Maine, on every side. But withholding funding from schools, meals programs, and kids to score political points isn’t leadership. It’s bullying, and Maine shouldn’t cave to it.”
Bennett also voted against state-level attempts to roll back those protections last year, breaking from his Republican colleagues before he left the party to run as an independent for governor.
Independent gubernatorial candidate and Sen. Rick Bennett from Oxford at Portland Pride in June. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)
He said he believes “schools should provide a safe and respectful learning environment for every student,” adding that laws should not change while there is pending litigation.
Charles has been outspoken in his opposition to Maine’s law. He supported a failed referendum aiming to restrict trans students’ rights to athletics, bathrooms and locker rooms, and has vowed to “drop the Title IX lawsuit” with the federal government.
“As an attorney and someone who believes in common sense, I think we should always follow the law, whether I agree with it or not,” he said when asked if he would attempt to change the Maine Human Rights Act if elected. “As far as working to change them, what I will not do is engage in petty arguments and insults with the federal government that sends hundreds of millions of dollars each year to our local public schools.”
Teacher salaries 
After many years of educators pushing for higher pay amid chronic staffing shortages, Maine recently raised minimum teacher salaries to $50,000 by 2029. Bennett, a co-sponsor of that bill, said it’s not enough, though added that “pay alone doesn’t solve the workforce crisis.”  
“Maine also needs to improve retention and strengthen the teacher pipeline through mentoring, support for new teachers, paying student teachers, and helping Maine students afford college if they commit to teaching here,” he added. 
In addition to increasing pay, Pingree focused on the need to tackle the broader cost of living challenges that many educators face.
Making childcare and energy costs more affordable, lowering housing prices and protecting collective bargaining rights are all part of the solution, she said. 
“If we want to recruit and retain great teachers, Maine needs to be a place where educators and school staff can actually afford to live and build a life,” Pingree added.
Charles said his campaign promises to cut income and property taxes, reduce state spending, lower energy bills, and grow Maine’s economy will “make it easier to live on a teacher’s salary and even attract more educators to our state.”
“As the son of a teacher who taught for 40 years and the grandson of a principal, I would love to pay all of them a million dollars a year, but obviously, we have limited resources,” he said. “I would aim to dramatically shift state resources away from Augusta bureaucracy to teaching.”

title: Less than 10% of Ohio lawmakers are moms of minor children. They say it informs their lawmaking.
description: About 9% of Ohio’s state lawmakers are moms of children under 18, according to a new report, giving them insight into issues impacting families with minor children, several said in interviews. The third Politics of Parenthood: Representation in State Legislatures report was recently published by the Vote Mama Foundation, a nonprofit organization that studies[...]
text:
The Ohio Statehouse. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal). About 9% of Ohio’s state lawmakers are moms of children under 18, according to a new report, giving them insight into issues impacting families with minor children, several said in interviews. 
The third Politics of Parenthood: Representation in State Legislatures report was recently published by the Vote Mama Foundation, a nonprofit organization that studies the political participation of mothers in the United States. 
About 4% of Ohio state lawmakers were moms of minors when the first report was published in 2022 and that number rose to 6% in 2024 for the second report. 
Of Ohio’s 132 state lawmakers in 2026, 12 are moms of minor children as of February, according to this year’s report. Ohio would need 13 total moms of minors to reach proportional representation among the population at-large, according to the report.
Only two states have reached proportional representation: California and Virginia.
Ohio ranks 23rd in this year’s report — a significant jump compared to being ranked 37th in 2024. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“It’s important to have well-rounded conversations, and the only way to do that on each piece of legislation is to have a variety of people in these elected positions,” said Ohio state Rep. Lauren McNally, D-Youngstown. 
Ohio lawmakers who are moms of minor children are:

State Sen. Susan Manchester, R-Waynesfield
State Rep. Ashley Bryant Bailey, D-Cincinnati
State Rep. Rachel Baker, D–Cincinnati
State Rep. Beryl Brown Piccolantonio, D-Gahanna
State Rep. Kellie Deeter, R-Norwalk
State Rep. Sarah Fowler Arthur, R-Ashtabula
State Rep. Latyna Humphrey, D-Columbus
State Rep. Crystal Lett, D-Hilliard
State Rep. Lauren McNally, D-Youngstown 
State Rep. Monica Robb Blasdel, R-New Waterford
State Rep. Allison Russo, D-Upper Arlington
State Rep. Heidi Workman, R-Rootstown

The Ohio Capital Journal talked to Fowler Arthur, McNally, Bryant Bailey, and Piccolantonio about balancing motherhood and their work in the legislature. 
“We need more moms in every state legislature across the country,” Bryant Bailey said.
“The ability to truly understand wholeheartedly a lot of the issues that plague our residents really starts with the lens of how we learn to be protectors as mothers, and it pains me that our government is not really suited for moms, I’ll even say for parents in general, especially of young kids.”
Nationally, 8.3% of state legislators are moms of minors — a 5.3% increase since the 2024 report. 
Of the 7,386 state legislators in the United States, only 613 were moms with children under 18, as of February, according to the report. 
State Rep. Monica Robb Blasdel, R-Columbiana,sitting on the House Floor with her daughters Presley, left, and Raegan, right. (Photo provided by Rep. Monica Robb Blasdel).
About 730 more moms with kids under 18 are needed to have proportional representation in state legislatures, according to the report. 
“(Being a mom) is one of the busiest phases of life,” Piccolantonio said. “That is one of the reasons why the numbers are so low, and also the reason why it is so important to have those voices at the table when making policy decisions.”
California and Virginia have reached proportional representation. 
“Getting mamas at every decision-making table requires paying attention to state legislatures, which pass tens of thousands of bills each year that affect nearly every aspect of families’ lives,” Liuba Grechen Shirley, founder and CEO of Vote Mama Foundation, said in a statement. 
This is the first year moms of children under 18 have been elected to all 50 state legislatures, according to the report. 
Challenges experienced 
An often mentioned challenge of balancing motherhood and being a lawmaker is the distance from a lawmaker’s district to the Ohio Statehouse and missing out on family activities. 
“I can’t just be home after session, regardless of what time session ends,” said McNally, who lives about three hours away from the Statehouse and has four children — ages 12, 10, 9, and 6. 
“I can’t come home for an emergency. I’m not home in time for their baseball game because committee ended at four. I’m doing homework in between committee on FaceTime at the Statehouse with them, or helping my daughter pick out her school outfit for picture day on FaceTime while I’m down in Columbus.” 
Ohio state Rep. Ashley Bryant Bailey, D-Cincinnati. (Photo from Ohio House of Representatives).
McNally acknowledged it can be hard to make it to events in the evenings or on the weekends. 
“I get that you want me to come to your event on Sunday, but I want to go to my kid’s soccer game on Sunday,” McNally said. 
To squeeze in extra time with her kids, she tries not to work on President’s Day or Martin Luther King Jr. Day when her kids are off school. 
“When I am home, I try really hard to make moments that are exciting for them.” 
But the work does not always stop, even when she is with her family.
“There’s very few places I go where I don’t get stopped to have a conversation about something, and that includes my kids’ baseball game or my kids’ dance competition, where my kids want me to focus on them,” McNally said.
Bryant Bailey has two children — ages two and seven — and she said there is some guilt at times when it comes to balancing legislative duties and motherhood. 
“I don’t live in Columbus, so when I’m there to do the legislative work — whether we’re in session or not — it’s always going to be time away,” she said. 
“Even when I am in Cincinnati, the work doesn’t stop. … There’s always that short-term feeling of are they seeing me enough?”
Ohio state Rep. Sarah Fowler Arthur, R-Ashtabula. Official photo.
Becoming a mom has changed how Fowler Arthur spends her time traveling to and from the Statehouse, which is at least a three hour drive.  
She typically leaves early Tuesday morning for committee meetings and goes back home Wednesday after session. 
“I really try hard to be here to tuck them in and be here when they wake up as much as I can,” Fowler Arthur said. 
“They’re always so happy to see that, but it is a lot more wearing, I think, on me personally just to be driving on top of these really full days that we already have.”
Even though Piccolantonio lives in Central Ohio, she’s not able to make it to everything for her sons. 
“There are definitely sacrifices missing out on activities or things that get scheduled,” she said.
Her youngest son plays tennis, but she’s only been able to make it to one of his matches. 
“I work to find ways to be constantly connected with him, even if I’m not physically there with him,” Piccolantonio said. 
“We try — in the times that I’m not as busy — to schedule more time together. I try as hard as I can to keep Sundays clear.” 
State Rep. Sarah Fowler Arthur
Fowler Arthur and her husband legally adopted their children — ages 8, 9, and 10 — almost three years ago after fostering them. 
Becoming a mom has made Fowler Arthur, who is the chair of the Ohio House Education Committee, more passionate about children learning how to read and the importance of math. 
“I didn’t really connect how absolutely unprepared for everyday life someone could be until my kids came into my house officially going into second grade and going into first grade in the public school, and still could not read, and seeing them struggle through the process,” she said.
“If they have those two basic fundamental skill sets (reading and math) they really do have the world at their fingertips. If they don’t, they are at such a huge disadvantage compared to their peers who can read.”
Fowler Arthur occasionally brings her children to the Ohio Statehouse — sometimes if they can’t find child care and other times as part of their homeschooling education. 
“They really love to come and to observe and be a part of just the day-to-day activities of the legislature, which I think is a really neat hands-on experience,” she said. 
“They love coming home and playing state representatives.” 
State Rep. Lauren McNally
Rep. Lauren McNally, D-Youngstown, delivering sponsor testimony. (Photo courtesy of the Ohio House Democratic Caucus.)
McNally had her three youngest children while serving on Youngstown City Council before being elected to the Ohio Statehouse. 
“Both times I ran for city council, I was pregnant,” she said. “They’ve been my winning lucky charm.” 
At the Statehouse, most of McNally’s testimony for bills includes a personal story about her children. 
When she testified in support of Ohio House Bill 63 — which would require security cameras at all rest areas — McNally talked about how her family decided where to stop on a road trip while driving through West Virginia. 
“I didn’t know it, but our then three-year-old was getting motion sickness,” she said in her April 2025 testimony. 
“Our family weighed the pros and cons of stopping … It wasn’t until we made it to a Welcome Center that we finally stopped, got her cleaned up, and went on our way. … (Travelers are) looking for locations with a presumption of safety.”
From wearing her campaign shirts during election season to conversations about McNally’s work during dinner, her children are “very much involved” in her job as a lawmaker. 
“It’s not a traditional job from that perspective,” McNally said. 
“Protecting your family unit while also being in the public eye like this is a balance.”
State Rep. Ashley Bryant Bailey
Being a mom impacts every decision Bryant Bailey makes and the implications it will have for her two children. 
She introduced Ohio House Bill 768 which would allow certain child care staff members to receive publicly funded child care. 
“My daughter goes to daycare, and I know full well there are teachers at her daycare that can’t afford to send their own kids there,” she said. 
“I talk to the child care workers at my daughter’s school all the time about how difficult it is, and I know firsthand how expensive childcare can be.”
State Rep. Beryl Brown Piccolantonio
State Rep. Beryl Brown Piccolantonio, D-Gahanna, speaks during an Ohio House session at the Statehouse in Columbus, Ohio. (Photo by Graham Stokes for Ohio Capital Journal. Republish photo only with original article.)
Piccolantonio said her sons — ages 22, 20, and 16 — are the reason she serves in the Ohio legislature. 
“It’s at the forefront of my mind whenever I’m thinking about any bills that we’re talking about,” she said. 
“When I’m making decisions, a lot of times I’m thinking about it from the perspective of what would my kids think about me doing this.” 
Piccolantonio often finds herself asking how a bill would affect young people and families. 
“How would this legislation make it easier or more difficult for a family, for a mom, to be able to afford to live in Ohio or to be able to have opportunities in this state?” she said.  
Piccolantonio wrestles with her children being part of public life. 
“You are a public servant, it really is a full family commitment … but for kids who are minors, they’re not consenting to be part of public life, and yet they are part of public life,” she said. 
Most people Piccolantonio’s sons interact with know their mom is a state representative. 
“Their identities are set in that way without them having made a choice about that,” she said.
“It weighs on me a lot. They are young people trying to forge their own identities. That’s a lot to carry on their shoulders.”
She often talks about that with her sons. 
“I have a lot of different roles, but in my mind, my first role is always as mom.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio lawmaker pushes for local hearings before PUCO decides on Dayton utility purchase
description: Ohio state Rep. Tristan Rader wants state regulators to take a close look at a plan to purchase Dayton’s electric utility, AES. The $10.7 billion deal would take the utility private — putting it in the hands of a group with few ties to the region and investments that might cause conflicts of interest down […]
text:
Ohio state Rep. Tristan Rader, D-Lakewood, speaking at an energy affordability press conference. (Photo by Nick Evans, Ohio Capital Journal.)Ohio state Rep. Tristan Rader wants state regulators to take a close look at a plan to purchase Dayton’s electric utility, AES. The $10.7 billion deal would take the utility private — putting it in the hands of a group with few ties to the region and investments that might cause conflicts of interest down the road.
Rader, D-Lakewood, wants the Public Utility Commission of Ohio to hold hearings in AES’ service territory to allow ratepayers, local governments, and other stakeholders to weigh in before making a final decision.
“This is a consequential decision for the future of Ohio’s electric system,” Rader wrote in a letter to PUCO chair Jenifer French.
“With rates increasing, data-center demand accelerating, and billions of dollars in new grid investment likely ahead, Ohioans deserve the opportunity to ask questions and be heard before control of their electric utility changes hands,” he went on.
A PUCO spokesman acknowledged they’d received the letter and filed it in the case docket.
The Commission set an Aug. 13 deadline for comments in the case, and it has yet to make a final decision on the deal. A staff review, however, indicated the buyers are a “suitable owner for AES Ohio.”
The consortium
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The buyers include the Qatari sovereign wealth fund, California’s public employee pension program, a Swedish private equity firm called EQT, and Global Infrastructure Partners, a subsidiary of the largest asset manager in the world, BlackRock. The consortium put up $10.7 billion in cash.
In a March press release, the parties said AES will have “improved access to capital to invest in critical energy infrastructure assets,” and it would “continue to invest prudently in utility assets to meet the growing energy needs of all 1.1 million customers.”
The consortium’s said it intends to leave the utilities’ management team intact and make additional investments in the competitive energy generation market.
The release plainly stated, “this acquisition is not expected to impact customer rates in AES’ regulated utilities.”
The PUCO staff report leans heavily on the consortium’s assurances that it won’t meddle in the utility’s day-to-day operations.
The report notes the company’s rates and management aren’t changing, the company isn’t rebranding, and merger costs won’t get recovered through rates. Customers will use the same website, call the same call center, and receive the same bills.
“Staff believe that a change in ownership has little to no foreseeable drawbacks for AES Ohio,” the report said. The new owners might even give the company more opportunities to invest energy infrastructure, PUCO staff added.
“The benefits of an active investing ownership outweighs the foreseeable drawbacks,” the report said.
It’s a point AES Board chairman Jay Morse brought up when the deal was announced. In the press release, he emphasized the benefits for current stockholders and noted the company had “significant need for capital to support growth beyond 2027.”
Without the acquisition, Morse warned, AES would have likely cut or eliminates dividends and might have issued a “substantial” number of new shares in the company — diluting current stockholders’ stake.
Skeptics concerns
The consortium aiming to purchase AES emphasizes the “enhanced financial flexibility” it will have as a private company, but Rader worries that also mean less transparency.
“It’s a big change,” he said. “Going from a publicly traded company to completely privately held. (It) closes some doors and makes it a little more opaque.”
He’s also concerned about conflicts of interest. BlackRock has substantial investments in artificial intelligence and data centers.
AES sees data centers as a significant growth opportunity within its service territory. So what happens when the company that controls the grid also has a stake in one of its biggest customers?
“It feels like, seems like to me, there might be some, if not double dealing, at least some incentives here to give data centers a great deal, (while) at the same time passing those costs on to customers,” Rader said.
“Incentives don’t seem to be quite lined up in my opinion,” he added.
Just east of Dayton, Kim McCarthy chairs the Greene County Democratic Party, and she’s running for a state House seat in November.
By day, she’s an accountant, and she isn’t thrilled about private equity taking over the local utility. She described losing her job in 2021 after a private equity firm bought the local IT company where she was working.
“So, when I heard that private equity groups were looking to purchase AES,” McCarthy said, “I couldn’t help but think, oh wow, they’re just going to hollow out our electrical system.”
As for Rader’s idea to holding public hearings in the Dayton area, McCarthy’s on board, so long as it’s “impactful,” rather than an exercise to “placate the public.”
“Qatar? BlackRock? And no offense to the California pension fund, but what do they care?” she said. “They want to make money. That’s all they want to do. They have no ties to this area, they’re not going to care about the lives that are impacted here.”
And she isn’t the only one skeptical of the consortium’s long-term plans.
In a filing with the PUCO, representatives from the city of Dayton pressed for binding assurances from the utility’s new owners.
If regulators are going to rely on the consortium’s claims to justify approving the purchase, the city reasoned, they should take steps to ensure the consortium sticks to its promises.
Among Dayton’s asks, PUCO should require the new owners maintain AES’ headquarters, senior leadership, and at least 90% of its baseline workforce in the area for the next 20 years.
And while the consortium plans to continue programs investing in local infrastructure and economic development, Dayton argued choosing not to eliminate that work isn’t the same as providing a benefit.
“The city would like to see how the merger improves upon the great work AES is already doing,” the city’s filing stated, “not whether the merger will simply maintain AES’ existing commitments.”
