title: Open letter to Ohio US Sen. Bernie Moreno: Haitian parents love their children too
description: Warning: This commentary discusses issues of torture, murder, and rape, including of children. An open letter to Ohio U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno Sen. Moreno, we can see that you love your daughter and granddaughter — it’s clear from the statement you released on X. Domestic violence is a national epidemic that scars families of every […]
text:
Signs of support for Haitians in Springfield, Ohio after temporary protected status ended on July 27. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).  Warning: This commentary discusses issues of torture, murder, and rape, including of children.
An open letter to Ohio U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno
Sen. Moreno, we can see that you love your daughter and granddaughter — it’s clear from the statement you released on X. Domestic violence is a national epidemic that scars families of every race and religion, in every neighborhood. It’s important that you are speaking up now, even though it’s difficult.
We have to talk about domestic violence and we have to develop new, visible approaches to addressing it. Keeping the problem hidden only allows it to continue, and passes the pattern on to future generations.
I think we can all agree that everyone deserves to live in a safe home and community. Which is why I hope you can see why Ohioans born in Haiti need to stay here. To paraphrase Sting, I know Haitian-Ohioans love their children too.
Any parent would do anything they could to keep their children safe. All Haitian-Ohioans are asking is that the government continue their Temporary Protected Status.
I know you said that “temporary is temporary.” That is true. The definition of temporary is “not permanent.” That doesn’t mean “short term.”
Now is not the time to pull the plug on legal status for Haitians. No one believes that country is a safe place to send anyone.
There’s a bill pending in the U.S. Senate that would extend Haitians’ Temporary Protected Status into 2029. It would bring relief and hope to these constituents’ lives. And if you don’t like the fact that it expires in 2029, the Senate has the power and authority to amend it and make their status permanent.
Members of Congress recently returned from Haiti, where they went to view conditions on the ground. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast (R-FL) led the delegation.
He told Fox News Digital about a 6 year-old girl — a U.S. citizen — who was raped while held hostage by gangs for at least six weeks. “It appears as though we were able to secure the release yesterday,” he said, citing an “agreement” on ransom money to be paid by her family.
Mast also described the torture and murder of a heavy machinery operator. The man had been assisting police. Gangs kidnapped his family and then offered a trade — his life for theirs.
“They brutally killed him. I mean it’s all on video. They cut off his ears, fed him his own ears… Then they hacked at him for probably at least five minutes with machetes. His limbs looked like a Christmas tree afterwards, with just bone and skin and other things coming off of him, until ultimately they killed him. That is who these gangs are.”
Many Haitians deported from the U.S. have been raped and murdered. They are seen as ripe targets, because gangs believe they have ransom money.
Already this year, more than 2,000 people have been killed, thousands have been raped, and nearly 1.5 million are internally displaced.
Haitians in Ohio already know all of this. They are connected to their home. They saw it happen while they were there.
“Nearly all of them have seen friends or family members killed,” said Springfield, Ohio Pastor Carl Ruby, one of the faith leaders leading the charge to keep Haitians in their Ohio homes.
It’s not only adults carrying these memories. Ruby frequently recalls how a 12 year-old told him about seeing feral hogs eating bodies when he was much younger, in Haiti.
Our own State Department says, “Do not travel to Haiti for any reason.”
If you decide to go, against their advice, the travel advisory instructs you to prepare a will, establish a proof of life protocol with your loved ones, and choose a family member to serve as a point of contact with kidnappers.
Ransoms run in the tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars; you may be killed; and if you are only injured, hospitals lack basic supplies.
The State Department also tells you to “have a plan to leave in an emergency that does not depend on U.S. government help.”
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine said deporting Haitian-Ohioans would be sending them “back to hell.”
As Catholics, we know that is a profound statement.
Senator, you know what it means to fear for your family’s safety. You know the relief of seeing them protected. Haitian-Ohioans are asking for the same relief — and the power is in your hands.
In his song “Russians,” Sting sang, “We share the same biology, regardless of ideology.”
You applied for your job as a Senator representing all of Ohio, and you applied for your job as a parent. This is a moment where both jobs point to the same decision.
When it comes to the U.S. Senate TPS bill for Haitians, your constituents’ lives depend on it.
Lynn Tramonte is a parent and Executive Director of the Ohio Immigrant Alliance. The organization’s resource website for people who want to protect immigrants, or immigrants who want to learn about their rights, is OhioIsHome.org.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska on course to approve new campaign donation limits in Ballot Measure 1
description: This article is developing and will be updated. Early tallies from Tuesday’s statewide primary election showed overwhelming support for a ballot measure that will restrict the amount of money that political candidates can accept from groups and individuals. With 242 of 403 precincts reporting by 10 p.m. Tuesday night, Ballot Measure 1 had the support […]
text:
Voters line up on Aug. 17, 2026, at the early voting station set up in Anchorage's Midtown Mall. Voters reported waiting about an hour to cast their primary election ballots. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)This article is developing and will be updated.
Early tallies from Tuesday’s statewide primary election showed overwhelming support for a ballot measure that will restrict the amount of money that political candidates can accept from groups and individuals.
With 242 of 403 precincts reporting by 10 p.m. Tuesday night, Ballot Measure 1 had the support of 71.8% of participating voters. 
That’s only slightly less than the 73% margin that a similar ballot measure received in 2006. 
The limits imposed by that 2006 measure remained in place until 2021, when a three-judge panel of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that Alaska’s limits on campaign contributions were so tight that they violated the First Amendment.
Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s administration declined to appeal that decision, and the state’s 2022, 2024 and 2026 elections have taken place without limits on the amount of money that candidates may accept. 
Vote-counting is expected to continue through Aug. 28, the deadline for mailed absentee ballots to reach the Alaska Division of Elections.
The measure will take effect after this year’s elections.

title: Trump administration advances plan to rescind protections for nearly 45 million wild acres
description: The Trump administration will move ahead with plans to end more than 25 years of sweeping protections for tens of millions of wild, federally managed acres across the U.S. Brooke Rollins, head of the U.S. Department of Agriculture, on Tuesday filed a rule to rescind “in its entirety” the national 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, […]
text:
The Still Creek area in the Mt. Hood National Forest is part of 2 million acres of Oregon land protected by the federal Roadless Rule. (Photo courtesy of the U.S. Forest Service)The Trump administration will move ahead with plans to end more than 25 years of sweeping protections for tens of millions of wild, federally managed acres across the U.S.
Brooke Rollins, head of the U.S. Department of Agriculture, on Tuesday filed a rule to rescind “in its entirety” the national 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, which prohibits road construction, logging and mining on about 30% of lands managed by the U.S. Forest Service, mostly in forested areas of the West. Rollins had last year filed a notice of intent that the agency was considering “rolling back” some protections under the rule.
A draft environmental impact statement will be posted Wednesday, and the public will have until 11:59 p.m. Eastern time/8:59 p.m. Pacific time on Sept. 21 to comment before changes are finalized.

Comment on the Roadless Rule termination and environmental impact statement here.

The Roadless Rule prohibitions are intended to protect wildlife, watersheds and old-growth forests from human development and human-caused wildfires. But in her announcement, Rollins said she was rescinding the rules on nearly 45 million acres under the banner of wildfire prevention, saying the protections instead have led to “overgrown stands, insect outbreaks and disease” turning “healthy landscapes into tinderboxes.”
“For too long, outdated restrictions have kept tens of millions of forested acres off-limits to the very treatments that improve forest health and reduce wildfire risk to our communities,” she said.
Rollins’ assertions are not borne out by research, including from Oregon State University Professor Chris Dunn, a forest ecologist and wildfire expert. Dunn and his colleagues found that most wildfires in Western national forests between 1984 and 2018 started near roads, showing an increased likelihood of wildfires where roads exist because the No. 1 cause of wildfires is people.
The U.S. Forest Service’s own research also shows the majority of human-caused ignitions occur on roadsides, and 20 years of monitoring data does not support assertions that repealing road prohibitions will improve forest health, researchers found.
 No public meetings

Rollins first proposed rolling back the rule in August 2025, saying at the time the move would support President Donald Trump’s executive orders meant to increase logging and energy development on federal lands.
That notice of intent set off a 21-day public comment period that brought in more than 600,000 comments, most of which expressed opposition to any changes that would erode the Roadless Rules prohibitions on development. Federal officials have not held a single public meeting since then.
In the two years leading up to final passage of the 2001 rule, Forest Service officials held 600 public meetings across Western states and received more than 1.6 million public comments.

Roughly 96% of the Forest Service’s inventoried roadless areas are located in 12 western states, including 2 million acres in Oregon within places like Iron Mountain in the Willamette National Forest, Joseph Canyon in Wallowa County, Tumalo Mountain in central Oregon and Lookout Mountain in the Ochoco National Forest.
Last year, U.S. Rep. Andrea Salinas, a Democrat representing Oregon’s 6th Congressional District based in the Willamette Valley, introduced the Roadless Area Conservation Act to enshrine the rule in federal law, but it does not yet have enough support to pass. In the House, 88 of her Democratic colleagues have signed on as co-sponsors, including Oregon Reps. Suzanne Bonamici, Janelle Bynum and Maxine Dexter, as have 25 U.S. senators. The state’s two other representatives, Democrat Val Hoyle and Republican Cliff Bentz, have not signed on as sponsors.
No state would be more affected by the rule termination than Alaska, which has almost a third of the 45 million acres affected by the pending change.
Alaska is home to the Tongass National Forest, a West Virginia-sized stretch of islands and waterways in the Southeast Alaska panhandle that make up the largest surviving temperate rainforest in the world.
Idaho and Colorado would not be impacted by the rule changes because the two states negotiated their own agreements with the federal government more than a decade ago to permit projects that would “reduce hazardous fuels” near wildfire prone communities and to allow some local and state decisions about development on the federal acres.
 Different takes on the past 25 years

U.S. Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz, who previously worked for one of the country’s largest lumber producers in Idaho, said in a statement last year that the Roadless Rule has frustrated land managers for years and served as a barrier to commercial logging.
“More than 40% of inventoried roadless areas, primarily in the West, have high or very high wildfire hazard potential. And only 5% of those areas have received hazardous fuels reduction treatments since 2014,” he said.
Rollins’ announcement included praise from the Republican governors of Montana, Utah and Wyoming, who said rescinding the federal protections would give their states flexibility to manage land locally. Democratic governors and other elected officials in states including Oregon, Washington and New Mexico have criticized the administration’s efforts and blame a century of largely unrestricted logging on federal lands, climate change and recent losses to Forest Service staff for worsening fires and declining forest conditions in the West.
Statements following Rollins’ announcement made clear conservation and logging groups have seen the last 25 years of the Roadless Rule quite differently.
Abigail Dillen, president of the nonprofit environmental legal group Earthjustice, said in a statement that the group will likely sue to stop the rule changes from moving forward.
“For 25 years, the Roadless Rule has kept our wildest forests intact. The benefits have been incalculable for people, for water, for wildlife, and for the climate,” she said. “Earthjustice has successfully defended the Roadless Rule for a quarter century, and we are not going to stop now.”
Travis Joseph, president of the American Forest Resource Council, a trade association representing the timber industry, said in a statement that the Roadless Rule is among “failed policies” meant to protect forests.
“The Forest Service is right to take a hard look at a policy that was written for forest conditions that looked very different 25 years ago,” he said. “Our national forests are experiencing severe wildfire, drought, insects and disease on a scale that few anticipated when the Roadless Rule was adopted.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: After historic crash, Yukon River’s iconic king salmon run shows early signs of rebound
authors: Max Graham, Northern Journal-Anchorage Press, Alaska Beacon
description: For the past few years, smokehouses in the Yukon River village of Anvik have sat empty. After salmon populations crashed, dozens of Alaska Native communities along the river faced a stark new reality, one without the fish that fed families and sustained Yup’ik and Athabascan traditions for generations. This summer, though, smoke once again wafted […]
text:
Boats pictured along the bank of the Yukon River in Grayling, Alaska. (Max Graham)

For the past few years, smokehouses in the Yukon River village of Anvik have sat empty.
After salmon populations crashed, dozens of Alaska Native communities along the river faced a stark new reality, one without the fish that fed families and sustained Yup’ik and Athabascan traditions for generations.
This summer, though, smoke once again wafted through Anvik, on the middle Yukon some 350 miles west of Anchorage.
The river’s two main species, chinook and chum, have recorded a surprising uptick in numbers. And in spite of state regulations that bar fishing for chinook, Anvik’s fishermen have caught dozens of the fish this year, plus even more salmon of other species — meaning that there are enough to share with elders, hang in smokehouses and store in freezers.
“It’s the first time I’ve seen the smokehouses smoking in five years,” said Robert Walker, former chief of the Anvik Tribal Council. “I was just amazed. People are so happy.”
The returning fish could represent a remarkable rebound for one of Alaska’s most iconic and culturally important salmon runs, though scientists caution that numbers are still relatively low and that more data are needed before they can be confident about a meaningful turnaround.
Salmon strips hang to dry in Anvik in 2023. (Max Graham)
The harvest in Anvik, announced by Walker on a public teleconference with fishery managers and local leaders in July, also has inflamed a long-running political debate over fishery closures and government policies aimed at rebuilding the runs.
In 2024, Alaska state officials agreed with the Canadian government to a seven-year ban on harvesting chinook along the Yukon, which flows from northwest Canada more than 2,000 miles through Alaska to the Bering Sea.
Even though many Alaska Native leaders generally agreed about the need to limit fishing, they also criticized Alaska’s government for not formally including tribal governments in the decision-making process.
The recent chinook harvest in Anvik came in spite of the official moratorium.
Walker, in a recent phone interview, described the state’s implementation of the ban without input from tribal leaders as a form of “dictatorship.”
Alaska’s fish and game commissioner, Doug Vincent-Lang, said state officials wouldn’t have been able to reach a timely agreement with Canada if they had formally consulted with every tribe along the river.
But he pushed back against the idea that they didn’t get input from local leaders before agreeing to the ban.
“We talked to a lot of people downriver,” Vincent-Lang said in a brief phone interview.
“I think it’s working,” he added, referring to the agreement. He also noted that the ban includes certain exceptions, such as allowing fishing on tributaries when local spawning goals are met.
During the July teleconference, Walker described a scene of joy in Anvik. People in the village are “eating fish like they never ate fish before,” he said.

Some salmon advocates and fisheries biologist say the chinook run isn’t yet strong enough to warrant fishing. The numbers are still well below targets set by fisheries managers.
Roughly 32,000 chinook have been counted so far this season at a sonar station in Eagle, Alaska, near the Canadian border. That’s more than the state had tallied by now in recent years. But it’s still below average, and the final count is expected to be substantially lower than the goal of 71,000 set by Alaska and Canadian fisheries managers two years ago.
“While it is a little bit more encouraging, the runs are still well below average,” said Deena Jallen, a Yukon area fisheries biologist for the Alaska Department of Fish and Game. “We’re still not meeting any goals in Alaska and Canada.”
In a statement posted on social media last week, a leading Alaska Native advocate described the painful decision not to fish during closures that she and many others along the Yukon have made, and she called on fishermen to continue cooperating with government agencies with the shared goal of restoring the salmon runs.
“I understand the importance of passing on our way of life, our traditional knowledge and our culture to our children and grandchildren,” said Serena Alstrom, the longtime executive director of Yukon River Drainage Fisheries Association, a conservation-focused advocacy group with board members from communities along the river.
“Because of that, I have made the difficult decision not to fish when regulations require it. I don’t do it because it is easy or because I always agree with management. I do it because I believe those sacrifices give our salmon the best chance to recover for future generations.”
In a phone interview, Alstrom said she has heard about more instances of illegal fishing this summer than usual — not only in Anvik but on other stretches of river, too.
“It’s upsetting,” she said.
Later, Alstrom released another statement, saying the boost in salmon numbers this year reflects the “diligence of those who have chosen to allow these salmon to continue their journey to the spawning grounds.”
Most families along the river are continuing to make that sacrifice, she said in the interview. They’re doing that not merely for the sake of following rules but because they “understand that we need to have salmon at the spawning grounds,” Alstrom said.
In Anvik, the fishermen used a traditional fishwheel to catch chinook and chum, according to Walker.
They released most of the fish, but kept a few dozen chinook and more than 100 salmon of other species, he said.
The fishermen took only what the village needed, he added. The fish “went in people’s freezers, and people are jarring them, too,” Walker said.

The Alaska State Troopers, which enforces state fisheries closures, have not observed an increase in illegal salmon harvests this season, according to spokesperson Austin McDaniel.
The agency issued five citations for illegal fishing along the lower Yukon during a salmon closure, including one for unlawfully possessing chinook, McDaniel said.
State wildlife troopers “are aware of reports of potential improper fishing practices near Anvik,” he said. “However, we have been unable to substantiate those claims at this time.”
But, McDaniel added, “our patrols indicate that compliance with Yukon River subsistence fishing restrictions remains high and has improved in many areas.”
On another river in Western Alaska, the Kuskokwim, fishing during state-imposed closures more than a decade ago led to prosecutions of Yup’ik fishermen, who unsuccessfully argued that harvesting was an expression of their constitutionally protected religious beliefs.
Chinook numbers in the Yukon initially plummeted more than two decades ago, and harvests have largely been limited since then. The run dropped to a record low of about 50,000 fish in 2022, down from closer to 300,000 decades ago.
This year’s run is now estimated at 103,000 fish, far exceeding pre-season forecasts.
Managers also counted nearly 1 million summer chum, which was more than forecasted and enough for limited fishing opportunities in Western Alaska communities, like Anvik, along the lower and middle river.
In a recent interview with KYUK, the regional public broadcaster, a Yup’ik elder in Russian Mission, 70 miles downstream of Anvik, described a sense of elation around the summer chum harvest.
“When I ate my fish,” said the elder, Alexandra Quak-aq Kozevnikoff, “I could feel that tingling from my stomach come out like [a] little quiver all the way around my body, even to the top of my head, and a big sigh of relief.”

name: WyoFile
title: Gray edges out Friess and Christensen in tight, crowded race for US House
description:
Wyoming’s current secretary of state walks away with a victory after a bruising, high-dollar, self-funded campaign and will likely soon be off to Washington.
The post Gray edges out Friess and Christensen in tight, crowded race for US House appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Republican Chuck Gray, who’s been the secretary of state since 2022, won a tight, crowded race Tuesday that puts him in a strong position to represent Wyoming in Congress. 
The former statehouse representative from Casper narrowly beat Jackson Hole businessman Steve Friess and retired Bureau of Land Management employee Kevin Christensen, who finished respectively as the second- and third-place vote getters. As of 10:50 p.m., with 81% of ballots counted, Gray had 25% of the votes while Friess had 20% followed by Christensen, with 18%. 
Gray has been a firebrand in state politics, frequently butting heads with Wyoming Gov. Mark Gordon. 
During a July candidate forum in Casper, he explained to Wyoming voters why he was investing large sums of personal and family money in his U.S. House campaign. “Like President Trump,” he said, he was making the investment “to take on the insiders and the media.”
“I don’t back down to the media and the insiders,” Gray said.
Gray declined an interview on Tuesday night, but sent WyoFile a statement thanking Wyoming voters. 
“This was a spirited race, but the primary is over,” he said. “Now is the time to come together, because what unites us is far greater than anything that divided us during this campaign.”
Gray’s statement called upon Republicans to work together to help President Trump “continue the work of rebuilding the country.”
FEC filing data shows that Gray gave himself a $1.38 million loan. That was supplemented by a PAC singlehandedly funded by Jan Gray, Chuck Gray’s father, who spent another $519,000 on Gray’s candidacy.
Gray becomes the heavy favorite to take over the seat currently occupied by outgoing U.S. Rep. Harriet Hageman. The sophomore representative  gave up her seat to run for the U.S. Senate after Cynthia Lummis announced she was retiring. On Tuesday, Hageman beat challenger Sam Mead handily, winning nearly two-thirds of the vote. 
An unusually deep field of candidates competed in the Republican primary. Ten candidates vied for the seat, though Frank Chapman, a Moran guest ranch owner and lawyer, dropped out after he and the Fighting for Wyoming PAC spent roughly $3 million on his campaign.
Besides Gray, Friess and Christensen, other candidates included former Superintendent of Public Instruction Jillian Balow, Wyoming Senate President Bo Biteman, actor and singer Richard Dodson, former Army Ranger David Giralt, Casper resident Keith Goodenough and Casper businessman Reid Rasner.
Big investments, often of personal and family fortunes, was a theme. Candidates making huge cash loans to their own campaigns is a change from previous competitive Republican primary races in Wyoming. 
When former U.S. Rep. Liz Cheney won the lone seat a decade ago, she attracted $1.6 million in individual contributions, versus $70,000 in personal loans. In 2022, Hageman easily ousted Cheney. She did so with Trump’s endorsement and a campaign that raised $5.7 million, with over 90% of that sum coming from individual contributions. 
The 2026 race was quite the contrast, with the overwhelming majority of campaign funds coming from the candidates themselves. Two of the three highest vote getters on Tuesday all spent a million-plus dollars on their races. Friess spent $3 million. Rasner also loaned his campaign $1.87 million. 
Christensen’s campaign operated very differently, relying on less than $36,000. He loaned and contributed $18,000 of his own money and solicited another $18,000 in donations, according to FEC data. 
There was never a crystal clear frontrunner. Gray likely had the greatest name recognition, having held a statewide seat for four years. Friess was the biggest spender, as of the last FEC filing deadline. Rasner, who’s been marketing his name for years and gained attention for a failed bid to buy TikTok, frequently made headlines for aggressive and bombastic campaign tactics. On Tuesday, Cowboy State Daily reported that an 11th-hour text to potential voters falsely claimed that Trump had endorsed Rasner. 
Gray, Friess and Rasner all consistently tried to position themselves as Trump acolytes, although the president never endorsed any of them. 
Gray will face Democrat Lisa Kinney, a former state senator who lives in Laramie, in the November general election. In a state where Republicans have long dominated statewide races, she’ll be a long shot to win. Wyoming hasn’t sent a Democrat to Congress since 1976, when Teno Roncalio was reelected. 
This is a breaking news story that may be updated.
The post Gray edges out Friess and Christensen in tight, crowded race for US House appeared first on WyoFile .

name: Colorado Newsline
title: ​Officials at ICE facility miss Colorado public health order deadline in tuberculosis case
description: The private company that runs Colorado’s only immigration detention center missed a compliance deadline set by the state’s health department to provide information about a recent tuberculosis case in the Aurora facility. The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment issued a public health order on the issue Thursday and gave The GEO Group until […[...]
text:
The sign outside the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment on Oct. 5, 2020. (Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)The private company that runs Colorado’s only immigration detention center missed a compliance deadline set by the state’s health department to provide information about a recent tuberculosis case in the Aurora facility.
The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment issued a public health order on the issue Thursday and gave The GEO Group until Monday to respond. GEO did not.
“The GEO Group has not complied with the public health order or provided the required information. While statements that there are no active or suspected cases may be reassuring, they are not a substitute for compliance,” CDPHE spokesperson Hope Shuler wrote in an email to Newsline. “Its continued refusal to cooperate significantly limits the investigation, but we remain determined to obtain the information needed to protect public health. We are actively coordinating with Adams County, the Colorado Attorney General’s Office, and Denver Health TB Clinic on next steps, including legal remedies.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
State law has long required that public health officials investigate confirmed active tuberculosis cases. GEO, which operates the detention center for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, first shared the laboratory-confirmed case with state and county officials June 22. The company then “ceased all communication” with the Denver Health Tuberculosis Clinic, according to the state’s public health order.
Colorado issues public health order over tuberculosis case at Aurora ICE facility

GEO did not comply with an Adams County Health Department order from mid-July. Public health officials need specific information about the infected person, their contacts and their medical treatment to complete an investigation. In various statements, ICE has said the sick person was quarantined, treated and removed from the country. The agency claims there are no active cases in the Aurora facility. GEO has referred requests for comment to ICE.
“Public officials must be able to verify the facts, identify people who may have been exposed, and ensure they receive appropriate follow-up care. GEO has a responsibility not only to the people in its facility, but also to its employees and surrounding community,” Shuler wrote.

title: Some rural Alaska polling stations opened late on election day, a sign of continuing problems
description: At least two polling stations in rural Alaska opened late for the Tuesday statewide primary election, the Alaska Division of Elections confirmed late Tuesday, and observers independently reported other sites also opened late. The problem was most acute in the southwestern village of Nunapitchuk, where bad weather grounded flights and kept elections workers f[...]
text:
Voters walk across the map of Alaska on the floor of the Alaska State Library, Archives and Museum on Tuesday, Aug. 20, 2024. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)At least two polling stations in rural Alaska opened late for the Tuesday statewide primary election, the Alaska Division of Elections confirmed late Tuesday, and observers independently reported other sites also opened late.
The problem was most acute in the southwestern village of Nunapitchuk, where bad weather grounded flights and kept elections workers from opening a polling place until 5 p.m. That gave local voters only three hours to vote before the scheduled 8 p.m. close.
Nunapitchuk has 343 registered voters, mostly independents. 
In the North Slope village of Point Lay, polls opened at 8 a.m., one hour later than scheduled.
Michelle Sparck is director of Get Out The Native Vote and has been working for months to help recruit local poll workers. 
Late Tuesday, she said polls in the North Slope village of Wainwright didn’t open until 4 p.m. due to staffing issues, and Anaktuvuk Pass in the central Brooks Range had similar problems, with the city mayor temporarily stepping in. 
The Division of Elections did not respond to a question seeking to verify Sparck’s report.
Tuesday’s issues followed a warning from the Alaska Federation of Natives and other groups.
The groups issued a public letter saying they were “deeply concerned by reports of significant vacancies among election workers in rural Alaska precincts, as well as reports that some election workers have waited for months to receive per diem following required election training.”
The letter called for the Division of Elections to take additional steps to ensure that rural polling locations were open on time before the primary. 
Earlier this year, the Alaska Legislature passed a bipartisan, bicameral election reform bill that would have mandated some actions to improve rural voting access. 
Gov. Mike Dunleavy vetoed that bill, and the Legislature failed to override the veto after two Republicans from Southeast Alaska reversed themselves and voted to sustain the veto after voting to pass the bill. 
Even with late openings in places across the state, the Division of Elections appeared to perform better in rural Alaska than it did in the 2024 and 2022 primaries. 
Two years ago, polling stations failed to open at all in Wales and Kaktovik for the primary election, and polling places in several other locations failed to open on time. 
In 2022, polling places in the southwest villages of Tununak and Atmautluak failed to open for the primary election, and a lack of poll workers meant two other communities could only vote by absentee ballot.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming Freedom Caucus faces loss of at least 10 incumbent lawmakers
authors: Maggie Mullen and Maya Shimizu Harris
description:
Meanwhile, the hard-line caucus failed to pick up new seats in some districts, early results show.
The post Wyoming Freedom Caucus faces loss of at least 10 incumbent lawmakers appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming Freedom Caucus members hoped to tip the Legislature’s balance of power in Tuesday’s primary elections. Early results show that balance could shift significantly, but not in the direction they hoped. 
According to the Associated Press and county-level preliminary results, Reps. Tony Locke, Ocean Andrew, Ken Pendergraft, Marlene Brady, Jayme Lien, Nina Webber, Mark Jennings, Gary Brown and Darin McCann and Sen. Bob Ide, all of whom are members of or aligned with the Wyoming Freedom Caucus, lost their seats in the state Legislature on Tuesday.
Meanwhile, the caucus failed to pick up new seats in some districts, preliminary results show. 
Republican Brian Costello defeated Freedom Caucus-aligned candidates Ross Schriftman and Donna Rice in House District 37. Incumbent Rep. Elissa Campbell defended her seat against Freedom Caucus candidate Pete Fox in House District 56. Another incumbent, Rep. Julie Jarvis, also kept her seat in House District 57 after facing former representative and Freedom Caucus member Jeanette Ward for a second time. 
Several other key races appear poised to end in losses for Freedom Caucus incumbents. With 65% of votes counted, results from the Associated Press show House Speaker and Freedom Caucus member Chip Neiman losing by almost 10 points in his bid to unseat Senate President Ogden Driskill in Senate District 1. 
Some Freedom Caucus incumbents have successfully defended their seats, such as Rep. Tomi Strock, R-Douglas and Rep. Bill Allemand, R-Midwest. 
After most of the Wyoming Freedom Caucus’ top legislative goals failed this year, Rep. Rachel Williams, who heads the hard-line conservative group, told reporters they needed “reinforcements in Cheyenne.” The caucus aimed to win a supermajority in the House, which it won control of in 2024, and a majority in the Senate. (Williams lost her secretary of state bid on Tuesday night to a more moderate candidate.)
To keep a simple majority in the House, the caucus and its allies need to win at least 32 legislative races. They need to win at least 42 races to gain a supermajority.
Seventeen of the Senate’s 31 districts were on the ballot this year. To gain a majority in the upper chamber, the Wyoming Freedom Caucus needed to win at least 14 of those races to bolster the two senators it endorsed in 2024 — Sens. Tim French of Cody and Laura Pearson of Kemmerer. Neither was up for reelection this year.
WyoFile reporter Maggie Mullen contributed to this story.

name: WyoFile
title: Short, Harshman and Meier take state executive seats in GOP primary
description:
The Campbell County rancher and state senator defeated candidates endorsed by Trump and the Wyoming Republican Party. 
The post Short, Harshman and Meier take state executive seats in GOP primary appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Robert Short, Steve Harshman and Curt Meier are the apparent GOP primary winners for secretary of state, superintendent of public instruction and state treasurer, respectively, according to preliminary results from Tuesday’s primary election.
State Auditor Kristi Racines, a Republican, is running for reelection unopposed, and Eric Barlow is the apparent GOP primary winner for governor.
In November’s general election, Short will face Democratic challenger Bryan McCarty, and Harshman goes up against Democrat Ana Cordova — who edged out Sergio A. Maldonado, Sr.
All three of the contested state primary challenges indicate Wyoming voters bucked against Freedom Caucus-aligned candidates, particularly in the secretary of state race where caucus chair Rachel Williams vied to succeed Freedom Caucus-aligned Chuck Gray who made his bid for U.S. House.
Secretary of state
“The people of Wyoming absolutely care about who works for them in the secretary’s office,” Short told WyoFile Tuesday night, “and the importance of having rational, balanced and thoughtful consideration for all decisions associated with the secretary’s office is paramount to the people of Wyoming. 
“If I’m the chosen person for that position,” Short added, “the people can expect a voice of reason, a very willing listener and a tireless advocate for all things Wyoming.”
From left, Republican candidates for Wyoming Secretary of State Qwenton Eagle Oviatt, Robert Short and CJ Young chat Wednesday, July 15, 2026, during a candidate forum at the Albany County Public Library in Laramie. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
After the governor’s office, secretary of state is perhaps the most high-profile elected state office, overseeing elections, registering businesses and recording and maintaining many state records. In a pinch, Wyoming’s secretary of state is also the first in line for gubernatorial succession.
Whether it’s Republican Short or Democrat McCarty who prevails in the general election, they will take the helm of a state office where outgoing Gray — with cooperation from Freedom Caucus members in the House — enacted several controversial election reforms during his four-year-term.
Gray, while still a Wyoming legislator, paved the way for a more restrictive voter identification law. As secretary, he successfully rallied the Legislature to limit the time voters are allowed to “cross-over” to another party during an election cycle — an effort to limit the success of moderate Republicans. Gray also clashed with county clerks over whether to restrict the use of “drop boxes” in elections.
Cody Republican Rep. Rachel Williams was seen as the most politically aligned successor to Gray’s election reform agenda running for the secretary’s post.
During a secretary of state forum, much of the GOP primary field — Short, Qwenton Oviatt and CJ Young — expressed confidence in the security of Wyoming elections and that county clerks are doing a good job of overseeing elections without major reforms. 
Short, a Converse County commissioner, raised $429,521 for his campaign and outspent his competitors by about $360,000 ahead of Tuesday’s primary election, campaign finance reports showed.
Superintendent of public instruction 
Harshman was among three Republicans in the primary running to replace current Superintendent Megan Degenfelder, who chose to run for governor rather than seek reelection. Degenfelder lost her bid for governor to Barlow.
The state’s education chief oversees considerable record-keeping, enforces provisions of the Wyoming Education Code, maintains a list of accredited schools and gathers reports and statistics. But the position is also one of political power, particularly when it comes to education funding and social issues.
Chad Auer, Steve Harshman and Tom Kelly take questions on Thursday, July 16, 2026, during a forum for candidates for the Wyoming Superintendent of Public Instruction at the Albany County Public Library in Laramie. (Molly Walters for WyoFile)
The Legislature passed a recalibration bill in March that represents a new funding model for school districts; Wyoming’s universal school choice program is being challenged in court and the state just overhauled literacy standards and instruction — a change fought for by Degenfelder.
Though the three Republican candidates mostly aligned on conservative ideals, they diverged in their philosophies for helming the Department of Education, particularly on whether to pursue a “top-down” approach to practical things like literacy instruction, as well as hot-button education issues like public funding for homeschooling.
The Legislature this spring passed a law spearheaded by Degenfelder that establishes new guidelines for literacy instruction based on “the science of reading.”
Harshman, a high school coach, has served as House District 37 representative since 2003, including two terms as Speaker of the House, and along the way earned a reputation as politically moderate while carrying institutional knowledge of the inner workings of the Legislature.
State treasurer
Two-term Treasurer Curt Meier easily topped Lingle Rep. Scott Smith, who is listed as a member of the Wyoming Freedom Caucus and who earned the state GOP’s endorsement. 
Marilyn Kite, former chief justice of the Wyoming Supreme Court, interviews Wyoming Treasurer Curt Meier during a July 15, 2026 candidate forum. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
Meier, regarded as a moderate in today’s Wyoming GOP, served for 23 years in the Wyoming Senate before running for treasurer back in 2018. He’s generally won accolades among supporters for overseeing a more aggressive approach — backed by the Legislature — in investments, playing a key role in making those returns Wyoming’s top source of revenue.
“What I think the voters that voted for me understood is that, you know, I’m kind of a big tent guy,” Meier told WyoFile Tuesday evening. “We’re doing this for all of Wyoming, we’re just not doing it for people that think the way that we think.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The science that protects our children doesn’t take a summer vacation
description: Connecticut's own biopharmaceutical community has played an important role in advancing vaccine science.
text:
For families, the end of summer can often seem like a never-ending to do list: enjoying the last pool and beach days, shopping for school supplies, and signing up for fall sports and after school activities. But for those in Connecticut’s life sciences community, back to school is also a reminder that protecting the next generation never pauses, and neither should our commitment to the science that keeps them safe.
As Connecticut families finish their summer breaks, allow me to offer an important reminder: vaccines are safe, effective, and backed by decades of rigorous scientific evidence.
Yet recent measles outbreaks across the country demonstrate how quickly vaccine-preventable diseases can return when vaccination rates decline. Many communities are still working to recover from the disruptions to routine healthcare during the COVID-19 pandemic, leaving some children behind on recommended vaccination schedules.
The consequences of falling behind are serious. Measles is not a minor childhood illness. It can cause pneumonia, brain swelling, permanent hearing loss, and in rare cases, death. With back-to-school season only a few days away, the window to act is now.
The good news is that the tools to protect our children are well-established and thoroughly tested. Vaccines undergo one of the most rigorous approval processes of any medical product. Before reaching patients, they are evaluated through years of research, clinical trials, and independent scientific review. Even after approval, they continue to be monitored through multiple safety systems designed to identify even the rarest potential concerns.
Connecticut’s own biopharmaceutical community has played an important role in advancing that science. Across our state, researchers, healthcare providers, manufacturers, and innovators work every day to develop treatments and technologies that improve and save lives. Their work is grounded in rigorous science, transparency, and an unwavering commitment to patient safety.
And yet, doubt persists, often fueled by misinformation that has been repeatedly disproven. Questions about vaccines are understandable, and science welcomes scrutiny. In fact, scientific progress depends on it. But after decades of research and millions of administered doses, the evidence remains clear that vaccines are one of the most successful public health interventions in history.
No issue better illustrates the importance of separating fact from fiction than the long-debunked claim linking vaccines to autism. The original study that sparked those concerns was retracted for serious ethical and scientific violations, and numerous large-scale studies conducted around the world have found no link between vaccines and autism. Yet the myth persists, highlighting how difficult it can be to rebuild trust once misinformation takes hold.
For parents navigating an increasingly complex information environment, there is a clear place to start. If you have questions about vaccines, ask your child’s pediatrician rather than social media. Use the start of the school year as an opportunity to schedule a wellness visit, review your child’s immunization record, and discuss any concerns with a trusted healthcare professional.
Connecticut’s life sciences community stands ready to help. They are your neighbors, your fellow parents, and your partners in building a healthier future. Connecticut families may be wrapping up their summer vacations, but the science that protects our children never takes a break.
Tony Sheridan is President of the Chamber of Commerce of Eastern Connecticut.

name: WyoFile
title: Republican Hageman will face Democrat Byrd after landslide victories in Wyoming’s US Senate primary
authors: Angus M. Thuermer Jr. and Maya Shimizu Harris
description:
Currently Wyoming’s lone representative in the US House, Hageman won by a landslide in Tuesday’s primary election for US Senate. 
The post Republican Hageman will face Democrat Byrd after landslide victories in Wyoming’s US Senate primary appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Republican Harriet Hageman, currently Wyoming’s lone U.S. House representative, will face Democrat James Byrd in the November general election after each won their party’s nomination in Tuesday’s primary, according to preliminary results.
The Associated Press called the Republican primary for Hageman at 8:52 p.m. with 26% of the votes counted and with Sam Mead as runner-up.  
In the Democratic tilt, the AP called the race for James Byrd with 27% of votes counted.
Hageman said in a statement that she is “grateful to the people of our great state for entrusting me with the responsibility of promoting and defending our ideals in Congress at this moment in history,” describing it as a “struggle for the existence of the United States of America as we know them, with patriots on one side and a rising tide of Marxists on the other.” 
She emphasized keeping taxes low, ensuring that “property rights mean something,” producing domestic energy “by responsibly accessing our natural resources” and enforcing immigration laws.  
“In short, we are a nation of laws and accountability, and we must make sure we continue to act like one,” Hageman concluded. “And we must aggressively defend freedom and capitalism, or we will descend into the dreary, soul-sapping, certain failure of communism.” 
Hageman thanked President Donald Trump for his endorsement, as well as Wyoming’s current U.S. Sens. John Barrasso and Cynthia Lummis. 
Voters elected Hageman to Congress in 2022 and again in 2024. Endorsed by Trump, she ran a $2 million MAGA campaign eight times larger than Mead’s.
Mead, the nephew and great-grandson of two former Wyoming governors, campaigned under the banner of protecting public lands. That struck a contrast with his opponent who signed onto a Utah lawsuit that claimed the U.S. government’s ownership of land in Wyoming amounted to a justification for war.
“I knew this was going to be a pretty big challenge,” Mead said Tuesday evening. “I wanted to make huge improvements to the state and country. 
To not have an opportunity to do that is disappointing.”
Mead said he is still seeking ways to help the state and will offer his services when needed. Meantime, he said, he will “get some tractor time in.”
In a July survey of likely GOP voters, taxes and government spending were listed by 14% of respondents as their top issue. Illegal immigration was the next most important subject, listed by 13%, jobs and the economy by 11% and public lands by 11%.
Hageman and Mead faced three other Republican opponents. 
Jimmy Skovgard, married, and the father of four, began his career as a data analyst and retired from his oil field business cleaning drilling sites and spills. 
Jill Edwards, a Laramie resident, is a self-described “Wyoming mom who works multiple jobs … busy putting food on my children’s tables.” 
John Allan Holtz, is a Laramie resident and former Douglas circuit court judge with a military, law and technical engineering background.
In the Democratic primary, Byrd, a former state representative who served from 2009-2019, also rode the public lands bandwagon, criticizing Hageman, now his opponent in the November election, for what he characterized as an anti-conservation position.
Billy Benavidez, a greenskeeper from Sheridan and the father of two, had to contend with the fact he is on probation. He was put on a year’s unsupervised probation on Aug. 20, 2025, for a breach-of-peace conviction, court records show.
This is a breaking news story and may be updated.

name: WyoFile
title: Eric Barlow wins GOP nomination for Wyoming governor
description:
The Campbell County rancher and state senator defeated candidates endorsed by Trump and the Wyoming Republican Party. 
The post Eric Barlow wins GOP nomination for Wyoming governor appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Sen. Eric Barlow, a Gillette rancher and former speaker of the House, won the GOP nomination for Wyoming governor Tuesday, making him the overwhelming favorite to become the state’s next chief executive officer. 
The Associated Press called the race at 8:54 p.m. with 21% of the votes counted.
Barlow triumphed over a Trump-backed opponent in a state where the president remains deeply popular. He also succeeded despite the Wyoming GOP endorsing another candidate and steady criticism from the right wing of the party that he was too moderate.
His election puts Wyoming on track to welcome another traditional Republican governor with ranching roots. Current Gov. Mark Gordon and former Gov. Matt Mead also won office despite skepticism from their party’s flank. 
Barlow will still face two challengers in November, but given Republican domination of Wyoming politics, they face long odds.
Barlow sought the nomination against three other Republican candidates including Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder, who President Donald Trump endorsed, and Brent Bien, who was backed by the Wyoming Republican Party. The fourth candidate, Curt Blake of Centennial, ran a more informal, “word-of-mouth” campaign. 
Born in Gillette and raised on the family ranch southwest of town, Barlow served as a U.S. Marine and worked as a large-animal veterinarian and a rancher before getting elected to House District 3 in 2013. Voters elected him to Senate District 23 in 2022. 
As a lawmaker, Barlow led the House as speaker in 2021 and 2022 and now chairs the Senate Labor, Health and Social Services Committee as well as the Mental Health and Vulnerable Adult Task Force.  
“I am a leader who stands firmly on sound, conservative principles and who will fiercely defend your rights, including the Second Amendment and the sanctity of life,” Barlow said in his announcement. “I will protect your private property rights, safeguard our public lands, and keep Washington, D.C. out of Wyoming’s business.”
Barlow kicked off his gubernatorial bid more than a year ago, and focused his campaign on protecting public lands, funding education and solving Wyoming’s healthcare access and affordability issues. 
Gordon did not run for re-election and was technically prevented from seeking a third term, though he could have challenged that, as the Wyoming Supreme Court has ruled that term limits on the other top elected positions in the state are unconstitutional. 
The last two times the governor’s seat was open in Wyoming, the Republican nominee handily won the general election after succeeding in the primary election. 
In late July, Barlow released internal polling that showed him with a comfortable lead. At that time, the polling indicated support for Barlow at 42%, followed by Degenfelder at 19%, Brent Bien at 14%, with 22% of respondents undecided.
A few weeks after Barlow released the poll, Trump hosted a telerally with Degenfelder. About 20,600 people joined the call, according to Degenfelder’s campaign, which is about twice as many as attended Trump’s 2022 in-person rally in Casper when he backed Hageman against Liz Cheney. 
When it came to fundraising, Barlow also pulled ahead of his opponents, raising $1.67 million since he announced his bid in August 2025. That beat out Degenfelder, who announced in January of this year, by about $380,000. Barlow’s fundraising also eclipsed the previous statewide record for individual fundraising. 
In November’s election, Barlow will face two opponents: Democrat Kenneth Casner of Casper and Constitution Party candidate Rebecca Bextel of Jackson. 
Bextel, the Teton County conservative activist at the center of the Checkgate controversy that dominated the 2026 legislative session, announced in May that she would run for the state’s post as an “insurance policy against Eric Barlow.” 
The most support a third party candidate for governor in Wyoming has received was in 1894, when Populist Party candidate, Lewis C. Tidwell, won 11.28% of the vote. 
The general election is Nov. 3.
