name: Mississippi Today
title: At first redistricting hearing, Mississippians call push for new maps a ‘power grab’
description: Teresa Roberts speaks to lawmakers at a redistricting public hearing in Tupelo on Aug. 18. 2026.
text:
TUPELO – Mississippi residents who spoke on Tuesday at the first of several public hearings on redistricting around the state urged lawmakers to not redraw electoral maps, calling the effort a needless power grab aimed at diluting Black political power in a state with a sordid racial history.  
The Republican-dominated joint House and Senate committee on redistricting kicked off its slate of public hearings in a nearly packed room at Itawamba Community College in Tupelo. Leaders of the committee say the hearings will allow lawmakers to solicit feedback before making recommendations on new voting maps to the full Legislature in a likely special session this fall. 
The push to redraw maps comes after the U.S. Supreme Court issued a decision in the Louisiana Callais case in May. The ruling gutted part of the Voting Rights Act and, by removing protections for minority districts, cleared the way for Republican-controlled state legislatures to redraw political lines in their favor. 
A crowd of residents attended a legislative redistricting public hearing in Tupelo on Aug. 18, 2026. Credit: Michael Goldberg / Mississippi Today
President Donald Trump, who is working to protect a slim GOP majority in Congress in this November’s midterm elections, has pressured states his party controls to redraw maps, and many have already complied.

In Mississippi, the joint House and Senate committee is expected to do the bulk of the work of redrawing Mississippi’s legislative, judicial and congressional voting lines. But with Mississippi having had its federal midterm primaries months ago, it appears unlikely congressional maps would be redrawn for November’s federal election.
Only 10 of the 20 members on the state joint committee were in attendance on Tuesday. 
The room was dominated by Mississippi residents who oppose redistricting. Many of those who spoke said the Callais decision doesn’t require Mississippi to redraw its maps, and that doing so would create confusion for voters and impose a financial cost on localities. They also said hard-won progress to increase Black representation in Mississippi since the Jim Crow era would be eradicated. 
The Reverend Jeffrey Gladney, pastor of a Church in Shannon, said redrawn maps would “eliminate Black districts” and attack “Black voices that represent the Black community.”
“If maps are redrawn, they will split neighborhoods, divide communities, take away resources from already weakened communities,” Gladney said. 
Resident Jim Newman speaks at redistricting public hearing in Tupelo. on Aug. 18, 2026.  Credit: Michael Goldberg / Mississippi Today
Jim Newman, chairman of the Lee County Democratic Party, said the Legislature should redistrict after the next U.S. Census in 2030 rather than rushing to redraw maps at President Trump’s urging as states such as Texas have done. 
“Y’all are looking for a power grab, plain and simple,” Newman said. “It didn’t have to happen. But the president asked for it, and by God, everybody bends over to take care of the president. And it’s not any different here in Mississippi.”  
Teresa Roberts said redistricting would impact the social and economic well-being of “marginalized people.” 
“These are people who need us, who need you, and you are going to take away what little strength they already have,” Roberts said. “Shame on you.”
Katie Gilbert said she came straight from work to attend Tuesday’s hearing. She was raised in Tupelo and went to Tupelo High School. She said redistricting would contribute to the “brain drain” flight of young people out of Mississippi.
“We wonder a lot of times why we have a brain drain in Mississippi, why a lot of educated young folks leave this state. It’s because of decisions like this that are leaving us in the past,” Gilbert said. “Mississippi has a very dark history, but we do not need to continue on with a dark future. Equitable maps lead to a stronger Mississippi.”
Walter Jones said his family lived down the street in Chicago from the family of Emmett Till, a Black youth whose murder in Mississippi helped spark the Civil Rights Movement. He said moved to Mississippi because of the progress the state had made in overcoming its history of racial discrimination, but he now wonders whether he made the wrong move.
“I came down here because things have changed. Mississippi was becoming a great place to stay. People was people. Everybody like everybody,” Jones said. “If this is what y’all want to do to Mississippi after all the hurt and struggles y’all went through to get to where we’re at today, I made a bad decision.”  
Only one person in attendance, Mike Walker, appeared to speak in favor of redistricting.
“All I’ve heard up here today is bashing these elected representatives for what they’re trying to do,” Walker said. “So let me ask you, what color is your soul? It’s a soul thing people. It ain’t Black or white. It’s a soul thing.” 
Many civil rights leaders, Black lawmakers and voting rights advocates believe the hearings are a pretext for the Legislature moving to dismantle majority-Black districts and weakening Black political power in the state.
Democratic Rep. Rickey Thompson of Shannon, who is not on the joint committee but attended the hearing, said he doubted his Republican colleagues would take community feedback into account.
“They already have their plans together,” Thompson told Mississippi Today. “They’re just going through the motions.”
Republican leaders believe that when the U.S. Supreme Court issued its ruling in the Callais decision, it ended an improper practice of allowing for the consideration of race in drawing political maps.  
Since the Callais decision, some GOP leaders in Mississippi and Washington, D.C., have called for heavy partisan gerrymandering, including redrawing of incumbent U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson’s district to help oust him, the state’s only Black member of Congress and only Democrat.
Cliff Johnson, a University of Mississippi law school professor who is the Democratic nominee challenging Republican U.S. Rep. Trent Kelly in this year’s midterms, attended the hearing and mingled with attendees. He said the hearing showed Mississippians didn’t want a redistricting process that inflamed racial and partisan divides.
“I thought it was very powerful to see people stand in front of a bunch of legislators and ask to have a say. My sense as a lifelong Mississippian is that our diversity is such a strength,” Johnson said. “The notion of having representatives chosen by a cross-section of our population is something that makes us stronger.” 
The committee is encouraging the public to participate in future hearings. The public can offer comments at any of the seven remaining public hearings, or submit written comments to Ted Booth, the committee’s attorney, at ted.booth@peer.ms.gov.
Below is the schedule of the future planned redistricting hearings. Each will start at 6 p.m. 

Aug. 27 at Northwest Mississippi Community College in Southaven 
Sept. 1 at Delta State University in Cleveland 
Sept. 8 at Alcorn State University in Natchez 
Sept.10 at Meridian Community College in Meridian 
Sept. 17 at the University of Southern Mississippi in Hattiesburg 
Sept. 22 at Mississippi Gulf Coast Community College in Gulfport 
Oct. 1 at the state Capitol in Jackson

name: Daily Montanan
title: Public Service Commission says NorthWestern’s energy plan ‘deficient’
description: NorthWestern Energy’s plan for energy resources for the next 20 years came up short on Tuesday at the Montana Public Service Commission. In a 3-1 vote, the PSC returned the plan to the utility with a revision request to address deficiencies identified by Public Service Commission analysts. Every three years, NorthWestern Energy must do an […]
text:
A power line is pictured crossing Beck Hill Road in Powell County, Montana on Thursday, June 11, 2026 (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)NorthWestern Energy’s plan for energy resources for the next 20 years came up short on Tuesday at the Montana Public Service Commission.
In a 3-1 vote, the PSC returned the plan to the utility with a revision request to address deficiencies identified by Public Service Commission analysts.
Every three years, NorthWestern Energy must do an assessment of how much power it will require to meet customer needs in the future and the resources it will use to meet those needs in a cost-effective way.
The PSC doesn’t have the authority to reject the plans, but it has the authority to review whether they meet minimum requirements and send them back if they don’t.
Based on a consultant’s report, public comments, and its own analysis, PSC staff found the plan had five shortcomings, meaning it doesn’t meet minimum requirements in Montana. Staff recommended the commission request improvements.
“Returning the plan isn’t necessarily a wholesale rejection of the plan,” said PSC Vice President Jennifer Fielder, who made the motion to request more work on the document. “It’s basically a quality control step.”
Commissioner Annie Bukacek, who raised concerns about the cost of the Integrated Resource Plan and its impact on customer bills, cast the only “no” vote.
(Only four commissioners voted because Commissioner Brad Molnar has been suspended, although he is fighting the suspension in court.)
In the report, the consultant, GDS Associates, found the draft 2026 plan was “a substantial step forward” from the utility’s 2023 plan and reflected NorthWestern’s “growing analytical capabilities.”
But GDS also said the plan fell short in a number of ways, including in its treatment of data centers.
The report said the plan identifies data centers as “potentially significant” drivers of energy needs, but NorthWestern isn’t transparent about how it is including data centers in its forecasts.
“As these customers become a larger component of future load growth, the methodologies used to evaluate and incorporate them into long-term forecasts will become increasingly important to resource planning outcomes and future customer costs,” GDS said in its report.
Commissioner Randy Pinocci said his constituents have expressed concerns that NorthWestern has power available for customers but is going to reserve it for data centers — and then charge customers if it needs more supply.
“Are they going to build something and charge a ratepayer?” Pinocci said.
The PSC staff report found NorthWestern evaluated short-term energy needs based on the requirements of a compliance program to which it belongs, but it didn’t take a comprehensive look at long-term needs — required by state regulation.
When NorthWestern runs forecasts, the consultants said it uses models in a way that could bias outcomes in favor of resources that are more expensive, such as a power plant.
The staff report said the PSC had raised a similar concern in NorthWestern’s 2023 resource plan, and it asked for more information again this time.
“GDS … notes the 2026 IRP (Integrated Resource Plan) does not resolve the transparency and documentation concerns the Commission identified with the 2023 IRP,” the staff report said. “Staff agrees with GDS’s assessment.”
Bukacek said the cost of the consultant’s report, up to $260,000, along with the cost of producing the resource plan itself would be passed onto ratepayers. She said Claude AI put the cost in the millions, although a PSC staff analyst said he wouldn’t be able to assess the accuracy of that estimate.
Fielder agreed the resource plan wasn’t a cheap undertaking. However, she said the plan drives expenses “that are exponentially greater” over the long run for Montanans, and it had to be done right.
In other words, an imprecise plan could result in costly, unneeded energy resources for which customers would have to pay — or in not enough power for customers.
“Having incomplete analysis at this point in an IRP actually increases the chance that there could be overbuilding, which would result in higher rates, or under-preparing, which results in those reliability risks,” Fielder said.
The PSC directed NorthWestern to correct its plan within 30 days or request an extension if needed.
A spokesperson for NorthWestern Energy earlier said the utility would review any recommendations from the Public Service Commission and in the GDS report, and it welcomes perspectives that “help strengthen energy planning efforts.”
“The 2026 IRP reflects extensive analysis, data and stakeholder engagement to evaluate how best to serve our Montana customers’ energy needs while maintaining reliable and affordable service,” said NorthWestern Energy’s Jo Dee Black in an email.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Donalds, Jolly emerge from primaries
description: Florida voters will pick either U.S. Byron Donalds or former Rep. David Jolly as the state’s next governor after both men won their primaries Tuesday. Donalds took 48% of the vote in a crowded primary that included nine other Republicans.  Jolly easily defeated five opponents in the Democratic primary, earning 61% of the vote. The […]
text:
David Jolly, left, and Byron Donalds, right, are the nominees for their respective parties. (Photos via each candidate's social media accounts)Florida voters will pick either U.S. Byron Donalds or former Rep. David Jolly as the state’s next governor after both men won their primaries Tuesday.
Donalds took 48% of the vote in a crowded primary that included nine other Republicans.  Jolly easily defeated five opponents in the Democratic primary, earning 61% of the vote.
The result was somewhat predictable, but the primary ended the early part of a campaign season that has been punctuated by some unusual side stories.
Both of the night’s primary winners jumped into the governor’s race last year but the contest took some unpredictable turns ahead of Tuesday’s primary.
Donalds posted about his victory on X shortly after 8 p.m. eastern time, after the polls closed in the western panhandle.

I am grateful to my family, my team, my volunteers, and every Floridian who powered us to this victory.
Now is the time for the Republican Party to unite. By working together, we can make Florida more affordable and defend the Florida Dream for our families, seniors, and young… pic.twitter.com/HZBtyaCS9G
— Byron Donalds (@ByronDonalds) August 19, 2026

And in a victory speech from Orlando, Donalds later said Jolly represents “everything that folks hate about Washington, D.C. Liberal David Jolly is the change that Florida cannot afford,” Donalds said.
Some of the other Republicans included former House Speaker Paul Renner, Lt. Gov. Jay Collins, and investor James Fishback. None of them could get enough traction to mount a serious challenge to Donalds, who won the president’s endorsement, but never Gov. Ron DeSantis’.
DeSantis, who for a while touted First Lady Casey DeSantis as a potential gubernatorial nominee before the Hope Florida Foundation scandal, never endorsed any of the Republicans in the primary.
Byron Donalds, Jay Collins, James Fishback, Paul Renner. (Photos via U.S. House, Florida House, Office of the Governor, and Fishback campaign)
Collins finished in second place with more than 25% of the vote. DeSantis named him lieutenant governor in August 2025 but he did not become a Republican gubernatorial hopeful until earlier this year. Collins sold himself as someone who would continue DeSantis’ legacy but the governor never endorsed his second-in-command. 
DeSantis also had a close working relationship Renner during his two years as House speaker but DeSantis initially called Renner’s run for governor “ill-advised.” DeSantis acknowledged earlier this month that Renner would make a “good” governor, but still there was no endorsement. Renner finished with 8.5% of the vote.
Fishback, who won slightly more than 10% of the vote, repeatedly insulted Donalds and called him a “slave” to donors. 
Collins, meanwhile, filed suit seeking to get Fishback knocked off  the ballot for not meeting eligibility requirements for governor. A state circuit judge tossed the lawsuit and let Fishback remain in the race.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Alleged liberal
There was less drama in the Democratic primary.
Jolly is a former Republican member of Congress who left the GOP after Trump was elected. 
He switched to the Democratic Party last year and appeared on the path to his own competitive primary against Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings. 
But Demings dropped out of the race after being diagnosed with cancer.
While Donalds has been attacking Jolly as a liberal, Jolly has had to defend some of his more conservative positions to Democrats.
For instance, Jolly does not want to eliminate Florida’s  universal school voucher program. “I’m a Democrat who’s not going to stand up and tell you we’re going to do away with choice,” Jolly told members of Capital Tiger Bay Club. “Choice is here. Choice is here to stay. However, Florida families are being left behind by the current choice program.”
Jolly said last year that he uses the state vouchers to help offset costs for both of his children, who attend faith-based private school.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Wasserman Schultz, Moskowitz advance in their congressional primary races
description: South Florida Democrats Debbie Wasserman Schultz and Jared Moskowitz won contested primary elections for Congress on Tuesday night, and there was a major upset in Florida’s 7th Congressional District. Several primary congressional elections Tuesday had national appeal. Coming into Tuesday night, the most vulnerable Republican incumbent was Cory Mills, runnin[...]
text:
Florida Republican U.S. Rep. Cory Mills (via U.S. House)South Florida Democrats Debbie Wasserman Schultz and Jared Moskowitz won contested primary elections for Congress on Tuesday night, and there was a major upset in Florida’s 7th Congressional District.
 District 7
Several primary congressional elections Tuesday had national appeal.
Coming into Tuesday night, the most vulnerable Republican incumbent was Cory Mills, running in District 7, which encompasses Seminole and Volusia counties.
He was defeated soundly by former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah.
Mills lost substantial support from Republicans amid a House Ethics Committee investigation into allegations of dating violence and campaign finance law violations. Mills has denied the accusations, but last week Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis became the latest Republican to say he was not supporting his re-election. Donald Trump also declined to endorse him.
GOP U.S. Reps. Anna Paulina Luna and Mike Haridopolos backed Elijah.
In the Democratic primary, former NASA administrator Bale Dalton defeated Navy veteran Marialana Kinter, and he will now face Elijah in November.
Before tonight’s results, pollster Nate Silver had predicted Dalton could defeat Mills. Whether a Democrat can win in CD 7 against a less controversial candidate in a district that is Trump +12 is uncertain.
 District 9
No congressional district has been more radically redrawn by the Republican-led Legislature and DeSantis than the seat Democratic Rep. Darren Soto has held for several election cycles.
CD 9 previously contained all of Osceola and parts of Polk and Orange counties, and Soto won it by more than 13 points in 2024. In addition to those counties, the new map adds parts of Indian River, Okeechobee, Highlands, and Glades counties, and is a seat Trump would have won by 18 points if in existence two years ago. That change led seven Republicans to get in the race, with the winner looking strong against the Democratic incumbent in November.
Dan Green, a veteran and former Trump administration official, narrowly defeated Ben Butler, a dairy and cattle farmer in Highlands County, by a single point, 25.39% to 24.38%.
Thomas Chalifoux, a businessman and former Osceola County school board member, finished in third place and Jorge Martinez was fourth.
 District 14
Coming a close second in the district most obviously redrawn to help a Republican win in November is Congressional District 14 in Hillsborough County, represented by Democrat Kathy Castor for 20 years. The new map removes most of downtown Tampa and all of St. Petersburg, historically Democratic strongholds.
In the GOP primary, former state Rep. Mike Beltran has defeated former Pasco County state Rep. Kevin Steele in a bitter affair, 46%-30%.
Steele had represented Pasco in the Legislature since 2022, but when the Phoenix asked him earlier this month if he intended to move into the district if elected (members of Congress are not required to live in the district they represent, but state lawmakers are), he told the Phoenix he had not only moved to Hillsborough County but had voted there the day before. He resigned from his legislative seat a day later.
Both political parties appear ready for an intense contest in the fall.
“Congratulations to Mike Beltran, who will be a MAGA Warrior and fight alongside President Trump,” the Republican National Committee said in a statement. “Kathy Castor is Florida last, and her far-left record of hiking taxes, defunding law enforcement, and shutting down FEMA ahead of hurricane season is a recipe for yet another loss for Democrats this November.”
“Mike Beltran is too extreme even for his own party,” said DCCC Chair Suzan DelBene.
“In Tallahassee, he attacked reproductive freedom and voting rights, and opposed investments that would lower health care and housing costs while Floridians struggled to get by. Now, he wants to take that same agenda to Congress and rubber-stamp policies that are raising the cost of gas, groceries, health care, and housing. Kathy Castor has spent her career delivering for the Tampa region and taking on powerful special interests to lower costs for Floridians. Tampa voters will resoundingly return her to office.”
The district is now Trump +10 points, but Castor and Democrats believe she has a chance to thwart the GOP’s goal of capturing the seat.
 District 19
Perhaps the wildest Republican congressional primary is for the Florida CD 19 seat being vacated by U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds.
There were 10 GOP candidates on the ballot, five of whom have previously run for Congress in other states.
Jim Schwartzel, who owns and operates a conservative radio station, overcame a Trump endorsement for Catalina Lauf to win the CD 19 seat. Schwartz got 29% of the vote to 22% for Lauf, who served in the Commerce Department during Donald Trump’s first term as president, was in second place.
Other Republicans in the race included former New Yorker Chris Collins, who pleaded guilty to a felony and later was pardoned by Trump. There was also Madison Cawthorne, who served one controversial term in Congress from North Carolina. There was also Jim Oberweis, a former Illinois state lawmaker who defeated Lauf in the 2020 Republican primary there and then lost in the general election.
There’s also Ola Hawatmeh, who lost a Republican primary in New York in 2020.
District 20
In one of the most observed congressional primaries this year, longtime Florida Democratic Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz won in a Broward County-based seat held by a Black representative since the early 1990s.
She defeated former Broward County Mayor Dale Holness, 45%-23%.
Young progressive Elijah Manley came in third at 14%.
Former CD 20 Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick was fourth, and Luther Campbell, a/k/a “Uncle Luke,” a former rapper with the Miami hip-hop group 2 Live Crew and now a football coach and community activist, came in fifth.
Cherfilus-McCormick had held the seat since winning a special election to succeed the late Alcee Hastings in early 2022. However, she resigned in April shortly before she was scheduled to go before the House Ethics Committee on allegations of stealing federal disaster money.
Wasserman Schulz had to make a choice after the Florida Republicans drew her out of her Congressional District 21 seat in May. Her decision to run in the historically Black-held district drew widespread criticism both in and outside of Florida.
 District 24
The redistricting map made this seat encompassing northern Miami-Dade and parts of southern Broward County even more Democratic-leaning. Six Democrats entered the race after longtime incumbent Frederica Wilson announced she would not run for re-election.
Oliver Gilbert III, chairman of the Miami-Dade County Commission, endorsed by Rep. Wilson, defeated state Sen. Shevrin Jones, 34%-32%.
The other candidates in the race included Kendrick Meek Jr., grandson of former Florida U.S. Rep. Carrie Meek and son of Kendrick Meek, who served in both chambers of the Florida Legislature before serving as a U.S. representative. Also running were Rudolph Moise, Marshall Davis Sr., and Roderick Vereen in the race.
 District 25
This is another one of the four congressional districts Florida Republicans hope they can flip red in November, and the Democratic primary between two-term U.S. Rep. Jared Moskowitz and his Democratic Socialists of America-backed opponent, Oliver Larkin, has received national attention.
Moskowitz crushed Larkin, 64%-36%
“Tonight, Democratic voters sent a clear message. I faced a challenge from the DSA. They threw everything at me and I didn’t change who I am or what I believe, and the voters overwhelmingly chose the independent-minded approach I’ve brought to Congress,” Moskowitz said in a press release.
“I led the effort to have Kristi Noem fired, I’ve taken on this Administration, and I’ve taken on extremes in the DSA and won. Now we’re running in a tough district hand-drawn by Republicans to defeat me, but I plan to win that too.”
Moskowitz will now face Republican Scott Singer in the general. Singer is the former mayor of Boca Raton.
Legislative battle
In perhaps the most interesting state legislative race in Florida, Democratic House Minority Leader Fentrice Driskell held off fellow Democratic Rep. Michele Rayner in state Senate District 16 in the Tampa Bay area, 60%-40%.
The seat has been held by Democrat Darryl Rouson for a decade.
That race became incredibly divisive, as the Phoenix previously reported.
Since there was no Republican in the race, Driskell will go immediately to Tallahassee and serve in the Senate this fall.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Candidates and supporters take to the streets of Anchorage to win attention and votes
description: Under low, gray clouds that spit occasional rain sprinkles, candidates running for office in Alaska stood on street corners in Anchorage on Tuesday waving signs, rallying supporters and trying to win the attention and votes of passing motorists. Tuesday’s primary election activities continued what is a longstanding tradition in Alaska politics, with the majo[...]
text:
Kendra Arciniega and Alissa Nelson, in an axolotl costume, hold signs on the morning of Aug. 18, 2026, urging support for independent gubernatorial candidate Meda DeWitt. They were among DeWitt supporters gathered on primary election day at the intersection of Northern Lights Boulevard and Minnesota Drive in West Anchorage. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon) Under low, gray clouds that spit occasional rain sprinkles, candidates running for office in Alaska stood on street corners in Anchorage on Tuesday waving signs, rallying supporters and trying to win the attention and votes of passing motorists. Tuesday’s primary election activities continued what is a longstanding tradition in Alaska politics, with the major statewide candidates gathering in the largest city to make their final pushes for votes.

U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III, a Republican running for re-election, gives a thumbs-ups to a passing motorists on Aug. 18, 2026. Next to him is Julie Sullivan, the wife of U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, another Republican running for re-election. Supporters of both incumbents were holding signs at the intersection of Northern Lights Boulevard and the Seward Highway in Midtown Anchorage. Tom Begich, a Democrat and Nick Begich’s uncle, is running for governor and was rallying that morning at the same intersection, but on the other side of the street. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

Both Begiches — gubernatorial candidate Tom Begich and incumbent U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III — spent part of the morning at the busy intersection of the Seward Highway and Northern Lights Boulevard. Tom, the Begich running for governor, is a Democrat and former state senator who represented an Anchorage district that is one of the most left-leaning in the state; Nick, his nephew, is a Republican and ally of President Donald Trump.
They and their sign-waving supporters stood on opposite sides of the street.
It’s an unusual situation, said the younger Begich, who was in a group that also included Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and his wife, Julie Sullivan.
“To my knowledge, there has never been an election in which two members of the same family have run for statewide office in the same cycle for different parties,” Nick Begich said.
Still, he believes the voters know the difference between him and his uncle, he said.
 

A pickup truck parked on Aug. 18, 2026, at the intersection of Northern Lights Boulevard and the Seward Highway expresses support for both U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and capitalism. The intersection, in Midtown Anchorage, is a favored spot for candidate sign-waving. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	“You know, Tom’s running his own campaign, and he’s got his own perspective. We have different issues that we think we touch on and at the end of the day, I’m focused on federal issues. And the governor’s race is very crowded right now,” the younger Begich said.
“I think most Alaskans know who’s who,” he added.
Less than two miles to the west along Northern Lights Boulevard, gubernatorial candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins was at the Minnesota Drive intersection, waving to morning commuters.
Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democrat and former state House member from Sitka who refers to himself as JKT, was in friendly territory. West Anchorage is a reliably Democratic part of Alaska’s biggest city.
Campaigning statewide was a fun experience, Kreiss-Tomkins said.
 

Gubernatorial candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins holds a campaign sign on the morning of Aug. 18, 2026, Alaska’s primary election day. Kreiss-Tomkins and his supporters spent part of the morning at the intersection of Northern Lights Boulevard and Minnesota Drive in West Anchorage. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	“The campaign has felt like a love letter to Alaska,” he said. He mentioned some places and events he visited: the Hmong Harvest Festival in Anchorage, the Fourth of July and Mount Marathon festivities in Seward and a 450-mile trip along the Yukon River. “We’ve seen all sides of this incredible state. So it’s been awesome,” he said.
Asked if there might be a reshuffling among candidates who wind up in the top four positions, with possible withdrawals to consolidate support in the general election, Kreiss-Tomkins suggested that might happen.
“It’s so hard to say. I think it just depends on the results. People are going to talk and might try to forge coalitions. I’ve personally spoken to some other candidates, and channels of communication are open,” he said.
Former Gov. Bill Walker, an independent who is now seeking to return to the office he held from 2014 to 2018, refrained from predicting that he would be among the top candidates advancing to the general election.
“We’ll respect the process and we’ll work with whoever moves on,” he said.
 

Former Gov. Bill Walker, an independent seeking to return to the position he held from 2014 to 2018, stands on Aug. 18, 2026, outside the church where he cast his primary election vote. Walker is among 17 candidates for governor. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Even if he is not among the top vote-getters, it was important for him to run to call attention to serious issues, he said after casting his ballot at a church in West Anchorage’s Turnagain neighborhood. Those issues are primarily the state’s unsustainable fiscal practice of living off its depleted savings, he said, along with the looming Cook Inlet natural gas shortfall that will affect the state’s most populous region.
Walker took a big political hit for reducing the Alaska Permanent Fund dividend in 2016. But that was a time when the state had a $4 billion shortfall and when oil prices were $26 a barrel, he said.
He and his administration took on “the hard stuff,” he said. “We kind of ran into the fire instead of running from it,” he said. Without using names, he said other candidates are making unrealistic promises about good times to come. However, “it’s not what you do in the good times. It’s what you do in the tough times,” he said.
There was some light-heartedness on the streets, as well.
Supporters of independent gubernatorial candidate Meda DeWitt wore costumes as they stood on the Seward-Minnesota corner opposite Kreiss-Tomkins and his supporters. DeWitt supporters were dressed as a blue and white shark, a white polar bear and a pink axolotl, which is a type of salamander.
 

State House candidate Lisa Keller, a Democrat running in House District 13, and supporters hold campaign signs in the early morning of Aug. 18, 2026, Alaska’s primary election day. Keller and her supporters were at the intersection of Dimond Boulevard and the Old Seward Highway, in the southern part of her Midtown Anchorage district. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Also hitting the Anchorage streets was Lisa Keller, a state House candidate with what appears to be only token opposition. A Democrat, she is running in House District 13, a slice of Midtown Anchorage that has been represented by retiring Rep. Andy Josephson, also a Democrat. Keller worked as aide to Josephson, and her only opponent is another Democrat, Felix Rivera, who has done little campaigning.
Waving campaign signs at the intersection of Dimond Boulevard and the Old Seward Highway as morning commuters drove by, Keller admitted that her race isn’t getting the same attention as the big statewide races.
“I think I know how the assembly candidates felt back in April because they were being overshadowed,” she said, referring to Anchorage’s municipal election that took place as the statewide races were heating up.
Her race also may lack the drama and excitement that is enveloping the statewide races, she said.
“It doesn’t feel like a very competitive race, but you can never take anything for granted. Just like in sports,” said Keller, who is a champion triathlete and a coach.
 

Colby McMichael, Ze (“It’s just Ze”), Curt Burgoyne and Jo Maillet wait in line to vote on Aug. 17, 2026, at the Midtown Mall in Anchorage. They got out their guitars when they saw how long the line was, and they played as they waited. The four, all from Anchorage, cast their votes early because they were to be working on a friend’s film on Aug. 18, primary election day. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	But a group of young Anchorage voters who cast their ballots on Monday at the Midtown Mall early voting site suggested that state legislative elections may be more important to them than the bigger races.
“I’m here voting because I think it’s important to participate in our local elections, and because I think that small-town elections, small stuff matters more than the big stuff, the big scale,” said Colby McMichael.
With him was Ze — “It’s just Ze,” she said of her name — who also attested to the importance of local elections. “Local change is the most important and most effective change,” she said.
McMichael, Ze, Jo Maillet and Curt Burgoyne were voting early because they were due to be on a friend’s film set on Tuesday. They were among more than 25,000 Alaskans who cast their ballots at the state’s 10 early voting stations.
As they waited in a line that was about an hour long, they took turns playing two guitars. The instruments were fetched from a car once they knew they would have to wait a long time to vote, they said. “We walked in the door, saw the line, and then walked right back out,” Maillet said.

title: The Florida Cabinet races are set for November
description: The races are now set for the three Cabinet positions on the ballot in this November’s elections, and the incumbent Republicans will be favorite in all three. Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson defeated Matt Taylor (a/k/a “Matt the Welder”) for the Republican nomination, 69%-31%, and he will be the prohibitive favorite against Democrat Joey Mendoza Atki[...]
text:
Attorney General James Uthmeier announces a new emergency rule regarding 7-OH and similar compounds. (Photo courtesy of the Attorney General's Office)The races are now set for the three Cabinet positions on the ballot in this November’s elections, and the incumbent Republicans will be favorite in all three.
 Agriculture Commissioner
Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson defeated Matt Taylor (a/k/a “Matt the Welder”) for the Republican nomination, 69%-31%, and he will be the prohibitive favorite against Democrat Joey Mendoza Atkins.
Atkins is a Miami trial attorney and former sports agent. Outside of an $8,400 loan to his campaign, he raised $1,685.
Meanwhile, Simpson is sitting on more than $30 million in combined fundraising through his four political committees.
 CFO
In the race for Florida chief financial officer, Republican incumbent Blaise Ingoglia crushed Frank William Collige, a U.S. Air Force veteran and licensed public adjuster from Baker County. The final tally was 61%-39%.
He will face former Miami-Dade County state Sen. Annette Taddeo, who defeated Earle Ford in the Democratic primary, 66%-34%.

“Tonight, Florida voters made their voices heard, and I am honored by their confidence and support. This victory belongs to every voter, volunteer, grassroots supporter, and family member who stood with us throughout this campaign. Now the real work begins. All gas, no brakes,” Ingoglia said.
“I congratulate Annette Taddeo on advancing to the general election. I look forward to a spirited, substantive contest on what the future looks like,” he added.


A native New Yorker, Ingoglia served in the Florida Legislature for more than a decade before being appointed by DeSantis to replace Jimmy Patronis as CFO last year.
“¡Ya basta! Enough is enough,” Taddeo said in a statement. “For too long, politically connected insiders have profited while Florida families paid the price. As Chief Financial Officer, I will be an independent watchdog for taxpayers — fighting for affordability, holding insurance companies accountable, and rooting out corruption wherever it exists.”

 Attorney General
There was no primary in the race for attorney general, because there were no challengers to either Republican incumbent James Uthmeier or his Democratic opponent, José Javier Rodríguez.
“JJR,” as he was known in Tallahassee, is a former Miami-Dade County state senator who narrowly lost a bitter primary re-election bid in 2020. He was later appointed to serve in the Biden administration as assistant secretary for employment and training at the U.S. Department of Labor.
Uthmeier has never faced an election. The former chief-of-staff to Ron DeSantis, he was the governor’s pick to replace Ashley Moody as attorney general in February 2025. He’s been adept at getting press coverage since he began serving, in some cases far outside of the purview of what any other Florida attorney general has ever done before.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Voters in Alaska’s deep red Mat-Su and Eagle River communities weigh in at the polls
description: In Southcentral Alaska, voters in some of Alaska’s most conservative regions, including the Matanuska-Susitna Borough and Eagle River, cast their votes in Tuesday’s primary election. Many voters said one of their biggest challenges was deciding which of the 17 candidates for governor they would like to vote for. Voters also said they found the crowded […]
text:
A polling site at the Mat Su Fire Station 5-1 in Palmer stages a sign reminding residents to vote in the primary election on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)In Southcentral Alaska, voters in some of Alaska’s most conservative regions, including the Matanuska-Susitna Borough and Eagle River, cast their votes in Tuesday’s primary election.
Many voters said one of their biggest challenges was deciding which of the 17 candidates for governor they would like to vote for. Voters also said they found the crowded congressional races daunting — there are 15 candidates for Alaska’s sole U.S. House seat and 16 candidates vying for the U.S. Senate seat.
At 8:30 a.m. in Eagle River, a northern suburb of Anchorage near Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, voters began to arrive in a steady stream to vote before work at the Eagle River Town Center polling station.     
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

Ken Slaughter of Eagle River said he was voting for Shelley Hughes and Blake Gettys for governor and lieutenant governor based on their pro-life stance, a priority for him voting down the ballot as a Republican. 
“I’m also a Christian. I’m very conservative in every category — socially, theologically, politically. I don’t like abortion, which to me is murdering babies,” he said. “So I do what I can as a citizen, and that’s vote.”
Farther north in the Matansuka-Susitna Borough, one of the state’s most Republican regions, many voters declined to say on who they picked for governor. 
A polling site at the Matanuska-Susitna Borough offices is seen on primary Election Day on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
In downtown Palmer, at the Matanuska–Susitna Borough offices, the polling station had been set up for the last two weeks since early voting began on August 3. On Tuesday morning, a steady stream of voters stopped by to cast their ballots. 
Charm Mastriano of Palmer declined to say who her top pick for governor is, but said she’s hoping for a new direction. “I’m not a Dunleavy fan, and I’m not happy with many of the things he’s done and his vetoes and things like this. So I am looking for a change and hoping for something better,” she said. 
Mastriano also declined to say who she voted for in the high-stakes congressional elections, but said she also wanted to see a new direction in the U.S. Congress. 
“I think they need to get their act together. I’m not at all happy with our Congress. Generally, in the United States, I’m not pleased with the way they behave and they piddle around and don’t do anything, so I think they need to get it together and get things done,” she said.
A few miles west across the valley, Will Lacy stopped to chat after voting mid-morning at Mat-Su Fire Station 51, where polls were set up beside a row of parked fire engines and ambulances.     

Poll workers pose for a photo at the polling site at the Mat Su Fire Station 51 in Palmer on primary Election Day on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Lacy said he voted for Shelley Hughes for governor, as he was familiar with her serving in the Alaska State Senate representing the region. 
“I just like her voting record and the things she stands for while she was serving as senator, and she’s always been consistent, and so that’s what I like most about her,” he said. 
He said for the U.S. Senate race he wants to see someone new but declined to say which challenger he voted for.
“I’m going for fresh blood this time around,” he said. “I’m giving somebody else a chance. There’s just some things that I didn’t like about the last two terms, and so I’m just looking for something fresh.”
Poll workers said it was fortunate there had been no fires the engines had to respond to that morning. 
Roughly five miles down the Palmer-Wasilla Highway at the Wasilla City Hall, voters stopped by during lunchtime. 
After casting her ballot, Evelyn Goughnour of Wasilla said she hoped to see more Alaska voters turn out at the polls. 
A polling sire at the Wasilla City Hall is seen on primary Election Day on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
“I’m feeling pretty positive, if we get enough voters,” she said. “But one thing that we are really lacking is people that really vote, and they don’t realize if they don’t vote, there’s nothing that can be done. And if they don’t vote, they can’t say anything about it, is my opinion, because they didn’t do anything to change things.”
Goughnour said she’s concerned about the rising cost of living in Alaska — for herself and for her children and grandchildren — and wants to see the next elected leaders address it. 
“The prices are being hiked on everything for all of us normal people — the groceries, the gas, how we can barely get by,” she said. “And it’s getting harder and harder to feed the families because the prices are so high. I’m a senior on Social Security, and it’s harder and harder to feed myself.”
Goughnour said she wants to see term limits of no more than eight years for all elected officials, and voted to limit campaign finance contributions, a “yes” on Ballot Measure 1. She declined to say who she voted for as a top pick for governor, but voted for a candidate with “a good moral background.”
“Honestly, I didn’t go for any of the top runners because I don’t think any of them are good. They’re all politicians,” she said. “I think we need somebody in there that is more down to earth and more in tune with the people, and so not the politicians.” 
Zach Scholl of Wasilla said he cast his primary ballot with some relief knowing the primary election would be over Tuesday and end the campaigning, candidate ads and what he called a “bombardment” of campaign flyers in his mailbox. 
“I would love to hear more of what people are going for instead of what they hate about the other person. The slander campaign, like, man, that gets old. I want to see, you know, what do you stand for? What are you doing that’s going to be good?” he said. “So that’s one thing that’s a little disappointing in politics in general.”
Scholl also declined to say who he voted for in the governor’s race, but added he has not heard much from Democratic candidates. 
“I don’t know anybody on the Democratic side,” he said. “I’ve heard a ton of Republicans just everywhere, and it might be me not paying attention enough, but I’ve heard a lot of the Republicans, so it’ll be interesting to see how that shakes out because that splits votes.”
Scholl said he would like to see fisheries, oil and gas, and energy supply issues addressed by new elected leadership. 
“We’re talking about these brownouts and blackouts with gas, that’s a big deal,” he said. “And I think a solution for stuff like that is something that’s you know where if those start happening, people are going to feel and see those effects in real time, and I think those are real issues that I would like to see addressed and talked about.”
Voters cast their ballots at a polling site in the school library of Tanaina Elementary School in Wasilla on primary Election Day on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Nixon advances to face Moody in U.S. Senate race with decisive win over Vindman
description: Angie Nixon will run against incumbent Republican Ashley Moody for the U.S. Senate, Florida Democrats decided Tuesday by double-digit margin. Nixon’s victory concluded a primary that had some wondering whether progressive Democrats’ wins around the nation would carry into Florida. Nixon, carrying endorsements of several of Florida’s progressive Democratic le[...]
text:
Rep. Angie Nixon talks to reporters after the House Rules and Ethics Committee reprimanded her on May 14, 2026. (Via Liv Caputo/Florida Phoenix)Angie Nixon will run against incumbent Republican Ashley Moody for the U.S. Senate, Florida Democrats decided Tuesday by double-digit margin.
Nixon’s victory concluded a primary that had some wondering whether progressive Democrats’ wins around the nation would carry into Florida.
Nixon, carrying endorsements of several of Florida’s progressive Democratic legislators, enjoyed a significantly smaller campaign account compared to challenger Alex Vindman.
With 88% of votes in, the Associated Press reported Nixon had captured 55.7% of votes to Vindman’s 44.3%. Nixon’s share of the votes equates to more than 660,000 while Vindman’s is about 530,000.
According to FEC reports through July 29, Nixon had spent nearly $710,000 and received nearly $975,000, with ending cash on hand of $264,978.
Vindman received $16.27 million and spent $9 million, leaving him with $7.26 million cash on hand as of July 29. 
The race, considered a special election, was for the seat vacated by now-Secretary of State Marco Rubio. He was elected to a six-year term in 2022 but, given the vacancy, the seat was up for grabs this cycle. Moody is in her position as Gov. Ron DeSantis’ appointee. This would be her first Senate election. She previously won two elections for Florida attorney general.
Moody won the GOP primary Tuesday with nearly 80% of votes, as of the same time the the AP posted the above Democratic results.
Who is she?
Nixon was born and raised in Jacksonville and bills herself as a union organizer and mother. 
She’s been a member of the Florida House since 2020. During the most recent legislative session, she was Democratic ranking member on the Education Administration Subcommittee and was a member of the State Affairs Committee, Information Technology Budget & Policy Subcommittee, and Industries & Professional Activities Subcommittee.
Her speeches at the Florida Capitol frequently referenced the middle class, with her closing arguments on Election Day advocating Medicare for all and that the decision is “OURS” not “billionaire donors or the establishment politics of DC.”
Her margin of victory seems to reflect that sentiment, beating a candidate by about 10% who out-raised her by about $15 million.
Nixon was endorsed by Democratic U.S. Reps. Maxwell Frost, Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib, and Ayanna Pressley.
She has support from a bundle of legislative Democrats including Sens. Rosalind Osgood, Tracie Davis, Lavon Bracy Davis, Kristen Arrington, and Reps. Yvonne Hinson, RaShon Young, Michele Rayner, Dianne Hart, Felicia Robinson, Ashley Gantt, and Anna Eskamani. 
During her six years in Tallahassee, Nixon hasn’t been able to get much passed in the GOP-controlled House — although she’s not the only one, given the GOP’s supermajorities in both legislative chambers.
Nixon made headlines earlier this year after she staged a sit-in in the governor’s office. She wanted him to reject the GOP-led congressional redistricting efforts. She’s become known for her activism, sometimes on the House floor, including protests against the Legislature’s approvals of Gov. Ron DeSantis’ congressional redistricting maps in 2022 and earlier this year.
Vindman did not commit to debating Nixon in the primary.
Middle East politics
One area the two differed on was Israel and Palestine. 
Vindman is a stalwart supporter of Israel, but critical of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and supportive of a two-state solution between Israelis and Palestinians.
Nixon has been outspoken in support Palestinian rights, sponsoring a Florida House resolution calling for a ceasefire just a month after the 2023 attack on Israel by Hamas.
Nixon was formally reprimanded by her colleagues after she blared a bullhorn on the House floor during a contentious fight over congressional redistricting. 
“I don’t care if I get a reprimand. I don’t even care if they expel me, because I’m standing up for my elders,” Nixon said. “Stop doing illegal things and I won’t call you out with a pink microphone.”
Vindman is a retired U.S. Army lieutenant colonel who was awarded a Purple Heart. He retired from the military in 2020, ending a 21-year career.
Vindman moved to Florida in 2023. He announced his candidacy in January. His twin brother represents Virginia’s 7th congressional district, elected two years ago. 
Vindman was a witness in the 2019 impeachment of President Donald Trump. He had listened to a phone call between Trump and Ukrainian PresidentVolodymyr Zelenskyy in which Trump asked Zelensky to investigate Hunter Biden.

name: Nevada Current
title: Hope for Prisoners founder Ponder arrested for sexual assault and more
description: Jon Ponder, a three-time bank robber who was pardoned by President Donald Trump, was arrested Tuesday by Las Vegas Metropolitan Police on 20 charges, including sexual assault. Other charges against Ponder include multiple counts of unauthorized contact with prisoners, attempted coercion that is sexually related, and open and gross lewdness.  The Current was[...]
text:
A screenshot from the RNC’s livestream of the August 2020 Republican National Convention, which was held virtually, and during which Donald Trump pardoned Jon Ponder. (Photo Courtesy of the Committee on Arrangements for the 2020 Republican National Committee via Getty Images)Jon Ponder, a three-time bank robber who was pardoned by President Donald Trump, was arrested Tuesday by Las Vegas Metropolitan Police on 20 charges, including sexual assault.
Other charges against Ponder include multiple counts of unauthorized contact with prisoners, attempted coercion that is sexually related, and open and gross lewdness. 
The Current was first to report in April that Ponder had been banned from Nevada prisons, where Hope for Prisoners, a non-profit organization, provides reentry services.  
Ponder has long been the subject of allegations of sexual misconduct. 
A motion to compel the production of documents in a 2024 lawsuit against Ponder and the nonprofit sought a “letter written by Kristina Wildeveld to the Board in September 2020 informing the Board of allegations of sexual misconduct with clients, mentors, and/or employees of the Company by Jon Ponder, CEO of the Company.”
The letter from Wildeveld was sent in 2020 to Clark County Sheriff Kevin McMahill, who was undersheriff to then-sheriff now Gov. Joe Lombardo, and to Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson at their government email addresses.   
Lombardo has long refused to say whether he, as sheriff, investigated the allegations against Ponder. 
Ponder was briefly suspended in 2020, however, the board, aware that Trump intended to expand Hope for Prisoners nationwide if re-elected, backed down after the pardon, according to Wildeveld’s letter, which the Current recently obtained. 
In June, Ponder’s wife, Jamie, filed for divorce in Clark County Family Court. On Monday, she requested a voluntary dismissal of the proceedings. She did not respond to the Current’s requests for comment.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa ethanol backers share concerns with Rob Sand
description: NEVADA — Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand did more listening than talking Tuesday during a meeting with members of Iowa’s ethanol industry at Lincolnway Energy in Nevada. Sand participated in a briefing and toured the biorefinery, which came online in 20o6, as part of his 100 Town Hall Tour. There are currently 42 operational biorefineries in […]
text:
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand, from left, with Scott Wheeler, Lincolnway Energy; Jeff Taylor, Lincolnway Energy; Chris Cleveland, Lincolnway Energy and Bill Couser, Story County farmer, tours the Lincolnway Energy ethanol plant in Nevada, Iowa, on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Joanna Schroeder for Iowa Capital Dispatch)NEVADA — Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand did more listening than talking Tuesday during a meeting with members of Iowa’s ethanol industry at Lincolnway Energy in Nevada.
Sand participated in a briefing and toured the biorefinery, which came online in 20o6, as part of his 100 Town Hall Tour.
There are currently 42 operational biorefineries in Iowa producing more than 5 billion gallons per year. The state produces approximately 28-30% of all fuel ethanol in the U.S., according to Story County farmer Bill Couser.
“There’s volatility, but we’ve created demand for the product here,” said Couser, who asked Sand to support year-round E15. He showcased Brazil; its current ethanol fuel blend is E32, or 32% ethanol.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“They’re just walking away with this game,” Couser said, “and how do we stay competitive?”
One solution? Diversification of Iowa’s ag industry, said Scott Henry, a fourth-generation Nevada farmer. With the complexities of agriculture in the industry today, diversification has been one way to continue to grow the industry, he said, and finding domestic end users for their product.
“There’s very few parts of our state where you can, from five miles from our headquarters, you can have a rail facility co-op, you can have a corn ethanol plant, and you have cellulosic and a corn ethanol plant next door,” Henry said.
A challenge, he said, is that it’s not getting any easier and requires significant capital investment.
“And it’s not getting any easier to try and deploy capital into furthering our operation, whether we’re fighting with groups that don’t understand livestock production, with groups that don’t understand what we’re doing on the farm to clean up Iowa’s waters and to keep them clean and to manage our nitrogen load,” Henry said.
He said farmers have a target painted on their backs at times and there is a disconnect between what people think they are doing and what they are actually doing.
“The last thing I want to do is take anhydrous ammonia and put it on every acre in the fall without a nitrogen stabilizer. It’s not only like environmentally wrong, it’s economically stupid,” Henry said. “So, we’re out here utilizing four different sources of nitrogen, applying it at different times, the bulk of it going on either right ahead of the plant or in this crop season. And nobody out here seems to understand that story.”
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand, second from left, talks to ethanol industry representatives outside the Lincolnway Energy ethanol plant on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Joanna Schroeder for Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Sand said this is why it’s important for people to talk to each other. “I think if we listen to each other more, we end up actually understanding our own thinking better and getting to the place where we can actually put together solutions that most people agree with.”
Tim Couser, who farms with his father, said it was important to him that he “pitch” Sand on the importance of ethanol to young farmers.
“That (ethanol) is our market. That’s our demand structure. If you’re a farmer in the corner of the state of Iowa, you’re outside of the metropolitan area, you know, most of what you have is agriculture. And people leave those small towns because there’s no market,” Tim Couser said. “And the cardinal sin with the consumer with ethanol is they think that the corn goes to an ethanol plant and the buck stops there. And they forget about the feed and the oil that comes off the back to feed the livestock. And then the investment in it, too.”
Tim Couser was the youngest investor in Linconway Energy at 18 while still in high school. He said he is also very concerned about Iowa’s water quality.
“I do truly believe that in the future, technology will play a part in solving this water quality issue,” he said. “So, one thing you’ve got to be careful about is looking at it today and saying this is the problem, and the only way we can solve it is with today’s current solutions.”
“You started this by saying you want to pitch me on ethanol,” Sand responded. “I’d reframe that in your mind, for where it comes to me personally, because when I hear people talking negative about agriculture in Iowa or about ethanol, one of the first things I remind them of is: well, you (ethanol) support Iowa public schools.”
“You want to have well-funded public schools?” posited Sand. “Okay, well, right now, today in the state of Iowa, we’re going to want agriculture and ethanol to be doing well because we want to have roads and bridges that work. We want to have public schools that are paying teachers well and getting our kids educated. We want to have good public safety. And we can have conversations around, like you’re talking about, the ways we can find to make it work better.”
Sand has said he supports Iowa agriculture and ethanol, but believes carbon pipelines used to support the ethanol industry should not be allowed to use eminent domain.
Tim Couser concluded the briefing with an anecdote about U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley and his wife Barbara. He sat with them in the pork tent at the Iowa State Fair while they were eating a pork sandwich.
“How cool is that in Iowa?” Tim Couser said. “And I would hope that if you become governor, that you walk down the main street of the state fair and anybody can stick their hand out. Oh, that is special to Iowa.”
Listening to people is Sand’s passion, he said. “I’ll tell you, I do it the way I do it because I remember growing up in Decorah seeing in the newspaper that Chuck Grassley’s coming to town. He’ll be here on this time and this day. And I just remember thinking as a kid, yeah, that’s democracy. That’s how it’s supposed to work. You’re supposed to be able to meet the people that represent you. And that level of accessibility is really important to me.”
