name: Rhode Island Current
title: As municipalities across Rhode Island resist Flock cameras, McKee orders review
description: A colleague’s empty seat separated Deborah Janick from the three other members of the Tiverton Town Council present at its July 27 meeting. So too did her perspective on Flock Safety.  Janick was the only no as the council voted 3-1 — with three members absent — to approve the installation of additional Flock automated […]
text:
The Tiverton Town Council voted last month to add more Flock automated license plate readers in town. But Gov. Dan McKee has called for a pause on new cameras for 60 days pending a statewide review. A Flock camera is shown on Main Road in Tiverton on Monday, Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Nolan Page/Rhode Island Current)A colleague’s empty seat separated Deborah Janick from the three other members of the Tiverton Town Council present at its July 27 meeting. So too did her perspective on Flock Safety. 
Janick was the only no as the council voted 3-1 — with three members absent — to approve the installation of additional Flock automated license plate reader cameras in town.
The decision following 40 minutes of deliberations interrupted by outbursts from opponents in the audience made the town an outlier in a summer of public resistance to Flock across the state and the country. The Atlanta-based private company’s 120,000 U.S. cameras photograph and identify vehicles using artificial intelligence to recognize license plates, bumper stickers, make, model and color. Police don’t need a warrant to search Flock’s system. 
On the very same night, just 20 miles away from Tiverton, the South Kingstown Town Council voted unanimously to cancel its contract with Flock, citing concerns about privacy and the potential for misuse. Since then, Narragansett, Glocester, Lincoln and North Kingstown have canceled or paused their Flock programs.
“I value protection, but I’m concerned,” Janick told the town’s police chief and a Flock representative before the vote.
Also concerned is Gov. Dan McKee. On Tuesday, he called for a pause on the installation of new Flock cameras for 60 days while the Rhode Island State Police lead a review of the technology. The order allows existing cameras to continue operating.
“Automated license plate readers can be an important tool for law enforcement to solve crimes, recover stolen vehicles, and locate dangerous or missing individuals, but Rhode Islanders also have legitimate questions about privacy, transparency, and how this information is collected, stored, and shared,” McKee said. 
In October 2025, when the state police launched a federally funded program to expand Rhode Island’s Flock network, 14 of the state’s 39 municipalities had active Flock cameras. Now at least 24 currently use or plan to install the technology.
The governor’s order renders Tiverton’s approval moot for the time being. It directs the Department of Public Safety to work with stakeholders like the Rhode Island Police Chiefs’ Association and the Rhode Island League of Cities and Towns to review the technology and make recommendations on statewide policy governing its use. 
The Rhode Island American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), a leading opponent to Flock cameras in the state, applauded McKee’s action but said it will continue to call for municipalities to cancel existing contracts with Flock. 

Flock has “kind of exploded” in the past two years, said Madalyn McGunagle, a policy analyst at the state’s ACLU and a leading critic of the technology in Rhode Island. She views the cameras as invasive surveillance that reveals “intimate and sensitive details about someone’s life.” 
“They’ve become increasingly more normalized, and that really just infringes on continuous expectations of privacy,” McGunagle told Rhode Island Current. “As they become more and more normal, that expectation just erodes more.”
The ACLU continues to support legislation that would establish “clear and strict standards” around automated license plate readers. Rep. Matthew Dawson, an East Providence Democrat, sponsored bills calling for uniform policies regarding the cameras in the last two General Assembly sessions. 



Quotation







I value protection, but I’m concerned.


– Tiverton Town Councilor Deborah Janick, who voted against adding more Flock cameras on July 27


His 2026 bill (H8077), a collaboration between legislators, the ACLU and law enforcement, would have restricted the type of cases the cameras can be used for, created guidelines for data access and retention, established standards for transparency and required municipal council approval to use the technology. The bill was held for further study by the House Judiciary Committee. 
The issue is Dawson’s “top priority” if he wins reelection, he said, and he’s optimistic about another bill’s chances in the legislature.
“I’m positive it’s going to happen next year,” the East Providence Democrat said. 
A solar panel-powered Flock automated license plate reader sits on a pole beside Route 24 North in Tiverton on Monday, Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Nolan Page/Rhode Island Current)
Piecing together a statewide network
Since 2021, Rhode Island municipalities have been independently signing contracts with Flock — starting with Cranston, Pawtucket and Woonsocket — without much pushback, gradually building a patchy network of the cameras in Rhode Island. A count last year by the ACLU estimated that Rhode Island had at least 295 of the cameras.
Much of the growth has come from the state police effort to unite the state’s splintered Flock landscape into a more cohesive network using $597,000 from a $4 million community policing grant. Rhode Island was one of three states — along with New Jersey and New York — to receive that amount, which is the maximum award given through the Anti-Heroin Task Force grant program designed to support heroin-related community policing. 
The goal of the state police program was “to get as much coverage statewide for the protection of the state,” Maj. Marc Alboum, who is heading the effort, said. 
Alboum said the cameras will lead to better surveillance to investigate drug trafficking cases in Rhode Island.
“It was to get the tools we need to properly investigate these cases and prosecute them,” he said. 
The state police began work on ramping up the state’s Flock network after signing its contract with the company on Oct. 10, 2025. Of the 23 municipalities the state police approached to install Flock cameras since last December, 21 approved the technology, Alboum said. Only Warren and Portsmouth rejected the agency’s proposal.
Funded for three years, the program is set to provide 39 cameras throughout the state, with the first batch of new cameras installed through the initiative on June 23 in Providence, North Kingstown and East Greenwich, Alboum told Rhode Island Current. 
Alboum said the cameras have already been useful in a murder investigation. He added that he feels people are quick to disregard positive stories about Flock, and that “nobody wants to hear it” when advocates try to disprove concerns about the technology. 
“It’s frustrating, and it’s exhausting to try to explain what it really does and what it doesn’t do,” Alboum said. But he hopes to apply for another federal grant to continue the program beyond its initial three-year period. 
﻿
Public safety vs. right to privacy
To law enforcement and other advocates for the cameras, the technology is an innovative tool that only photographs license plates, which are already in public view on the road. 
Supporters of the cameras regularly credit Flock’s role in the break in the investigation of the Brown University mass shooting last December. Providence police used an image that a Flock license plate reader captured of the suspected shooter’s vehicle to identify and track the rental car tied to his name. The photograph is branded with the company’s wordmark in the bottom left corner. 
But McGunagle argued that history and recent terminations of Flock contracts weaken that argument. “We’ve seen public safety objectives met without the use of these cameras,” she said.
McGunagle also contended that Flock’s systems violate privacy by taking a public license plate and using it to create a traceable profile that can reveal details like where someone lives, works, attends school or goes to the doctor. 
Critics raise other concerns about the security of information collected by Flock, with some claiming the data is accessible to hackers. In response, congressional lawmakers have called for an investigation into Flock’s data security. The company’s website says data is encrypted from creation to deletion.
Flock’s website also features an Aug. 13 announcement revising the company’s safeguards, part of its efforts to win stronger public trust as more and more communities push back against its cameras. Those efforts have also involved sending representatives to municipal council meetings across the country, including in Tiverton and South Kingstown. 
“It is not judge and jury and executioner,” Flock’s senior public affairs director, Trevor Chandler, said of the technology at the South Kingstown Town Council’s July 27 meeting. “It is a tangible piece of evidence that your officers are trained to use so that they can take action.”
Flock’s new policy shortens how long data is retained from 30 days to seven. The ACLU has called the decrease “a step in the right direction” but said it doesn’t go far enough, instead recommending deleting data after 48 hours unless it’s flagged for an investigation. 
Among other changes, Flock will also now require every search in its systems to be accompanied by a case number, which was previously optional, as well as mandate use of its auditing tool to flag suspicious use. 
“We are not perfect, so we will keep listening, improving, and building a better standard for public safety technology together,” Flock CEO Garrett Langley wrote in the announcement. 
The company did not immediately return a request for comment.
A Flock automated license plate reader records data on Main Road in Tiverton on Monday, Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Nolan Page/Rhode Island Current)
‘Not just a local problem’
A June lawsuit filed by an East Providence woman against Cumberland and its police department shows a potential downside to giving law enforcement more access to the surveillance equipment.
The plaintiff, Eva Pizzarelli of East Providence, claims she was wrongfully arrested for reckless driving and eluding police after police allegedly misidentified her as the driver of a car who was failing to signal turns and led police on a brief chase before Cumberland officers called off the pursuit. Police relied on an image taken by a Flock camera, the lawsuit claims. 
The lawsuit alleges that the officers compared the Flock image with Pizzarelli’s Facebook profile and driver’s license photo to conclude that she matched the driver they were looking for. Police described the offending driver as having red hair, but Pizzarelli claims the photos the officers used were outdated and that her hair was dyed brown at the time of the incident on March 26, 2025. Cumberland officials have denied Pizzarelli’s allegations in court documents.
The case prompted neighboring Lincoln’s town administrator to pause installations of 12 approved Flock cameras, the Valley Breeze reported. Flock has said its license plate readers are only designed to capture photographs of passing cars and use technology to identify vehicles, not for facial recognition. 



Quotation







It’s frustrating, and it’s exhausting to try to explain what it really does and what it doesn’t do.


– Rhode Island State Police Maj. Marc Alboum


McGunagle also highlighted examples of the technology being used for federal immigration enforcement, as well as of police officers using Flock to track people seeking gender-affirming care and even romantic partners. A New Bedford police officer is under investigation for allegedly using Flock to follow her ex-girlfriend, The New Bedford Light reported.
“It’s also equally as troubling for the idea that someone way across the country could be misusing this information,” McGunagle said. “It’s not just a local problem. It’s this nationwide sharing model that makes it a big issue.”
But McGunagle said legislation and guidelines — like those ordered by McKee — around the technology’s use could alleviate some critics’ concerns. Dawson, who was also an opponent to the cameras when he first sponsored a bill regulating them, agreed.
Dawson said he initially wanted to halt the use of cameras entirely. But that changed when he was filling out paperwork at the East Providence police station and witnessed Flock’s utility firsthand. He said that officers and dispatchers used the cameras to locate and stop an individual believed to be suicidal in just 10 minutes. 
“I don’t want Big Brother watching me,” Dawson said. “But it’s proven as a successful tool for law enforcement.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: CCC hoping for funding infusion as it implements new law, policies
authors: Katie Castellani | State House News Service
description: Cannabis regulators are planning a sweeping overhaul of the state's marijuana industry while also advancing plans to let adults buy and use marijuana at the same establishment.
text:
CANNABIS REGULATORS ARE seeking millions of dollars more from Beacon Hill, money they say is necessary to implement this spring’s sweeping overhaul of the state’s marijuana industry and simultaneously advance long-discussed plans to let adults to buy and use marijuana at the same establishment.
The ask is split between two buckets: To take on the additional responsibilities this year’s law places on the Cannabis Control Commission, including making both consumer- and business-facing changes, the agency needs more than $7.9 million in additional fiscal year 2027 funding, Executive Director Travis Ahern said in an April letter to state budget writers. And the CCC is also seeking IT funds from the Executive Office of Technology Services and Security to help replace the “antiquated” licensing and registration platform known as MassCIP, according to an agency spokesperson.
During a meeting last week, Ahern said the CCC is seeking funds to upgrade MassCIP as part of rolling out regulations governing sites where people could consume marijuana in social settings.
Those regulations include creating three new license types, one of which Ahern said is expected to be open for applications in December. That’s the “supplemental” license available for existing marijuana businesses to allow customers to consume products they’ve purchased on-site. Commissioners said during the meeting that they are still determining when applications for the other two social consumption license types – hospitality and event organizer – are expected to open.
That timing aligns with the CCC’s projections of rolling out the new licenses when the body approved social consumption regulations in December 2025, Ahern said. The agency has also assigned a “significant amount of personnel assigned to this implementation to move it as quickly as we have been,” Ahern said.
“And so, in this regard, what I’d highlight again is to maintain the speed and the emphasis we have on the implementation of social consumption, while also getting into the very robust conversation we’ll have later on implementation of Chapter 65 in the regulatory process, we are going to need additional resources to maintain the pace that we’re on. And we’ll hopefully have updates for that as we get into our September meeting,” Ahern said August 13, referring to the sweeping cannabis reform legislation signed in April.
Most of the approximately additional $7.9 million the CCC has requested would go to “information technology development, consultant support, and the establishment of new regulatory infrastructure, including public-facing portals and data systems” along with new staff to implement the law, Ahern wrote in the April letter, which was sent the same day lawmakers shipped the industry overhaul legislation to Gov. Maura Healey’s desk.
“Absent this funding, the Commission will be required to implement sweeping statutory changes without the staffing, systems, or resources necessary to do so,” Ahern wrote  in the letter. “This would create immediate operational risks, including delays in implementation, an inability to meet statutory deadlines, reduced oversight capacity, and increased strain on an already constrained workforce.”
In June, the CCC adopted a set of emergency regulations in order to meet a deadline embedded within the cannabis law. Those regulations were “just the beginning of a comprehensive policymaking process that will unfold over the next year,” CCC Chair Chris Harding said at the time.
A CCC spokesperson told the News Service the agency “followed the standard process” of requesting a supplemental budget from the Executive Office of Administration and Finance. 
Each fall, the governor files a supplemental budget closing the books on the prior fiscal year. Last month, Healey filed a $100 million fiscal year 2027 supplemental budget (H 5586) that’s pending in the House Committee on Ways and Means. And several supplemental spending budgets typically arise throughout the fiscal year.
Earlier this year, commissioners asked lawmakers for $32.9 million in funding for fiscal year 2027. That would have been a roughly $13 million increase over the CCC’s fiscal 2026 operating budget of $19.7 million. The agency’s request included an additional $3.88 million for the rollout of the social consumption regulations along with $2.8 million for IT costs to support licensing upgrades and replacements. The fiscal year 2027 budget allocated approximately $20.9 million for the agency.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Under new legislation, restaurants prep to post origin country for shrimp
description: Coastal Georgia is known for its hospitality as well as its shrimp-abundant waterways and estuaries. However, not all restaurants along the coast source their seafood from local waters, while allowing people to assume they do. Foreign imports have flooded the market in the United States, selling farm-raised shrimp for lower prices and making it difficult […]
text:
A basket of freshly caught Atlantic white shrimp ready to be put on ice. Credit: Justin Taylor/The CurrentCoastal Georgia is known for its hospitality as well as its shrimp-abundant waterways and estuaries. However, not all restaurants along the coast source their seafood from local waters, while allowing people to assume they do.
Foreign imports have flooded the market in the United States, selling farm-raised shrimp for lower prices and making it difficult for local shrimpers to compete.
A new state law, House Bill 117, took effect on July 1, turning the tide for both Georgia shrimpers and the state’s restaurants. The bill requires that all Georgia restaurants, excluding those operated by a state agency, disclose whether the menu items they serve contain foreign imported shrimp.
The disclosure can be labeled either on the menu or on signs visible to the public. While HB 117 has officially been signed into law, it will not be enforced until January in order to give restaurants time to prepare. Chefs and restaurant owners around downtown Savannah, many food service establishments who sell imported shrimp say they are in no hurry to update their menus.
Rep. Jesse Petrea. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
State Rep. Jesse Petrea, who represents parts of Chatham and Bryan counties, sponsored HB117. Petrea drafted the bill with the intent of providing transparency for consumers to make informed decisions about the seafood that they choose to buy.

“There’s a lack of information by consumers,” said Petrea, “and what you discover, if you dig superficially, is that we have huge problems with foreign imports having a multitude of things that cause them to be sent back.”
According to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), 94% of all seafood consumed in the U.S. is imported, with shrimp being the most popular seafood product in the nation. Although federal programs serve to ensure the safety of our food, foreign imports are sometimes flagged or recalled by the FDA as unfit for consumption.
A notable instance of shrimp contamination that reached the mainstream media was coined as “radioactive shrimp.” In 2025 the FDA announced a recall on frozen shrimp imported from Indonesia for testing positive for Cesium-137 (Cs-137).
But the impacts of HB 117 doesn’t just concern safety, it’s also intended to keep Georgia shrimpers in business.
“If people think they’re eating domestic, as they usually do when they aren’t, then we have almost lost our entire shrimp and fleet,” said Petrea. “And when we lose that, when America can’t feed itself, that’s a loss that you don’t just fix overnight.”
Captain David Attia unloads his catch of Atlantic white shrimp from the freezer hold of his boat. David and his brother Marcus make up the crew of the James W. Salyers. Being a “freezer boat,” the shrimp caught on this vessel are de-headed, bagged, and then stored below deck at zero degrees to be frozen and ready to ship. Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current
 From boat to fork

Dockside restaurants are a main attraction on Tybee Island, Savannah and Brunswick, drawing in both locals and tourists with the full experience of Georgia’s marshes and rivers. With the sound of seagulls and the smell of salty air, diners at these dockside restaurants expect their dinner to come from the coast. However, several establishments serve imported shrimp despite being near shrimp-abundant waters.
Some Tybee Island businesses such as Bubba Gumbo’s and Sea Wolf Tybee, take pride in serving fresh seafood and supporting local shrimpers.
Tom Worley, owner of Sea Wolf Tybee, explained that a shortened supply chain can lead to a better product when it comes to shrimp. By cutting out the middle distributors, restaurants are able to ensure that the safety and quality of the shrimp doesn’t degrade in transportation due to temperature fluctuations. Sourcing from local shrimpers also has the benefit of building trust and clear communication between restaurant owners and suppliers.
“You have a better control over what you’re eating when it comes from a closer source,” said Worley.
Sea Wolf head chef Justin Waldman prepares a dish with fresh local shrimp at his restaurant on Tybee Island. August 14, 2026. Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current GA/CatchLight/Report for America
Food service establishments that sell imported shrimp for some portions of the year benefit from getting more bang for their buck as food distributors allow them to buy imported shrimp at a lower price for large purchases.
A general manager at Dockside Seafood in Savannah, Chase Crenshaw, said that the restaurant buys shrimp from Ecuador, a decision he said “just made sense” to them. He claimed that shrimp imported from Ecuador and Georgia shrimp is similar as far as taste and quality. Crenshaw said that while many restaurants use low quality shrimp to make a couple extra dollars, Dockside is willing to narrow its margins a little more to buy Ecuadorian shrimp. Crenshaw described local shrimp as being something that is hard for their restaurant to find due to the inflated cost.
“At the end of the day, we’re all out here trying to survive, and you know, we try and give the customers the best quality we can while also being able to make a couple dollars ourselves,” he said.
But while making a profit is, of course, essential for running a business, a disclosure on shrimp origin is long overdue as customers are often misled as to who is serving local shrimp and who isn’t. Even restaurants who decorate their walls with fishing nets and model shrimping boats may not be meeting the standards that their customers expect.
DNA tests conducted in 2025 found that only 10 of 47 samples of shrimp from 44  restaurants tested in Savannah, Tybee Island and Port Wentworth were American species. Tests from the Golden Isles — Darien, Jekyll Island, St. Simons Island and Brunswick — showed 43 out of 44 restaurant samples were wild-caught, American shrimp. This study ultimately boosted the approval of HB117 and revealed mislabeling and false perceptions about shrimp served in restaurants tested.
SeaD Consulting, the firm hired to conduct DNA tests, released a list of 10 restaurants that passed the test but did not name the restaurants that failed the test for locally sourced shrimp.
Some restaurant owners and managers say they felt the DNA results weren’t communicated fairly because the list released only names of those that tested positive for local shrimp. For example, Bubba Gumbo’s, a locally owned restaurant and marina on Tybee Island which serves shrimp fresh off the nearby dock, wasn’t tested, and therefore did not make it onto the “nice” list.
“It left all of it up to the consumer’s assumption, you know, with them saying only these restaurants were tested positive for selling domestic shrimp,” said Chris Gulser, executive chef at Bubba Gumbo’s. “That meant people immediately thought that we weren’t selling domestic shrimp.”
In spite of the initial public misunderstanding that resulted from Bubba Gumbo’s being excluded from the DNA testing, Gusler expressed the importance that restaurants on Tybee be transparent as to where they source their shrimp. When vacationing diners come to Tybee Island, they likely expect to get fresh, Georgia shrimp, he said.
“They’re expecting a specific product and they should be able to get that product,” said Gusler.
Workers at the Smith and Sons Seafood company in Darien tediously de-head shrimp in a large refrigerated room. It’s a job that has to be done by hand. Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current
John Wallace, shrimper and owner of Anchored Shrimp Company in Brunswick, says that HB117 can be nothing but good for shrimpers and shrimp sellers. Wallace explains how foreign imports have the largest hand in controlling the cost of staying in business. In recent years, the profit margin for the local shrimping industry has dwindled, with the price of shrimp rarely keeping up with inflation.
“I was actually getting more for shrimp in 1979 than I am today,” said Wallace. “In 1979, my net cost me $400, which now has cost me $4000. Also, fuel back then was less than a dollar, and sometimes it gets between $4 and $5 now.”
Wallace believes that as HB117 begins to take effect, many consumers will begin to take interest in supporting local shrimpers.
“We can already see interest changing. You know, we’re getting more and more calls for the product,” said Wallace.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT winter heating benefits tick up but still lag pre-pandemic levels
description: The number of fuel distributors participating in the Connecticut Energy Assistance Program is up, but some fear the number could shrink.
text:
Connecticut’s chief heating and energy assistance grant will increase this winter, according to a plan recently approved by state legislators, but aid remains below pre-pandemic levels.
And while the number of fuel distributors participating in the Connecticut Energy Assistance Program also jumped last year, the head of a key trade association said he fears those numbers could shrink dangerously unless reforms are made.
Households that purchase heat from vendors and earn 60% or less of the statewide median income — less than roughly $57,630 per year — are eligible for a base benefit ranging from $355 to $705, depending upon earnings, household size and other factors. That’s up from last year’s range of $295 to $645.
That’s according to a CEAP budget prepared by the state Department of Social Services and approved recently by the General Assembly’s Appropriations, Energy & Technology and Human Services committees.
Some of these households covered by that plan also can receive from one to three “crisis assistance” payments of $430 each this winter, up $5 per payment from one year ago.
Renters who meet income guidelines and do not purchase fuel from vendors can receive a benefit ranging from $145 to $90. Last year’s range was $125 to $75.
But those grant levels are all down from the plan adopted in August 2019, the last one before COVID struck Connecticut in early 2020.
Households deemed the poorest and most vulnerable could receive up to $2,980 in the winter of 2019-20. The maximum possible grant in the latest plan is $1,995, down more than 49%.
Pre-pandemic renters’ benefits ranged from $190 to $150.
“I worry that if we have another winter like we did last winter — one that is exceptionally cold — that we’re not going to have enough resources to provide people with the support that they need,” said Sen. Cathy Osten, D-Sprague, co-chairwoman of the Appropriations Committee.
Osten also noted that fuel prices have been generally unstable and subject to multiple surges since the U.S. war with Iran began in late February.
Though the energy assistance service is run by the state, its chief source of funding is federal Low Income Household Energy Assistance Program dollars. And while Connecticut’s $86.3 million LIHEAP grant this year is up from $81.7 million 12 months ago — and $10 million greater than pre-pandemic levels — things have worsened overall since 2020.
That’s because 94,280 households are projected to seek energy assistance this winter, up 12.4% from last year and 15% from seven years ago.
Connecticut has used state dollars in recent years to bolster LIHEAP, and Osten and Sen. Norm Needleman, D-Essex, said there likely will be another conversation about shifting state funds into the program when the 2027 General Assembly convenes in early January.
“Based on current pricing, I almost don’t see a way we’re not going to have to” have that conversation, said Needleman, who co-chairs the Energy & Technology Committee. “We’re not going to have people freezing in their houses.”
But the president of the Connecticut Energy Marketers Association, Chris Herb, said this week that unless other reforms are made to the winter assistance program, there soon may not be businesses available to deliver fuel to all households in need.
Increasing demand for services and growing vendor fears about participating are, collectively, “a train wreck in the making,” Herb said.
According to the state Department of Social Services, 212 fuel vendors delivered to CEAP clients last winter. And while that was up considerably from the 123 served two years ago, it still is down 60 vendors or 22% from 2019.
“Most look at it as strictly a community service,” Herb said, adding that delivering to CEAP clients can strain a small business’s finances quickly and significantly.
CEAP relies on a complex system that limits how much participating businesses can charge program-eligible households. 
That retail price isn’t set at the same time a fuel distributor purchases home heating oil at one of the terminals spread across Connecticut. And given the unstable political situation in the Middle East, fuel prices can vary by as much as 40 cents per day.
In other words, the price a distributor purchases for fuel and the price it can charge CEAP customers could leave a significant gap.
“We have an adequate vendor network,” said Social Services Department spokeswoman Christine Stuart. But Herb warned the number of available vendors will continue to drop unless policymakers look more closely at the system.
Most fuel vendors “are small mom-and-pop places,” Osten said. “We need to remember that these are small businesses who do a critical job.”
“Your [CEAP] benefit is meaningless if you can’t get anybody to deliver,” added Nora Duncan, who is director of the Connecticut chapter of AARP and vice chairwoman of the state’s Low-Income Energy Water Advisory Board.
The AARP also has been pressing for state lawmakers to increase Connecticut’s role in keeping vulnerable residents warm as aid from Washington shrinks.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana governor secures FEMA grant for Sand Creek Fire
description: As Montana’s largest wildfire exceeds 30,000 acres, Gov. Greg Gianforte announced the state secured a grant from the Federal Emergency Management Agency to help with costs associated with fighting the Sand Creek Fire. The blaze, which started Aug. 1 in Beaverhead County, is only 1% contained, according to Monday’s reports from fire crews. It burned […]
text:
The Federal Emergency Management Agency building is seen on May 15, 2025 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Kayla Bartkowski/Getty Images)As Montana’s largest wildfire exceeds 30,000 acres, Gov. Greg Gianforte announced the state secured a grant from the Federal Emergency Management Agency to help with costs associated with fighting the Sand Creek Fire.
The blaze, which started Aug. 1 in Beaverhead County, is only 1% contained, according to Monday’s reports from fire crews. It burned through parts of Maverick Mountain Ski Area and has prompted evacuation orders in the region surrounding Elkhorn Hot Springs.
The federal assistance from FEMA is through a Fire Management Assistance Grant, which provides funding for up to 75% of a state’s eligible firefighting costs. Those include materials and supplies, mobilization and demobilization, equipment use and other expenses.
“The state of Montana has been in constant contact with the U.S. Forest Service since the Sand Creek Fire first began,” Gianforte said in a press release. “We’re asking all Montanans to follow all necessary precautions and take the evacuation warnings and orders from local law enforcement seriously.”
The governor asked the public to stay updated on restrictions at mtfireinfo.org as Montana enters “the core of fire season” and firefighters and law enforcement work to protect communities.
The state Department of Natural Resources and Conservation and the state Disaster and Emergencies Services submitted the funding request to FEMA.
Firefighters are continuing to prioritize structure protection and have prevented loss, with the only confirmed impact being to the Maverick Mountain upper lift shack and the Maverick Mountain U.S. Forest Service repeater, according to the Governor’s Office. Emergency evacuation orders are in place for all communities north of Clark Creek and Shale Creek, including Elkhorn Hot Springs and Maverick Mountain.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Lahn says cancer crisis isn’t partisan and it must be solved in Iowa
description: Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn said Tuesday that Iowa’s cancer crisis was one the reasons he entered the race and said regardless of party, it’s a problem that has to be solved.  Lahn spoke in Urbandale with cancer survivors and volunteers with the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network as part of the organization’s “coffee […]
text:
Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn at an American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network in Urbandale Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn said Tuesday that Iowa’s cancer crisis was one the reasons he entered the race and said regardless of party, it’s a problem that has to be solved. 
Lahn spoke in Urbandale with cancer survivors and volunteers with the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network as part of the organization’s “coffee cancer chat” event series which asks politicians about their stances on key cancer policy issues.
After listening to testimonies from more than a dozen event participants about their struggles with cancer diagnoses, paying for treatment, losing loved ones and living with the after-effects of cancer treatment, Lahn shared his own story of his father’s fight with non-Hodgkin lymphoma. 
Lahn choked up as he explained his father’s diagnosis several years ago that led to a rapid cognitive decline, and other calls he has received about friends diagnosed with cancer. 
“It’s not normal. It’s not right,” Lahn said. “Cancer has become a flashpoint in my own campaign, and the reason it has is because, I think I’ve been giving a voice to people who traditionally didn’t think they had a person to talk about it, especially in the Republican Party.”

He said he was under “no illusion” that he would win the Republican primary in June, considering people in his own party told him he wouldn’t win if he talked about water quality and cancer. Lahn said a “serious discussion” about cancer must include a discussion on nitrate load and water quality. 
“It doesn’t matter if you’re left or right – you’re drinking the water, you have a family member who’s got cancer, we all have,” Lahn said. “ … We have to solve it.” 
Lahn is the latest in a slew of candidates on the November ballot who have participated in the organization’s coffee cancer chat series, including Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand, who participated in late July.
Advance testing 
Lahn said he was supportive of programs that improved access to screening and early detection of cancers. Many of the cancer survivors in the room noted that they developed their cancers at a younger age than when most doctors would screen for the diseases. 
Lahn said he and his wife use a screening tool that detects early cancer signs via a blood test. He said he would like to initiate large contract pricing through the state to offer the tests, which cost more than $800 for an individual, to the “most vulnerable populations” in the state. 
When speaking with reporters after the event, Lahn also said he wants Iowa to research the safety of certain products, including pesticides. He noted similar efforts have been done in Florida to test products like bread, candy and infant formula for harmful ingredients. 
Redirecting university priorities to cancer research
Lahn said he would continue to support state funding for pediatric cancer research at the University of Iowa, but also suggested university funding that currently goes to other departments and degrees be redirected to things like pediatric cancer research, which he said has a higher “value proposition.” 
“It’s not just adding more on top, but it’s also shifting the buckets that our money is going into right now, because it can’t just be that everything has the same sort of value proposition attached to it,” Lahn said. “Saving lives of people, and especially children, is one of the highest value propositions you could have.” 
Sand, when asked the same question during his coffee chat, said he supported expanding the up to $3 million in pediatric cancer research funding approved by the state Legislature and Gov. Kim Reynolds in May. 
That funding will come from the state’s new 5-cent tax on vapes and alternative nicotine products purchased in the state. 
Tobacco tax 
As part of the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network event, volunteers asked participating politicians if they would support raising tobacco taxes by $1.50 per cigarette pack, and making taxes on other tobacco and nicotine products equivalent to 50% of the products’ wholesale price. These figures, the organization argued, would help reduce lung cancer rates in the state. 
Lahn said he wants to see tobacco use decrease, but didn’t commit to the “very specific” policy proposals presented.
He said while there is “something positive to be gained” out of raising taxes to those levels, he wants to be cognizant of the “second order consequences” of raising the price of an addictive product.
“If we were to raise a tax on cigarettes or nicotine products, I would not support it if there was not a commensurate increase in the ability for us to help people get off of the product in the first place,” Lahn said. “Because otherwise, what we’re doing there is essentially a poverty tax, and you’ll hurt the people that are actually in the most need in our society.” 
Sand also did not commit to the tax rates proposed by the organization when asked in July, but said he supported raising the taxes. 
Medicaid expansion 
While Lahn’s opponent has said he wants to end the privatization of the state’s Medicaid program, Lahn said Tuesday he believes using managed care providers, or MCOs, is the “right idea.” 
“My goal is to make sure that with Medicaid that we’re getting good service, prompt payment, we’re not using AI in the decision making of claims … and also that we are not having vertical integration to make sure that the price is affordable,” Lahn said. 
Lahn said he was “committed” to maintaining Medicaid access and Medicaid expansion for Iowans. He noted criticisms of his past, when he worked for a group that advocated against Medicaid expansion, and said there were some “real problems” with Medicaid expansion when it first came out. Namely, he said there was “no mechanism” to stop the federal government from “ratcheting down” its support, which would leave states with an “unbelievable burden.” 
He also defended work and volunteer requirements in the program and said he believes “there’s a benefit” to being out in the community for those who are able to do so. 
Democrats have argued work requirements, as laid out in a state law and in the 2025 federal budget reconciliation bill, will push eligible Iowans out of the program.
Vaccines
While Lahn has been critical of vaccine policies, especially mRNA vaccines and the COVID-19 vaccines, he said didn’t have a plan to restrict  human papillomavirus, or HPV, vaccinations, which the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network holds can help prevent cervical cancer.
Cervical cancer was the most common cancer among the survivors at the event. Earlier this year, the Iowa Legislature passed a law that restricts minors from receiving HPV or hepatitis B vaccines without parental consent. 
“I think it’s between you and your doctor, also between a parent and their doctor for their children,” Lahn said. “So, my goal is to have safe, effective, and tested products available to people that would like to use them.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: KY county clerks say state mapping prompted local questions about voting, taxes and more
description: Jefferson County Clerk David Yates told lawmakers Tuesday that as a result of a review of registered voters’ information after a “clerical error” prevented a handful of voters from casting a ballot in the correct precinct, about 290 voters on the county line must now vote in Jefferson County rather than a surrounding county.
text:
Jefferson County Clerk David Yates held a press conference about voting problems on July 1, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)Jefferson County Clerk David Yates told lawmakers Tuesday that as a result of a review of registered voters’ information after a “clerical error” prevented a handful of voters from casting a ballot in the correct precinct, about 290 voters on the county line must now vote in Jefferson County rather than a surrounding county. 
Earlier this year, Yates said “a clerical error by a former employee” prevented eight voters from casting a ballot in the 44th House District during Kentucky’s May primary. At the time, Yates had said 30 registered voters were assigned to an incorrect precinct and called for further review of registered voters’ precinct information within the state’s most populous county. 
Yates, a former Democratic state senator, told the State Government Committee a 2022 law to centralize a state mapping system may not reflect what’s happening at the local level. Yates said in some cases where a person resides on a county line, they may pay taxes in one county but vote in another. 
“We have a discrepancy,” Yates said. “Now, the lines didn’t change; the technology got better to lay it out there.”
In response to questions, Yates said his office’s review flagged 290 new voters in Jefferson County and about 35 voters who need to vote in another county. 
The situation isn’t only affecting Jefferson County. Rep. James Tipton, R-Taylorsville, said he recalled that about 200 constituents told him ahead of the 2024 primary they received notice they no longer resided in Spencer County and had to vote in neighboring Shelby County. The matter “caused a lot of confusion” and some voters ultimately didn’t vote because of it, Tipton added. It also raised questions about where school buses should go and which first responder departments served those residents. 
“There’s a lot more issues than just voting is what I’m trying to point out here,” Tipton said. 
Franklin County Clerk Jeff Hancock, who joined Yates for the presentation, said the Voter Registration System (VRS) and the Geographic Information Systems (GIS) “needs to be interactive” and able to “keep up with the changes of today’s pace.” He added that there is no federal or local money to make the changes. 
“This is going to have to be funded from the honorable gentlemen and ladies that are sitting right in front of me, and it needs to be done,” Hancock said, referring to the lawmakers. “You have a rainy day account, we all need some umbrellas at this point.” 
The rainy day fund, which is also known as the budget reserve trust fund account, is based on the state’s previous revenues. 
Constitution in schools
The committee also heard a presentation from Joni Bryan, the founder and executive director of The 917 Society, about a request to designate the group as an “official resource” for education materials for Constitution Day, which is Sept. 17. The 917 Society distributes copies of the U.S. Constitution to students around the country. Bryan said some distribution already happens in a few Kentucky schools. 
While Bryan said The 917 Society is nonpartisan and works with a variety of groups, she listed some conservative groups like Moms for Liberty and Hillsdale College, which was on the advisory board for Project 2025. That was created as a guiding document for the Trump administration leading up to the 2024 presidential election.
“We don’t tell teachers what to teach,” Bryan said. We give them the book for the kids, and then they can decide what they want to do.” 
Democrats on the committee expressed skepticism. 
“As much as I want to see our kids understanding all of the civic education, getting them involved in our government, and understanding how it all works — just because something is free doesn’t always mean that it’s without side costs,” said Rep. Anne Gay Donworth, D-Lexington. 
Rep. T.J. Roberts, R-Burlington, said the back of one of the materials Bryan brought to the committee included quotes from President John F. Kennedy and U.S. Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg. 
“This doesn’t seem to be a partisan organization,” Roberts said. “This seems to be a no-tax resource for our schools to fulfill our federal obligation to educate our students on the Constitution.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: An entire school board in central Georgia is fired, kicking off search for new members
description: Gov. Brian Kemp hopes a newly appointed panel can help clean up a financial mess in Dublin City Schools. Kemp suspended all seven of the board’s members via an executive order Monday and appointed five local leaders to help select temporary replacements. Their dismissal followed a unanimous recommendation from the state Board of Education issued […]
text:
Gov. Brian Kemp speaks at a Georgia Chamber event in Athens, Aug. 5, 2026. Kemp suspended all seven members of the Dublin City School Board after its accreditation came under threat following years of financial instability. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderGov. Brian Kemp hopes a newly appointed panel can help clean up a financial mess in Dublin City Schools.
Kemp suspended all seven of the board’s members via an executive order Monday and appointed five local leaders to help select temporary replacements. Their dismissal followed a unanimous recommendation from the state Board of Education issued last week.
The nominating committee announced Tuesday that it is accepting letters of intent and resumes from those interested in serving on the local school board. The deadline to apply is 5 p.m. Aug. 26. Usually, the school board members are elected.
Dublin is located in Laurens County in central Georgia. The school system serves about 2,300 students in five schools.
In April, Cognia, the private agency which accredits the district, downgraded Dublin City Schools from “accredited” to “accredited with conditions,” its lowest ranking and a step toward removing the district’s accreditation entirely.
The system’s financial difficulties reached a breaking point last August when it became clear that the district had not paid into the state health plan for over a year, but during an 11-hour hearing last week, Georgia Department of Education Chief Financial Officer Rusk Roam testified that the district’s financial woes started as early as 2009.
Amy Rowell, director of financial review at the state Department of Education, said an influx of federal funds during the COVID-19 pandemic allowed the district to show a positive balance of funds, but the district was still engaging in deficit spending during that time.
Roam testified that the district is the “worst financially managed school system” he had seen in his nearly 20-year career.
In October, the district adopted a deficit reduction plan that resulted in the surprise dismissal of dozens of employees.
“It’s heartbreaking,” said suspended Board Chair Amanda Smith. “You recruit people to your district because you love the school and you know how much it does for children and how much ability it does have and you have these wonderful programs and you’re looking at some of your best friends and saying ‘I’m sorry, and there’s nothing I can do about it.’”
Smith, who was elected chair early this year after serving on the board for two years, testified the current board, in contrast with previous boards, has made efforts to increase transparency as well as the district’s financial stability.
Kemp’s appointees will be tasked with proposing temporary nominations to replace her and the other board members following the governor’s suspensions.
Members are set to include State Board of Education member Matt Donaldson, who will serve as chairman and represents the congressional district in which the Dublin City Board of Education is located; former Dublin Mayor Phil Best; Edwin May, a member of the Dublin-Laurens County Economic Development Authority and Rep. Matt Hatchett and Senate President Pro Tempore Larry Walker, Republicans who represent Dublin in their respective chambers.
“This is an important moment for Dublin City Schools, and our focus must remain squarely on improving outcomes for students, families, educators and ultimately taxpayers who fund the school system,” Walker said.
The committee is accepting nominations by email at DublinCityNominatingCommittee@doe.k12.ga.us. Letters of intent should include the board district where the applicant resides and include their address.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Egg-static: NC food bank receives first delivery from 3 million egg antitrust settlement
description: One of the most requested items at North Carolina’s food banks is food that’s high in protein. Starting this week, hungry families will see their wish fulfilled dozens and dozens of times over. State Attorney General Jeff Jackson, joined by state food bank leaders, received 270,000 eggs on Tuesday, the first in a series of […]
text:
N.C. Attorney General Jeff Jackson, with Ann Edmondson of Feeding the Carolinas (left) and Amy Beros of the Food Bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina (right), points to 270,000 eggs that will be distributed to N.C. food banks. The eggs are the first shipment in a three million egg settlement in a recent antitrust case. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) One of the most requested items at North Carolina’s food banks is food that’s high in protein. Starting this week, hungry families will see their wish fulfilled dozens and dozens of times over.
State Attorney General Jeff Jackson, joined by state food bank leaders, received 270,000 eggs on Tuesday, the first in a series of deliveries of three million eggs from an antitrust lawsuit.
Jackson and 16 other attorneys general reached a settlement in July with three of the nation’s largest egg producers over allegations they violated the law and worked together to set higher egg prices.
Grocery stores and restaurants typically buy eggs at prices that are tied to industry benchmarks. In this case, the state attorneys general alleged Cal-Maine Foods, Hickman’s Family Farms, and Versova worked together to game the system and charge more for eggs.
North Carolina’s share of the 53 million egg settlement is about 3 million eggs. Over the next six weeks, those eggs will be distributed to food pantries across all 100 counties.
Ann Edmondson, executive director of Feeding the Carolinas, said the settlement arrives as more than 1.7 million North Carolinians face food insecurity.
“That’s the highest in a generation – families who don’t know where their next meal is coming from,” said Edmondson.
No yolk: NC AG Jeff Jackson settles antitrust lawsuit for 3 million eggs

Jackson said the attorneys general could have pushed for more money in the litigation against the egg producers, but decided a more creative solution would benefit more people.
“The harm here was [to] people’s grocery bill. Why not try and do something more direct and targeted towards the neediest families in America?” Jackson told NC Newsline. “This doesn’t undo the fact that people paid too much for groceries, but it is genuine accountability in a way that will actually help people immediately.”
Amy Beros, president of the Food Bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina, said they will be coordinating distribution of the fragile cargo through September. And partner agencies are egg-static to receive the unexpected windfall. With rising food costs, fresh eggs are often considered a luxury by needy families.
“What we hear directly from neighbors facing hunger – eggs are so critical to making a meal feel whole,” said Beros. “Protein is such a key piece of dignity for our neighbors. We have heard over and over again how critical eggs have been, because they’ve been priced out of them for a while.”
Jackson pauses to thank a forklift operator at the Food Bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina, which is handling the distribution of three million fresh eggs. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: UW system to propose two-year tuition freeze in exchange for infusion of state funds
description: The University of Wisconsin system says it will freeze tuition for two years and keep potential increases in the following two years capped at the rate of inflation if the state provides $190 million in the next state budget. “This proposal means four years of predictable tuition with costs that remain well below inflation,” UW […]
text:
The proposal comes as complaints mount about a fourth consecutive year of tuition increases. Photo of UW-Superior campus. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)The University of Wisconsin system says it will freeze tuition for two years and keep potential increases in the following two years capped at the rate of inflation if the state provides $190 million in the next state budget.
“This proposal means four years of predictable tuition with costs that remain well below inflation,” UW Regent President Kyle Weatherly said in a statement, defining the system’s “4-Year Tuition Pledge.” 
“It represents an important commitment to Wisconsin families and helps ensure the Universities of Wisconsin remain the Midwest leader in tuition affordability,” he said. 
The money is just a portion of the system’s $730 million biennial budget request the UW system plans to submit for consideration. 
The proposal comes as complaints mount about a fourth consecutive year of tuition increases and as the state enters a critical election year with control of the governor’s office and the state Legislature up for grabs. 
“To make the 4-Year Tuition Pledge a reality and deliver the quality of education students deserve and parents expect, we need a state partner to fund ongoing operational expenses and help us, as was done for previous generations, fund basic education costs,” Weatherly said.
The UW system and outgoing Gov. Tony Evers have requested significant investments from the Legislature to prevent tuition increases, but Republican lawmakers have opposed the spending increases. The UW Board meeting briefing notes that Wisconsin currently ranks 43 out of 50 states in public funding to support four-year universities.
The last round of budget negotiations led to a $250 million increase for operational costs under the 2025 biennial state budget, well below the $855 million operational budget increase that former UW President Jay Rothman said would be needed to avoid tuition increases.
The UW’s entire proposed funding request, which would allocate $347 million in the first year of the budget and $383 million in the second year, is tied to the advancement of three goals: helping the UW system provide access to affordable, high-quality education; building the state’s workforce; and advancing life-saving discoveries as well as access to healthcare.
If the budget request is fulfilled, the Board of Regents plans to commit to a two-year tuition freeze for undergraduate residents. It says it would also limit potential increases in the 2029-31 biennium to no more than the rate of inflation.
The request also includes $45 million that would go towards developing the UW’s AI capabilities in an “ethical manner”. The investment would cover hardware, software, and networking infrastructure required to run advanced AI systems, as well as staff to manage AI and support faculty and students. 
“Rather than renting computing power from commercial vendors at escalating costs, this infrastructure would be owned and operated by the Universities of Wisconsin, giving Wisconsin universities reliable, affordable access to the computing resources needed to train and develop AI tools,” the briefing states. 
The request also includes $35 million to raise starting salaries to be more competitive and $33 million for the Wisconsin Work & Learn program, which would cover eligible students’ tuition and fees. Students will in turn work while they attend school. 
The system is requesting another $240 million to strengthen economic and workforce competitiveness through investments in technology, research, workforce training, expanded dual enrollment opportunities for high school students as well as academic and career services. 
Another $115 million would be used to grow healthcare education programs. 
The UW Board of Regents will consider the request during its meeting this week.

name: Source New Mexico
title: What spending reports can’t tell us about the opioid settlement
description: Doña Ana County's special project manager responds to state auditor's report on opioid settlement spending.
text:
Doña Ana County's special project manager responds to a recent state auditor report that found more than three years after New Mexico counties and towns received the first installments of a nearly $1 billion opioid settlement fund, almost half of them had failed to report any spending, as of July of 2025.(Douglas Sacha/Getty Images)
The New Mexico Office of the State Auditor’s recent report on opioid settlement spending raises important questions about how communities are using these historic resources. The report found that many counties and municipalities reported little or no expenditures through June 2025.


Those findings deserve careful consideration. Expenditure reports capture only one part of implementation. They tell us how much money has been spent, but they reveal much less about whether communities have built the capacity to use these resources well.


As the special project manager for Doña Ana County Health and Human Services, I help coordinate our county’s opioid settlement work. I’ve learned that spending these resources responsibly involves much more than identifying a worthy project and writing a check. Local governments are being asked to strengthen behavioral health systems that, in many parts of New Mexico, have been under-resourced for decades. Before services can expand, communities often have to establish governance, engage stakeholders, navigate procurement, develop contracts, create evaluation plans and determine how programs will be sustained after settlement payments end.


Much of that work never appears in a financial report, yet it often determines whether these investments produce lasting change.


In Doña Ana County, our first priority was to build framework for decision-making. Rather than working separately, Doña Ana County and the City of Las Cruces established a joint Opioid Settlement Advisory Council bringing together local government, healthcare, behavioral health, recovery, public safety and community partners. That collaboration allows us to coordinate priorities across jurisdictions while reducing duplication of effort, an approach that our Health and Human Services Director, Jamie Michael, recently presented at the National Association of Counties (NACO) Annual Conference.


Vital Strategies provided funding for an opioid settlement coordinator and much of the early convening and planning work of the advisory council. That support allowed Doña Ana County and the City of Las Cruces to build the administrative and collaborative foundation for this work. Building implementation capacity before launching major funding initiatives was a deliberate decision because we believed the community would be better served by thoughtful, coordinated investments than by spending quickly.


The State Auditor’s report also identifies a challenge that many local governments know well: the shortage of qualified providers, particularly in rural communities. Funding alone cannot create services where organizational capacity does not exist.


When Doña Ana County offered opioid settlement funding to expand services for pregnant and parenting people, infants, and families affected by substance use disorder, no organizations applied. The response made clear that while the need is significant, the local provider capacity to deliver these services remains limited.


Those challenges have also shaped how we finance this work. Rather than viewing opioid settlement dollars as a stand-alone funding source, we intentionally pursued a braided funding strategy that aligns these investments with other opportunities. Our work is coordinated with the Region 3 Behavioral Health Regional Plan developed under New Mexico’s Behavioral Health Reform and Investment Act (BHRIA). Early Access BHRIA funding supports projects such as transitional housing for people leaving incarceration and the expansion of Assertive Community Treatment (ACT) services.


No single funding source will rebuild New Mexico’s behavioral health system. Settlement dollars represent an extraordinary opportunity, but they are finite. Coordinating them with state investments, Medicaid, philanthropy and local partnerships offers a stronger foundation for developing services that communities can sustain over time.


None of this diminishes the importance of accountability. The public deserves transparency in how settlement dollars are being spent. Expenditure reports are an important part of that accountability, but they should be understood alongside the planning, collaboration and capacity-building that make meaningful investments possible. If we focus exclusively on dollars spent, we risk overlooking the work required to ensure those investments achieve the outcomes communities expect.


Doña Ana County is also committed to making this work transparent as it evolves. Information about the County’s opioid settlement efforts is available on the Doña Ana County Opioid Settlement webpage and will continue to expand as our public dashboard is developed.


The State Auditor’s report should encourage important questions about how these funds are being used. I also hope it encourages a broader conversation about what successful implementation looks like, particularly in rural states where provider shortages, workforce challenges and fragmented systems make this work especially complex. New Mexico has an opportunity to invest these dollars wisely while strengthening the partnerships and infrastructure that will improve lives long after the settlement funds are exhausted.

title: Trump’s ballroom ‘illegal’ without congressional approval, high court told
text: WASHINGTON — Historic preservationists asked the U.S. Supreme Court Tuesday to deny President Donald Trump’s appeal to continue construction on his $400 million White House ballroom on the grounds of the demolished East Wing.In response to Trump’s application to the high court, the National Trust for Historic Preservation argued irreparable harm would result if construction continued, and that the project is “illegal” without authorization from Congress.The Trust lawyers highlighted that the Trump administration has argued in court the ballroom will be “virtually impossible to deconstruct” because it will be constructed out of nuclear power plant-grade concrete.“That is the essence of irreparable harm,” the Trust argued in the 48-page filing.“Petitioners make no secret of the fact that if the Court permits construction to continue, they will declare the case over,” according to the Trust, a private nonprofit chartered by Congress in 1949 to encourage the protection of historic sites.By contrast, the organization argued, the president and his administration would not be harmed if the Supreme Court left intact a lower court order halting above-ground construction.Security complexCourt filings from the administration have publicly revealed that a security complex under the ballroom will descend five stories, and is well on its way to completion. The concrete-and-steel “superstructure,” reaching five stories deep and 70 feet high, already encompassing about 50,000 square feet, is 65% finished, according to the administration. Plans include a 1,000-seat ballroom incorporated into a “highly integrated military complex” with drone-proof ceilings, bomb shelters, sniper nests, “military-grade venting,” and “state-of-the-art hospital and medical facilities.” The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit panel on Aug. 7 upheld, 2-1, the lower court order blocking all but underground construction while litigation continued.The Trust further argued Tuesday that any above-ground construction happening is already illegal because Congress didn’t authorize it, which means the administration would not likely win the case should the Supreme Court take it up. “The question is simply who decides whether a ballroom can be built on federal property. Our constitutional system and federal law commits that choice to Congress,” the Trust argued. “If Petitioners believe there is a pressing need for a ballroom, nothing prevents them from asking Congress for one — today, tomorrow, or any time in the future,” the brief reads. “But Petitioners’ efforts to foil judicial review and arrogate Congress’s exclusive powers should not be rewarded with a stay that allows Petitioners to complete a ballroom they lacked any authority to commence in the first place.”Democrats back preservationistsMore than 30 Democratic U.S. senators, U.S. House Democratic leaders and committee ranking members from both chambers filed a brief Tuesday in support of the Trust.Lawmakers who signed the brief are from California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, New Hampshire, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia and Washington.“The White House is, indisputably, federal property. It was built only after Congress authorized its construction and appropriated funds to cover that expense,” the lawmakers wrote. “And for over two centuries since, the White House has been renovated and maintained pursuant to congressional authorizations and appropriations.”But Congress “neither authorized the demolition of the White House’s East Wing and construction of a ballroom nor appropriated funds to carry out that project,” they continued.Trump maintains the ballroom project is being funded entirely by private donations. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer, who was Trump’s personal attorney before joining the government, told the Supreme Court in the administration’s application last week that $200 million has already been spent or committed to the project. Sauer argued that a statute governing the Department of the Interior allows private donations to cover projects on land administered by the National Park Service. The service, an agency within the Interior Department, manages the White House and President’s Park.The Democratic senators who signed onto the amicus brief were Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse and Jack Reed of Rhode Island, Dick Durbin of Illinois, Angela Alsobrooks and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, Martin Heinrich and Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico, John Hickenlooper of Colorado, Mazie Hirono of Hawaii, Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, Gary Peters of Michigan, Adam Schiff of California, Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Ron Wyden of OregonThe Democratic House leaders who joined the brief were Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, of New York, Minority Whip Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California. The other representatives who signed on were Robert Garcia, Jared Huffman, Ro Khanna, Mark Takano, Maxine Waters and Zoe Lofgren of California; Jim Hines of Connecticut; Rick Larsen and Adam Smith of Washington state; Jamie Raskin of Maryland; Bobby Scott of Virginia; Bennie Thompson of Mississippi; and Gregory Meeks and Joe Morelle of New York.Republican AGs want ballroomA brief led by the Republican Attorneys General Raúl Labrador of Idaho and Todd Rokita of Indiana argued the Supreme Court should side with Trump because the National Trust allegedly built its case on the “associational standing” of one of its board members who would not suffer harm.“This case is about more than a ballroom. It is about whether a passerby’s aesthetic objection to a government construction project furnishes not just the passerby standing, but an uninjured association standing to air its grievances in court,” the attorneys general wrote. The argument echoed Trump’s many public statements that the case against his ballroom rests on the objection of one person who sometimes walks by the White House.That risk is “of significant interest to States across the Nation,” they wrote.  “Amici States have extensive experience litigating against organizations that invoke associational standing as their ticket into court.”The attorneys general concluded: “The Court should not allow groups whose members claim offense to sue over virtually anything and everything.” A federal district judge in December had already denied the Trust’s initial request for a temporary restraining order based on the lack of irreparable harm for an initial plaintiff.The most recent lower court decision is based on an amended complaint filed by the Trust in early March.In addition to Idaho and Indiana, the Republican attorneys general who signed the brief are from Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee and Texas. Two members of the Arizona state legislature also signed it.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska AG sues City of Omaha over minimum wage ordinance
description: Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers announced he is suing the City of Omaha to enforce Nebraska’s minimum wage law against city ordinance.
text:
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers. Oct. 9, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers on Tuesday announced he is suing the City of Omaha to enforce Nebraska’s minimum wage law against its new city ordinance.
The lawsuit follows one against Lincoln city leaders who passed a similar measure. Hilgers’ office argues the state’s two largest cities are seeking a “power grab” after a supermajority of state lawmakers set a 1.75% annual growth rate for the minimum wage and said employers “may” pay 14- and 15-year-old workers $13.50, down from the current $15 minimum wage.
“Our Constitution does not permit the City of Omaha to repeal any portion of a statewide law passed by the Legislature,” Hilgers said in a Tuesday statement.
The local ordinances seek to maintain the 2022 voter-approved annual adjustment to the minimum wage based on inflation and prohibit paying any workers less than $15, except for a $13.50 training wage eligible for 16- to 19-year-old workers for the first 90 days of employment.
Under current state law, the minimum wage will increase to $15.26 on Jan. 1. The youth minimum wage will remain at $13.50 through 2029 and remain below $15 for nearly 40 years.
Legislative opponents had argued 1.75% annual increases would likely lag inflation.
Lancaster district judge grants injunction in state lawsuit against Lincoln’s minimum wage ordinance

Lancaster County District Judge Lori Maret on July 17 blocked Lincoln from enacting its ordinance. The order came one day before the Lincoln ordinance was set to take effect in tandem with the amended law. Maret stopped short of extending her order statewide.
Hilgers is asking a Douglas County District Court judge to similarly block the Omaha order, which is set to take effect Oct. 1, absent court action.
The Attorney General’s Office argues the ordinances will “inevitably” cause the cost of goods and services statewide to increase and require other communities to adjust to keep up. Hilgers’ team says the issue is a “matter of statewide concern,” so the Legislature has the final say.
Omaha Mayor John Ewing Jr. and Lincoln Mayor Leirion Gaylor Baird, both Democrats, signed their respective ordinances after they passed on a party-line vote with only Democratic council members in support in each city. In Lincoln, the ordinance passed 6-1. In Omaha, it passed 4-3.
The Omaha lawsuit names Ewing, Director Cailin Daly Dejillas of the City of Omaha Human Rights and Relations Department and all seven Omaha City Council members: Danny Begley, Aimee Melton, Pete Festersen, LaVonya Goodwin, Ron Hug, Don Rowe and Brinker Harding.
Begley, council president, sponsored the measure and cited residents’ overwhelming support for the 2022 ballot measure. Ewing said it would help families and was the “right thing to do.”
“I am aware of the legal issues surrounding this legislation,” Ewing said July 21 as his justification for signing the ordinance. “I am confident the city can successfully argue for Omaha having its own minimum wage ordinance.”
Others, such as Melton, urged caution and doubted whether Omaha had such authority.
In a June 4 letter to the Omaha City Council, City Attorney Matt Kuhse told the Omaha City Council that it could enact such an ordinance as a “home rule charter city,” which also faces a higher cost of living than other parts of the state. Hilgers disagrees.
Kuhse wrote: “Given the higher costs in Omaha, compared to the balance of Nebraska, the Legislature-enacted minimum wage increases may not be sufficient to deal with costs unique to Omaha. By utilizing its local control and ability to address issues distinctive to Omaha, this ordinance addresses that issue.”
