name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: New Orleans could have right-sized its courts, and now it’s happening the hard way
description: An inconvenient truth is being overshadowed by an increasingly tedious melodrama between Gov. Jeff Landry and Mayor Helena Moreno, and not many of my fellow New Orleanians are willing to admit it.
text:
Orleans Parish Criminal District Courthouse. (Louisiana Illuminator photo)An inconvenient truth is being overshadowed by an increasingly tedious melodrama between Gov. Jeff Landry and Mayor Helena Moreno, and not many of my fellow New Orleanians are willing to admit it.
It’s that the city’s court system is long overdue for a right-sizing to adjust for its roughly 25% population loss since Hurricane Katrina in 2005. Until Landry and the Republican-dominated legislature forced the issue this year, status quo was permitted for two decades. As a result, local leaders lost their opportunity to shape changes to their bloated judiciary.
Unlike the other 41 state judicial districts in Louisiana, New Orleans has separate civil and criminal courts along with a host of specialty venues.    
Until this year, New Orleans counted:

 12 criminal court judges and a magistrate; 
 14 civil court judges;  
 four juvenile court judges; 
 four city court judges who handle small claims and eviction cases; and
 another seven judges at its Municipal and Traffic Court.

New state laws have removed three criminal court judges and two from traffic court, and New Orleans’ separate criminal and civil clerks of court have been consolidated into a single agency. Landry and lawmakers have implied they’re not done with courthouse cuts, with the governor indicating he’s willing to call a special session for specifically that reason.
There was an opportunity, albeit slim, that the reductions could have been reasonably well received had Republicans made an efficiency argument. The governor and his boosters have instead turned up the volume on an anti-New Orleans campaign that got us to the current state of political discord.    
Any chance at harmony crumbled back in May when Republican Attorney General Liz Murrill sent pointed letters to Moreno, District Attorney Jason Williams and five New Orleans City Council members in May. It warned them they could be removed from office for attempting to call an election to fill the city’s consolidated clerk of court seat. 
The local reaction was equally unreasonable: An New Orleans grand jury indicted Murrill in July for intimidation and malfeasance over her letter. The charges were ultimately dropped, but Landry has launched a Louisiana State Police investigation into who initiated the indictment. 
Moreno and Williams have denied any involvement, and the governor says he’ll keep giving the mayor the silent treatment at least until the investigation concludes. 
This theater of the absurd might have ideological curtains, but make no mistake that this entire saga is about who’s in power behind the scenes.
Rewind back to the months immediately after Katrina when there was a grass-roots movement to merge New Orleans’ seven district assessors, each with disparate approaches to assigning property values, into a single agency. A group of influential and vocal citizens convinced state lawmakers, and then voters statewide, to change the Louisiana Constitution in 2006 to consolidate the assessor’s offices.
That same year, the legislature voted to combine Orleans Parish’s two sheriffs into a single seat. Civil Sheriff Paul Valteau opted not to run against Criminal Sheriff Marlin Gusman, who easily won the first election for the consolidated sheriff’s office in 2010. Gusman’s political clout was all the more remarkable, considering he oversaw a city jail under federal supervision for pervasive violence, contraband and abusive personnel.
The desire to continue streamlining in New Orleans waned as the city’s population recovered from Katrina. It dipped from 455,000 in July 2005 to just more than 200,000 immediately after the storm, peaking in 2018 at around 392,000. Its resident count has fallen by about 30,000 since then, and there’s still no local talk of scaling down the judiciary.
Instead, Landry, Murrill and the GOP-led legislature have steered the conversation, and they aren’t likely to give up that control even if New Orleans leaders indicate they’re willing to pare back on judge numbers.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: The Arctic Report Card is a unique asset to Alaska and the nation
description: For 20 years, the Arctic Report Card, supported by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, has delivered timely and accurate information on the Alaska and Arctic environment that takes raw observations and makes them understandable to anyone interested in what’s happening across the top of the world.
text:
An arctic fox on the tundra of the north slope of Alaska near a field camp of the Alaska Science Center.
(Photo by Ryan Askren
USGS, Alaska Science Center)Have you ever wondered about how sea ice and ocean temperatures are changing, marine debris in the Bering Strait, the spread of beavers into northwest Alaska, “rusting rivers” or community-based observations of Bering Sea salmon? For 20 years, the Arctic Report Card, supported by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, has delivered timely and accurate information on the Alaska and Arctic environment that takes raw observations and makes them understandable to anyone interested in what’s happening across the top of the world.
The rapidly changing Arctic environment brings challenges and opportunities to Alaska communities, our state and the United States, including food security and cultural continuity, commercial sustainability and development options, and national energy and security concerns. Nearly 20 percent of the United States’ land area is in Alaska, and Alaska is part of the much larger Arctic. But on August 10, 2026, as reported by the Alaska Beacon, NOAA ended support of the long-running Arctic Report Card.
Since 2006, the Arctic Report Card, supported by NOAA, has delivered timely and accurate information on the Alaska and Arctic environment in formats from plain language essays to a professional video to social media bites. Alaskans use the Arctic Report Card for many reasons, because it is a trusted, understandable and vetted source of environmental information and on-the-ground impacts across the Arctic. Starting in 2019, the Report Card has included perspectives rooted in the lived experiences and cultural knowledge of Indigenous peoples in Alaska and elsewhere in the Arctic. These are not models or projections or policy. The essays in the Report Card describe what’s happened in our part of the world.
Every autumn more than 100 authors from a dozen or more countries come together, volunteering their time and expertise to create a report, not for other specialists or academic journals, but for anyone who needs timely and accurate information about what’s happening in the Arctic environment. While written for non-specialists, the Arctic Report Card maintains strict scientific integrity through the peer-review process. That is coordinated by the Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme, and neither Report Card editors nor authors have any say in reviewer selection, nor do they know who provides reviews. 
Professional societies and international organizations around the world issue several annual reports summarizing yearly weather and climate conditions, but not all include the Arctic; all are released months after the fact and are largely or entirely focused on atmosphere and ocean conditions. The Arctic Report Card is unique in providing both timeliness of the information and the wide range of topics and is the only report that provides broad review of the climate and ecosystems of the Arctic.
The loss of NOAA’s support for the Arctic Report Card does not mean that observations go away, or that change stops. But without the Arctic Report Card, the broad array of information will be harder for non-specialists to find and interpret. I work as an Alaska climate specialist, but as a user of the Arctic Report Card for 20 years and an editor since 2020, I have learned so much about topics outside of my specialty. Over the years, I’ve heard similar comments from Alaskans across the state. 
The Arctic Report Card editorial team, dedicated authors and supporters are working hard to keep timely, accurate and accessible Arctic environmental observations available to everyone who relies on this annual report. However, the break in continuity with the first 20 reports and the elaborate interface developed during that time to make this information readily available will make it harder for Alaskans to find what they need in this time of rapid change. 
Rick Thoman works as a Climate Specialist with the Alaska Center for Climate Assessment and Preparedness at the International Arctic Research Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks. The views expressed are solely the author’s and do not constitute the university’s official position.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Emergency management director resigns to join Collins campaign for governor
description: Florida Division of Emergency Management Director Kevin Guthrie has resigned to join Lt. Gov. Jay Collins’ campaign for governor.  Gov. Ron DeSantis said Tuesday he accepted Guthrie’s resignation to avoid “a situation where there’s politics and emergency management. I think you got to choose one or the other.” Collins’ campaign for governor could end Tuesday[...]
text:
Kevin Guthrie, director of the Florida Division of Emergency Management, fields questions from reporters at the state emergency operations center in Tallahassee in advance of a winter weather storm on Jan. 21, 2025. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Florida Division of Emergency Management Director Kevin Guthrie has resigned to join Lt. Gov. Jay Collins’ campaign for governor. 
Gov. Ron DeSantis said Tuesday he accepted Guthrie’s resignation to avoid “a situation where there’s politics and emergency management. I think you got to choose one or the other.”
Collins’ campaign for governor could end Tuesday, the day after he announced Guthrie as his running mate.
Florida’s primary election will decide who Republican voters want to run as their nominee for the next governor. Collins, once seen by some as a potential successor to DeSantis, did not receive the governor’s endorsement. Polls have not indicated Collins is a favorite to win Tuesday.
DeSantis said Guthrie has “done a great job” responding to hurricanes, flying Floridians caught in harm’s way overseas back to the state, responding to the COVID-19 pandemic, and enforcing immigration laws.
“If people want to choose politics, more power to them. I didn’t necessarily think that was something that Kevin aspired to but, given that he’s doing that, I think it’s important that we have emergency management just focused on emergency management,” DeSantis said.
Guthrie, commonly accompanying DeSantis during TV hits to tell Floridians about hurricanes hitting the state, has held the position since May 2021. He took over from Jared Moskowitz, now a Democrat in the U.S. House.
Florida Department of Transportation Secretary Jared Perdue will take the reins at FDEM, DeSantis said during a higher education roundtable in Sarasota Tuesday.
“It’s a well-oiled machine, we’ve got a lot of great people over there. We’re not going to miss a beat,” DeSantis said. 
Although DeSantis has not endorsed in the GOP primary, he wished Guthrie well.
“This is something that I think he believed in and wanted to do and I wish him all the luck in the world,” DeSantis said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi Today welcomes new multimedia producer
description: Barnes joins a multimedia team responsible for collaborating with reporters and editors to produce social videos based on Mississippi Today’s reporting.
text:
Mississippi Today is pleased to welcome Blake Barnes as its new multimedia producer.
Barnes joins a multimedia team responsible for collaborating with reporters and editors to produce social videos based on Mississippi Today’s reporting. He will also contribute to the production of the newsroom’s video podcasts, as well as long-form video projects. He began work Monday.

The hire reflects Mississippi Today’s commitment to reaching audiences and creating impact across multiple mediums.

“Blake is a proven producer whose work I’ve respected and admired,” said Michael Guidry, Mississippi Today’s editorial director of multimedia. “His passion for telling Mississippi stories makes him an awesome addition to this newsroom, and I am excited for what he will deliver for our audiences.”

Barnes most recently served as a producer at Mississippi Public Broadcasting, where he directed Everlasting: The New Generation.
He grew up on a farm in Ludlow, Mississippi with a family of storytellers. He attended East Central Community College, then Delta State University. He’s called Jackson home for the last five years.
“I’ve always loved Mississippi,” said Barnes. “This is my home, and I think telling stories is a way I can help push the state forward. I’m looking forward to the opportunities Mississippi Today will offer me in this way, and continuing to tell and to preserve these local Mississippi stories.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Every SC student to get free breakfast with state funding
description: Legislators spent $2.8 million to cover breakfasts not already included in a federal program.
text:
South Carolina students who don't already receive free breakfast could have their meals covered with funding included in the state budget that went into effect Monday, Aug. 17, 2026. (File/Spenser Heaps for the Utah News Dispatch)COLUMBIA — Every K-12 student in the state will be able to eat breakfast for free at school this year with funding included in the state budget.
The $2.8 million included in the spending package that went into effect Monday is expected to cover the cost of breakfasts this school year for all students who don’t already qualify under another program, regardless of their parents’ income, according to the Department of Education.
“Every student deserves the opportunity to reach their full potential, and access to a healthy breakfast is one important way to support that goal,” agency spokesman Kinard Lisbon said in a statement.
The agency is still determining the exact number of meals the money will cover and the details of rolling out the program, Lisbon said.
Gov. Henry McMaster recommended paying for all students’ breakfasts in his budget proposal at the beginning of the year.
In his executive budget, the governor suggested spending $8.7 million to cover an estimated 4.1 million meals, saying every student should get breakfast for free at school.
In actuality, because of federal funding that already provides free meals to most students, McMaster’s budget proposal would have been enough to also provide lunches at no cost across the state, according to the Department of Education.
“Providing students with access to breakfast at school will help ensure they have the support they need to focus, learn, and succeed in the classroom,” McMaster said in a statement to the SC Daily Gazette about the Legislature’s designation.
More SC schools are offering free meals to all. A new law encourages participation.

Students can already receive free meals at school if their parents’ income is 130% of the federal poverty level or less. For a family of four, that’s $42,900 or less each year.
If a quarter of a school district’s population meets that requirement, the district can sign up for a federal program that allows every student to receive free meals without needing to apply.
Just one school district, Fort Mill (York 4), doesn’t qualify for the federal program. During the 2025-2026 school year, 10 qualifying districts opted not to participate, though all but one offered the program at some schools, according to state Department of Education data.
The districts that haven’t signed up pointed to the cost of running the program. The federal government pays for a portion of the meals, but districts must make up the rest, depending on how many students qualify.
The extra state funding will make sure that’s no longer a concern.
“This is one of the best investments in K-12 in this year’s budget,” said Patrick Kelly, lobbyist for Palmetto State Teachers Association.
If a student’s physical needs aren’t meant, such as eating a balanced meal in the mornings, they aren’t going to be able to learn as much or perform as well in the classroom as their peers, said Kelly, who also teaches advanced government classes in Blythewood.
“It’s impossible to learn and do the work of learning if a student is hungry,” Kelly said.
Making the program widely available could help reach students who qualify but whose parents didn’t know about the help, said Sue Berkowitz, director of policy for Appleseed Legal Justice Center. In districts that don’t offer free meals at every school, parents must submit an application.
Even if a student’s family doesn’t qualify for free meals, the offer can make life a little easier, Berkowitz said.
Many families live just above the cutoff line for certain benefits, meaning they might be struggling to pay their bills as well, she said. All families have seen grocery prices, along with other costs, rise with inflation in recent years.

“All families can use that help right now,” Berkowitz said.
At the same time, the number of people using grocery benefits has decreased, helping fewer people keep their pantries stocked, she said.
Last month, more than 235,200 families (with nearly 482,000 total South Carolinians) received federal grocery aid. That’s about 35,000 fewer households — 83,000 fewer people — than a year earlier, according to state Department of Social Services data.
Students whose families are enrolled in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, commonly known as food stamps, automatically qualify for free meals, meaning students whose parents stopped receiving SNAP might also lose their school meals, according to the federal think tank Food Research and Action Center.
Statewide free breakfast “couldn’t have come at a better time,” Berkowitz said.
Berkowitz hopes future budgets make all meals free for all students, she said.
“Kids need lunch, too,” Berkowitz said.

text:
Gov. Abigail Spanberger. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)Gov. Abigail Spanberger announced Executive Order 19 Tuesday afternoon, which is designed to strengthen Virginia’s preparedness for natural disasters and other emergencies and streamline the state’s response to crises.
The announcement comes ahead of hurricane season for states along the country’s southeastern coast. But the order extended beyond natural catastrophes, with the governor saying Virginia “faces an increasingly dynamic and complex threat environment that demands a modern, integrated approach to preparedness.” 
She named “public health emergencies, cyber incidents, threats to critical infrastructure, supply chain disruptions, acts of violence, emerging technologies, and other complex hazards” that the order addresses by creating a “unified readiness framework,” Spanberger wrote. 
The measure is meant to strengthen emergency communications, operations and planning, bolster retention and training for emergency response workers, promote community partnerships and enhance digital security. 
This means that executive branch agencies with responsibilities related to emergency management, public safety and public health will designate a Unified Readiness Coordinator, participate in implementing the framework, share requested data and participate in statewide assessments and planning.
Private-sector entities, local first responders and nonprofit organizations will also be involved in the endeavor. 
The coordination “breaks down operational silos and builds a stronger, more resilient Commonwealth,” Spanberger said in a press release announcing the order. 
“By bringing together our first responders, state agencies, businesses, and community partners, we are ensuring Virginia is fully equipped to anticipate, respond to, and recover from any threat,” she added.

description: The interim dean of Drake University’s law school said the institution is in the process of finding both a permanent replacement for the former dean and the leader of one of its clinics as students come back to campus. Jerry Anderson stepped back into the role of Drake Law dean this month following the announcement […]
text:
Drake University has selected faculty member Jerry Anderson to serve as interim dean of its law school. (Photo courtesy of Drake University)The interim dean of Drake University’s law school said the institution is in the process of finding both a permanent replacement for the former dean and the leader of one of its clinics as students come back to campus.
Jerry Anderson stepped back into the role of Drake Law dean this month following the announcement that then-dean Roscoe Jones would step down. Anderson will remain in the position, which he also served in from 2016 to 2024, until a national search has yielded a new dean.
Provost Joseph Valenzano III, also appointed to his position this summer, is heading the national search effort, Anderson said, and is currently putting together a search committee. The job application will open Oct. 1.

“The provost is planning to have the search concluded by February, so that we can expect a new dean to start next summer,” Anderson said. “It’s always the best time for a new dean to start.”
Drake isn’t working with any outside firms currently to aid in the search, he said.
Also without a leader is Drake University’s Wrongful Convictions Clinic, which has paused its operation since the firing of former director Erica Nichols Cook in January. Job advertisements have already been released for the director position, Anderson said, with the same goal of having someone selected and starting on campus next summer. This search is also a national one, he said, saying the clinic is “a very specialized kind of practice.”
William Amor, who spent 22 years in prison for murder before being acquitted in a new trial, left around $3 million to the wrongful convictions clinic, Anderson said. The clinic is described in the director job posting as an entity that “provides meaningful experiential learning opportunities for students related to wrongful convictions and manifest injustice work.”
According to reporting from the Des Moines Register, conflicts over how the funds should be used and legal misunderstandings between Drake and the trustee for Amor’s estate led to Nichols Cook’s firing. She said to the Register that Amor, who died in 2023, wanted to leave the money to her as she had represented him previously.
“We’re excited by the possibilities for new leadership in that role,” Anderson said. “It’s definitely something that we’re committed to, and we have this endowment now that is supporting that work, that means that we have a long-term commitment to that clinic.”
A “really robust” cohort of 140 new students started their first-year orientation Tuesday, with the most out-of-state students the school has had in his 35 years working there, Anderson said. Application numbers have increased by 75% over the past four years, a trend Anderson attributes to top-100 rankings in the past few years and efforts Jones took to travel the country and “raise the national profile of Drake.”
One of Anderson’s main focuses in his temporary role is rural practice and ensuring students have the ability and training to work in rural areas, something he said is helped by a new law passed in the 2026 legislative session providing a framework for attorney loan forgiveness.
He said he will also continue to “seek alumni support” for scholarships for students, as new borrowing limits have been placed on federal loans.
“We definitely want to keep the momentum going, and I think they selected me because … I’ve done the job before,” Anderson said. “We cannot have any downtime in terms of keeping the momentum going.”

title: Ferguson, Baumgartner seek meeting with Trump on WA wildfires
description: Washington’s Democratic governor and a Republican congressman are asking President Donald Trump to meet with them to discuss the wildfires that have devastated parts of the state this summer. In their letter Monday, Gov. Bob Ferguson and U.S. Rep. Michael Baumgartner, who represents eastern Washington, told the Republican president they want to discuss the s[...]
text:
A Cal Fire firefighter works amid the remains of homes destroyed in the Old Trails Fire on Aug. 6, 2026 in Spokane, Washington. (Photo by Mario Tama/Getty Images)Washington’s Democratic governor and a Republican congressman are asking President Donald Trump to meet with them to discuss the wildfires that have devastated parts of the state this summer.
In their letter Monday, Gov. Bob Ferguson and U.S. Rep. Michael Baumgartner, who represents eastern Washington, told the Republican president they want to discuss the state’s forthcoming request for federal recovery aid after the fires in Spokane and elsewhere. 
“Thank you again for your help with the devastating fires in our state and your personal engagement on this disaster,” they wrote. “We appreciate all that you and your team are doing to provide assistance during this very difficult time.”
They wrote that Ferguson’s staff was communicating with White House officials to see if the meeting is doable. 
The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Nearly 800,000 acres, or upward of 1,200 square miles, have burned in wildfires this year in Washington, making it already one of the worst fire seasons in history.
In and around Spokane, the state’s second-largest city, more than 800 buildings were destroyed and tens of thousands of residents were ordered to evacuate when a trio of fires erupted in early August. Other major fires have burned across central and eastern Washington, with some of the smoke descending at times into western Washington. 
Ferguson earlier this month invited Trump, who he’s criticized fiercely over other issues, to tour the damage in Spokane. It’s unclear if the president responded, but Interior Secretary Doug Burgum came in the aftermath of the fires there and on the Colville Reservation in northeast Washington.
Baumgartner, a former state senator and Spokane County treasurer, said on social media that he appreciates “how responsive the White House has been to the E. Washington fires.”
“And I’m pleased at how unified both Republican and Democrat elected leaders at the Federal, state and local level have been in working to get those impacted the help they need,” the first-term congressman continued. “Much work to do.”
The state’s request for a major disaster declaration will follow a previous one Trump approved to provide federal emergency support for the eastern Washington wildfires. If approved, the disaster declaration through the Federal Emergency Management Agency will allow residents who lost their homes or were otherwise affected by the fires to get federal aid. 
Ferguson and Baumgartner believe this would help thousands of Washingtonians. 
“Many of those individuals have lost everything,” they wrote in their letter. 
The disaster declaration would be similar to what Trump OK’ed after the historic flooding last December, which resulted in the distribution of upward of $14 million in federal assistance. In that case, it took about five weeks for the governor’s request for individual aid to be submitted. 
The federal government can also provide money for governments and tribes to deal with infrastructure damage.
Ferguson last week signed an emergency proclamation to expand state assistance for fire victims.
Ferguson and Baumgartner have rarely found common ground since they both took office last year. Baumgartner even challenged Ferguson to a debate last year during the federal government shutdown.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: New poll: Most in NC don’t see themselves as primarily political
description: About one-third of North Carolinians identify with President Donald Trump’s “make America great again” movement.
text:
(Image: AdobeStock)More extreme ideological groups like MAGA and Democratic Socialists have dominated the national headlines in recent months. But a new poll by Elon University shows most North Carolinians prefer to describe themselves in less political terms. 
The poll, released Tuesday, asked 800 North Carolina adults how they described themselves across 30 different political, economic, cultural, and lifestyle identities. They were offered labels ranging from capitalist to politically moderate to beach person, with respondents answering how much they identified with each, if at all.
About one-third of North Carolinians identify with President Donald Trump’s “make America great again” movement.
At the same time, about 30% of North Carolinians identify as democratic socialists, and one-fifth identify as libertarian.
By contrast, many more respondents identified more strongly with broader group identities like working class at 78%, anti-racist at 74%, and proud North Carolinian at 74%. 
The findings indicate that political identities receiving the greatest public attention represent a smaller share of the electorate than broader groups that unite many residents, according to Jason Husser, director of the Elon University Poll. 
While political polls typically ask candidates who they’re likely to support in an election, there haven’t been surveys in North Carolina about what percentage of people are part of larger social groups and political movements, Husser told NC Newsline.
“For instance, prior to this survey, I wouldn’t have been able to tell you what percent of North Carolinians were democratic socialists or considered themselves LGBTQ-rights advocates,” he said. “We know that many of these political identities end up shaping how people align with parties.”
Among the least frequently chosen affinity groups for all respondents, 39% said they were an LGBTQ rights advocate, 32% said small business owner, and 41% said fiscally conservative. 
With three months remaining before the midterm elections in November, the results could shape how candidates orient their campaigns. 
Some campaigns run on appealing to the largest possible voter group, even if it means they lose support from their own party, Husser said. Others focus more on their dedicated voter base, aiming for high turnout, before turning to picking up independents. 
A candidate running on the former strategy could target, for example, voters identifying as working class, since it’s a large portion of the electorate. 
Poll: Majority of NC voters oppose data centers, aren’t worried about voter fraud

MAGA identity could play a pivotal role in North Carolina’s U.S. Senate race, where Republican U.S. Sen. Thom Tillis’ retirement leaves an open seat. Trump has endorsed former Republican National Committee chair Michael Whatley, who trailed Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper by 11 points in a poll released by Elon last week. 
Husser said winning coalitions of voters are often built by attachments that go beyond party labels alone.
“Outcomes in North Carolina elections are driven not only by whether the state has more Democrats or more Republicans, but also whether politicians can move those who identify with groups like working class, progressives or Second Amendment advocates,” he said in a statement. “We measured the scope of some of the largest politically relevant group identities in North Carolina to offer insight into why some ideas stick in the state and others struggle.”
Elon University and YouGov surveyed 800 North Carolina adults between July 23 and July 31. The margin of error is plus or minus 4.42 percentage points.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana GOP selects Kronebusch as replacement candidate in disputed Senate race
description: Members of the Montana Republican Party on Monday nominated Ted Kronebusch as a replacement candidate for Senate District 9, even as a lawsuit filed by current candidate Rep. Llew Jones to stay on the ballot is ongoing.  Kronebusch is chairman of the Pondera County Republican Central Committee and a close friend of Jones for decades. […]
text:
Rep. Llew Jones, R-Conrad, chair of the Appropriations Committee, chats with lawmakers on the House Floor. (Micah Drew/ Daily Montanan)Members of the Montana Republican Party on Monday nominated Ted Kronebusch as a replacement candidate for Senate District 9, even as a lawsuit filed by current candidate Rep. Llew Jones to stay on the ballot is ongoing. 
Kronebusch is chairman of the Pondera County Republican Central Committee and a close friend of Jones for decades. Both are longtime businessmen from Conrad.
Jones has sued to stay on the ballot because a new interpretation of term limits by Attorney General Austin Knudsen would mean he’s out of time despite his primary win in June. Kronebusch is a fellow plaintiff in the lawsuit.
During a Zoom meeting Monday of the 12-person appointing committee, Kronebusch received roughly three-quarters of votes from representatives of the four counties comprising SD 9.
“I’ve also been involved in politics from the Republican side for as long as I’ve been around,” Kronebusch said at the meeting. “I’m a conservative person, and I’m concerned about what my constituents feel and what’s important to them. And using the conservative values, I would vote in that manner.”
Also nominated was Rep. Zach Wirth of Helena. Wirth lost to Jones in the June primary in one of the most contentious races that embodied the split between a more moderate faction of Republicans, represented by Jones, and hard-line conservatives such as Wirth backed by the state GOP. 
Jones has served continuously in the Legislature since 2005, moving between the House and Senate regularly, and as the architect of the state budget is often considered one of the most powerful lawmakers in the state. He spent the last eight years in the House and filed to run for the Senate this year. 
But Jones’ status as a candidate is in limbo following the new legal opinion by Knudsen reinterpreting the state’s constitutional term limits and ending the practice by lawmakers to serve indefinitely, so long as they routinely switch Legislative chambers. 
A lawsuit filed on behalf of Jones, Republican Rep. Steve Fitzpatrick of Great Falls, and Kronebusch last week argued that the Attorney General cannot alter the rules so close to Election Day, and that the request for a legal opinion from Senate President Matt Regier, a Kalispell Republican and hardline Republican, was improper. 
The Montana secretary of state must certify ballots by Thursday, putting the legal process on a tight timeline. A hearing before Lewis and Clark District Judge Christopher Abbott to stop the new interpretation from taking effect so close to ballot certification is scheduled for Tuesday afternoon. 

Because of the quick turnaround for ballot certification, the state GOP convened a nominating committee of the four affected counties to select a replacement candidate Monday evening. 
Each committee questioned the two nominees, asking them about their respective stances on abortion, Medicaid expansion, and limiting government and the state budget. 
“We have laws that say we have to be budget neutral and so we already have a surplus,” Kronebusch said. “I would ask that we continue on … and I would also look to keep our budgeted surplus as low as possible.”
Wirth took a harder line on the budget, following criticisms lobbied by more conservative lawmakers against the latest Jones-engineered budget. Jones served as chairman of the House Appropriations Committee.
“We’ve got to rein ourselves in,” Wirth said. “ Then, if we lower the taxes that we have — on the state income tax and the state property taxes — if we can bring that down, that’s going to leave a little bit more room down there for the counties and the cities.“
Both candidates spoke about being Catholics staunchly against abortion.
Wirth received 25% of the vote from committee members. 
Though Kronebusch is an ally of Jones, who has been a thorn in the side of the state GOP, party Chairman Art Wittich said he believed in the process that played out. 
“I think the process was fair, and the counties spoke,” Witch told members of the press after the meeting. “I’m just satisfied that we’ll be able to have a Republican name on the ballot, so that a Democrat doesn’t win by default.”
Wittich said he wasn’t sure if the party would make it a priority in the upcoming legislative session to more clearly define term limits, but added that in Montana, having strict term limits is popular among voters. 
“Obviously, the initiative passed almost 30 years ago, and it still continues to poll highly for people,” Wittich told reporters. “People don’t want professional politicians, and you know, our platform is to follow the Constitution.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma Republicans raise millions ahead of key runoff elections
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Millions more dollars have poured into an already historically expensive GOP primary race for Oklahoma governor leading up to an Aug. 25 runoff. Campaign finance reports filed Monday with the state Ethics Commission — the first reports since the June 16 primary election — show Attorney General Gentner Drummond raised $2.47 million […]
text:
Gentner Drummond, left, and Mike Mazzei are pictured with their wives. Both are running for the Republican nomination for Oklahoma governor. (Photos by Nuria Martinez-Keel and Ace Cuervo/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Millions more dollars have poured into an already historically expensive GOP primary race for Oklahoma governor leading up to an Aug. 25 runoff.
Campaign finance reports filed Monday with the state Ethics Commission — the first reports since the June 16 primary election — show Attorney General Gentner Drummond raised $2.47 million from individual donors and political action committees over the past two months. Drummond, a rancher from Hominy who narrowly led the Republican primary, also loaned his campaign $500,000 over that time, bringing the total amount of his personal loans to $3 million since launching his bid for governor.
His runoff opponent, financial planner and former state Sen. Mike Mazzei, of Tulsa, has loaned his campaign $11.6 million in total, including $710,000 since the June primary election, according to his campaign finance reports.
Mazzei, who is endorsed by President Donald Trump, raised more than $1.54 million from political action committees and individual contributors in the two months between the primary and runoff elections. Among his campaign donors were term-limited Gov. Kevin Stitt and First Lady Sarah Stitt, who each gave $3,300.
Drummond and Mazzei advanced to the Aug. 25 runoff election as the top two vote earners from the Republican primary, where four of the leading candidates poured more than $22 million of zero-interest personal loans into their campaigns.
In an interview with Oklahoma Voice ahead of the campaign finance filing deadline, Mazzei said he views his campaign loans as “an investment in the people of Oklahoma.”
Drummond said he wishes the state had limits on how much political candidates can self-fund. Under the current rules, highly qualified men and women can’t afford to run a competitive campaign unless they have personal wealth, he said.
“I wish that we had a restriction in Oklahoma,” Drummond said. “I think that that would create greater parity for non-independently wealthy candidates to get in the race.”
Hundreds of thousands contributed to other statewide campaigns
No other statewide race this year comes close to the gubernatorial election in the amount of fundraising and self-funding involved. But multiple candidates have raised hundreds of thousands of dollars in other runoff elections between Republicans, who hold every statewide office in Oklahoma.
In the high-interest Republican primary for state superintendent, Robert Franklin and James Taylor advanced to a runoff by defeating opponents who had out-fundraised them.
James Taylor, left, will face off against Robert Franklin, right, in the Republican runoff for state superintendent on Aug. 25. (Provided photos)
Taylor, a teacher and pastor from Oklahoma City, ran a mostly self-funded $7,600 campaign before the June primary. Support for him has swelled since he made the runoff election. 
He has raised $42,462 from individual donors over the past two months, according to his campaign finance reports.
Franklin, a longtime educator and school administrator from Sand Springs, has raised $128,446 from individual contributions and political action committees since he finished in the lead of the crowded GOP primary. That’s more than double the amount of money his campaign collected before making the runoff.
Franklin, who has been endorsed by over 200 current and former local district superintendents, received many of his campaign contributions from fellow educators and education-focused groups, Ethics Commission records show.
The race for Oklahoma labor commissioner also features a Republican runoff between state representatives John Pfeiffer and Kevin West. 
John Pfeiffer, left, and Kevin West, who are vying for the Republican nomination for Labor Commissioner, are pictured. (Provided photos)
Pfeiffer, of Orlando, received $93,550 in individual and political action committee contributions since the primary election while West, of Moore, raised $39,855, according to their campaign finance reports.
In the GOP runoff race for insurance commissioner, Marty Quinn leads Bob Sullivan in fundraising since June. 
Quinn, an insurance broker and former state lawmaker from Owasso, reported raising $153,302 in individual contributions, political action committee donations and a personal loan of $6,000. 
Marty Quinn, left, and Bob Sullivan, who are vying for the Republican nomination for Insurance Commissioner, are pictured. (Provided photos)
Sullivan, an insurance agent from Inola, raised $100,410 from donors and political action committees. His latest campaign finance reports show no personal loans over the past two months, though he poured $50,000 of his own money into his campaign before the June primary.
Senior reporter Barbara Hoberock contributed to this report.

name: VTDigger
title: Psychiatric hospital beds save lives
description:
Closing beds for acute psychiatric care leaves people in crisis with nowhere to go, and medication alone hasn't filled the gap.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Psychiatric hospital beds save lives.
text:
Dear Editor,
The closure of beds for patients suffering from severe mental illness is the worst news possible for those in the midst of a psychotic episode. In 1960, I spent five months at Forest Hospital in Des Plaines, Illinois, living through a horror that, in the end, turned out to be a gift to all my relationships: with my husband, three tiny daughters, parents, brothers and a host of extended family going through their own agony. 
If there had not been a hospital for me, I don’t know whether I would be the healthy, contributing individual with a loving mate, devoted daughters and sons-in-law, four grandchildren, two great-grandchildren, and friends and colleagues on both coasts today, who are inspired by our longevity. I give talks all over Vermont and California, our winter home, to encourage Americans to recognize the need for hospitals.
With the Lanterman-Petris-Short Act going into operation in 1972, large state psychiatric hospitals closed due to the general opinion that they violated patients’ rights. Psychotic and schizophrenic patients are a hard population to deal with, as any family who has suffered along with their affected loved one can tell you. We see those patients homeless today on the streets. Among that population are some like me, who could have been living productive lives if there had been a hospital bed for them at the critical moment. 
A major reason private hospitals like Forest and metropolitan facilities closed was the improvement of medication and diagnosis, which were far cheaper options for governments. The thought was that medication would supplant hospitals, and all those suffering from mental illness would soon be well, if the diagnosis could just zero in on the right medication. 

READ MORE

We see the failure of that hope today. 
Some of our brightest and most sensitive human beings are being lost due to the lack of hospital beds in the early stages. Psychosis is a wild, altered reality, an extreme aberration, and tends to settle down after a period, like any overly excited condition. The missing element today is a place apart for that first wildness to spend itself, so the patient can be worked with through the marvelous therapies available now.
Julie Howard ParkerGranville, Vt.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Lisa Demuth keeps focus on fraud, ties Klobuchar to Minnesota’s fraud scandal
description: Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth said Tuesday that if elected governor in November, she will tackle Minnesota’s fraud crisis by banning transfers of public dollars to foreign countries; recouping public dollars lost to fraud; and firing all current agency heads and deputy commissioners. Firing commissioners wouldn’t be groundbreaking: Demuth would be the[...]
text:
House Speaker Lisa Demuth, the GOP nominee for Minnesota governor, and her running mate Ryan Wilson spoke at a Capitol press conference on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Michelle Griffith/Minnesota Reformer)Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth said Tuesday that if elected governor in November, she will tackle Minnesota’s fraud crisis by banning transfers of public dollars to foreign countries; recouping public dollars lost to fraud; and firing all current agency heads and deputy commissioners.
Firing commissioners wouldn’t be groundbreaking: Demuth would be the first Republican governor in 16 years and a housecleaning would be expected.
Demuth, who gave her first press conference since winning the GOP nomination last week, said she would implement the proposals in her first 90 days as governor as part of an updated fraud prevention plan. Fraud in Minnesota’s social safety net programs has exploded in recent years and has caused intense national scrutiny of state Democratic leaders. Backlash to the fraud scandal led to Gov. Tim Walz terminating his bid for a third term earlier this year.
Demuth sought to tie Democratic-Farmer-Labor nominee for governor U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar to the fraud in Minnesota’s public programs, even though the majority of the theft came from state-administered programs.
“Fraud was exploding here in the state of Minnesota (and) Amy Klobuchar continually praised Tim Walz as a great governor and an incredible leader,” Demuth said. “Now she is Gov. Walz’s handpicked candidate to replace him. That is not what Minnesota needs.”
The House speaker also criticized Klobuchar’s lack of action and public statements about fraud since the scandal became public. Demuth’s campaign printed out over 1,000 press releases from Klobuchar’s office from 2022 to 2025, and placed the tall stack of papers on a stool. Demuth said there was not one mention of fraud.
“This is not taking fraud seriously. Three years, 1,000 press releases, no mention of the taxpayer fraud that was happening here,” said Ryan Wilson, Demuth’s running mate.
House Speaker Lisa Demuth’s campaign for governor printed out over 1,000 press releases from Sen. Amy Klobuchar from 2022 to 2025. Demuth said none of them mention the fraud in Minnesota’s social safety net programs. (Photo by Michelle Griffith/Minnesota Reformer)
Klobuchar also has proposed a fraud prevention plan that includes a top-to-bottom audit of state government, a “do not pay” database for providers convicted of fraud and creating anti-fraud units in state agencies.
The DFL Party Chair Richard Carlbom released a statement after Demuth’s press conference noting that former U.S. Attorney Andy Luger, who prosecuted the Feeding Our Future scheme, is supporting Klobuchar’s campaign and said Demuth’s plan is “empty political rhetoric.”
“Their records are clear: Amy Klobuchar fought for and delivered more prosecutors to go after the fraud, while Lisa Demuth has spent her many years in state government on political posturing instead,” Carlbom said.
Demuth’s fraud prevention plan — which was light on details — includes banning “all transfers of fraud to foreign countries,” she said. It’s unclear how she would implement such a ban, but she said she would work with the Legislature to get it done. Demuth also said she would pass legislation so the state can more easily recoup the dollars lost to fraud and seize a fraudster’s assets, though again, it’s unclear what that legislation is.
Demuth also touted legislation she shepherded earlier this year that created an independent office of inspector general and allocating millions to update technology in Minnesota’s counties, which administer many public programs.
As much as Demuth and Republicans would like to make the election about fraud, however, she’s also tied to an unpopular Republican presidential administration.
Reporters asked Demuth to comment about court documents showing that federal investigators engaged in a wide-ranging surveillance effort of labor unions and progressive groups during Operation Metro Surge. Demuth refused to answer.
“We are absolutely focused on what is going on here in the state of Minnesota. As I mentioned: fraud, affordability, education. That’s where my focus is,” Demuth said.
Reporters pressed her on whether she had thoughts on the government surveilling Minnesotans.
“I’m going with what I hear from Minnesotans right now, which is top of mind: fraud,” she said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Bridgeport exhibit shows Greene Homes through residents’ eyes: ‘It’s our story to tell’
description: Photos documented deteriorating buildings, while challenging the idea that the Bridgeport complex can be reduced to a collection of problems.
text:
Inside the Charles F. Greene Homes public housing complex, residents have learned to live with elevators that break down often, mold in aging buildings, broken windows, unsafe basements and hallways where strangers sometimes gather.
But the photographs residents took this year as part of a photovoice project were never meant to tell only the story about what is broken.
They also captured the people who live there, the places they find comfort, the friendships, the beauty and the community they fear could disappear as Greene Homes moves toward demolition and an uncertain future.
For five weeks this spring, eight Greene Homes residents worked on the photovideo project with the organization PT Partners and Sacred Heart University staffers Tricia Lewis, an assistant professor, and Julia Bates, an assistant teaching professor. Residents took photographs of their community, discussed what the images meant to them and selected the work they wanted to share publicly.
The resulting exhibit at BPT Creates took place earlier this week and gave residents control over how their community was represented. 
Greene Homes resident Deshawn Russell shares his experiences and concerns about life in the development. Credit: Gary Judkins / Pivot Language Media
Greene Homes, in Bridgeport’s Hollow neighborhood, is home to more than 700 residents, most of whom identify as Black or Latino. Historical material displayed alongside the photographs describes the original purpose of the public housing as providing decent and safe homes for families.
More than seven decades later, residents say the conditions inside Greene Homes tell a different story.
Deshawn Russell, who has lived there since 2009, said the project gave residents a way to document what they experience every day.
“I had to pause and really look at the bigger picture and realize, OK, this is really happening,” Russell said. “We’re finally going to basically bring receipts on what’s really going on, put it in the face of society, and show them what we are going through.”
Built in 1950, the development’s five eight-story buildings are equipped with elevators. But the photographs document one elevator that residents say is frequently out of service, along with mold, damaged windows, broken areas of the grounds and poorly maintained laundry facilities. One photograph shows a basement where residents said people sleep, with the smell of urine lingering in the space. 
For Russell, those problems are not occasional inconveniences. They affect the most basic parts of daily life. He recalled recovering from surgery while an elevator was out and watching people climb the stairs to bring him paperwork. 
He also photographed the hallway outside his apartment for the photovideo project. “I hate walking through my hallway and seeing garbage and writing on the walls and stickers on the doors,” Russell said.
The exhibit’s five themes — damage and disrespect, addictions and bad habits, escape, once a community and “who is this for?” — reflect the complicated picture residents wanted to present. Alongside photographs of deterioration and neglect are images of fashion, nature, the sky and places where residents find comfort.

Greene Homes resident Otika Fulton speaks about the conditions residents face and the importance of having their voices heard. Credit: Gary Judkins / Pivot Language Media

Otika Fulton, a former Greene Homes resident, said outsiders can easily see public housing only through the problems they associate with it. She said that misses the people who live there.
“It’s not the projects; it’s the people in the projects,” Fulton said. “It’s never the building; it’s the people in the building.”
Fulton said residents are grateful to have housing, but that gratitude should not mean accepting poor conditions.
“They’re making the outside look beautiful, and we look, and we’re living horrible at the inside,” she said.
She compared it to “putting glitter on mold.”
Still, Fulton said the conditions have not erased the sense of community among residents. She described neighbors looking out for one another and said she often thinks about residents whose apartments are in worse condition than the one she lived in.
That sense of community is part of what former residents fear losing.
Angie Rendon lived at Greene Homes for three years beginning in 2021. She said those who’ve lived in the buildings should be the ones telling the story because they are the ones who lived it.
She said people in positions of power can take residents’ experiences, reinterpret them and make decisions based on what they want rather than what residents need. “When you let other people tell it, it doesn’t get told in the way that it needs to,” Rendon said.
Greene Homes residents have been living with the possibility of demolition for years. Mayor Joe Ganim announced plans in 2018 to demolish and rebuild the development. In 2023, Park City Communities, which manages Bridgeport’s public housing, received a Choice Neighborhoods Initiative grant to begin planning for the demolition and redevelopment of Greene Homes as part of a broader effort to revitalize the Hollow neighborhood. 
But residents say the future remains unclear while repairs go unaddressed.
“What stood out to me with some of the disturbing photos is the fact that housing and maintenance see the issues, and they ignore it,” Rendon said. “It doesn’t matter how many work orders you put in. It doesn’t matter how many times you go to the office. Their excuses for the past two years have been the same thing. Well, demolition is coming. Demolition is coming. But no one should have to live like that.”
Greene Homes residents Otika Fulton and Deshawn Russell join former resident Angie Rendon to reflect on life, community and change. Rendon laughs during a lighter moment shared by the panelists. Credit: Gary Judkins / Pivot Language Media
Park City Communities did not respond Tuesday to questions about the concerns raised by residents.
Lanice Johnson, who has lived at Greene Homes for five years, said the elevators are among her biggest concerns, particularly for older residents who cannot easily use the stairs when they stop working. She said the elevators can break down frequently, leaving some older residents unable to leave their apartments.
“And I feel sorry for the older people. They can’t walk up and down the steps and stuff. They gotta stay in until they get fixed,” Johnson said.
Johnson said residents also need to come together and support one another.
“We have good residents,” she said. “We just got to get them to come out and support more. If they don’t, nothing’s gonna happen. We gotta support each other. We gotta help each other out.”
For some residents, the question of what happens after demolition is not theoretical.
Charlene Colson, a former Marina Village resident, participated in a panel with Greene Homes residents during the exhibit’s opening events. She spent much of her childhood and adult life connected to Marina Village, a South End public housing complex which was demolished in 2018.
Colson remembers Marina as a place where neighbors relied on one another. “It didn’t matter who you were. Everybody was family there,” Colson said. “Everybody came together.”
She said neighbors shared what they had when someone else was without, teaching her lessons about survival, empathy and caring for others.
Today, the site where Marina Village once stood is home to the Windward Apartments, a mixed-income development. Colson said the Marina buildings may be gone, but the memories remain.
“They could knock it down. The memories are still here,” she said. “We still talk about it.”
Her experience has shaped the advice she gives Greene Homes residents now facing possible displacement. Ask questions before the buildings come down, she said.
“What’s going to happen for us?” Colson said residents should ask. “Do we get a choice of where we’re going to go? Are we getting vouchers? And what are these vouchers going to entail?”
On the second day of the Greene Homes Photovoice exhibit in Bridgeport, attendees listen to a panel discussion featuring former Marina Village residents, who shared their experiences of community, displacement and life after the demolition of their former homes Credit: Gary Judkins / Pivot Language Media
Colson urged residents to attend meetings, understand their options and develop a plan rather than wait for decisions to be made for them.
Residents need to be included in decisions about their future, she said.
“We are important. We matter,” Colson said. “You guys, you have to use your voice.”
That idea is at the heart of the photovoice project.
Lewis, a housing scholar at Sacred Heart University, said the project grew from her interest in housing inequality in Bridgeport and her desire to conduct research differently. Rather than arriving with questions of her own, she wanted residents to help shape the research.
In 2023, residents helped create a survey about conditions at Greene Homes. Eighty-nine households responded. Residents wanted to understand living conditions, mental health and what people knew about the demolition and relocation process.
The photography project took that approach further.
“It’s not really about like what I want because we made sure this was very resident driven — 100%,” Lewis said. “These pictures are all, you know, from the residents and what they wanted to show their community as.”
Lewis said her role was to provide a platform for residents to share their stories in their own way.
Bates said the researchers also found a connection between the photographs residents took in 2026 and the history of Greene Homes.
An attendee views one of the Greene Homes Photovoice displays titled “Once a Community,” which explores the connections, memories and sense of community among residents Credit: Gary Judkins / Pivot Language Media
Archival materials, including old news clippings and documents, displayed alongside the photographs document decades of elevator failures and resident complaints. The development was originally built with elevators to serve elderly residents and others who needed them, yet the archive includes accounts of residents becoming trapped inside them.
For Bates, that history shows why it matters who gets to preserve a community’s story.
“Usually history is told by those in power,” Bates said, “and so the archive usually doesn’t actually provide voice to the people who are actually living through things.”
The photographs, she said, create something different: a “living archive” made by the people experiencing the history themselves.
For residents, the cameras became more than a way to document deteriorating buildings. They became a way to challenge the idea that Greene Homes can be reduced to a collection of problems.
Rendon sees the project as a beginning.
“If us eight could get together and just do this, what could we do with bigger numbers?” she said.
For residents who have spent years hearing that demolition is coming, the immediate request is more basic.
Make the homes livable now.
And when the time comes to decide what replaces them, they want to be in the room.
“It’s our story to tell,” Rendon said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Ann Arbor area legislators, election officials respond to election security concerns at town hall
description: State legislators and local and state election administrators joined U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell in seeking to assuage concerns and answer questions from voters about election security in the upcoming midterm general elections at a town hall in Ann Arbor on Monday night. Michigan Deputy Secretary of State Aghogho Edevbie emphasized throughout the event that, th[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Ann Arbor) and Michigan Deputy Secretary of State Aghogho Edevbie respond to questions from Washtenaw County voters about election security. Aug. 17, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. State legislators and local and state election administrators joined U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell in seeking to assuage concerns and answer questions from voters about election security in the upcoming midterm general elections at a town hall in Ann Arbor on Monday night.
Michigan Deputy Secretary of State Aghogho Edevbie emphasized throughout the event that, though no election system is perfect — and in response to concerns about noncitizens voting illegally in Michigan’s elections, that there were very few such cases in 2024 — elections in Michigan are extremely secure and, in cases of illegal voting, safeguards are in place so that those individuals are prosecuted. 
Asked about proposals that would establish strict voter identification laws in Michigan, Edevbie pointed to examples of why those are not the necessary solution to the problem. 
In Georgia, he explained, there are laws that only allow people with IDs indicating citizenship to vote — and in an audit two years ago, there were 20 noncitizens on their voter rolls. And in Arizona, when what Edevbie described as a “one-size-fits-all system” was put into place to try to eliminate noncitizen voting, 40,000 people who should have been eligible to vote were disenfranchised. 
Dingell, a Democrat from Ann Arbor, also raised her own concerns about voter ID proposals — including both the federal SAVE Act, which she defended her “no” vote on, as well as the state-level citizens-only voting ballot proposal that on Monday the Bureau of Elections suggested did not submit enough valid signatures to appear on November’s ballot.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Specifically, she said that the federal SAVE Act would have made it difficult, if not impossible, for a woman who had changed her last name by marriage to vote without a copy of their marriage license — which she noted she does not have a copy of her own. 
“The other thing I want to add is that I worry about suppressing and disenfranchising your military and stationed overseas,” she continued. “You don’t have the ability to come back and show your ID if you’re a senior citizen who has a hard time getting to the polls.”
Washtenaw County Clerk Larry Kestenbaum also repeatedly reassured those in attendance that Michigan’s electoral system — especially when backed by poll workers, challengers and other officials from both political parties — has only gotten more secure since he took his position in 2004. 
“I should say that I’ve been involved in election administration probably longer than anyone else at this table, and I have seen this from the 70s, the 80s, the 90s into the 21st century, the election system has steadily gotten in Michigan more standardized, more exact,” he said. “The fairness and accuracy has been tremendously protected and enhanced every step of the way. Every new change has gotten more rigorous.”
State Rep. Morgan Foreman (D-Pittsfield Township), who previously worked in a clerk’s office and has experienced processing absentee and in-person ballots, also explained the process of verifying individual ballots — including checking signatures on ballots themselves to match the signature on file for a voter. 
“It’s so safe and so secure that yes, things do happen, and no, the system is not perfect, as has been said,” she said. “But the people behind it are people you can trust, and the people right now in Lansing, at least on my side of the aisle, are people you can trust to preserve your right to vote in every way.”
Edevbie also responded to numerous questions from audience members to explain the state’s procedures on ensuring the security of elections. For example, when one audience member asked why USB drives with voting data are destroyed seven days after an election, he explained that the paper voting records are kept for a full 22 months after an election and are available to the public through a records request. 
Another audience member raised concerns about voters who are deceased remaining in the qualified voter file, to which Edevbie explained that, in addition to removing those who have died based on the Social Security Death Index, anyone who has not voted in six consecutive elections is designated an “inactive voter,” and must show further proof of identity and eligibility.
“I’m not going to stand here and say, ‘Gosh, we have the most perfect system. There’s nothing wrong with it at all,’ because that would be a lie, but we have a system that works, and I would submit to you that 16 votes out of 5.7 million in 2024 is a pretty good system,” Edevbie said. “It’s a system that we can all be proud of. There’s no evidence that we have these thousands and thousands and thousands of non-citizens voting in our election. It just doesn’t exist. And if there is evidence, please report it to law enforcement because they’ll investigate it and we’ll get to the bottom of it and we’ll prosecute the people who are responsible.”
Heather Smiley, the Republican nominee to face Dingell in the November general election for Michigan’s 6th Congressional District, also took the chance to both ask a number of questions about Michigan’s election procedures as well as to attack Dingell’s voting record.
In response to her concerns about potential artificial intelligence or hacking threats to Michigan’s elections, Edevbie again noted that the paper ballots used in Michigan provide a backstop that cannot be hacked.  
Heather Smiley, the GOP nominee in Michigan’s 6th Congressional District, criticized Dingell’s voting record at the town hall event. Aug. 17, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Smiley, along with other audience members raising skepticism on the security of elections, repeatedly referenced a case in the 2024 election in which a Chinese citizen and student at the University of Michigan illegally voted and later faced criminal charges, though he fled the country before he could stand trial. 
“I believe that that was a very deliberate effort to vote, and that that person, individual, signed an affidavit saying that he was an American citizen and eligible to vote,” Dingell said of that instance. “I think that that was a deliberate attempt to cause people to undermine their confidence in the election. But the fact of the matter is, there were audits of millions at every affidavit, and they are verified.”
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel’s office identified 16 cases of suspected non-citizen voting in the 2024 November general election throughout 2025, and on Thursday, announced charges against five noncitizens who allegedly cast ballots in that election.
Edevbie also noted that, because of the constitutional guarantee of a secret ballot, once a vote is cast, it cannot be discounted — though one audience member, a clerk herself, did note that poll challengers are able to flag legitimate concerns about voters that allow those ballots to be verified before they are counted. 
“I cannot put a code on every single person’s ballot so that I can go in and look at a tabulator and take it back out. That applies to people who vote legally and illegally,” he said. “But I emphasize, the 16 votes we have never had any evidence that the number of votes by a noncitizen or noncitizens changed the outcome of a statewide election. It just doesn’t happen.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Did Gov. McKee really create 37,000 jobs? It’s complicated.
description: Among Gov. Dan McKee’s favorite statistics: the 37,000 jobs “created” under his administration. But his recent boast drew a strong rebuke from his Democratic primary challenger, Helena Buonanno Foulkes. “This is a lie he’s telling all of you, and I really want to clarify that,” Foulkes said in response to McKee during an Aug. 12 […]
text:
Gov. Dan McKee emphasizes jobs during a Aug. 25, 2025, press conference at Quonset point in North Kingstown demanding the Trump administration reverse the Revolution Wind stop work order. (Photo by Laura Paton/Rhode Island Current)Among Gov. Dan McKee’s favorite statistics: the 37,000 jobs “created” under his administration.
But his recent boast drew a strong rebuke from his Democratic primary challenger, Helena Buonanno Foulkes.
“This is a lie he’s telling all of you, and I really want to clarify that,” Foulkes said in response to McKee during an Aug. 12 televised debate hosted by NBC10 and Coastal ABC. “Most of those jobs were coming out of COVID, which every state in this country did.” 
Unlike other moments of disagreement between the two rivals, this dispute can be easily fact-checked using federal labor market information.
So who’s right?
Technically, both of them.
As of June 2026, the most recent data available through the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Rhode Island’s seasonally adjusted nonfarm payroll — a.k.a., jobs count — stood at 514,200. That’s 39,700 more jobs in the state than when McKee took office in March 2021.
But, as noted by Foulkes, the Ocean State was still climbing out from the pandemic, which almost instantly slashed 108,700 jobs — more than one in five positions.
As mask requirements and social distancing rules lifted, businesses reopened, and seasonal tourism rebounded, so jobs increased. Slowly.
It took almost three years, until December 2023, for Rhode Island to reach its pre-COVID jobs level — the first New England state to do so, according to the Rhode Island Department of Labor and Training.
Yet, the comeback became a comedown a year ago. After reaching a record 517,800 jobs in May 2025, Rhode Island, like much of the nation, began to see employers pull back amid economic uncertainty posed by Trump tariffs, and later, the war in Iran.
The state’s current job count stands at 0.06% higher than in January 2020. In other words, there are 7,200 more jobs in Rhode Island now versus before the pandemic took hold.
Foulkes suggests the much smaller employment gains are evidence of McKee’s economic failure, and that any post-COVID rebound would have happened anyway.
She has hammered McKee over the loss of Hasbro, which is in the process of moving its headquarters to Boston. More recently, Foulkes accused McKee of attacking CVS Health, another major employer, because of his campaign critiques of her role as former head of its retail pharmacy division.
McKee, in turn, points to major employment expansions by Fidelity and Anduril Industries, along with the successful ploy to secure a long sought-after Amazon warehouse in Johnston, as proof of his leadership success.



It’s all relative 
To Edi Tebaldi, economics professor at Bryant University, the best way to measure Rhode Island’s record is not in any single statistic, but its performance relative to neighboring states and the rest of the country.
“How did we do compared to other states like Massachusetts and Connecticut?” Tebaldi said. “I think that’s more meaningful than anything else.”
On the jobs front, Rhode Island surpassed at least one of its New England neighbors, up 1.4% in total jobs compared with January 2020. Connecticut also saw jobs rise 1.4%, while Massachusetts lost 0.4% of its jobs during that time frame. Massachusetts and Vermont have yet to regain all their pandemic job losses.
Nationwide, jobs are up 4.5% since January 2020.
“Rhode Island is doing very well representing New England,” said Kate Greenwell, assistant director of labor market information for the Rhode Island Department of Labor and Training. 



Quotation







 How did we do compared to other states like Massachusetts and Connecticut? I think that’s more meaningful than anything else. 


– Edi Tebaldi, economics professor at Bryant University


Yet, Rhode Island lost a greater share of its jobs than any other New England state in the last year, down 0.4% from June 2025 to June 2026. Maine was the only other regional state to report year-over-year job losses (down 0.1%) while Massachusetts and Connecticut grew by half a percentage point each. And labor force participation — the number of people employed or looking for work — is down, another troubling sign to economists like Tebaldi.
“Our population is getting older, and all the data suggests that is not going to be changing any time soon,” he said. 
No single governor or leadership team can be held responsible for demographic realities.
But state policies can help, specifically taxes.
“We know states with tax-friendly environments tend to do better with population, tend to be better with the labor force,” Tebaldi said.
Infrastructure, including access to private and public transportation, is also a well-documented method to boost business growth. Hasbro CEO Chris Cocks cited Boston’s public transportation system and proximity to other major employers and talent as reasons for the move. The global gaming company is also receiving $14 million in tax credits through a Massachusetts economic development program.
“When we lose jobs, you’re going to blame the governor and the leadership,” Tebaldi. “When we gain jobs, it’s somewhat fair to give credit to whoever is in power.”
Do voters care? 
Rhode Island voters are looking for a candidate who they think can ease the affordability crisis gripping the state, and nation, said Joe Fleming, a political analyst for WPRI-TV 12. 
But they don’t put much weight on specific labor force statistics.
“In this election, I don’t think it’s going to have a great impact,” Fleming said of McKee’s 37,000 jobs claim. “Most people, by this point, have opinions of both candidates already and who they think will do a better job.”
Yet 22% of Democratic voters remain undecided in the gubernatorial primary, according to the latest public polling via The Pell Center at Salve Regina University. McKee, down 20 points to Foulkes among survey respondents, continues to put his economic record at the center of his appeal to voters. Foulkes, meanwhile, frames her campaign around a shift from a status quo that is not working, pledging to increase efficiency and eliminate cronyism in government.
Asked by debate moderator Gene Valicenti how she would improve Rhode Island’s lackluster business climate, Foulkes suggested a “one-stop shop” modeled after Worcester, Massachusetts, to ease the regulatory burdens associated with business creation and development.
Foulkes was unavailable for additional comment.
Sophie Mestas, a McKee campaign spokesperson, shifted focus back to Foulkes’ record, including as CEO of Hudson Bay Company from 2018 to 2020. Foulkes was charged with stabilizing the struggling Canadian retail company in a restructuring that included laying off 2,000 workers.
“McKee has spent his career fighting for Rhode Island workers,” Mestas said in a response sent via text message. “That’s not changing.”
McKee and Foulkes will square off for a third and final debate at 8 p.m. Tuesday at Rhode Island College, hosted and livestreamed by WPRI-TV 12. Early voting begins Thursday ahead of a Sept. 9 primary.
