title: With PNW electricity demand surging, planners map out major grid upgrades
description: The Pacific Northwest will need a massive buildout of new energy infrastructure over the next six years to meet rising electricity demand, according to a draft regional power plan released this month. Implementing the plan will cost the Pacific Northwest approximately $2.3 billion. And the rate of building will need to quicken to make it […]
text:
Oregon’s Bonneville Dam is the last of 14 dams on the Columbia River before it empties into the Pacific Ocean. (Courtesy of the Bonneville Power Administration/Flickr)The Pacific Northwest will need a massive buildout of new energy infrastructure over the next six years to meet rising electricity demand, according to a draft regional power plan released this month.
Implementing the plan will cost the Pacific Northwest approximately $2.3 billion. And the rate of building will need to quicken to make it happen by 2032.
Last year, the Northwest Power and Conservation Council forecast regional electricity demand to increase anywhere from 50% to 100% over the next 20 years. That’s largely due to data centers, the electrification of vehicles and buildings, and population growth.
On Thursday, the council released a draft of its Ninth Power Plan. Deemed by one councilmember as the “roughest of drafts,” it will serve as a guide on the region’s path to meeting future electricity demand. Public comment for the draft is open until Oct. 16.
The plan calls on Washington, Oregon, Idaho and western Montana to add 11,000 megawatts to the region’s grid. That’s about 16% of the total capacity on the Northwest’s power system today.
Getting there won’t be easy, and the plan doesn’t rely solely on renewable energy.
“No single resource on its own will be able to meet our growing need for energy in the future,” said Jennifer Light, director of power planning. “Rather, a regional portfolio of cost-effective resources will achieve the right balance of economics, efficiency, reliability, and adequacy.”
Across the four-state region, the plan includes 9,000 megawatts of renewables and 2,100 megawatts of natural gas.
In Washington, the plan calls for adding between 500 MW and 1,250 MW of natural gas to the grid by 2032. That is in accordance with the state’s clean energy policies, said Peter Jensen, a spokesperson for the council.
While the plan directs the largest power wholesaler in the region, the Bonneville Power Administration, on which resources it should acquire, it also influences the decisions of other electricity providers in the region. The BPA operates under the U.S. Department of Energy and owns approximately 75% of the Pacific Northwest’s grid.
Throughout the two-year planning process, the BPA has “consistently expressed concerns” over the costs and complexity of the council’s energy conservation recommendations.
This part of the plan focuses on how technology like efficient appliances, as well as building code changes, can reduce electricity demand. The region has spent billions on these types of upgrades over the last decade, according to the plan.
The BPA also questions whether the council’s proposed strategy would be less favorable for utility customers in Idaho and Montana, compared to Oregon and Washington, when it comes to providing access to energy efficiency assistance programs.
The plan was created amid a great deal of uncertainty. Council staff pointed out that it was a challenge to predict how much electricity will be needed to supply data centers. Also unknown is how fast the region can upgrade and expand transmission line capacity and how extreme weather events could strain the grid.
The council has published regional power plans about every five years since 1983, to lay out how the region will maintain an affordable and adequate power supply. The latest plan is expected to be finalized either by the end of this year or the beginning of 2027.
The Northwest Power and Conservation Council was formed in 1981 following the passage of the federal Northwest Power Act. That act directed the four states to work together on regional energy planning and to stop the decline of native Columbia Basin fish species, which is primarily due to the development of hydroelectric dams in the region.

name: VTDigger
title: New funds for Alburgh rail bridge could boost future Amtrak link to Montreal
description:
Upgrading or replacing the bridge across Lake Champlain is one of the hurdles left in the way of restarting cross-border passenger rail in Vermont.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  New funds for Alburgh rail bridge could boost future Amtrak link to Montreal.
text:
Construction work continues on the railroad trestle bridge across Lake Champlain between Swanton and Alburgh on Monday, August 17, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Long-stalled plans to restart the Amtrak connection between Vermont and Montreal are getting a boost from the federal government.
The U.S. Department of Transportation on Friday announced a $4 million grant to plan out repairing, or possibly replacing, an ailing bridge that carries the cross-border rail route over Lake Champlain. Funding for the project was originally set out in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, a sweeping 2021 federal law.
The East Alburgh Bridge is well over a century old, according to the Transportation Department, and its poor condition means trains can only traverse it as fast as 5 mph, too slow for efficient passenger service. Funds are being directed to the Northwest Regional Planning Commission, which oversees development in Franklin and Grand Isle counties.
“Having that Canadian connection would be just one more enticement to bring our Canadian visitors back,” said Catherine Dimitruk, executive director of the regional planning commission.
The trestle bridge parallels Route 78 between Alburgh and Swanton and is owned by the New England Central Railroad, a freight rail company. It’s a key link along the route that carried Amtrak trains between Washington, D.C., and Montreal from 1972 to 1995. At that point, Amtrak shortened the “Montrealer” to run only as far north as St. Albans during a push to cut the train operator’s costs. Today, that route is known as Amtrak’s Vermonter.
In the decades since, passenger rail advocates have pushed for the Quebec link to be restarted, saying it would be an economic boon for the region. The effort has taken on renewed importance today with so many Canadians choosing to spurn the U.S. over President Donald Trump’s tariffs and disparaging rhetoric, Dimitruk said. 
Vermont’s award is a slice of $5.3 billion in funding for rail projects that the Transportation Department announced last week, about $2 billion of which it said came from clawing back money for a high-speed rail project in California that has faced significant cost overruns and delays.
While the money is earmarked for planning work in Vermont, it will not actually fund any construction, Dimitruk said.
To be sure, upgrading the East Alburgh Bridge is not the only hurdle left to clear before service to Montreal could resume. More track upgrades are needed on the Canadian side of the border, said Carl Fowler, a longtime member of the Vermont Rail Advisory Council.
By far the biggest challenge, though, is the need to construct a facility at Montreal Central Station to allow customs officials to screen passengers traveling between the countries. U.S. and Canadian officials have long said restarting the Montreal-Vermont link hinges on this preclearance facility.
That project remains in the planning phase, with a Canadian official telling the Saint Albans Messenger in April that more studies are needed before it can advance.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  New funds for Alburgh rail bridge could boost future Amtrak link to Montreal.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Leader of Montana Freedom Caucus defends push to steer state money to private company
description: Montana Freedom Caucus Chairman Jerry Schillinger tried to direct $600,000 of state money to a private company even after it lost the bid for a state contract. The contract, to provide training for post-traumatic stress disorder therapy, came from House Bill 832 in the 2025 session of the Montana Legislature. A public records request by […]
text:
Montana Freedom Caucus Chairman Jerry Schillinger, center, is defending a push to steer state funds to a company that lost a state contract because he believes the company could help veterans. Schillinger is pictured here during the 2025 Montana Legislature. (Keila Szpaller/The Daily Montanan)Montana Freedom Caucus Chairman Jerry Schillinger tried to direct $600,000 of state money to a private company even after it lost the bid for a state contract.
The contract, to provide training for post-traumatic stress disorder therapy, came from House Bill 832 in the 2025 session of the Montana Legislature.
A public records request by The Daily Montanan uncovered the effort to steer the money to Quresta.
Quresta is based in New York and describes itself as offering a “life-changing” PTSD treatment without medication.
HB 832 called for a competitive bidding process, and records show Quresta was rated last among the three companies that submitted proposals.
Rep. Jerry Schillinger, R-Circle, said he advocated for state money to go to a company that didn’t get a state contract partly because he believes it’s what legislators wanted. (Provided by the Montana Legislature)
In an email to the Montana Department of Labor obtained in the public records request, Schillinger argued the state should ignore the results of the competitive process and give the contract to Quresta anyway — or to no company at all.
Schillinger, a bill sponsor, defended the email last month in an interview with the Daily Montanan. The Republican from Circle said legislators intended the money to go to Quresta.
Bill drafting documents show Rep. Ron Marshall, who originally requested the bill, and Larry Anderson, a former county commissioner who worked on the legislation, wanted to fund the treatment by Quresta. But even in draft form, the bill called for a competitive selection.
“I think it’s just a shame that as promising as that treatment method sounded, it’s not going to get an opportunity to be tried here in Montana,” Schillinger said.
Correspondence obtained in the public records request by the Daily Montanan indicates the request from a legislator about a preferred vendor isn’t unusual.
In an email about Schillinger’s request, Department of Administration Director Misty Ann Giles told the Department of Labor commissioner and officials from the governor’s office “it is worth noting, I get these calls often.” Giles said if Schillinger had wanted a specific company to do the training, that information should have been included in the bill, but it wasn’t.
“While we want to have good working relationships with the legislature, it is not our job just to keep everyone happy when doing so violates the law,” Giles said in the email.
Bill sailed through the 2025 Montana Legislature
Anderson, a former Missoula County Commissioner and Vietnam War veteran, told the Daily Montanan the idea for the bill came when he read an American Legion article about treating PTSD without medication.
The treatment is called the RTM Protocol, or Reconsolidation of Traumatic Memories Protocol. It aims to help patients change the way they store memories in three-to-five 90-minute sessions so they don’t “relive” a traumatic experience.
The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs says there is insufficient evidence to recommend it, but a clinical study showed patients who underwent the therapy reported fewer PTSD-related problems.
Anderson said he was impressed with the results, and he connected with a representative of RTM Global. In 2026, Quresta registered in New York to do business as RTM Global.
Montana has a high rate of veterans. U.S. News and World Report ranks the state No. 3 with nearly 9% of the population having served in the military.
House Bill 832 appropriated $600,000 to train health care providers in therapy for PTSD. It passed with strong support. Just seven legislators opposed it in its final vote in the Senate.
As head of the Freedom Caucus, Schillinger typically advocates for fiscal conservatism and limited government. In this case, he said he believed the money was worth spending compared with the social and criminal costs of letting PTSD go untreated, especially given testimony from the company.
“The results that they had documented were phenomenal. It just seemed like it would be ridiculous to not give that a try,” Schillinger said.
Quresta loses bid, Schillinger fights for it
On Dec. 24, 2025, the Department of Labor and Industry announced it planned to award the contract to a different company, Scaling Up LLC, of Utah.
Scaling Up also describes itself as offering a treatment that helps clients process difficult experiences and heal from trauma. In a scoring summary, evaluators praised both companies for different aspects of their programs, but Scaling Up’s proposal edged out the other two, in part because it proposed a cost $60,000 less than Quresta.
In an official protest of the award in January 2026, CEO Mark Ackermann of RTM Global, formerly Quresta, argued the state hadn’t properly evaluated the proposals, and he asked the Department of Administration to take “corrective action.”
In January and again in March, Schillinger stepped into the debate.
In an email to Department of Labor and Industry Commissioner Sarah Swanson obtained in the public records request, he said the contract needed to go to Quresta, “the only company to make a presentation to the Legislature.”
He said the program it offers has the potential to “deliver life altering and life saving help,” and fellow legislators agreed with him as evidenced by their votes.
“If for some reason the Administration feels constrained from awarding the contract to Queresta (sic), I would urge that no contract be awarded, no taxpayer money be spent on a program that received no hearings, no votes and no legislative support,” Schillinger wrote in the email.
Misty Ann Giles, director of the Montana Department of Administration, testifies in front of the Senate Judiciary Committee in February 2025. (Nathaniel Bailey for the Daily Montanan)
An email in March shows Swanson sought guidance from other state officials, Giles of the Department of the Administration, and Ryan Osmundson and Mark Blasdel in the governor’s office.
Giles shot back a message that said Schillinger was unequivocally in the wrong, and the Department of Labor and Industry must go with the winning vendor, as she had advised in January.
“As a baseline matter, the legislature has zero authority to dictate that the executive (or judicial for that matter) select a particular vendor for any action. Period,” Giles wrote, bolding and underling part of the message.
Giles said the state ran a request for proposals, the competitive process ran without errors, and the state made the award to the winning vendor, not the “subpar” one Schillinger preferred.
“If you opt to attempt to cancel the RFP, we will require documentation and a legislator being mad is not a valid reason,” Giles said.
Giles also said if DLI tried to cancel the RFP, the company that won the contract would protest, and the state wouldn’t have a solid case in court “as the underlying reason that we are catering to a legislator will come to light.”
Complaint filed
Republican Rep. Ken Walsh believes the process still needs scrutiny. He filed a complaint with the Legislative Audit Division in June after learning about the push to send state funds to the company that hadn’t won the bid.
Rep. Ken Walsh, R-Twin Bridges, believes the push to steer state funds to a vendor that didn’t win a state contract merits scrutiny. (Provided by the Montana Legislature)
“This post-passage lobbying to circumvent a competitive process in favor of a company registered by a high-ranking party official raises serious questions regarding the legislative intent and the integrity of the procurement,” Walsh said in the complaint that he also sent to the Daily Montanan.
By state statute, the Legislative Auditor is charged with investigating lawmakers’ concerns but cannot release information about a pending complaint or acknowledge an investigation.
Walsh said last week the Legislative Audit Division said it does not believe the issue is waste, fraud or abuse, and recommended he refer the complaint to the House Ethics Committee instead.
“I think there’s more to the story,” Walsh said.
In a brief follow-up phone call, Schillinger said he will withstand any scrutiny. “I didn’t do anything wrong,” he said.
Ackermann said no one in Montana has a financial interest in the company.
Quresta has an active business license with the Montana secretary of state registered in November 2025 by The Montana Law Company, operated by Montana Republican Party Chairman Art Wittich.
It is not unusual for a lawyer to be asked to register a business for an out-of-state company.
In an email last month, Wittich described Walsh’s complaint as a “baseless, politically motivated whine from a sore loser.” (Walsh lost his primary election in June.)
Wittich also said that his involvement with Quresta is part of his business as an attorney, not his volunteer role as the leader of the state’s most powerful political party.
In a brief exchange in June at the state GOP convention in Missoula, Wittich told the Daily Montanan he wasn’t familiar with Quresta. He declined to clarify his response when reached by email in July.
Schillinger said he didn’t know that Wittich was involved until a few weeks ago when he learned about the complaint.
Walsh told the Daily Montanan he isn’t jumping to conclusions about this case.
“If everything is above board, that’s fine,” Walsh said. “But I think there’s enough questions there that should be answered.”



Timeline
March 13, 2025: Rep. Jerry Schillinger sponsors HB 832 for PTSD training funding.
June 9, 2025: Gov. Greg Gianforte signs the legislation, which calls for a competitive bidding process.
Oct. 23, 2025: The proposal period opens.
Nov. 12, 2025: Montana GOP chairman Art Wittich registers Quresta in Montana.
Nov. 21, 2025: The proposal period closes with three bids.
Dec. 24, 2025: The state issues a notice that it will award the contract to Scaling Up LLC. The company’s bid was $60,000 less than Quresta’s.
Jan. 22, 2026: Quresta CEO Mark Ackermann submits a protest with the state.
March 16, 2026: Rep. Schillinger argues the state should award the bid to Quresta or to no company at all in an email to the Department of Labor and Industry.
June 2026: Rep. Ken Walsh files a complaint about Schillinger’s push for Quresta to be awarded the contract.
Sources: Legislative files; Montana Legislature’s bill tracking database; documents from a public records request to the state of Montana for information about Quresta; Montana Secretary of State registration forms; New York Department of State records.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: One year after Pillen announced McCook ICE jail, protests continue, governor doubles down
description: McCOOK — The sun was still rising as nearly 60 “mothers and others” boarded an Omaha bus and headed across the state to protest what goes on at the ICE detention facility in rural McCook. Their nearly 10-hour round trip marked a year since Gov. Jim Pillen announced the deal he made with U.S. Immigration […]
text:
A full bus traveled about 10 hours on the road to attend an Aug. 15 rally within eyeshot of a McCook, Nebraska-based U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention center that started holding migrants last November. The rally marks a year since Gov. Jim Pillen's administration announced a partnership with ICE to house immigrant detainees. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner) McCOOK — The sun was still rising as nearly 60 “mothers and others” boarded an Omaha bus and headed across the state to protest what goes on at the ICE detention facility in rural McCook.
A full bus heads from Omaha to a peaceful protest near the McCook migrant detention facility on Aug. 15. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
Their nearly 10-hour round trip marked a year since Gov. Jim Pillen announced the deal he made with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to convert the state’s rehabilitative-focused Work Ethic Camp into a 300-bed jail for migrants. The bus passengers, set to join other like-minded rallygoers Saturday, wanted McCook, the state and nation to know that time had not dulled their contempt for that decision or concern for those detained. 
They carried signs: “We have not forgotten.” 
Despite attempts by some state lawmakers and a lawsuit by 13 McCook residents to halt the plan, the ICE jail began accepting foreign-born detainees in November and the daily population count through March fluctuated between about 100 and 171, according to the Deportation Data Project, a repository of immigration enforcement data maintained by the University of California Berkeley Law School and obtained through the Freedom of Information Act.
Pillen last year said he expected the feds would pay the state a $2.45 million “base” fee each month. But to date, the state has received $14.6 million: $9.3 million based on occupied beds and $5.3 million for one-time costs such as vehicles and equipment, said a spokesperson for the Nebraska Department of Correctional Services.
Spokesperson Dayne Urbanovsky, in an email to the Examiner, said the higher amount could come when the facility is able to house 300. She said renovations are to be completed later this summer. 
Responding to the rally, Pillen spokesperson Laura Strimple said the governor remains committed to the ICE partnership and to “safe and secure detention of illegal detainees accused of either criminal or civil violations of our nation’s laws.”
The “McCook detention center has served that purpose for ICE and the Department of Homeland Security and will continue to do so throughout its contract with the state,” Strimple said. The contract is valid through at least September 2027.
A Lincoln bus arrives at rally site protesting  Trump Administration’s mass deportation movement that includes new migrant detention centers such as one in McCook. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
As the Omaha bus pulled up to the rally site, a private lot within eyeshot of  the detention facility, passengers held up letters that spelled “Omaha Cares.” The bus was hosted by “Mothers and Others: Justice and Mercy for Immigrants,” but carried representatives of assorted organizations, including a Nebraska lawmaker.
They joined a rally that grew to about 300 people. Lead organizers — including McCook-based Nebraska Voices, Lincoln-based Taco Tuesday Familia and American Civil Liberties Union Nebraska — said the turnout, higher than previous protests, signaled a continued resolve to fight for due process and legal reform for migrants. 
Organizers said participation, spanning the state, reflected a growing network of advocacy entities watching actions of ICE and the McCook facility.
“It’s galvanized people’s sense of injustice,” said Nebraska Voices’ Lorri Sughroue, who helped form the McCook group last year.
‘This began in 1492’
Kevin Abourezk, a Lakota elder whose journalism career documented stories of indigenous people, kicked off the rally’s lineup of speakers, saying the only people who aren’t immigrants are Native Americans.
Abourezk touched upon U.S. history  and  said the reason for Saturday’s gathering did not begin just last year. “This began in 1492, when Columbus landed …”
Demonstrators at the McCook immigration rally wave to traffic passing by on U.S. Highway 83. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
He told demonstrators that perhaps it is “good and right to have standards by which people are allowed to come here” to carve out homes for their families. He pointed toward the nearby McCook detention center: “But in terms of smart immigration reform — it ain’t that.” 
The two-hour program that unfolded without incident also included musicians, bilingual poets, red-robed Handmaids of Nebraska, hatted “Pissed Off Grandmas,” words from Las Voces Nebraska, clergy and local McCook residents. 
Most wore shirts with immigrant-friendly messages. Dozens held signs and waved to passing motorists on U.S. Highway 83 in the Red Willow County town of about 7,500. 
Co-organizer Holly Burns spoke of her Latino family’s Nebraska roots, which started with her grandparents’ farm work in Scotts Bluff County and led to Lincoln where she and sister Tiffany last year formed the TacoTuesday Familia advocacy group.
She spoke of how certain U.S. states were once part of Mexico. “Truly in my family’s history, the border crossed us,” said Burns.
State Sen. Margo Juarez of South Omaha got one of the louder reactions when recounting a meeting she and another lawmaker had the prior week with state officials about “isolation rooms” under construction at the McCook facility. She said she has asked for an accounting of how they are used.
Mindy Rush Chipman, executive director of ACLU Nebraska, harked back to Pillen’s August 2025 announcement that the state would convert the Work Ethic Camp into an ICE jail. 
“Those plans were shrouded in secrecy,” she told those sitting in lawn chairs, on the ground and under tents.
Rallygoers listen to speakers at a private lot within eyeshot an ICE detention facility for migrants established last year in McCook. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
Out of 49 lawmakers in an officially nonpartisan Nebraska Legislature, a group of 13 Democrats and one independent demanded more transparency and questioned whether Pillen violated the Nebraska Constitution by repurposing the state correctional facility without direct legislative approval. Pillen has argued that he is doing his duty to help the federal government enforce immigration laws.
A Red Willow County district judge ruled in favor of the governor and later dismissed a lawsuit filed by Nebraska Appleseed on behalf of a group of McCook residents and former State Sen. DiAnna Schimek. The judge said that the Legislature had previously tasked the executive branch with managing state prisons, and that the Pillen administration legally entered into the ICE contract. Appleseed has appealed the decision.



Quotation







It’s a perfect location, right? Rural Nebraska, nobody is going to complain.


– Deborah Walters, McCook area resident



Rush Chipman also told rallygoers that most ICE detainees are not dangerous or criminals, though held for civil violations of being in the country without authorization. The Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse at Syracuse University (TRAC), a nonprofit that tracks immigration trends, showed about 70% of migrants in ICE detention have no criminal convictions.
“They’re people that are being taken away from their families, taken away from their jobs and taken away from the communities they call home,” Rush Chipman said.
ACLU attorney Grant Friedman said that in his experiences, the McCook detention center provides the “worst lawyer-client accommodations.” He said, for example, he can’t get a message to an inmate without a full name and immigration identification number, which he said detainees don’t always have.
At the same time Pillen announced the facility, he disclosed a new 287(g) pact between ICE and the Nebraska State Patrol — a move Rush Chipman said essentially turned the state agency into an extension of immigration enforcement.
In August 2025, Gov. Jim Pillen announced the  state McCook Work Ethic Camp would be converted to an ICE detention facility. Detainees began arriving in November. The Work Ethic Camp sign is still up on Aug. 15, 2026. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
Initially, six troopers were trained as 287(g) task force officers. A patrol spokesman confirmed that the number has grown to 16.
Spokesman Cody Thomas said that since August, state troopers have assisted in about 275 immigration-related detentions or transports in 30 Nebraska counties, and that Homeland Security has reimbursed the patrol $277,037.
A few recent encounters he cited included a case when a trooper detained an undocumented migrant with several prior convictions including disorderly conduct and DUI, and another in which the person had a prior child sexual assault.
Thomas said the near tripling of troopers trained for immigration duties was due to unpredictable scheduling demands and new state participation in a program to “locate and ensure the safety of unaccompanied children.” 
No detentions have resulted in the program to find unaccompanied children, he said, but the task force helped find over 10 youths “and ensured they were safely with family.” 
Nationally, 287(g) partnerships have increased from 135 to 2,179 since the beginning of President Trump’s second term, a Homeland Security spokesperson said.
Solidarity appreciated
For some residents of McCook, a High Plains town historically tied to railroads and agriculture, the weekend gathering was a welcome sign of solidarity.
A protester holds a sign to passing motorists along U.S. Highway 83. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
Sughroue said many locals are fervent in their support for toughened ICE enforcement, though she also believes a good chunk don’t want the detention facility in their backyard. She believes they’re silenced by potential “repercussions” in the largely conservative area.
Indeed, a few asked not to be identified in a story.
John and Deborah Walters are registered Republicans who said they won’t hold back their objections.
The couple owns ag land in the area, including the few acres on which the rally was held. They said  they learned about the plan for the McCook ICE facility on a national newscast while eating breakfast at a hotel in Iowa.
“We were shocked,” said John, born in McCook 79 years ago. He believes state officials did not weigh future effects on the area. Deborah described as “our neighbors” most of the immigrants arrested in President Donald Trump’s mass deportation movement. Both were disturbed when federal and state officials dubbed the facility the “Cornhusker Clink.”
“Everything’s been so secretive, that’s what bothers us,” Deborah said. “It’s a perfect location, right?  Rural Nebraska, nobody is going to complain.”
John and Deborah Walters offered their land for groups to peacefully protest immigration enforcement actions. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
The couple viewed Saturday’s turnout as “tremendous.”
Gary Power, 84, said he endured the afternoon heat to register support “for democracy” and against inhumane tactics. He said he was somewhat surprised to see so many McCook folks.
“Six months ago I would never have seen something like this,” said Power. “They woke up. They’re paying those gas prices, wouldn’t that wake you up?”
McCook resident Diane Lyons told the group that part of her anxiety is not knowing what will come later of the converted facility now surrounded with new “rows and rows and rows of barbed wire.” She said she valued its previous use as a work ethic camp whose inmates helped set up various community events, including Santa Claus Lane.
“We feel your fear,” she told the group. “We feel the anxiety. We feel the anger about the people that are being wrongfully detained there … we also have lost a lot.”
Helping hands
Looking back over the past year, advocates said they are encouraged to see a stronger network emerge to help respond to immigration-related needs.
A Husker bus unloads a group traveling from Lincoln to the McCook rally, and they take a moment to pray. The McCook immigration detention facility is within eyeshot, down the highway about a quarter of a mile. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
The connections played out in a recent situation when a former McCook detainee from Minnesota called a North Platte advocacy group about his friend newly released from the McCook facility. The friend, a Spanish-speaking Venezuelan, wound up in Omaha without a phone, food or resources. The North Platte advocate called a representative of Omaha Welcomes the Stranger nonprofit, who contacted a member of Mothers and Others, who found the former detainee (via help of a photo) sitting alone in a lot near the Omaha immigration court complex. Volunteers at Omaha Welcomes the Stranger provided the Venezuelan a place to stay and helped him return to his family and friends in Minnesota.
Looking ahead, rallygoers in McCook are seeking to build a fellowship program that interacts with detainees. Appleseed continues its legal quest to close the facility.
“Working together helps protect our communities and encourages others around us to demand better from our elected officials,” Rush Chipman told the rally. “If Florida can close its detention center, so can we.” 
As the Omaha bus returned about 8 p.m., riders were signing up for another peaceful protest at a Council Bluffs ICE detention facility.
Juarez was planning another visit with McCook detainees. She had asked to do so the day of the rally, but was told more notice was needed.
Musicians play as people start to arrive at an afternoon protest about a quarter mile from the McCook, Nebraska-based U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention center. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
“We need to continue to monitor what goes on at the facility especially now that they have those isolation rooms,” she said.
The South Omaha lawmaker, a member of Mothers for Others, said she will work to end the McCook ICE partnership when the current contract ends in fall 2027. She said she left the rally energized by the geographic representation, diversity and number of young participants. 
“There were so many young people there who saw the wrong in the facility — that’s inspiring to me,” she said. “I hope they continue with their concern and leadership and always speak out on issues they don’t feel are humane.”
 



NE lawmakers question new ‘isolation’ area at McCook
McCOOK — State Sen. Margo Juarez, an outspoken critic of immigration enforcement tactics, said she is worried about “isolation rooms” being built at the state-owned McCook ICE detention facility, and wants to see records kept on usage. 
The South Omaha lawmaker and Sen. Terrell McKinney of North Omaha met last week with Nebraska Department of Correctional Services staff. She said they were told the solitary confinement space was a requirement of the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
On Monday, a Correctional Services representative confirmed that additional space is part of a federal agreement.
State Sen. Margo Juarez of Omaha speaks with an ICE detainee last year at the Lincoln County Jail. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
Dayne Urbanovsky, the spokesperson, said in an emailed statement that the McCook facility has had a “short-term observation area” for individuals with self-harm thoughts or combative behavior and those who request separation. She said additional spaces are expected to be finished this summer as part of the expansion.
“I told them I want accountability for them being used,” Juarez said during a weekend address in McCook. A peaceful protest was held Saturday on private land near the McCook facility, which before its conversion last year served as the state’s rehabilitation-focused Work Ethic Camp.
McKinney said he wants to know “why people are being placed in those rooms in the first place.” He said most ICE detainees are not being held for violent offenses and are in removal proceedings based on civil violations for being in the country without authorization.
McKinney, known as a watchdog of the state prison system, called ICE enforcement overall “super concerning.” Of possible isolation  of McCook-based migrant detainees, he said: “What’s the purpose?”
Juarez first learned of a planned solitary confinement area during a repeat visit to the McCook facility in March. She said state escorts at the time “spinned” the space as where detainees would go if they needed a “time out” or a spot alone.
State Sen. Terrell McKinney of Omaha. July 21, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
In an interview this weekend, Juarez said increased concern led her and McKinney to meet with state officials. The McCook facility is owned by the state but operates under federal rules.
Juarez said she wants a record of who is kept in isolation and for how long. 
“Absolutely I am worried about it,” she told the Examiner. “My main concern is how long somebody would be confined in one of the rooms.”
Of Juarez’s call for accountability, Urbanovsky said “room usage documentation is maintained in alignment with Department of Homeland Security ICE standard procedures.”











Protesters arrive at rally held on private land near the McCook, Nebraska-based U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention center that started holding migrants last November. name: Nevada Current
title: Kalshi and NV Gaming Control Board spar over geolocation mandate
description: Attorneys for Kalshi say Nevada gaming regulators are targeting the prediction market and wasting taxpayer money on behalf of casinos. The state contends Kalshi is dragging its feet when it comes to complying with a court mandate to prohibit people in Nevada from placing bets on the platform.  Kalshi is engaged in a high-stakes lawsuit […]
text:
The state’s goal “is not protecting consumers," said a Kalshi attorney. "It's just a vindictive waste of taxpayer dollars at the bidding of casinos.” (iStock/Getty Images)Attorneys for Kalshi say Nevada gaming regulators are targeting the prediction market and wasting taxpayer money on behalf of casinos. The state contends Kalshi is dragging its feet when it comes to complying with a court mandate to prohibit people in Nevada from placing bets on the platform. 
Kalshi is engaged in a high-stakes lawsuit with state regulators, who are trying to prevent it from gobbling up Nevada bettors without being taxed, licensed, or regulated. 
“Nevada’s investigators broke federal law when they used false information to hunt for loopholes in our geofence,” Kalshi General Counsel Rick Heaslip said in a statement this weekend after the Nevada Gaming Control Board asked a judge to fine Kalshi $120,000 a day for failing to geofence would-be customers in Nevada. 
The state’s goal, Heaslip said “is not protecting consumers. It’s just a vindictive waste of taxpayer dollars at the bidding of casinos.”
The platform has been under court order since May to stop taking bets from those in Nevada on sports, elections, and entertainment-related matters, but has flouted judicial orders by accepting dozens of bets, according to a motion filed Friday by Attorney General Aaron Ford’s office, which represents the GCB. 
Regulators are asking a judge to fine the ubiquitous betting platform $120,000 a day, a sanction Kalshi agreed to in July when it pledged to stop accepting bets from within the state by Aug. 12. 
Kalshi contends it complied, but that GCB agents placed bets using fake addresses to thwart the platform’s geofencing mechanism. 
In a letter Friday to the GCB, Kalshi’s attorney Andrew Porter notes the platform engaged the services of a vendor, GeoComply, at the request of Nevada regulators, and made good on its agreement to geofence bettors in Nevada by Aug. 12.
The GCB says Kalshi informed it on Aug. 11 that the geolocation function would not be active on mobile accounts until users updated their apps and said it was implementing a requirement that they do so. Kalshi, the state says, notified the GCB on August 12 that geofencing was activated on mobile devices. 
Despite Kalshi’s assurance, the GCB says that state investigators, using standard iPhones, were able to place nine bets on contracts that should have been prohibited.
When provided with details of the transactions by the GCB, Kalshi said the investigators were able to “trade” because their devices carried the previous version of Kalshi’s app, which was not subject to geofencing.  Additionally Kalshi acknowledged it had only required clients registered in Nevada to update their apps.  
Kalshi subsequently said it would require other users to update their apps in three to five days. 
Kalshi contends the GCB investigators violated federal law by falsifying their location, “and, in at least one instance, actively worked to circumvent the Kalshi restrictions that blocked the investigator from trading.”
The company did not elaborate when contacted by the Current. 
“Kalshi’s accusations are baseless, and they cannot obscure the fact that Kalshi missed its agreed-upon deadline to comply with Nevada law,” the GCB said in a statement. “Kalshi’s consistent failures to comply with the court’s orders left the Board with no choice but to advise the court of Kalshi’s noncompliance.”
Kalshi, according to court documents, has ignored several court orders to stop taking bets from individuals in Nevada. 
At a June hearing to show cause why it should not be held in contempt, Kalshi said it had spent $190,000 on internal compliance efforts to track locations, “a notoriously unreliable way to determine users‘ location,” the state wrote in its motion.  
A Kalshi executive had previously sworn in federal court that effective geolocation could cost the company “tens of millions of dollars” a year, according to the state’s motion.
Kalshi was also ordered by a Michigan court to stop taking bets in that state by Aug. 12 or pay a daily fine of $500,000. However, geofencing “system in Michigan only works after an app update that is not required,” according to an InGame reporter, who “was able to place bets on sporting events from Michigan, using an account registered to an Indiana address.”
Last week, a Washington state judge ordered Kalshi to curtail its operations and impose geolocation compliance measures.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Deery asks Indiana Supreme Court to take recount case, seeks emergency ballot pause
description: Three votes now separate Republican Paula Copenhaver from state Sen. Spencer Deery, but a dispute over six rejected ballots could reverse the outcome of their Indiana Senate primary for a second time. Deery’s attorneys on Monday asked the Indiana Supreme Court to take the recount case and the Court of Appeals to suspend the result […]
text:
Sen. Spencer Deery, R-West Lafayette, laughs at a joke from a member of the public during testimony on a bill in February 2022. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Three votes now separate Republican Paula Copenhaver from state Sen. Spencer Deery, but a dispute over six rejected ballots could reverse the outcome of their Indiana Senate primary for a second time.
Deery’s attorneys on Monday asked the Indiana Supreme Court to take the recount case and the Court of Appeals to suspend the result while judges determine whether the six ballots were wrongly rejected over omissions by election workers.
The Indiana Recount Commission unanimously dismissed Copenhaver’s election contest on Aug. 10 but issued a recount certificate showing her with 6,332 votes and Deery with 6,329.
That reversed the original certified results, which showed Deery winning the May 5 Republican primary by the same three-vote margin, 6,337 to 6,334.
Deery’s appeal is limited to six ballots from Montgomery, Vermillion and Warren counties that lacked a circuit court clerk’s seal and signature. The ballots were cast for Deery, according to his filings, so counting them would put him back ahead by three votes.



Quotation







We’re not talking about mysterious absentee ballots showing up in the dumpster that we’re trying to count. We’re talking about people that showed their ID and were there in person.


– Sen. Spencer Deery, R-West Lafayette


One of Monday’s filings asks the Indiana Supreme Court to accept an emergency transfer of the case from the Court of Appeals.
The other asks the appeals court to stay the Recount Commission’s certification and temporarily stop election officials from placing Copenhaver’s name on general-election ballots while the dispute is reviewed.
The question for the courts is whether the clerk errors require rejection of ballots that Deery says were otherwise valid.
Deery is represented by Samantha DeWester, who handled the recount proceedings, along with Karen Celestino-Horseman and William Groth. Celestino-Horseman and Groth, both of whom have extensive election-law experience, were added to Deery’s legal team for the appeal.
Copenhaver did not respond Monday to the Indiana Capital Chronicle’s request for comment.
Clerk errors at heart of case
Some of the ballots are classified as absentee ballots under Indiana law but were cast in person before Election Day, Deery said Monday during an interview on the Rob Kendall Show.
“We’re not talking about mysterious absentee ballots showing up in the dumpster that we’re trying to count,” Deery said. “We’re talking about people that showed their ID and were there in person.”
The senator maintained that election workers forgot to affix a stamp, however.



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



Indiana law requires the back of an absentee ballot to bear the circuit court clerk’s official seal or signature. Deery’s appeal asks whether a clerk’s failure to meet that requirement prohibits an otherwise valid ballot from being counted.
His attorneys point to another provision of Indiana law addressing mistakes by election officials.
“A ballot that has been marked and cast by a voter in compliance with this title but may otherwise not be counted solely as the result of the act or failure to act of an election officer may nevertheless be counted … unless evidence of fraud, tampering, or misconduct affecting the integrity of the ballot is presented by a party to the proceeding,” the statute says.
The law also states that, “The act or failure to act by an election officer is not by itself evidence of fraud, tampering, or misconduct affecting the integrity of the ballot.”
Deery’s attorneys argue that language allows the six ballots to be counted because their defects resulted from election worker omissions rather than anything the voters did.
They also contend Indiana law specifically excludes ballots lacking bipartisan election worker initials from that protection but does not impose the same explicit exclusion on ballots lacking a clerk’s seal and signature.
Deery said votes should not be thrown out solely because of worker incompetence.
“This may be the single biggest threat to election security we’ve seen in Indiana in decades,” he said on Kendall’s show.
Deery noted, too, that election workers could purposefully “forget” to stamp ballots cast by people they believed would vote a particular way based on a person’s hat, skin color or another factor.
“We know these are real ballots. We know these are real voters,” he continued. “We know how they wanted to vote.”
Supreme Court intervention sought
Deery also asked the Indiana Supreme Court to accept an emergency transfer of the case from the Court of Appeals.
Indiana appellate rules permit such a transfer “upon a showing that the appeal involves a substantial question of law of great public importance and an emergency exists requiring a speedy determination,” according to the motion.
His attorneys argue the case meets both conditions because it presents an unresolved question about the effect of election worker errors and because counties are quickly approaching deadlines for preparing, printing and transmitting ballots.
Republican state Senate candidate Paula Copenhaver speaks with reporters on July 28, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
“Because of the error of law by the Commission, an election has been overturned and the clear and undisputed intent of those voters to nominate Spencer Deery has been disregarded, through no fault of their own,” the motion said.
An emergency exists because county clerks need to prepare ballots for the Nov. 3 general election, Deery contends. His attorneys argue the ordinary appellate process might not resolve the case before those ballots must be printed and distributed.
The motion asks the Supreme Court to accept the case and impose an expedited schedule.
Under Deery’s proposal, any party opposing the transfer or proposed schedule would have two days to respond. Deery would have two days to reply after the latest response.
His opening brief would be due five days after the court grants transfer. The other parties would then have five days to respond, followed by three days for Deery to file a reply brief.
Deery has already ordered transcripts and exhibits from the recount proceedings and provided the materials received so far to the other attorneys in the case, according to the motion.
Months-long recount dispute
The court case is the latest turn in a Republican primary that has gone unsettled for more than three months.
Both candidates originally claimed victory, but completed county tallies later gave Deery a three-vote win after provisional ballots were reviewed.
Copenhaver requested a recount and election contest. She alleged that some people improperly voted in the Republican primary despite identifying as Democrats or progressives.
Copenhaver’s lawyers initially sought to question 14 voters under oath about whether they complied with Indiana’s primary-election law and, potentially, how they voted.
The request prompted objections that voters could be compelled to disclose private political information or reveal their ballots.
Trump-backed challenger jumps ahead of Republican senator in Indiana recount

Deery denounced the effort as an attempt to intimidate voters and discard lawful votes. His attorney argued that voters can change their party preference and that Indiana does not require formal party registration before someone participates in a primary.
The Recount Commission denied the proposed voter subpoenas but continued reviewing ballots disputed for other reasons.
The recount ultimately reduced both candidates’ totals. Deery lost eight votes from his certified total, while Copenhaver lost two, leaving Copenhaver ahead by three.
Copenhaver had the endorsement of President Donald Trump. Deery was among the Republican senators Trump targeted after they opposed the president’s push for a mid-decade redrawing of Indiana’s congressional districts.
The hostile primary attracted millions of dollars in outside spending as Trump and his allies sought to defeat Republican senators who opposed the redistricting plan.
Copenhaver is a staffer for Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith and a Fountain County clerk. She is also serves as the Fountain County Republican chair.
Deery, a first-term senator from West Lafayette, represents the heavily Republican district spanning all or parts of six counties between Lafayette and Terre Haute.
The eventual Republican nominee is set to face Democrat David Sanders, a West Lafayette City Council member, in November.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Mazzei releases drug test in Oklahoma gubernatorial race. His opponent immediately cries foul
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – Amid growing public pressure from his fellow Republican gubernatorial opponent, Mike Mazzei on Monday reversed course and released the results of a test that came up negative for drugs and other substances. His opponent, Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond, though wasted no time criticizing the results, accusing Mazzei of attempting to[...]
text:
Mike Mazzei addresses his supporters on Tuesday, June 16, 2026, during Mazzei’s watch party in Bixby, Okla. Supporters gathered to watch results in the Republican primary election.
(Photo by Ace Cuervo/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Amid growing public pressure from his fellow Republican gubernatorial opponent, Mike Mazzei on Monday reversed course and released the results of a test that came up negative for drugs and other substances.
His opponent, Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond, though wasted no time criticizing the results, accusing Mazzei of attempting to mislead voters by taking a urine test instead of completing hair follicle screening like Drummond did.
Both are vying for the Republican gubernatorial nomination in the heated Aug. 25 primary runoff.
The results of Mazzei’s urine test, which he took on Thursday, showed he tested negative for about a dozen substances, including oxycodone. 
Gentner Drummond visit with guests on Tuesday, June 16, 2026, during Drummond’s watch party at VFW Post 577 in Tulsa, Okla. Supporters gathered to watch results in the Republican primary election. (Photo by Ace Cuervo/For Oklahoma Voice)
Drummond’s results show he submitted to a hair follicle test, which experts say provides a lengthier look at an individual’s drug use history than a urine test.
“It looks like Mike is trying to pull a fast one on Oklahoma voters by taking a test that avoids the longer window,” said Matt Parker, Drummond’s campaign manager.
Mazzei’s campaign said Drummond doesn’t want to defend his record, so he is spreading lies about Mazzei’s health.
“Mike took the same standard drug test used by the NCAA and NFL, and passed,” said Jahan Wilcox, a Mazzei spokesperson. “Drummond won’t accept the result because the truth exposes his attack for exactly what it is, a lie.”
A urine test will show if a person has used a drug recently, while a hair test will indicate if a person has used a drug over a longer period of time, said Joseph Reilly, president of the Florida-based National Drug Screening, which provides services in the management of drug and alcohol testing programs.
“They’re definitely different,” he said. “They’re not apples to apples at all.”
A urine test will show use going back five or six days, but it will probably not show if someone was under the influence of drugs two weeks ago, Reilly said.
A hair follicle test will pick up drugs about seven days to about 90 days after ingestion, he said.
“One is not better than the other,” he said. “Are we trying to find out recent use of drugs? Are we trying to find out maybe more of a lifestyle pattern of past use of drugs?”
He said it is easier to be deceptive on a urine test than a hair test because someone could try to bring something with them to add to the specimen or try to substitute it.
While there are claims that cheating can occur on a hair follicle test, Reilly said it is very difficult, because a person is watching the specimen being collected by the donor, he said.
Both men have faced pressure to release their medical and financial records after a debate moderator asked if they’d agree to do so earlier this month. 
While it is common for U.S. presidents to release annual physicals and tax returns, it is not a common request for Oklahoma’s gubernatorial candidates.
Still, both candidates had said they would  release records. Drummond went a step further and released a drug test. He also called on his opponent to do the same.
Neither had released their financial records as of Monday.
Drummond, 62, released a letter from his physician last week stating he was healthy enough to serve.  
Mazzei, 61, on Monday also released a letter from his physician stating that he has no underlying health issues that would impact his ability to serve. 
“Based on my ongoing care of Mr. Mazzei, my review of his medical history, and my most recent clinical assessment on September 25, 2025, it is my professional medical opinion that he is in very good overall health,” the doctor wrote. “He is fully functional and has no medical condition that, in my judgement, would prevent him from carrying out the physical, cognitive, or professional responsibilities” for the public office he is seeking.
Mazzei said earlier this month that he has not been on medication since a 2008 car accident left him with a back injury and nerve damage. Mazzei missed a significant number of votes following the accident when he was in the Senate, where he served for 12 years.

text:
Iowa Valley Community College District will provide free technical training and assistance to small manufacturers through a federal grant. (Photo by Matthias Ritzmann/Getty Images)Iowa Valley Community College District will use a multimillion-dollar federal grant to expand manufacturing training and assistance to companies across its service area.
The Marshalltown-based community college district announced in a news release it has received $5 million from the U.S. Small Business Administration to provide free technical instruction for small manufacturers in Hardin, Marshall, Poweshiek and Tama counties.
According to the release, training and assistance for these manufacturers will span robotics, automation, industrial software, welding, industrial maintenance and more, building off the district’s existing Iowa Valley Business and Community Solutions program and offerings at Marshalltown Community College and Ellsworth Community College.

“The SBA looked at our proven outcomes-based training, which puts people directly into jobs across our region, and decided to invest in it,” said Iowa Valley Community College District President Anne Howsare Boyens in the release. “This grant lets us take what’s working in our BCS programs and MCC’s manufacturing pathways and put it directly in the hands of the small manufacturers who need it most.”
Iowa Valley Community College District was one of 11 institutions selected to receive grants from the Small Business Administration’s Manufacturing in America Empower to Grow Grant Initiative, the release stated. The combined $50 million in grants are aimed at bolstering capacity among small manufacturing companies in critical areas.
Marshalltown Community College is also launching a new associate degree program in robotics and automation, the release stated, which will also help in the grant-funded training.
“We’re building the pipeline local employers will need five and ten years from now,” said Marshalltown Community College Provost Matt Schmit in the release. “A lot of small manufacturers in our region may not have their own training department, and they can’t always spare employees for the time needed to get certified.
