name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Environment Department proposes mandatory investigations, fixes for major methane leaks
description: The New Mexico Environment Department is proposing beefed up rules for monitoring methane leaks in order to help reduce both air pollution and natural gas waste.
text:
A pumpjack between Hobbs and Lovington in the Permian Basin as seen on Aug. 7, 2025. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)The New Mexico Environment Department is proposing beefed up rules for monitoring methane leaks in order to help reduce both air pollution and natural gas waste.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The proposal, which the department announced Friday, would create a new statewide program to identify large methane leaks through satellite and aircraft imagery. When the program flags possible large leaks, NMED officials would then notify oil and gas operators in the area and require them to investigate.
If an operator finds a leak during the course of the investigation, they’re required to repair it and file a report with the Environment Department. Most investigations and repairs would need to be done within three days of the initial notification, NMED noted in a news release.
In addition, the new rules would increase requirements for oil and gas operating equipment to more closely align with federal standards by 2031.
“Methane leaks result in climate change, air pollution and waste of New Mexico’s natural resources,” NMED Secretary James Kenney said in a statement. The proposal, he noted, “builds on New Mexico’s nationally-leading oil and gas rules,” and will help oil and gas operators address leaks faster to keep “more natural gas where it belongs — in the pipeline.”
Members on the governor-appointed Environmental Improvement Board will decide whether to proceed with a public hearing on NMED’s proposal.
In a statement Monday, officials with the national Environmental Defense Fund praised the proposed rules, which they said would be “significantly stronger” than the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s.
“New Mexico is standing against the Trump administration’s reckless attack on our health and standing up for state climate action,” Environmental Defense Fund Senior Regulatory and Legislative Manager Nini Gu said in a statement.
Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham last year announced that New Mexico’s methane emissions were half of those measured in neighboring Texas, although wells across the state still experience “venting,” a term that refers to methane leaking into the air.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Three more NC localities weigh pauses on data centers as developer backs away from Raleigh project
description: Recent polling shows growing opposition to data centers in North Carolina.  That trend is being reflected across the state Monday, with three more cities and counties considering putting data project developments on pause, while a proposal to build one in Raleigh was withdrawn Saturday. Greensboro City Council will hold a Monday public hearing as the […]
text:
Data centers are energy-intensive, running servers around the clock to power streams of computer computations. (Image: Adobe Stock)Recent polling shows growing opposition to data centers in North Carolina.  That trend is being reflected across the state Monday, with three more cities and counties considering putting data project developments on pause, while a proposal to build one in Raleigh was withdrawn Saturday.
Greensboro City Council will hold a Monday public hearing as the city considers a 120-day moratorium on large data centers or similar facilities using more than 10 megawatts of electrical power. After rejecting a formal moratorium in July in a 5-4 vote, council members now say they need time to hear from the public and experts about the impact data centers would have on water, the energy grid, and the environment.
Poll: Majority of NC voters oppose data centers, aren’t worried about voter fraud

Greensboro Mayor Marikay Abuzuaiter said that there are currently no plans to bring or recruit a data center to the city.
Further west, Yadkin County will consider a 12-month moratorium on data centers.
A draft resolution that will be considered Monday evening by county commissioners states that the temporary moratorium would apply to “data centers, data processing facilities, cryptocurrency mining operations, and uses associated with data processing facilities not yet defined.”
The moratorium would also apply to artificial intelligence computing, weather modeling, genome sequencing, cloud storage and video and technical streaming services.
Yadkin, Alamance, and Greensboro are the latest municipalities to consider data center moratoriums. (Map: NCDOT)
Yadkin County’s planning department is in the process of updating its land use plan and wants more detailed information before greenlighting such facilities.
“The County has determined that to simply allow this intensive land use to be permitted without regard to location, height, size, density, population and type of trade would be counter to the County and its citizens,” the draft ordinance reads.
Residents of Alamance County are expected to flood the historic courthouse in Graham Monday evening for a special hearing on data centers. Like residents in Greensboro and Yadkin County, residents are worried about the environmental impact of  data centers in their community.
The North Carolina Environmental Justice Network and the Haw River Assembly are asking Alamance County Commissioners to approve a two-year moratorium on new data center development in unincorporated Alamance County. Proponents of the 24-month moratorium say that would allow time to complete a land use study, adopt appropriate zoning, and most importantly, confirm the area has a safe and adequate water supply for homes and farms already in the region.
The data center industry’s PR blitz is backfiring

If Alamance County commissioners approve a two-year pause, they would not be alone: Surry County commissioners also unanimously approved a 24-month moratorium last month.
The three local governments holding hearings Monday need to look no further than Raleigh to see how quickly public opposition to data center projects can snowball..
An annexation hearing for a data center in southeast Raleigh had only been public knowledge for a few days when the project came to an abrupt end on Saturday.
Citizens opposed to the plan flooded the email of city council members and quickly filled all 30 public comment slots available at Tuesday’s hearing. Raleigh Mayor Janet Cowell told WRAL-TV that her sense was that the council did not view the project favorably.
The drumbeat of opposition to the project prompted the Raleigh city government to take the unusual step Saturday of posting on social media that the annexation hearing had been cancelled, noting it was the developer who withdrew the request.
Neither Mayor Cowell nor a spokesperson for the city immediately responded to NC Newsline’s request for comment on the cancellation.
While several Wake County municipalities have enacted data center moratoriums in 2026, neither Raleigh nor Wake County has considered one to date.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kentuckian Scott Jennings may face defamation action from Hasan Piker over edited clips
description: Kentuckian and conservative political commentator Scott Jennings may soon be facing a defamation lawsuit.  Hasan Piker, a progressive Twitch streamer who often discusses politics, told Status, a media news site, that he and his legal team were preparing a defamation lawsuit against Jennings and Salem Media, the company that syndicates Jennings’ radio show. L[...]
text:
Daniel Cameron, former Kentucky attorney general, will speak for former President Donald Trump, the Republican candidate for president, Saturday at the 144th annual Fancy Farm Picnic. Last year, the Trump banner was carried by Bailey Canamore, 11, of Clinton, as GOP political consultant and pundit Scott Jennings spoke live on CNN, Aug. 5, 2023. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)Kentuckian and conservative political commentator Scott Jennings may soon be facing a defamation lawsuit. 
Hasan Piker, a progressive Twitch streamer who often discusses politics, told Status, a media news site, that he and his legal team were preparing a defamation lawsuit against Jennings and Salem Media, the company that syndicates Jennings’ radio show. Last week, Jennings shared an edited video on Aug. 11 of Piker online claiming Piker had said “the USA should resume lynchings against black people.” 
A Snopes review found that Piker was sarcastically mimicking others’ opinions and the clips were from hours-long streams and heavily edited without full context. 
Jennings, who now frequently appears on CNN to discuss Republican politics, is a former staffer of Kentucky U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell. In recent days, Jennings has become a rumored candidate to be President Donald Trump’s next press secretary after Karoline Leavitt said she plans to leave the role at the end of August. 
Jennings’ Aug. 11 post referred to Piker as “Abdul El-Sayed’s best pal and campaign partner.” El-Sayed, a progressive, became the Democratic nominee in Michigan’s U.S. Senate race earlier this month. 
“ive never seen a more clear cut instance of defamation than this in my entire life. blatant disregard for the truth,” Piker said on X in response to one of Jennings’ clips. 
Jennings didn’t immediately return a texted request for comment Monday.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Veteran pollster David McLennan discusses attitudes toward online gambling
description: As anyone who’s watched a college or professional sporting event in recent years is well-aware, the rapid spread of online gambling has brought transformative – and many would say deeply troubling – change to what has long been one of the most important social institutions in our country. In just a very few years, sports […]
text:
Meredith College political scientist and pollster David McLennan (File photo)As anyone who’s watched a college or professional sporting event in recent years is well-aware, the rapid spread of online gambling has brought transformative – and many would say deeply troubling – change to what has long been one of the most important social institutions in our country. In just a very few years, sports gambling has gone from an unlawful underground activity into a huge and ubiquitous business run by giant corporations.
So, what do average North Carolinians make of this rapid change in our society and how it’s affecting the people – a high percentage of them young men – for whom it has become a big and expensive part of their lives? Recently, veteran pollster David McLennan – the long-time director of the Meredith College Poll – conducted a new survey to examine these issues, and this past week, he joined me for an extended two-part conversation to discuss some of his findings.
Click here to listen to the full interview with veteran pollster David McLennan.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Federal judge denies hemp entrepreneurs’ request to overturn Virginia’s new THC limit
description: A federal judge in Roanoke on Friday declined seven Virginia business owners’ request to eliminate a new regulation that removes an exception to the state’s limit of 2 milligrams of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) per product package. The new standard took effect Aug. 15.  The entrepreneurs had asked the U.S. District Court for the Western District of […]
text:
A hemp plant at Redfern Hemp Co. in Caroline County. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)A federal judge in Roanoke on Friday declined seven Virginia business owners’ request to eliminate a new regulation that removes an exception to the state’s limit of 2 milligrams of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) per product package. The new standard took effect Aug. 15. 
The entrepreneurs had asked the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Virginia in Roanoke for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction to block the rule stemming from the state budget lawmakers passed and Gov. Abigail Spanberger signed in late June.
They said the removal of the 25-to-1 ratio, which allowed hemp products to exceed the 2 mg THC limit if they contained 25 times as much cannabidiol (CBD), would devastate their businesses, cause severe financial strains and undermine Virginia’s small business owners.
Hemp businesses ask federal judge to block Virginia’s new THC cap

The court found that the plaintiffs did not prove that the new standard would significantly harm their businesses, and determined that the new rule was created in the public’s best interest. 
“Because Plaintiffs have not demonstrated either a likelihood of success on the merits or irreparable injury if HB 30 becomes effective, and because the balance of equities and the public interest weigh in favor of Defendants, the Motions for Preliminary Injunction … and Temporary Restraining Order … are DENIED,” Judge Robert S. Ballou wrote on Aug. 14. 
The plaintiffs and other hemp industry representatives reacted quickly, expressing disappointment in the judgment, requesting lawmakers discuss the matter in a special legislative session and asking authorities to pause the new law. 
“We are incredibly disappointed with today’s news. The judge himself acknowledged that this was rushed legislation, leading to complications and unintended consequences,” Barbara Biddle, president of the Cannabis Small Business Association and owner of District Hemp Botanicals, said in a statement. “We are calling on legislators to convene a special session to address the gap in access for consumers, protect businesses from bankruptcy, and reinstate the previous definition of hemp.”
Biddle added: “We’re also asking the Virginia Cannabis Control Authority, Office of the Attorney General, and local law enforcement to consider halting enforcement of the redefinition until legislators are able to resolve this issue.”
Travis Lane, owner of Northern Virginia Hemp & Agriculture LLC, placed blame for the new standard squarely on Spanberger and her administration.
“If Virginia small businesses are pushed toward bankruptcy while a new state-regulated cannabis market is being built for 2027, voters deserve to remember who made that choice, and our elected leaders still have an opportunity to change it,” Lane said in a statement.
Spanberger has not commented on the ruling but earlier this month, her spokesperson said gaps between the state’s marijuana and hemp laws created dangerous conditions.
“For years, untested and highly-intoxicating products have flooded Virginia with little oversight, inadequate protections for kids and teenagers, and few tools for law enforcement to address the illicit market — all because of a loophole in state law that bad faith actors have exploited and pushed the limit of its intended use,” the spokesperson said.
He added that the state’s adult-use cannabis market, slated to open next year, will streamline the industries, shore up safety and create new opportunities for small businesses owners.
Learn more about the new regulation and other hemp and marijuana changes in the state at the Virginia Cannabis Control Authority’s website.

The Heflin-Torbert Judicial Building in downtown Montgomery, Alabama, seen on January 24, 2023. Justices on Monday extended a briefing deadline for Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville in a case that is challenging his candidacy. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama Supreme Court on Monday extended a briefing deadline for Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville’s responses in a lawsuit challenging his ability to run for the office. 
The court moved the briefing deadline from Friday to Aug. 27. Earlier this month, plaintiffs in the case also sought and received an extension to file their motions with the state’s high court. In a motion filed on Friday, Tuberville’s lawyers said they are busy with a civil lawsuit against Tuberville in Jefferson County filed by former Republican gubernatorial candidate Ken McFeeters. It is McFeeters’ fourth attempt to remove Tuberville from the ballot in some way.
“That case is filed by a different plaintiff, and involves a pleading of over 100 pages as well as exhibits totaling 400 pages,” the motion said.

According to the Friday motion, the appellants had no objection to the extension. In a statement Monday morning, Barry Ragsdale, an attorney for the plaintiffs challenging Tuberville, said he had no problem with the extension because “the case cannot possibly be resolved before the deadline for the GOP to replace Tuberville on the general election ballot.”
A message seeking further comment from Tuberville’s lawyers and campaign was sent Monday morning. 
Plaintiffs allege that Tuberville does not meet the state’s seven-year residency requirement to run for governor, citing reporting from several state outlets. Tuberville maintains that he meets the seven-year residency requirement.
The case made its way to the Alabama Supreme Court after a Montgomery County Circuit Judge dismissed the case due to a lack of jurisdiction. She did not rule on the merits.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Voters deserve a say as counties consider shifting property tax burden to sales taxes
description: South Dakota’s new optional half-percent county sales tax is being sold as property-tax relief. It is relief only in the sense of moving money from one pocket to another. The cost of county government does not fall. The law changes who pays it. Meade, Pennington, Custer and Codington are among the counties that have enacted […]
text:
A Minnehaha County property tax bill delivered in early 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota’s new optional half-percent county sales tax is being sold as property-tax relief.
It is relief only in the sense of moving money from one pocket to another. The cost of county government does not fall. The law changes who pays it.
Meade, Pennington, Custer and Codington are among the counties that have enacted the tax. Codington County opponents are gathering signatures to force a public vote. Brown and Fall River counties decided voters should make the choice. Other counties are still studying it.
The benefit goes to owner-occupied homeowners, who will receive a reduction in the county government portion of their property taxes. In Codington County, the projected reduction is about 23% of the total property tax bill. 
That is real money. But everyone who makes taxable purchases in the counties that enact the tax will help pay for it — including many who can least afford another tax.


Learn more

Black Hills counties among first to adopt new sales tax option for homeowner property tax reduction
How and when new South Dakota laws will reduce property taxes for homeowners
Here’s how much South Dakotans could save on property taxes after accounting for higher sales taxes



Start with renters. About one-third of South Dakota households rent. They will pay more tax on clothing, furniture, restaurant meals and everyday purchases, but receive no direct property tax credit.
The renter share is higher in parts of western South Dakota. Census data show about 37% of Rapid City households rent and 52% rent in Box Elder. Those renters will help pay the county sales tax but are unlikely to receive a benefit. Nothing in the law requires a landlord to pass along property tax savings.
The tax also lands harder on lower-income South Dakotans. Households in the lowest 20% of income pay about 7.4% of their income in sales and excise taxes. Among higher-income households, the share falls below 4% and keeps dropping as income rises.
Same cash register. Very different bite.
Farmers and ranchers have another reason to look closely. Not every farm expense is taxable. Seed, fertilizer, livestock feed and agricultural fuel are exempt inputs, while machinery and titled vehicles are handled under separate tax laws.
But farms and ranches still make taxable purchases for fencing, tools, shop equipment, building supplies and other things most households never think about.
The first property tax benefit goes to the farmhouse and homesite. Agricultural land receives nothing until the county generates enough revenue to fully offset its owner-occupied levy.
Then there is geography. Tourism counties have an advantage. Black Hills visitors buy gas, eat supper and fill the backseat with souvenirs proving they survived Needles Highway.
Most counties, however, do not have Mount Rushmore or the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. Their outside shoppers are usually other South Dakotans.
Governor signs bills to reduce homeowner property taxes with higher sales taxes

A Hamlin County renter shopping in Watertown may help finance relief for Codington County homeowners. Sioux Falls, Rapid City, Aberdeen, Watertown and Mitchell pull spending from surrounding counties, while smaller counties have no similar advantage.
Tourism counties can shift part of the bill to visitors. Regional shopping counties mostly shift it among South Dakotans.
Same half-cent. Very different results.
That is why the potential Codington County referendum matters.
County commissioners may have the legal authority to impose a tax paid by a broad group in order to provide a direct benefit to a narrower group. But legal authority and political fairness are not the same.
If the idea is sound, explain it. Put the numbers on the table. Tell renters, homeowners, farmers and businesses what they are likely to pay and who benefits.
Then let them vote.
A statewide Mason-Dixon poll commissioned by South Dakota News Watch and the Chiesman Center for Democracy found 49% of South Dakota registered voters opposed giving counties the authority to exchange higher sales taxes for lower property taxes, while 33% supported it and 17% were undecided.
That sounds like a conversation worth having before the tax is imposed, not afterward.

title: State suspends license of Davenport nurse who admitted stealing patient medications
description: The Iowa Board of Nursing has suspended, for at least one year, the license of a Davenport nurse who has pleaded guilty to criminal charges of stealing patient medications at a surgical center. The decision follows a May 2026 emergency order by the board immediately suspending the license of Glenn Thronson of Anamosa, who has […]
text:
The Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing is responsible for overseeing Iowa's licensing boards. (Photo illustration via Getty Images; logo courtesy of the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing) The Iowa Board of Nursing has suspended, for at least one year, the license of a Davenport nurse who has pleaded guilty to criminal charges of stealing patient medications at a surgical center.
The decision follows a May 2026 emergency order by the board immediately suspending the license of Glenn Thronson of Anamosa, who has been an Iowa-licensed nurse since 2021.
At the time, the board said only that Thronson was “seeking out and applying for nursing jobs in the state of Iowa and poses an immediate danger to the public,” and it charged Thronson with falsification of records related to nursing, misappropriating medications or supplies, habitual intoxication or addiction to the use of drugs in a manner that might impair his ability to practice nursing, and failing to properly document or perform the disposal of medications.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
On June 12, 2026, Thronson appeared before an administrative law judge for a closed-door hearing on the matter.
According to the judge’s findings of fact, which stem from evidence presented at that hearing, Thronson worked as a nurse in Texas for five years, although his employment there was intermittent due to his use of methamphetamine. After becoming homeless, he moved to Iowa and from August 2025 through April 2026 he worked at Spring Park Surgery Center in Davenport.
On April 7, 2026, a Spring Park employee spotted a discrepancy in the medication count, with unspecified amounts of fentanyl, Dilaudid and Demerol unaccounted for. According to the judge’s findings, an investigation by Spring Park indicated Thronson had completed 23 entries in the medication-administration records using fake patient names.
He was also alleged to have completed one entry using a real patient’s name to sign out fentanyl, despite the lack of a physician’s order for the narcotic. In addition, the investigation was also alleged to have shown that witnesses’ signatures, indicating others had watched Thronson dispose of unused medications, were mere scribbles that didn’t correspond to actual employee names.
At the hearing, a Spring Park administrator allegedly stated that when questioned Thronson admitted stealing patient medications for his own use and admitted falsifying records.
Court records show Thronson was criminally charged with three counts of prohibited acts involving a controlled substance and three counts of tampering with records. That case is still pending, although Thronson recently pleaded guilty to all six charges, with the state agreeing to recommend a six-year suspended prison sentence.
Board records indicate that at his disciplinary hearing Thronson acknowledged his substance abuse issues and indicated he was enrolled in inpatient treatment. He also indicated he wanted to continue practicing nursing, according to the judge’s findings.
Citing what she called Thronson’s “lack of disciplinary history,” as well as his “previously imposed discipline for similarly situated offenses,” Administrative Law Judge Kristine Dreckman recently issued an order suspending Thronson’s license. After one year, she ruled, Thronson can apply for reinstatement, but will not be reinstated until he has established that such action is in the public interest.
Prior to submitting an application for reinstatement, Thronson must also complete a comprehensive substance abuse and mental health evaluation and show evidence of 12 continuous months of sobriety, the order states.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Thronson for comment.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: New minimum wages for Minnesota nursing home workers to take effect in September
description: New minimum wages for Minnesota nursing home workers received final federal approval and will take effect on Sept. 10, more than three years after the state Legislature created a nation-leading labor standards board to set pay and working standards for some of the state’s lowest-paid workers. Thousands of workers will receive raises with the new […]
text:
(Photo by Getty Images) New minimum wages for Minnesota nursing home workers received final federal approval and will take effect on Sept. 10, more than three years after the state Legislature created a nation-leading labor standards board to set pay and working standards for some of the state’s lowest-paid workers.
Thousands of workers will receive raises with the new hourly wage floors across four job categories: $22.50 for certified nursing assistants, $23.50 for trained medication aides, $27 for licensed practical nurses, and $19 for all other nursing home workers. The hourly wages will increase another $1.50 per hour across all job categories on Jan. 1.
The minimum wages are the culmination of a yearslong campaign by the Service Employees International Union — representing nearly 50,000 Minnesota healthcare and long-term care workers — to increase pay across the entire nursing home sector despite fierce resistance from industry leaders, who warn tight margins keep them teetering on the brink of closure.
“These workers are a lifeline to our elders and most vulnerable residents, and they deserve financial peace of mind so they can provide the best care possible,” said Dr. Rasha Ahmad Sharif, executive vice president of SEIU Healthcare Minnesota & Iowa, in a statement celebrating federal approval of the new minimum wages.
Democrats created the Minnesota Nursing Home Workforce Standards Board in 2023 as part of a slew of pro-labor laws, giving it broad authority to regulate working conditions in nursing homes.
The nine-member board — made up of equal numbers of worker representatives, nursing home leaders and state officials — approved the wage floors in April 2024 and also mandated time-and-a-half pay for 11 holidays. The rules, which set wages far above the state’s $11.41-per-hour minimum wage for all workers, were approved without the support of the industry representatives, who abstained from voting.
The nursing home industry, represented by LeadingAge Minnesota and Care Providers of Minnesota, has filed a lawsuit in federal court seeking to dissolve the labor standards board after unsuccessfully suing to block the holiday pay rules. Industry leaders argue the unelected board has too much authority over labor standards and could force nursing homes to shutter even as demand grows from the state’s aging population.
Many workers — particularly licensed practical nurses — are already earning more than the minimum wages, according to a 2024 fiscal analysis by the Department of Labor and Industry. Those who are earning less than the new wage floors will receive about a $2-per-hour raise.
The rules set by the board were approved by the Minnesota Legislature with bipartisan support last year. The Minnesota Legislature already appropriated an additional $37 million to fund the raises in its 2024 health and human services budget bill, and the federal government will contribute a comparable amount.
The minimum wages were supposed to take effect on Jan. 1 but were delayed because the Minnesota Department of Human Services failed to complete the necessary steps to receive approval and funding from the federal government. The federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services gave the necessary approval on Aug. 11.
The Department of Human Services plans to pay nursing homes the higher reimbursement rate retroactive to Jan. 1. SEIU expects nursing homes will then pay workers at the higher rate retroactively, though it would be voluntary.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Gov. Reeves appoints Oxford attorney Amanda Tollison to state Supreme Court
description: Attorney Clay Baldwin with the State Auditor's Office, presents his case before the Mississippi Supreme Court, Tuesday, Jan. 20, 2026 in Jackson.
text:
Gov. Tate Reeves on Monday appointed Amanda Jones Tollison, a private-practice attorney in Oxford, to a vacant seat on the Mississippi Supreme Court. 
Tollison is currently a partner with the law firm Butler Snow, where she has practiced since 2012. Before this, she served as legal counsel to Governor Haley Barbour from 2008 to 2012. In that role she advised Barbour on legal, legislative, and policy matters, including judicial appointments, elections, budget issues, and disaster recovery efforts. 
“Amanda has distinguished herself throughout her career as an excellent attorney, respected leader in The Mississippi Bar, and dedicated public servant,” Reeves said in a statement. 
Tollison earned her law degree from the University of Mississippi School of Law and an undergraduate degree from Mississippi State University. She has served as president of The Mississippi Bar, as a member of the Board of Bar Commissioners and as a trustee and fellow of the Mississippi Bar Foundation. 
“I am deeply grateful to Gov. Reeves for this appointment and humbled by his trust in me to fulfill the duties of a justice on the Mississippi Supreme Court,” Tollison said in a statement.
Gov. Tate Reeves appointed Oxford attorney Amanda Jones Tollison to a seat on the Mississippi Supreme Court  Credit: Courtesy: Gov. Tate Reeves' office
Tollison’s term will begin on September 1, 2026, and continue until a special election fills the seat.
She replaces James Maxwell, also from Oxford, who left his seat on the state Supreme Court after being confirmed by the U.S. Senate as a federal judge in northern Mississippi. The appointment now fills all vacancies on the nine-member court.
When Tollison is sworn in, she will become the third woman on the court, serving alongside current justices Jenifer Branning from Philadelphia and Celeste Wilson of DeSoto County. This is the largest number of women who have served on the state’s highest court at the same time. 
She is also the wife of current 3rd Circuit Court Judge and former state Sen. Gray Tollison.

name: Delaware
title: Hockessin Wawa employees subdue knife-wielding man after worker injured
description:
The Delaware State Police have arrested 36-year-old Matthew Ralston, of Hockessin, Delaware, for felony assault and related offenses following a stabbing incident that occurred Sunday morning at a Wawa in Hockessin. […]
The post State Police Arrest Hockessin Man for Stabbing Incident at Wawa in Hockessin appeared first on Delaware State Police - State of Del[...]
text:
State police charged a 36-year-old Hockessin man with six felonies following the early-morning confrontation
HOCKESSIN — Wawa employees disarmed and subdued a knife-wielding man after he allegedly cut a co-worker’s hand during an altercation early Sunday, Delaware State Police said.
Troopers responded shortly before 3 a.m. Aug. 16 to the Wawa at 605 Yorklyn Road, near Lancaster Pike. When they arrived, employees were restraining 36-year-old Matthew Ralston of Hockessin, police said.
Investigators said Ralston initially entered the store, made a purchase and went outside but remained in the parking lot. He later returned, went behind the counter, displayed a knife and allegedly threatened and attempted to stab an employee.
Ralston then left the knife on the counter and walked outside, police said. He allegedly returned again, retrieved the knife and waved it above his head before leaving the store once more.
Police said Ralston entered the store again and approached an employee who was calling 911. He allegedly lunged at her and swung the knife, cutting her hand.
Other employees disarmed and restrained Ralston until troopers arrived. The injured employee was taken to an area hospital with injuries that were not considered life-threatening.
Ralston was charged with three counts of possession of a deadly weapon during the commission of a felony, second-degree assault, attempted second-degree assault and aggravated menacing.
Following his arraignment, Ralston was committed to the Delaware Department of Correction in lieu of a $46,000 cash bond.
Ralston is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty.

name: VTDigger
title: Dartmouth Health says it needs to close telehealth services for emergency and intensive care
description:
Five Vermont hospitals rely on the remote care to reduce costs of specialists and transfers while still providing high-acuity care close to home. Dartmouth Health says the costs are “simply unsustainable.” 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Dartmouth Health says it needs to close telehealth services for emergency and intensive care.
text:
Dr. Roslinde Collins-Gibbard consults on critically ill patients from Dartmouth Health’s Telehealth hub.  Photo courtesy of Dartmouth Health
Dartmouth Health expects to end its Tele-ICU and Tele-ED services, a move that would affect five Vermont hospitals and more across the region. 
They “are two services whose costs, at our current scale, without external support, are simply unsustainable,” Audra Burns, a spokesperson for the New Hampshire-based health network, told VTDigger. The network, which has two affiliate hospitals in Vermont and its flagship academic medical center minutes across the border in Lebanon, New Hampshire, is the second-largest healthcare provider to Vermonters.
Burns declined to comment on how much the two services cost Dartmouth Health.
Tele-ICU and Tele-ED are two of the nearly 20 kinds of remote healthcare Dartmouth provides. Both are designed to give rural hospitals access to specialists at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center.
A representative for Grace Cottage Hospital, in Townshend, which uses the Tele-ED services, confirmed that Dartmouth Health informed the Vermont hospital of its decision to close on Friday and is now working through the timeline of the closure.
The remote intensive care unit services connect Dartmouth’s intensive care physicians and critical care nurses with a patient’s bedside team, so rural hospitals can care for patients needing acute care and so clinicians can do more high-level, continuous monitoring. Dartmouth Health says the service reduces mortality rates and the length of stay in the ICU. The network also says it reduces the need for a patient to be transferred  — allowing them to stay in a less-expensive local setting.
Northwestern Medical Center in St. Albans and Southwestern Vermont Medical Center, a Dartmouth affiliate in Bennington, both use the network’s Tele-ICU, according to materials Dartmouth Health shared with VTDigger in 2025. Dartmouth Hitchcock, in Lebanon, also uses its own service internally to help avoid staff burnout and improve safety and quality of patient care, the Tele-ICU medical director told the New Hampshire Union Leader when they launched the service line in 2019. Three other New Hampshire hospitals use Dartmouth Health’s Tele-ICU. 
The remote emergency department services are meant to help providers with higher-level care and documentation as they transport an emergency patient, transfer a patient to a higher-acuity hospital or treat them in a smaller hospital setting.  
In promotional materials, Dartmouth Health called the service “a life-saving connection.” The health network says it reduces transfers, staffing costs and the need for more expensive temporary clinicians. The network also says the service helps open up emergency department capacity. 
In Vermont, Brattleboro Memorial Hospital, Grace Cottage Hospital in Townshend, Southwestern Vermont Medical Center and Mt. Ascutney Hospital and Health Center, a Dartmouth Health affiliate in Windsor, all use the service, according to Dartmouth Health’s 2025 list. 
In May, Dartmouth Health reported an overall $63.5 million operating deficit, as expenses — things like staffing and pharmaceutical costs — outpaced the hospital’s revenue, the Valley News reported. 
Burns cited these “significant financial challenges” as the push to evaluate the cost of continuing the Tele-ICU and Tele-ED services.

READ MORE

“External funding for these telehealth programs that often serve rural critical access hospitals, but rarely reach the scale to account for the 24/7 staffing required, is often critically scarce, yet is vital to maintaining these services,” she wrote in a statement to VTDigger. 
“As the nation’s most rural academic medical center and health system, we are steadfast in our commitment to deliver exceptional care to the farthest corners of our service region. Our sustainability during challenging financial times will require changes and new approaches to this important care model,” she added.
Burns said the health network will “be working closely” with the hospitals that rely on these services to make sure that alternatives are in place before Dartmouth Health finalizes its closures. 
This story will be updated.

title: Two Indiana secretary of state debates planned
description: Indiana’s secretary of state race tops the election ballot this year — and at least two debates are planned so far. The Indy Chamber’s HobNob legislative forum returns Aug. 26 at The Crane Bay Event Center and will feature a moderated conversation between Republican Max Engling, Democrat Beau Bayh, Libertarian Lauri Shillings and Greg Ballard […]
text:
Secretary of state candidates, from left: Independent Greg Ballard, Democrat Beau Bayh, Republican Max Engling and Libertarian Lauri Shillings. (Photos provided by campaigns)Indiana’s secretary of state race tops the election ballot this year — and at least two debates are planned so far.
The Indy Chamber’s HobNob legislative forum returns Aug. 26 at The Crane Bay Event Center and will feature a moderated conversation between Republican Max Engling, Democrat Beau Bayh, Libertarian Lauri Shillings and Greg Ballard of the Lincoln Party.

It will be hosted in collaboration with media partners Fox59 & CBS4 and IBJ Media, and coverage of HobNob will be shared with viewers and voters.


“HobNob reflects the Indy Chamber’s commitment to informed civic engagement,” said Taylor Hughes, chief strategy officer and chief of staff at the Indy Chamber. “Bringing candidates together in one forum gives our business community and voters the opportunity to hear directly from those seeking office and better understand the issues that will shape Indiana’s future.”
To purchase tickets to HobNob, visit the Indy Chamber Eventbrite.


The Indiana Debate Commission will host a more typical debate with the candidates at 7 p.m. on Oct. 7 inside WFYI studios in Indianapolis.

It will be moderated by Laura Merrifield Wilson, professor of political science at the University of Indianapolis — who hosts Positively Politics on WICR and is a member of the Indiana Debate Commission.

While there will be no audience, the public can submit questions through www.indianadebatecommission.com using the “Ask Your Question” link on the homepage. Hoosiers whose questions are selected may also be invited to ask their questions via pre-recorded video during the debate. Consistent with commission practice, candidates will not receive the questions in advance.

The race for secretary of state is one of the Indiana’s most closely watched contests, featuring candidates representing four different political parties. As Indiana’s chief elections officer, the secretary of state oversees election administration, business services, securities regulation and campaign finance reporting.
“The Indiana Debate Commission is committed to helping voters make informed decisions by providing opportunities to hear directly from the candidates,” said Elizabeth Bennion, president of the Indiana Debate Commission. “The secretary of state plays a vital role in Indiana’s elections and civic life, and this four-candidate debate will give Hoosiers an opportunity to compare different perspectives on the future of the office. We are grateful to WFYI and media partners across the state for helping make this conversation accessible to voters wherever they live. We hope the debate sparks conversations in communities across Indiana and encourages Hoosiers to learn more about the candidates before casting their ballots.”
Hoosiers can watch live on WFYI Public Television, streamed on WFYI’s YouTube channel, and streamed at www.indianadebatecommission.com. The debate feed will also be made available to media organizations across Indiana for broadcast, streaming and embedding.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Redistricting hearings across the state are open to the public, with tight security planned
description: Rep. Missy McGee, R-Hattiesburg, reads a document during the Joint Redistricting and Reapportionment Committee organizational meeting at the Capitol in Jackson on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026.
text:
When a panel of state lawmakers convenes in Tupelo on Tuesday to hear from the public on how, or whether, the state should redraw Mississippi’s legislative, judicial and congressional districts, the hearings will be open to the public. 
State and local authorities plan to provide security for the hearings before a joint House and Senate committee on redistricting on what has become an intensely debated topic.
Alex Gibert, spokesperson for the Mississippi Department of Public Safety, said no threats have been made against any legislator. Still, the Mississippi Highway Patrol will work alongside other divisions within the agency to “ensure the safety of legislators and civilians who are present.” 
Many civil rights leaders, Black lawmakers and voting rights advocates believe the hearings are a pretext for the Legislature moving to dismantle several majority-Black districts and weakening Black political power in the state.
Republican leaders believe that when the U.S. Supreme Court issued its ruling in the Callais decision on a Louisiana casae, it cleared the way for the Legislature to redraw political lines to make it easier for Republicans to get elected.
The committee is encouraging the public to participate. The public can offer comments at any of the eight public hearings, or submit a redistricting plan to the committee, according to the directions on the committee’s website. 
This is not the first time state police have protected board members during an impassioned policy debate.
In 2000, former Gov. William Winter led a 17-member advisory council on changing Mississippi’s former state flag that featured a Confederate battle emblem in the upper left canton that many Black citizens viewed as racist and white citizens viewed as part of the state’s history. 
The council conducted hearings across the state to gather input on how state officials should proceed after it was revealed that the state never actually adopted an official state flag. Some of the hearings grew heated and saw citizens argue with one another.
Below is the schedule of planned redistricting hearings. Each will start at 6 p.m. 

Aug. 18 at Itawamba Community College in Tupelo 
Aug. 27 at Northwest Mississippi Community College in Senatobia

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Morrisey ‘closely monitoring’ storms, says last month’s emergency declaration still in effect
description: Gov. Patrick Morrisey says his office is “closely monitoring” the storm that brought hard rain and flash flooding to parts of West Virginia beginning Sunday evening.
text:
Many streets on Charleston, West Virginia's West Side, including Greendale Drive, experienced severe flooding on Sunday, Aug. 16, 2026. (Photo by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)Gov. Patrick Morrisey says his office is “closely monitoring” the storm that brought hard rain and flash flooding to parts of West Virginia beginning Sunday evening. An emergency declaration due severe storms and flooding in July remains in effect throughout the state until Aug. 20, will allow the state to respond to severe weather in affected communities, the governor said. Morrisey previously extended the state of emergency through Sept. 12 for 12 counties in the state. 
“Please stay off flooded roads, never attempt to drive through high water, and give our first responders the room they need to do their jobs safely,” Morrisey said on the social media platform X Sunday night. 
“We are praying for everyone in harm’s way and for the first responders working through the night to keep West Virginians safe,” he said. 
According to the National Weather Service, more than 4 inches of rain fell at Yeager Airport in Charleston on Sunday, leading to reports of high water throughout Kanawha County, including Cross Lanes and Cabin Creek. Flooding was also reported in Fayette County, Braxton County and Nicholas County, said Simone Lewis, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Charleston.
More storms and rain in the forecast Monday could lead to more flooding, Lewis said. 
“We’re expecting more showers and storms to develop today, particularly this afternoon into the early evening,” Lewis said. “With the ground being as wet as it is, and a lot of the area creeks and streams running high, we do have the threat for flash flooding continuing through late tonight.”
After Monday, there will be a break in the rain this week with an occasional shower, she said. 
“People who are in flood-prone locations (shouldn’t) let their guard down,” Lewis said. “Monday is another day to kind of keep an eye out for the potential of flooding.”
This is a developing story and may be updated.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska gubernatorial candidates weigh in on working with the press, public engagement, AI use
description: Nine of 17 candidates for Alaska governor weighed in on plans for communicating with the media and the public. They touched on a variety of topics,  including town halls, news conferences, public records, use of artificial intelligence and the role of their communications teams.  The candidates are vying for the top four spots to advance […]
text:
The Alaska governor's mansion in Juneau is seen on Aug 14, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Nine of 17 candidates for Alaska governor weighed in on plans for communicating with the media and the public. They touched on a variety of topics,  including town halls, news conferences, public records, use of artificial intelligence and the role of their communications teams. 
The candidates are vying for the top four spots to advance to the ranked choice general election in November. The primary election is on Tuesday, August 18. 
The Anchorage-based public relations firm Thompson & Co. conducted a survey of 12 candidates on communications with the public “whose campaigns have demonstrated significant organizational capacity, fundraising, and public support,” according to a statement announcing the survey results.
The candidates that chose to participate answered an 18 question survey. The respondents were Democrats Tom Begich and Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins; Independent Bill Walker; and Republicans Adam Crum, Lesil McGuire, Click Bishop, Edna DeVries, Shelley Hughes and Matt Heilala. 
Republicans Dave Bronson, Treg Taylor and Bernadette Wilson received the survey but did not respond. 
“Candidates answered the same questions on press access, crisis communications, social media, rural and language accessibility, public records requests and staffing for the governor’s communications office,” the statement said. 
Transparency and public access
All nine candidates that responded agreed that a free press providing information to the public is critical to democratic government. Several candidates committed to an open and transparent relationship with the press, including Kreiss-Tomkins.
“If I find myself annoyed as Governor by seemingly pesky questions from the media, I think that is a good thing for Alaskans, for transparency, and for a healthy democracy,” he said. 
Hughes and Heilala noted the press also should be held to a standard of fairness. Hughes said she would be more responsive to “those who are fair.”
“I want journalists to report in a balanced fashion and strive to be unbiased – the way they should be in a healthy democracy (in our case, constitutional republic) – but that rarely is the case,” Hughes said. “I will give more time to those who are fair. I will be more apt to provide written comments to those who aren’t.”
Candidates varied on how often they would hold open press conferences and public town halls.
Bishop, McGuire and Hughes said they would hold weekly press conferences, with some flexibility due to scheduling Hughes added. Crum and Walker committed to two press conferences a month. 
DeVries and Heilala said they would hold conferences as events warranted; Begich and Kreiss-Tomkins were unsure.
Seven candidates promised to hold regular town halls and public events across the state, with DeVries and Crum saying they were unsure of frequency. 
“I intend to hold regular town halls and community visits across Alaska, including remote communities,” Bishop said. “My goal is to maintain a visible statewide presence through in-person visits and virtual options so Alaskans know their governor is accessible and engaged.”  
Candidates split on their willingness to publish a public-facing calendar of the governor’s official schedule. 
Currently Dunleavy’s calendar isn’t officially published publically, but has been available through a public records request. 
Bishop, Walker, McGuire, and Heleila said they would publish a public-facing calendar. Kreiss-Tomkins said he would publish a schedule of public events. 
Begich and DeVries said they were unsure, and Crum and Hughes said it would depend on security considerations. 
Limiting media access and non-traditional media 
Candidates were asked under what circumstances they would refuse to take press questions or limit media access to them personally. 
McGuire and DeVries said “None.” 
Kreiss-Tomkins, Crum, Bishop and Heilela said the default would be to answer questions. 
Begich noted the line between personal and professional life should be respected.
“However, when the personal veers into the professional, it is fair for the press to question those actions, and it is essential that a Governor respond to them in the interest of public integrity and the truth,” Begich said. 
Several candidates noted access may be limited on issues related to ongoing law enforcement investigations, active litigation, personnel issues or public safety. 
Hughes said media access would be limited: “Would limit if information is confidential, uncertain, or would jeopardize a positive outcome. Would limit access if a safety issue,” she said.
Candidates agreed that their media distribution lists would be broad and inclusive, and they would host virtual online press conferences. They agreed their administrations would be available to rural reporters and give them access equivalent to that of reporters in urban areas. 
The majority of candidates agreed they would grant access to “non-traditional” media organizations, including podcasters, bloggers, independent journalists and online-only outlets. 
Begich said he would evaluate such interview requests on a case-by-case basis depending on his availability. He said in the past he’s done interviews for outlets that were “inherently biased,” but said “as long as they and I acknowledged that, it was fine.”
Social media and artificial intelligence use
All candidates said they plan to maintain active social media accounts across major platforms, including Facebook, Instagram, X (formerly Twitter), YouTube and others.
Candidates varied on whether they plan to use artificial intelligence-generated content on their social pages.
McGuire and Heilala said yes.
Hughes said she would on occasion. “It would be the exception rather than the rule,” she said.
Begich and Bishop said no.  
Kreiss-Tomkins, Crum, Walker, and DeVries answered “unsure at this time.”
Candidates were also asked under what circumstances they would mute or block members of the public from government social media accounts. 
DeVries answered she would not block anyone. The majority of candidates said they would keep social media pages open and welcome criticism or differing opinions, but would consider blocking accounts for hate speech, threats, intimidation or spam. 
Heilala said his administration would monitor such blocked accounts. “Any blocks will be documented, applied consistently, and reviewed periodically. Viewpoint discrimination will never be tolerated. Alaskans have a right to speak to their government, even critically. I expect robust debate, not an echo chamber,” he said. 
Public records
All the candidates said their administrations would comply with public records law, under the Alaska Public Records Act. 
Kreiss-Tomkins and McGuire said they would not charge any fees.
Currently the law allows public agencies to charge after the first 5 hours of work on filling public records requests for personnel time based on their salary. 
Walker said he would “like to avoid fees if at all possible” and would assess once in office. Bishop noted that fees should reflect actual costs and not be a barrier to accessing public records. Hughes said a small fee would be necessary for large projects. 
Language access and communication with non-English speaking communities
Alaska is home to 21 official languages including Inupiaq, Yup’ik, Alutiiq, Tlingit and others. 
Candidates were asked how their potential administrations would communicate with non-English speaking communities, and what resources would be committed to making official information available across languages. 
Begich, Kreiss-Tomkins, Walker and Bishop said they would work with tribal and community organizations to translate government communications and make translation services available, particularly for emergencies. 
Kreiss-Tomkins pointed to his legislative record officially recognizing Native languages. “I’ll prioritize it in emergencies, when a delay in someone’s own language can cost lives. I’ve worked on this issue dating back to my service as a Representative, when I sponsored the bill that made Alaska’s 20 Native languages official languages of our state alongside English,” he wrote.
Crum said his administration would follow current law which “requires broad availability of public material.”
Hughes and Helaila said they would use AI translation tools and refer the public to AI translation services— “While always having human review for important documents,” Heilala added. 
McGuire said she would build on the Division of Elections translation model, and also seek bilingual team members in her administration. “I would also consider sight and hearing impaired Alaskans,” she said. 
Staffing communications teams 
Bishop, Heleila and McGuire provided some details on their potential communications offices, which would include a communications director, press secretary, digital communications and outreach coordinators. 
Walker pointed to his previous term as Alaska governor, from 2014 to 2018, with staff including a communication director, deputy communication director and several assistants to the director. 
Hughes said she would have a minimum of two communications staff, and possibly task others with communications duties. 
Several candidates responded that plans on staffing their communications teams are premature, and would be determined if elected to office. That included Begich, Kreiss-Tomkins, Crum and DeVries.
“We are focused on campaigning, listening to Alaskans, and getting our message out,” Kreiss-Tomkins said. “If we win the election, that is when we will make decisions on staffing the administration.”

name: National
title: ‘Hidden homicides’: Families push states for more scrutiny of domestic violence deaths
description: Families who believe local officials prematurely ruled their loved ones’ deaths suicides or accidents — rather than investigating whether domestic violence played a role — are pushing lawmakers in a growing number of states to require additional scrutiny. Advocates call the deaths “hidden homicides” — killings they say may be staged to look like suicides, […[...]
text:
Dr. William Smock, medical director of the Training Institute on Strangulation Prevention, part of the Alliance for HOPE International, speaks to students about evidence and how to detect staged scenes during a mock crime scene exercise. This year, at least five states have considered “hidden homicide” legislation. (Photo courtesy of Gael Strack/Alliance for HOPE International)Families who believe local officials prematurely ruled their loved ones’ deaths suicides or accidents — rather than investigating whether domestic violence played a role — are pushing lawmakers in a growing number of states to require additional scrutiny.
Advocates call the deaths “hidden homicides” — killings they say may be staged to look like suicides, overdoses or accidents and then overlooked by investigators. Some advocates argue that requiring additional investigative steps could prevent potential evidence from being lost before a case is closed.
This year, lawmakers in at least five states — Illinois, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New York and Oregon — have considered legislation aimed at identifying homicides or unexplained deaths involving domestic violence that might otherwise be misclassified. All of the bills have stalled in legislative committees amid concerns over financial and administrative constraints, including requirements for law enforcement training. 
California in 2024 became the first state to enact a law addressing the issue when lawmakers approved Joanna’s Law, or Senate Bill 989, which took effect last year. The law requires police officers, in certain cases, to interview family members before determining the manner and cause of death and allows families to request a complete autopsy when specific indicators of domestic homicide are present.
The law was inspired by the death of Joanna Lewis, whose family argued her death had been misclassified as a suicide. She had previously sought restraining orders against her husband, Mark Lewis, accusing him of domestic violence.
Alliance for HOPE International, an anti-domestic violence advocacy organization that helped develop the legislation, said that case reflects broader concerns about how suspicious deaths involving intimate partner violence are investigated nationwide. 
The group has also helped families conduct independent investigations into their loved ones’ deaths. 
“We’ve come across some tremendous obstacles and have felt the pain and the frustration that family members have gone through,” said Gael Strack, co-founder of Alliance for HOPE International. 
The group would also like to help introduce similar legislation in Alaska, Arizona and Nevada.
Police officers can help prevent domestic violence killings by asking the right questions

Advocates acknowledge that not every suspicious death involving domestic violence is a homicide, but argue certain circumstances should prompt investigators to slow down and ask additional questions.
“In many of our cases, they make a conclusion on the manner of death within 30 minutes of arriving at the scene. They don’t know anything about the family, the relationship, the history,” said Casey Gwinn, co-founder of Alliance for HOPE International.
Advocates point to several reasons they believe deaths can be misclassified, including the limited number of autopsies, inconsistent death investigation practices and a lack of coordination among law enforcement, medical examiners, prosecutors and domestic violence experts.
In many cases, advocates say, a death that appears to be a suicide is treated differently than a homicide investigation — meaning investigators may not conduct the same level of scene analysis, interviews or evidence collection.
Families seeking answers also often face additional hurdles after a death is classified as a suicide or accident, some advocates say. They may struggle with obtaining police records, challenging a medical examiner’s findings or commissioning an independent investigation. 
Among those pushing for legislation is Kellee Harris of Oregon, whose daughter, Kelsey Harris, was found dead in her Linn County home in 2021 a week after she had reported that her boyfriend had strangled her.
Local authorities ruled Kelsey’s death a suicide. Harris says investigators failed to fully consider the circumstances surrounding her daughter’s death, including the recent strangulation report and the history of abuse she says occurred in the relationship.
“I just think that they wanted me to go away,” Harris told Stateline, referring to local authorities. “It’s real easy to slap a suicide determination on on a death, and then they don’t have to do anything else.”
When families question a death investigation, getting a second autopsy can be complicated

Linn County Sheriff Michelle Duncan told Stateline that her office stands by its determination that Kelsey died by suicide.
Oregon lawmakers are now working to revive a proposal that stalled during this year’s legislative session. Democratic state Sen. Sara Gelser Blouin, one of the bill’s sponsors, said the original version of the legislation needed revisions after medical examiners and law enforcement raised concerns about its scope and cost.
The earlier proposal was interpreted by some stakeholders as requiring significantly more autopsies, leading to concerns about the financial impact. Gelser Blouin said the next version, which she plans to introduce next year, will take a narrower approach. She plans to update the bill’s language to more explicitly require additional evaluation in certain domestic violence-related deaths rather than automatically requiring an autopsy.
Those additional steps could include further documentation, toxicology testing, additional imaging or interviews before investigators determine the manner of death. Her goal, she said, is to make the death investigation process in the state more transparent in hopes of helping people find some sense of closure.
“People want to do this, and they want to get it right. They don’t want us to pass a law that can’t be implemented because it’s too confusing or that makes it worse,” Gelser Blouin said.
Duncan, the Linn County sheriff, said she generally supports efforts to strengthen Oregon’s death investigation system and said she would like to see more autopsies completed.
But Duncan said she has concerns about making certain investigative steps mandatory in every case, such as requiring law enforcement to contact family members, because sometimes investigators are unable to locate next of kin.
“There’s often people that we just can’t even find family for,” she said.
Stateline reporter Amanda Watford can be reached at awatford@stateline.org.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: This was my experience of Operation Metro Surge as a Somali home care worker
description: This is the story of Nazra Ahmed’s experience during Operation Metro Surge. She’s a home care worker and member of SEIU Healthcare Minnesota and Iowa. As told to Phillip Cryan, SEIU Healthcare Minnesota and Iowa executive vice president.  When Operation Metro Surge first happened, I was talking with my family: “How are we going to […]
text:
ICE agents arrest two men during a traffic stop Wednesday, Feb. 11, 2026 on Bottineau Blvd. in Robbinsdale. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)This is the story of Nazra Ahmed’s experience during Operation Metro Surge. She’s a home care worker and member of SEIU Healthcare Minnesota and Iowa. As told to Phillip Cryan, SEIU Healthcare Minnesota and Iowa executive vice president. 
When Operation Metro Surge first happened, I was talking with my family: “How are we going to get groceries?” We were scared. Somebody could kill us, because we’re Somali. And President Trump is just spreading all this hate against us. 
There were Somali people who wouldn’t leave their houses, because of their trauma from the Somali civil war. They were used to seeing dead bodies everywhere during the war. Because my people, we didn’t even go to therapists to heal after the war, displacement and coming to the U.S. as refugees. We never sat down with someone to talk about it all. When Trump was reelected for a second term, I couldn’t sleep for night after night. I was back in the civil war in Somalia in my mind. Fear had damaged me, too. 
My son needs a special diet. He’s non-verbal. “What’s going to happen to him if ICE takes me?” It was a horrible feeling.
Everybody in the Somali community was saying: How can this be happening here, in the United States?
But it didn’t go the way we’d feared. Minnesotans stood up and said: “No. You’re not going to get my neighbor.” We have people here who actually believe in us, who love us. The opposite thing to what we had feared happened. I’d go to the grocery store, and people would say “We love Somalis.” They would say “We love you.”
Then I felt power. We have power. We have people behind us.
Trump thought people wouldn’t have documents, but well over 90% of Somalis here are American citizens. And we’re not a scared people. We stood up to him.
Once we realized they weren’t going to be able to do much against us Somali-Americans, I started checking in on my neighbors. 
When I first bought this house a couple years ago, I met one of my neighbors. He had legal status, not citizenship or a green card but political asylum. He has worked on my house, fixing things, doing my kitchen. He and his wife don’t speak much English, so we use Google Translate to talk to each other. He has asylum and his kids are citizens, but his wife is undocumented. And they have a 9-month-old baby who was born premature and has special needs. I was scared for them. 
“How can I help them?” I talked to another SEIU organizer and my son’s therapist, and we figured out together how to pay their rent, and to go to the grocery store for them. But then ICE took his wife, one day while she was on her way to work as a house cleaner.
They have three other kids, and the baby. And he’s looking after all of them. 
He and his wife are very hard-working. They don’t ask anyone for help. They’re proud. I could see that he was feeling shame about accepting help. But I told him: We’re family. He started crying, and he was saying he will never forget us. I told him: That’s why we’re here. We’re here for each other. We are all God’s children.
We paid his rent from December to March. Now he feels safe enough that he can go back to work, so we aren’t paying his rent anymore. And he has a pro bono lawyer helping his wife.
I never thought I would see ICE come out to the suburbs. But one day, all of a sudden, they stopped me in my car. And that was my nightmare. 
My son had therapy that day. We had been carrying our identification everywhere because we never knew what was going to happen. We had just finished his therapy and were coming home. I saw this big SUV behind me. Right away, I felt like “Uh oh. Is that them?” But then I thought, “Maybe I’m overthinking this, it’s nothing.” But they just kept coming coming coming behind me. And then I saw: There’s no license plate. That’s when I knew for sure. That’s when I slowed down and stopped. 
And the masked people came out. How could I know if they were even real agents? There’s no license plate, no name badge. Just a number on their chest. So you don’t know who you’re even talking to.
Oh my God. I didn’t show them, but my heart was sinking. And I started shaking. One of them approached the car. 
“Are you an American citizen?” 
“Yes, I am. Why are you guys doing this?” 
“We’re just doing our job, you know.” 
“What would you think if this happened to you? Or your sister? Or your wife? If someone harassed them like this?” 
“We’re just doing our jobs.” 
“Okay. But why are you covering your face to do your jobs? I want to see you. … Have you ever heard of Al Qaeda? Al Shabab?” 
“Yes.” 
“That’s exactly how they look. They look like you. That’s why I’m scared now.” 
“No, no. You’re doing great. You can just go ahead and go.”
I couldn’t go. I was stopped there, shaking in my car, for about 10 minutes. When you have that kind of anxiety, you can’t drive a car. Every time bad things like that happen, you flashback: back home, the civil war. It’s all in there somewhere — the memory of people attacking you. So I had to breathe and say to myself, “It’s okay, it’s okay.” 
When he pulled me over, he had been thinking that maybe I would yell at him or call him names. But I never call people names. You’re not going to win by calling people names. 
The only way you can win, with the cowards, is by showing them strength. If they see that you’re scared, they will come after you. That’s the way I’ve always done it: Anyone who’s coming after me, attacking me, I will smile at them and talk to them. I’ll attack them, but in the nicest way: Hit them in their heart. 
When I asked what he’d do if something like this happened to his sister or his wife, I could see his eyes — that was the only part of him I could see — tear up. That got him in his heart.
It’s what people who are cowards try to do: they try to scare you.
But we’re not going to stop for fear. We’re not going to stop. We’re going to go vote. We’re going to knock doors and make calls. We won’t be scared. Minnesotans are warriors. On Jan. 23, the day of the general strike and march, it was like -30 degrees with windchill, but Minnesotans didn’t care! I wish I could have been there, but I couldn’t bring my son with me and I didn’t have a caregiver for him that day. I wish I could have been there that day with everyone. I would have brought so many sambusas.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Desperation and a double bind for Quabbin towns
description: For the towns around the Quabbin Reservoir, managing worsening drought seasons comes with a bitter irony: they surround the essential clean water source for distant Greater Boston, and that means harsher water restrictions than the populous downstream cities. This week on The Codcast, Jennifer Smith talks with fellow CommonWealth Beacon reporter Jordan Wolma[...]
text:
EPISODE INFO

HOST: Jennifer Smith
GUEST: Jordan Wolman







THE COMMUNITIES THAT ring the Quabbin Reservoir have long found themselves in a double bind. They protect the state’s largest drinking water source, but don’t get to drink from it. And they’re barred from developing the land around it, but say they aren’t compensated enough to make that tradeoff fair. 
That tension has only grown with persistent drought. The Central Massachusetts region, where the Quabbin sits, remains at Level 2 – Significant Drought status even as other parts of the state have recovered somewhat. 
This week on The Codcast, Jennifer Smith talks with senior reporter Jordan Wolman about his recent reporting on the towns surrounding the reservoir — a manmade lake built a century ago that now supplies drinking water to 3.1 million people in and around Greater Boston. The surrounding towns rely on smaller wells and municipal sources that are far more exposed to drought and contamination. 
Wolman noticed the board of the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority, which operates the Quabbin, was holding a rare meeting in Belchertown, one of the Quabbin’s seven “host communities,” and once he tuned in, he said, “there was this just sense of desperation.” 
The first half of 2026 was so dry it wasn’t safe for Belchertown athletes to play soccer and football on their home fields this fall. The well serving New Salem’s town hall ran dry, forcing staff without water and workable restrooms into borrowed office space. 
The mood is dour, Wolman said. “It just creates this dynamic that’s festering of, ‘Why do we live near the biggest body of water in Massachusetts and we can’t drink from it? And we’re struggling ourselves with access to water because of drought, because of contamination, whereas Greater Boston is fairly insulated from this,’” he said. “And so it creates that sort of us-versus-them mentality, I think, that’s started to really spill over here.” 
Underneath it is a fight about money and equity. 
The towns get payments in lieu of taxes, or PILOTs, for the state-owned land around the reservoir that they can’t develop to protect the critical watershed, but they say those payments aren’t cutting it. Five of the Quabbin’s seven host communities have received flat PILOT payments for five straight years running. New Salem’s payment works out to $21 an acre, against a statewide median of $127.  
Wolman said MWRA officials counter that raising those payments could mean higher water rates for customers in lower-income communities served by the Quabbin, like Chelsea and Everett. 
That fight is now tucked into an environmental bond bill in closed-door conference committee negotiations. Gov. Maura Healey has waded in, too, writing a letter to the MWRA this month urging it to “more fully recognize” Quabbin communities. Wolman said the letter matters more for what it signals politically than any specific policy requirement. 
“She’s asking not necessarily directly for increased pilot payments, not necessarily for a permanent seat on the board of the authority,” he said. “She’s asking the MWRA to sort of take good faith measures to collaborate and partner with and coordinate with these towns on their water access concerns, on their local police and fire response.” 
On the episode, Smith and Wolman discuss the roots of the PILOT payment disparity (8:00), how drought restrictions fall unevenly on Quabbin towns versus Boston-area MWRA customers (18:00), and what Healey’s letter to the MWRA does and doesn’t accomplish (28:00).

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Wake Ed Partnership President Keith Poston on their efforts to equip public school classrooms
description: All across North Carolina, students, parents and teachers are preparing for the start of a new school year and, unfortunately, one of the most vexing challenges that’s accompanied this time of year for the last several is the struggle many public school teachers face in properly equipping their classrooms. Thanks to the state legislature’s […]
text:
Keith Poston, Wake Ed Partnership  (Courtesy photo) 
All across North Carolina, students, parents and teachers are preparing for the start of a new school year and, unfortunately, one of the most vexing challenges that’s accompanied this time of year for the last several is the struggle many public school teachers face in properly equipping their classrooms. Thanks to the state legislature’s serial underfunding of basic things like school supplies, teachers in our state typically resort to spending an average of more than $1,600 of their own funds per year just to get their classrooms up to snuff.
It’s a maddening situation but for now – at least here in Wake County – an excellent and inspiring partial solution has been provided by the private nonprofit Wake Ed Partnership. Thanks to the group’s Tools-4-Schools program, hundreds of Wake County teachers will be able to collect the classroom materials they need at no cost over the coming days, and recently to learn more about the program and how listeners can help out, Newsline caught up with Wake Ed Partnership President Keith Poston.
